research.area: Merge gates and branch protection for a PHI-handling application (GitHub Actions CI, 2-developer team)
research.standard_summary: The 2026 standard is: one protected default branch, changes only via pull request, a small number of REQUIRED status checks that always report, and no silent bypass path. GitHub has consolidated this into repository rulesets (an automatic branch-protection-to-ruleset migration tool shipped 2026-08-11) and classic branch protection still works with no announced sunset. NIST SSDF PW.7.1 explicitly leaves the human-vs-automated review mix to the organization, so a defensible minimum is one human approval plus an automated gate, not a fixed reviewer count; CIS Software Supply Chain Security Guide 1.1.3 asks for two approvers, which is arithmetically impossible for two developers because GitHub forbids self-approval. HIPAA names no gate at all: 164.308(a)(1)(ii)(B) requires "security measures sufficient to reduce risks and vulnerabilities to a reasonable and appropriate level", 164.312(b) requires audit controls, and 164.316(b)(2)(i) requires the resulting documentation be retained six years — so what matters for compliance is that the gate config is versioned, its bypasses are reviewable, and the record outlives GitHub's 180-day audit log. The evidence on gate count is one-directional: DORA found no evidence that heavier external approval lowers change failure rate, while the CI Theater study of 1,270 projects and 534,417 builds found 85% had at least one build broken for more than four days, with the smallest projects averaging 40 days to fix — i.e. gates that are slow or ignorable decay into theatre. For this team the defensible set is roughly five required things (one aggregated CI check, one approval, most-recent-push approval, conversation resolution, no force-push/delete) plus a monthly bypass review, and the single highest-leverage engineering decision is to expose exactly ONE required check name backed by an `if: always()` aggregator job.

standards.claim: GitHub repository rulesets are the direction of travel and can now be auto-migrated from classic branch protection, but classic branch protection is not deprecated and has no announced sunset date. Rulesets differ operationally in that multiple rulesets can target the same branch and are aggregated with the most restrictive version of a rule winning, and they layer with any classic branch protection rules still in place (all applicable rules are enforced).
standards.threshold: Migration tool shipped 2026-08-11; no deprecation date announced
standards.source_name: GitHub Changelog - Automatically migrate branch protection rules to repository rulesets
standards.notes: Changelog wording is strategic, not terminal: "As we continue investing in rulesets as the foundation for repository governance on GitHub, this tool makes it easy to bring your existing policies forward." Practical consequence for this team: pick ONE mechanism. Running a classic rule and a ruleset simultaneously means both are enforced and you will spend an afternoon working out which one is blocking you. Recommend rulesets, because they are readable by anyone with repo read access, have a REST API with version history, and default to nobody bypassing.

standards.claim: The branch ruleset rules available in 2026 are: Restrict creations, Restrict updates, Restrict deletions (selected by default), Require linear history, Require deployments to succeed before merging, Require signed commits, Require a pull request before merging, Require status checks to pass before merging, Block force pushes (enabled by default), Require code scanning results, Require code quality results, Restrict code coverage (public preview), Restrict file paths, Restrict file path length, Restrict file extensions, Restrict file size.
standards.threshold: Required approvals configurable 0-10; required reviewers up to 15 teams; Restrict file paths and Restrict file extensions limited to 200 entries each
standards.source_name: GitHub Docs - Available rules for rulesets
standards.notes: Sub-options under "Require a pull request before merging": required approvals, "Dismiss stale pull request approvals when new commits are pushed", "Require approval of the most recent reviewable push", "Require review from code owners", restrict review dismissal, required reviewers, "Require all comments on the pull request to be resolved before it can be merged", allowed merge methods. Sub-option under status checks: "Require branches to be up to date before merging" and "Do not require status checks on creation". Note that "Require code scanning results" and "Require code quality results" exist in the UI but are unusable on a private repo without a paid licence (see separate entry) - the UI will show you rules you cannot actually turn on.

standards.claim: Classic branch protection does NOT apply to repository admins unless you explicitly enable "Do not allow bypassing the above settings". Rulesets invert this: enforcement is the default and bypass is an explicit list you populate (repository admins, organization owners, enterprise owners, the maintain or write role, custom roles based on write, teams excluding secret teams, GitHub Apps, and Dependabot), with each bypass actor set to either "Always allow" (the default) or "For pull requests only", the latter meaning the actor "is now required to open a pull request to make changes to a repository, creating a clear trail of their changes".
standards.threshold: Classic BP: admin exemption is the DEFAULT. Rulesets: bypass list is empty unless populated.
standards.source_name: GitHub Docs - About protected branches
standards.notes: Verbatim from the docs: "By default, the restrictions of a branch protection rule do not apply to people with admin permissions to the repository or custom roles with the 'bypass branch protections' permission." On a two-person repo both developers are almost certainly admins, so classic branch protection configured without that checkbox protects nobody. CIS makes this its own control (1.1.14). This is the single most common false sense of security in small-team GitHub setups.

standards.claim: A pull request author cannot approve their own pull request, and repository owners/administrators can merge a pull request even if it has not received an approving review. Both facts constrain what a two-person team can promise.
standards.threshold: Self-approval: prohibited outright. Admin merge without approval: permitted unless bypass is closed off.
standards.source_name: GitHub Docs - Approving a pull request with required reviews
standards.notes: Verbatim: "Pull request authors cannot approve their own pull requests." and "Repository owners and administrators can merge a pull request even if it hasn't received an approving review, or if a reviewer who requested changes has left the organization or is unavailable." Consequence: with 2 devs, "1 required approval" already means genuine second-person review 100% of the time, and "2 required approvals" is unsatisfiable. Also: the admin-merge escape hatch is exactly why the ruleset bypass list must be empty and reviewed.

standards.claim: A required status check behaves differently depending on WHERE you skip it, and one of the two behaviours silently disables your gate. If a workflow is skipped due to path filtering, branch filtering or a commit message, the associated checks remain in a Pending state and block merging forever. If a JOB inside a workflow is skipped by a conditional, it reports its status as Success and does NOT prevent merging even when it is a required check.
standards.threshold: Workflow-level skip => Pending => PR permanently blocked. Job-level `if:` skip => Success => required check silently satisfied.
standards.source_name: GitHub Docs - Troubleshooting required status checks
standards.notes: Verbatim from About status checks: "A job that is skipped will report its status as 'Success'. It will not prevent a pull request from merging, even if it is a required check." GitHub's own remediation is to avoid requiring workflows that can be skipped, and to use `always()` with `needs` for aggregating jobs. Also verbatim: "If a check and a commit status have the same name, both must pass when that name is required" - so name collisions between an Action and an external app both block. A GitHub staff member acknowledged the path-filter papercut on 2024-09-19 in community discussion 44490 with no timeline; it is still open. This is the technical justification for exposing exactly one required check name.

standards.claim: GitHub merge queue is not available for private repositories except on GitHub Enterprise Cloud. Where available it is configured through the ruleset rule "Require merge queue" with build concurrency between 1 and 100, minimum and maximum pull requests to merge between 1 and 100, a wait time to meet the minimum group size, a status check timeout, and a "Require all queue entries to pass required checks" toggle. CI workflows must add the `merge_group` event, and it creates temporary `gh-readonly-queue/{base_branch}` branches that consume additional CI minutes.
standards.threshold: Private repos: GitHub Enterprise Cloud only. Concurrency 1-100; group size 1-100.
standards.source_name: GitHub Docs - Managing a merge queue
standards.notes: The numeric ranges and settings are verified from pages I opened. The plan-availability sentence ("available in any public repository owned by an organization, or in private repositories owned by organizations using GitHub Enterprise Cloud") appeared consistently in docs.github.com search result snippets across the github.com, Enterprise Cloud and Enterprise Server variants of the page, but the availability banner did not render in the page bodies I fetched, so I could not quote it from a page I opened. Verify in your own repo settings before planning around it. Docs also warn that jumping to the front of the queue triggers full rebuilds of in-progress PRs.

standards.claim: GitHub auto-merge is the correct latency mitigation for a small team: it is offered only on pull requests that cannot be merged immediately - specifically when a rule enforces required pull request reviews or required status checks - and it merges automatically once all required reviews and checks are satisfied. It is disabled automatically if someone without write access pushes to the branch or the base branch changes.
standards.threshold: n/a
standards.source_name: GitHub Docs - Automatically merging a pull request
standards.notes: This is the feature that makes a real gate survivable for two people: the reviewer approves, walks away, and the merge happens when CI finishes. Without it, every gate adds a context switch at the end of a 10-minute CI run, which is precisely the friction that produces admin merges. Enable "Allow auto-merge" in repository settings at the same time you create the ruleset - it is one checkbox and it is the difference between a gate people use and a gate people route around.

standards.claim: Rulesets are addressable as configuration-as-code and carry their own version history and bypass telemetry, which is the mechanism that turns a merge gate into retainable audit evidence: GET/POST /repos/{owner}/{repo}/rulesets, GET/PUT/DELETE /repos/{owner}/{repo}/rulesets/{ruleset_id}, GET /repos/{owner}/{repo}/rulesets/{ruleset_id}/history and .../history/{version_id}, plus GET /repos/{owner}/{repo}/rules/branches/{branch}. Rule Insights shows actions that passed, failed, or "where someone has bypassed one or more rulesets", with a dashboard of successes/failures/bypasses over time and "Top bypassers" for GitHub Team and Enterprise Cloud, and an "Evaluate" enforcement mode that shows what would have passed or failed.
standards.threshold: n/a
standards.source_name: GitHub REST API - Repository rules
standards.notes: This directly satisfies SSDF PO.3.2 Example 3 ("Use code-based configuration for toolchains (e.g., pipelines-as-code, toolchains-as-code)") and PO.3.3 Example 1 (use tooling "to create an audit trail of the secure development-related actions that are performed"). The ruleset history endpoint is the under-advertised one - it means you can answer "who loosened the gate and when" without an enterprise audit log. "Top bypassers" being available on Team is the cheapest possible implementation of CIS 1.1.19.

standards.claim: GitHub's own security merge gates are paywalled on private repositories: "You need to pay to use Advanced Security features in private repositories on GitHub.com." This covers CodeQL code scanning (and therefore the "Require code scanning results" ruleset rule) and dependency review, which is available for "all public repositories" and "private repositories that have GitHub Code Security or GitHub Advanced Security enabled". Code scanning alerts carry a level of Error, Warning or Note, and CodeQL security alerts additionally carry Critical/High/Medium/Low; the newer "Require code quality results" ruleset rule blocks on thresholds of "Errors", "Warnings and higher", "Notes and higher" or "All".
standards.threshold: Code quality merge-gate thresholds: Errors / Warnings and higher / Notes and higher / All. Alert levels: Error, Warning, Note. CodeQL security severities: Critical, High, Medium, Low.
standards.source_name: GitHub Docs - GitHub Advanced Security license billing
standards.notes: Also opened: https://docs.github.com/en/code-security/supply-chain-security/understanding-your-software-supply-chain/about-dependency-review (dependency review action "will fail if it discovers any vulnerable packages" and supports fail-on-severity plus license allow/deny lists) and https://docs.github.com/en/code-security/code-scanning/managing-code-scanning-alerts/about-code-scanning-alerts (severity levels). Cost is out of scope for this exercise, but FEATURE AVAILABILITY is not: half of the standard 2026 merge-gate advice assumes CodeQL and dependency review are free, and on your private repo they are not. The free substitutes below (NuGet audit, yarn npm audit, gitleaks) cover the dependency and secret cases well; SAST is the genuine gap.

standards.claim: CIS Software Supply Chain Security Guide section 1.1 (Code Changes) is the most prescriptive branch-protection checklist an auditor is likely to use, and its controls are: 1.1.1 changes tracked in a version control platform; 1.1.2 every change traceable to its associated task; 1.1.3 approval of two strongly authenticated users (Automated); 1.1.4 previous approvals dismissed when updates are introduced; 1.1.5 restrictions on who can dismiss reviews; 1.1.6 code owners set for extra sensitive code or configuration; 1.1.7 code owner review required when a change affects owned code; 1.1.8 inactive branches periodically reviewed and removed; 1.1.9 all checks passed before merging; 1.1.10 branches up to date before merge; 1.1.11 all open comments resolved before merging; 1.1.12 signed commits verified before merging; 1.1.13 linear history required; 1.1.14 branch protection rules enforced for administrators; 1.1.15 pushing/merging restricted to specific individuals or teams; 1.1.16 force push denied; 1.1.17 branch deletions denied; 1.1.18 any merging of code automatically scanned for risks; 1.1.19 any changes to branch protection rules are audited.
standards.threshold: 1.1.3 requires TWO approving reviewers. 19 controls in section 1.1.
standards.source_name: CIS Software Supply Chain Security Guide v1.0, June 2022 (PDF copy distributed with aquasecurity/chain-bench)
standards.notes: I downloaded and extracted the v1.0 PDF text directly, so the control IDs and titles are quoted from the document, not from memory. CIS now also publishes platform-specific benchmarks - the cisecurity.org page I opened lists "GitHub (1.2.0)" and "GitLab (1.0.1)" as current - but those downloads are form-gated and I could not read v1.2.0, so control numbering may have shifted; treat the v1.0 numbering as indicative. 1.1.14 rationale verbatim: "Administrators by default are excluded from any branch protection rules. This means these privileged users ... are not subject to protections meant to prevent untrusted code insertion, including malicious code." 1.1.19 asks only for "a tracking system ... that logs changes in branch protection rules" - GitHub's ruleset history API satisfies it.

standards.claim: NIST SSDF (SP 800-218 v1.1) does NOT mandate human code review. PW.7.1 says to "Determine whether code review (a person looks directly at the code to find issues) and/or code analysis (tools are used to find issues in code...) should be used, as defined by the organization." PW.7.2 then says to "Perform the code review and/or code analysis based on the organization's secure coding standards, and record and triage all discovered issues and recommended remediations in the development team's workflow or issue tracking system", with Example 4 being a static analysis tool with a human reviewing the reported issues, and Example 6 being "Use automated tools to identify and remediate documented and verified unsafe software practices on a continuous basis as human-readable code is checked into the code repository."
standards.threshold: PW.7.1, PW.7.2 - no reviewer count specified; the mix is explicitly the organization's decision
standards.source_name: NIST SP 800-218, Secure Software Development Framework (SSDF) Version 1.1, February 2022
standards.notes: Text extracted from the PDF itself. This is the load-bearing citation for a two-person team: anyone who says "NIST requires two reviewers" is wrong, and PW.7.1's phrasing ("as defined by the organization") is the language to quote back. PW.8.1/PW.8.2 apply the same risk-based framing to executable-code testing. SP 800-218 v1.1 remains the current final version as of 2026-08-28; SP 800-218A is a companion part on generative AI, not a successor.

standards.claim: SSDF places the merge-gate obligations in three places that a two-person team can actually evidence: PS.1.1 (store all forms of code by least privilege) with Example 2 "Use version control features of the repository to track all changes made to the code with accountability to the individual account", Example 3 "Use commit signing for code repositories", and Example 4 "Have the code owner review and approve all changes made to the code by others"; PO.4.1 (define criteria for software security checks, with Example 3 "Add software security criteria to existing checks (e.g., the Definition of Done...)" and Example 5 recording "security check approvals, rejections, and exception requests"); PO.4.2 Example 4 "Only allow authorized personnel to access the gathered information, and prevent any alteration or deletion of the information"; and PO.3.3 (configure tools to generate artifacts of secure development practices) Example 1 "Use existing tooling ... to create an audit trail of the secure development-related actions that are performed".
standards.source_name: NIST SP 800-218, SSDF v1.1
standards.notes: PO.3.2 Example 3 is "Use code-based configuration for toolchains (e.g., pipelines-as-code, toolchains-as-code)" - this is the SSDF hook for committing your ruleset JSON to the repo. PS.1.1 cross-maps to OWASPSAMM OE3-B, OWASPASVS 1.10 / 10.3.2, and SP800-53 SA-11 in the SSDF's own reference column, which is convenient if a customer questionnaire asks for a control mapping.

standards.claim: HIPAA's Security Rule names no merge gate, no code review and no CI check. What it requires is 164.308(a)(1)(ii)(B) Risk management (Required): "Implement security measures sufficient to reduce risks and vulnerabilities to a reasonable and appropriate level"; 164.308(a)(1)(ii)(D) Information system activity review (Required): "Implement procedures to regularly review records of information system activity"; 164.312(b) Audit controls (Required): "Implement hardware, software, and/or procedural mechanisms that record and examine activity in" systems containing ePHI; and 164.316(b)(2)(i) Time limit (Required): "Retain the documentation required by paragraph (b)(1) of this section for 6 years from the date of its creation or the date when it last was in effect, whichever is later."
standards.threshold: 164.316(b)(2)(i): 6 years retention. 164.308(a)(1)(ii)(A)-(D) are all Required, not Addressable.
standards.source_name: 45 CFR 164.308 / 164.312 / 164.316 (Cornell Legal Information Institute)
standards.notes: Also opened https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/45/164.312 - 164.312(a)(1), (a)(2)(i), (b) and (c)(1) are Required; 164.312(c)(2) Mechanism to authenticate ePHI is Addressable. The practical translation for merge gates: the gate itself is a security measure you selected under (a)(1)(ii)(B) and must be able to justify; the PR record and ruleset history are your (b) audit controls and (a)(1)(ii)(D) activity review; and the six-year clock in 164.316 is why you should not rely on GitHub's audit log as your record. Note that eCFR blocked automated fetching (302 to unblock.federalregister.gov), which is why I used Cornell LII.

standards.claim: A proposed rule published in the Federal Register on 2025-01-06 would materially tighten this: it proposes to "Remove the distinction between 'required' and 'addressable' implementation specifications and make all implementation specifications required with specific, limited exceptions", to "Require written documentation of all Security Rule policies, procedures, plans, and analyses", to require vulnerability scanning "at least every six months", penetration testing "at least once every 12 months", a technology asset inventory refreshed "at least once every 12 months and in response to a change", and a compliance audit "at least once every 12 months". As of 2026-08-28 I found no evidence it has been finalised.
standards.threshold: Vulnerability scanning every 6 months; pen test every 12 months; asset inventory every 12 months; compliance audit every 12 months; proposed 180-day compliance period after any final rule
standards.source_name: HHS - HIPAA Security Rule NPRM Fact Sheet
standards.notes: The proposed content is verified from the HHS fact sheet. The NON-finalisation is where I am only partial: the HHS Regulatory Initiatives page I opened was last reviewed 2025-06-27 and still describes it as a proposed rule, and the January 2026 OCR cybersecurity newsletter (on system hardening) I opened makes no statement about it. I could not find an affirmative 2026 HHS statement either way. Check https://www.hhs.gov/hipaa/for-professionals/security/hipaa-security-rule-nprm/index.html before you rely on this. Why it matters for merge gates: if finalised, the removal of "addressable" plus the written-documentation requirement means your gate configuration and your bypass log stop being nice-to-have and become documentation you must produce - which is a strong argument for committing the ruleset JSON now rather than later.

standards.claim: The evidence does not support adding approval weight. DORA found "no evidence was found to support the hypothesis that a more formal, external review process was associated with lower change fail rates" and that heavyweight approval "tend[s] to slow down the delivery process leading to the release of larger batches less frequently, with an accompanying higher impact on the production system"; its recommendation is peer review during development captured at code check-in plus automation. DORA's associated operating thresholds are: merge to trunk at least once a day, three or fewer active branches, and tests that "should not take more than a few minutes to run, with an upper limit of about 10 minutes", with a broken build taking priority over other work and being reverted if not fixable in a few minutes.
standards.threshold: Build/test feedback upper limit ~10 minutes; merge to trunk >= daily; <= 3 active branches
standards.source_name: DORA - Streamlining change approval
standards.notes: Also opened https://dora.dev/capabilities/trunk-based-development/ (three or fewer active branches; branches lasting no more than a few hours) and https://dora.dev/research/ (most recent State of DevOps report listed is 2025). The 10-minute number is the single most useful design constraint here: it is the budget your entire required-check set has to fit inside. If your aggregated gate exceeds it, the gate will be routed around regardless of what the ruleset says.

standards.claim: Gates decay when they are slow or ignorable, and small projects decay worst. The "Continuous Integration Theater" study (Felidre, Furtado, da Costa, Cartaxo, Pinto; ESEM 2019; arXiv 1907.01602, 2019-07-02) analysed 1,270 open-source projects and 534,417 builds and found that 85% of the analysed projects had at least one build that took more than four days to be fixed, that these long-to-be-fixed builds on very small projects are fixed on average in 40 days, and that 60% of projects had fewer than 2.36 commits per weekday. Build duration was NOT the problem - almost all projects built in under 10 minutes.
standards.threshold: 85% of projects had a build broken >4 days; smallest projects averaged 40 days to fix; 60% below 2.36 commits/weekday
standards.source_name: Continuous Integration Theater (arXiv 1907.01602 / ESEM 2019)
standards.notes: I extracted the numbers from the PDF text directly rather than the abstract. This is the strongest available empirical answer to "how many gates before people start bypassing": the literature does not give a gate-count threshold (I looked and could not find one - treat any specific number as unsourced), but it does show that the failure mode in small projects is a red gate that stays red, not a bypassed gate. The design implication is the opposite of what teams assume: the risk is not that two devs will click admin-merge, it is that they will leave main broken for weeks and stop trusting the signal. Hence: few checks, fast, and a rule that a red main is the top priority.

standards.claim: OWASP SAMM v2 puts the merge gate at maturity level 3 of Secure Build Stream A - "Define mandatory security checks in the build process and ensure that building non-compliant artifacts fails" - with level 2 being "Automate your build pipeline and secure the used tooling. Add security checks in the build pipeline" and level 1 merely "Create a formal definition of the build process so that it becomes consistent and repeatable". Security Testing Stream A is level 1 "Utilize automated security testing tools", level 2 "Employ application-specific security testing automation", level 3 "Integrate automated security testing into the build and deploy process".
standards.threshold: Secure Build A: L1 formal definition, L2 automated + checks added, L3 mandatory checks that fail the build
standards.source_name: OWASP SAMM v2 - Secure Build
standards.notes: Useful for calibrating ambition honestly: a two-person team that gets to Secure Build A2 and Security Testing A1 before public launch is doing well, and SAMM says so. Secure Build Stream B (Software Dependencies) L1 is "Create records with Bill of Materials of your applications and opportunistically analyze these" - the free NuGet/Yarn audit gates below already exceed that.

standards.claim: Free, first-party dependency gates exist for both stacks and do not require GitHub Advanced Security. For .NET, NuGetAudit defaults to true, NuGetAuditLevel defaults to low, and NuGetAuditMode "defaults to `all` when a project targets `net10.0` or higher. Otherwise NuGetAuditMode defaults to `direct`" - meaning a .NET 10 project already audits transitive dependencies. Findings surface as warnings NU1901 (low), NU1902 (moderate), NU1903 (high), NU1904 (critical), and Microsoft documents a CI-only pattern using `<WarningsAsErrors Condition=" '$(AuditPipeline)' == 'true' ">` with `dotnet restore -p:AuditPipeline=true`. For Yarn, `yarn npm audit` accepts `--severity` with values info/low/moderate/high/critical plus `-A/--all` and `-R/--recursive`, and "the process will exit with a non-zero exit code if a report is found for the selected packages".
standards.threshold: NuGetAuditMode default `all` on net10.0+; NuGetAuditLevel default `low`; NU1903 = high, NU1904 = critical; yarn npm audit --severity high
standards.source_name: Microsoft Learn - Auditing package dependencies for security vulnerabilities
standards.notes: Microsoft Learn page updated 2026-07-07, and the feature table lists NuGet 7.0 / .NET 10 SDK (10.0.100) / Visual Studio 2026 for the NuGetAuditMode default change and `dotnet package update --vulnerable`. This is the single best effort-to-value gate available to this team: the audit already runs, you are just choosing to fail on it. The CI-only conditional pattern matters because it means a new advisory published overnight breaks your audit gate but not the other developer's local build.

standards.claim: The trust model for workflow files changed twice in the last year and both changes affect merge gates. From 2025-12-08, for pull_request_target "The workflow file and checkout commit will always be taken from the repository's default branch, regardless of the pull request's base branch", GITHUB_REF resolves to the default branch, and environment branch protection rules evaluate against refs/pull/{number}/merge for pull_request events and against the default branch for pull_request_target. From 2026-06-18, actions/checkout v7 is GA and "refuses common pwn request patterns by default", blocking fork-PR checkouts of fork refs, PR head SHAs and merge commit refs unless you opt out with `allow-unsafe-pr-checkout`; enforcement was backported to v5/v6 on 2026-07-20.
standards.threshold: pull_request_target default-branch resolution effective 2025-12-08; actions/checkout v7 GA 2026-06-18; backport enforcement 2026-07-20
standards.source_name: GitHub Changelog - Safer pull_request_target defaults for GitHub Actions checkout
standards.notes: Tool-maintained evidence: actions/checkout latest release is v7.0.1, published_at 2026-07-20T15:10:05Z (https://api.github.com/repos/actions/checkout/releases/latest). If your workflows pin `@v4` or `@v5` you received behaviour changes on 2026-07-20 without editing anything. Note the residual gap this does NOT close: for ordinary `pull_request` runs the workflow file is still read from the PR branch, so a PR that edits .github/workflows/ci.yml runs the edited workflow as its own check while the required check name stays green.

recommended_checks.what_it_does: A single aggregator job named `gate` that declares `needs: [backend, frontend, deps-audit, secrets, tenant-isolation]` and runs with `if: always()`, failing unless every needed job result is success or skipped. This is the ONLY check name you add to the ruleset's required list. Everything else - build, unit tests, lint, audits - hangs off it. Adding, renaming or splitting a job never requires touching branch protection again, and a job legitimately skipped by an `if:` condition cannot silently satisfy a required check because `gate` inspects `needs.*.result` explicitly rather than relying on GitHub's skipped-equals-success behaviour.
recommended_checks.tool: GitHub Actions (first-party)
recommended_checks.tool_maintained_evidence: actions/checkout v7.0.1, published_at 2026-07-20T15:10:05Z per https://api.github.com/repos/actions/checkout/releases/latest ; GitHub documents the `always()` + `needs` aggregation pattern at https://docs.github.com/en/pull-requests/collaborating-with-pull-requests/collaborating-on-repositories-with-code-quality-features/troubleshooting-required-status-checks
recommended_checks.rationale_for_two_person_team: This is the highest-leverage decision in the whole area and it costs one extra job. It removes three failure modes at once: (1) required-check names orphaned by a job rename, which blocks every PR until an admin notices; (2) path-filtered workflows sitting in Pending forever, which GitHub's own docs tell you to avoid by not requiring skippable workflows; (3) the political cost of asking two people to agree on which of fifteen check names should be required. From the outside the team sees exactly one green tick. Keep the whole chain inside DORA's ~10 minute upper limit - if it exceeds that, split the slow parts into a scheduled run rather than adding a second required name.

recommended_checks.what_it_does: A job feeding `ci / gate` that runs the cross-tenant test suite against at least two seeded tenant databases and asserts that a request carrying office-a's Host header cannot read, write or enumerate office-b data through any anonymous-reachable endpoint (registration, login, password reset, document upload) or any authenticated endpoint. It should fail closed: if the harness cannot prove it exercised both tenants, the job fails.
recommended_checks.tool: GitHub Actions + your existing xUnit/integration test harness
recommended_checks.tool_maintained_evidence: Runs on the same first-party GitHub Actions runner as ci / gate; no third-party dependency introduced. Content of the suite is the testing area's remit, not this one.
recommended_checks.effort_hours: 12-24 to author the suite; ~1 to wire it into the gate
recommended_checks.rationale_for_two_person_team: You have stated that tenancy resolves from the Host header only and that cross-tenant leakage is the highest-consequence failure mode. A gate is worth its friction in proportion to the consequence it prevents, and this is the only check on this list whose failure mode is a reportable breach across eleven offices. It is also the check most likely to catch a regression that two SDE 1s reviewing each other's PRs would not spot by reading. Everything is synthetic data today, so build and break this now while destructive testing is free. If you only fund one thing on this list beyond the branch ruleset, fund this.

recommended_checks.what_it_does: Fails the build on known-vulnerable dependencies in both stacks without any paid licence: for .NET, `dotnet restore -p:AuditPipeline=true` with an MSBuild property group that adds NU1903 and NU1904 (high and critical) to WarningsAsErrors only when AuditPipeline is true; for the frontend, `yarn npm audit --all --recursive --severity high`, which exits non-zero when a report is found. Both feed ci / gate.
recommended_checks.tool: NuGet Audit (built into the .NET SDK) + `yarn npm audit` (Yarn 4)
recommended_checks.tool_maintained_evidence: Microsoft Learn 'Auditing package dependencies for security vulnerabilities' updated 2026-07-07 and documents NuGet 7.0 / .NET 10 SDK 10.0.100 / Visual Studio 2026 behaviour including the NuGetAuditMode default change and `dotnet package update --vulnerable` (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/nuget/concepts/auditing-packages). Yarn CLI docs for `yarn npm audit` at https://yarnpkg.com/cli/npm/audit document --severity values and non-zero exit.
recommended_checks.rationale_for_two_person_team: Nearly free: on .NET 10 NuGetAuditMode already defaults to `all`, so your build is already computing transitive vulnerability data and discarding it as warnings. You are only choosing to fail on the top two severities. Microsoft's `AuditPipeline` conditional is specifically designed so a newly published advisory breaks CI without breaking a teammate's local build at 11pm - which is exactly the property that stops this gate from becoming the reason someone starts using admin merge. Cap it at high+critical: auditing at the default `low` level on an ABP Commercial dependency tree will produce noise you cannot action and the gate will be disabled within a month.

recommended_checks.what_it_does: Runs gitleaks over the PR's commit range and fails on any finding, feeding ci / gate. Add a committed `.gitleaks.toml` with allowlist entries for known synthetic test fixtures so that false positives are fixed once, in version control, rather than by re-running the job.
recommended_checks.tool: gitleaks
recommended_checks.tool_maintained_evidence: Latest release v8.30.1 dated 2026-03-21, previous v8.30.0 dated 2025-11-26, per https://github.com/gitleaks/gitleaks/releases - actively maintained within the last 12 months.
recommended_checks.rationale_for_two_person_team: GitHub secret scanning push protection is an Advanced Security feature and 'You need to pay to use Advanced Security features in private repositories on GitHub.com', so the built-in option is not available to you by default. A leaked OpenIddict signing key, SQL Server connection string or MinIO credential in a repo that is about to face the public internet is a materially worse outcome than a leaked API key in a hobby project, because the connection strings are per-tenant database credentials. This is a ten-line workflow step with a well-maintained single binary and no service to run.

recommended_checks.what_it_does: Static analysis on PRs. On a private repo this requires a paid GitHub Code Security licence; if that is not available, the free substitute is to enable the .NET built-in code-quality and security analyzers with `<EnableNETAnalyzers>`/`<AnalysisMode>` plus ESLint security rules for the Angular side, run inside ci / gate at warning level and reviewed rather than enforced.
recommended_checks.tool: GitHub CodeQL (paid on private repos) or .NET analyzers + ESLint (free)
recommended_checks.tool_maintained_evidence: GitHub documents the 'Require code scanning results' and 'Require code quality results' ruleset rules with thresholds Errors / Warnings and higher / Notes and higher / All (https://docs.github.com/en/code-security/how-tos/maintain-quality-code/set-pr-thresholds), and the paid-on-private-repos constraint at https://docs.github.com/en/billing/concepts/product-billing/github-advanced-security
recommended_checks.rationale_for_two_person_team: Advisory, not a merge gate, and deliberately so: SAST on a 53k-line ABP codebase will produce a first-run backlog that two people cannot triage in a week, and a required check with an unclearable backlog is the fastest route to bypass culture. But it must EXIST and have been triaged once before you face anonymous internet traffic, which is why launch_blocking is yes while gate_or_advisory is advisory. Promote it to a required gate at the 'Errors' threshold only after the initial backlog is at zero - which is a decision for month three, not week one.

recommended_checks.what_it_does: One branch ruleset targeting the default branch, enforcement Active, bypass list EMPTY. Rules: Require a pull request before merging with 1 required approval, 'Dismiss stale pull request approvals when new commits are pushed', 'Require approval of the most recent reviewable push', and 'Require all comments on the pull request to be resolved before it can be merged'; Require status checks to pass with exactly one entry, `ci / gate`; Block force pushes; Restrict deletions; Require linear history. Do NOT enable 'Require branches to be up to date before merging'. Also enable repository-level 'Allow auto-merge'.
recommended_checks.tool: GitHub repository rulesets
recommended_checks.tool_maintained_evidence: Rule names and options verified at https://docs.github.com/en/repositories/configuring-branches-and-merges-in-your-repository/managing-rulesets/available-rules-for-rulesets ; GitHub shipped automatic branch-protection-to-ruleset migration on 2026-08-11 (https://github.blog/changelog/2026-08-11-automatically-migrate-branch-protection-rules-to-repository-rulesets/), confirming active investment.
recommended_checks.rationale_for_two_person_team: This is the whole defensible minimum in one screen, and it is five rules, not thirty. 'Require approval of the most recent reviewable push' is the one people skip and the one that matters most here: it means the person who last pushed cannot be the approver, which is the only mechanical separation of duties available to a two-person team. 'Require conversation resolution' costs zero CI minutes and is what makes SSDF PW.7.2's 'record and triage all discovered issues' true by construction rather than by promise. Leaving the bypass list empty is what distinguishes this from classic branch protection, where admins are exempt by default and both of you are admins. Auto-merge is what keeps the approval from becoming a scheduling problem.

recommended_checks.what_it_does: A scheduled workflow (weekly) that calls `GET /repos/{owner}/{repo}/rulesets` and `GET /repos/{owner}/{repo}/rulesets/{id}`, normalises the JSON, and diffs it against a committed baseline at `.github/rulesets/main.json`. On any difference it opens an issue naming the changed fields. The baseline file is itself covered by CODEOWNERS so changing it requires the other developer's approval.
recommended_checks.tool: GitHub Actions + GitHub REST API (repository rules endpoints)
recommended_checks.tool_maintained_evidence: Endpoints documented at https://docs.github.com/en/rest/repos/rules including GET/POST /repos/{owner}/{repo}/rulesets, PUT/DELETE /repos/{owner}/{repo}/rulesets/{ruleset_id}, and GET /repos/{owner}/{repo}/rulesets/{ruleset_id}/history for versioned history.
recommended_checks.rationale_for_two_person_team: CIS 1.1.19 is a control entirely about auditing changes to branch protection rules, and it exists because in a small team the people who can loosen the gate are the same people the gate constrains. This is the cheapest possible compensating control for having no separation of duties: the config becomes a reviewed artefact in the repo, and any out-of-band change produces an issue rather than passing unnoticed. It also produces the SSDF PO.3.2 'pipelines-as-code' and PO.3.3 'audit trail' artefact for free, and gives you something concrete to hand an auditor asking how change control is enforced.

recommended_checks.check_name: Monthly ruleset bypass and gate-health review
recommended_checks.what_it_does: A recurring 20-minute review: open Rule Insights filtered to bypasses (the dashboard shows successes, failures and bypasses over time plus 'Top bypassers' on GitHub Team), check the ruleset history endpoint for config changes since last month, and record the result - including 'no bypasses' - in a dated CHANGE-CONTROL.md committed to the repo. Also note any period main was red for more than 24 hours.
recommended_checks.tool: GitHub Rule Insights + ruleset history API + a markdown file in the repo
recommended_checks.tool_maintained_evidence: Rule Insights behaviour verified at https://docs.github.com/en/repositories/configuring-branches-and-merges-in-your-repository/managing-rulesets/managing-rulesets-for-a-repository ; the organization audit log is documented as retaining 180 days at https://docs.github.com/en/organizations/keeping-your-organization-secure/managing-security-settings-for-your-organization/reviewing-the-audit-log-for-your-organization
recommended_checks.effort_hours: 1 to set up, ~20 minutes per month
recommended_checks.rationale_for_two_person_team: This is the only item here that is compliance-shaped rather than engineering-shaped, and it is the one that turns everything above into evidence. 164.308(a)(1)(ii)(D) requires you to 'regularly review records of information system activity' and 164.316(b)(2)(i) requires the documentation be retained six years - GitHub's audit log gives you 180 days, so the durable record has to be a file in your own repo. Twenty minutes a month is affordable at one developer-week per month, and 'we reviewed bypasses monthly and here are 24 dated entries' is a materially different conversation with an auditor than 'branch protection is on'. It also gives you an early signal if the gates are being routed around, which is the failure mode you cannot see from inside.

not_worth_it_here: GitHub merge queue. It is not available on private repositories outside GitHub Enterprise Cloud, and even if it were, it exists to solve semantic conflicts between many concurrent PRs landing on a busy branch. DORA's own guidance for a healthy team is three or fewer active branches and merging to trunk at least daily; with two developers you will rarely have two mergeable PRs in flight simultaneously. It also multiplies CI minutes (every queue entry rebuilds on a gh-readonly-queue branch) and GitHub's docs warn that jumping the queue triggers full rebuilds of in-progress entries. The thing merge queue buys you - main is never broken by a combination that individually passed - is worth real money at 50 engineers and roughly nothing at two.

Two required approving reviews (CIS Software Supply Chain Security Guide 1.1.3, 'approval of two strongly authenticated users'). This is not merely expensive here, it is arithmetically impossible: GitHub states plainly that 'Pull request authors cannot approve their own pull requests', so two approvals requires three humans on a two-person team. Do not attempt a workaround. Instead write a one-paragraph compensating-control note now - one approval, plus author-cannot-approve, plus 'Require approval of the most recent reviewable push', plus an automated gate - and keep it with your risk analysis. You will be asked for it by a customer security questionnaire before you are asked for it by OCR.

'Require branches to be up to date before merging' (the strict status-check option; CIS 1.1.10). Without a merge queue this serialises every merge: dev A merges, dev B must rebase and re-run the full CI suite, and with two people alternating you burn a 10-minute build per merge for a conflict class that a fast test suite would catch anyway. Enable it later if you ever see a semantic conflict reach main; do not pay for it prospectively.

Required signed commits (CIS 1.1.12, SSDF PS.1.1 Example 3). Genuine supply-chain value, but the setup cost lands on both machines, both IDEs, any bot account, and every rebase, and CIS's own note is that pull requests with unsigned commits simply cannot be merged - so a misconfigured key becomes a hard stop on a Friday afternoon. This is a good month-six item once the rest is stable and habitual, or a good item to add the week a third developer joins. Not a launch blocker.

CODEOWNERS with required code-owner review across the whole repository (CIS 1.1.6/1.1.7 applied broadly). With two people, repo-wide code-owner review means one named person is a single point of failure for every merge; when they are on leave the team's only options are to wait or to bypass, and bypass wins. Scope CODEOWNERS narrowly to `.github/**` (so nobody can quietly weaken the pipeline) and to the tenancy-resolution and multi-tenant data-access code. That is two lines in the file and it targets the two things where a second pair of eyes is actually load-bearing.

A separate required check per analysis type - SAST, DAST, IaC scanning, licence compliance, container scanning, coverage threshold, bundle-size budget, each with its own name in the required list. This is the shape most enterprise pipelines take and it is the specific failure this brief warns about. Every additional required name is another string that can be orphaned by a rename, another workflow that can sit Pending after a path filter, and another negotiation about whether it may be bypassed. Consolidate behind one `ci / gate` name and manage the contents in code.

A formal change advisory board, release sign-off tickets, or any approval step outside the pull request. DORA's finding is direct: 'no evidence was found to support the hypothesis that a more formal, external review process was associated with lower change fail rates', and heavier processes correlate with larger, less frequent batches and higher production impact. For a HIPAA system the temptation is to add ceremony because the data is sensitive; the evidence says the sensitivity argues for faster, smaller, better-tested changes, not slower ones.

Organization-level rulesets, enterprise policies, 'Evaluate' enforcement rollouts, required workflows sourced from a central repository, and the whole governance-at-scale layer. These are GitHub Enterprise features designed to enforce policy consistently across dozens of repositories. You have one repository and two people who talk to each other every day. Revisit only if the codebase splits into several repos.

Full build provenance, SLSA attestation, reproducible builds and signed release artefacts (SSDF PS.2, PS.3, PO.3.2 Example 4). These matter when third parties consume your build output and need to verify it independently. You are operating a hosted multi-tenant application for eleven offices; nobody downloads your artefacts. The archive-and-retain obligation in PS.3.1 is worth satisfying cheaply (keep tagged releases and their CI run records), but signing infrastructure is not.

Coverage percentage as a merge gate (including GitHub's new 'Restrict code coverage' rule, currently public preview). A coverage floor on a 53k-line C# plus 27k-line TypeScript codebase written without one will either be set so low it certifies nothing or so high it blocks every PR. Report coverage as a comment, watch the trend, and spend the effort on the tenant-isolation suite instead - that is coverage that maps to your actual worst-case failure.
surprises: The same 'only run this when relevant files change' optimisation either deadlocks you or silently disables your gate, depending on which line you put it on. GitHub's docs are explicit: a workflow skipped by path filtering, branch filtering or a commit message leaves its checks Pending and blocks merging forever, while a JOB skipped by a conditional 'will report its status as Success. It will not prevent a pull request from merging, even if it is a required check.' So `on: pull_request: paths:` wedges every PR until an admin force-merges, and `jobs.x.if:` makes your required security check green while it does nothing. Both are things a team adds in week two to save CI minutes. GitHub acknowledged the path-filter case as a papercut in community discussion 44490 on 2024-09-19 with no timeline, and it is still open in 2026.

Classic branch protection does not apply to you. Verbatim from GitHub's docs: 'By default, the restrictions of a branch protection rule do not apply to people with admin permissions to the repository.' On a two-person repo both developers are admins. If you configure classic branch protection and do not tick 'Do not allow bypassing the above settings', you have built a gate that constrains nobody and will pass a superficial audit anyway. CIS considers this important enough to be its own control (1.1.14). Rulesets reverse the default - enforcement applies and bypass is an explicit list - which is on its own a sufficient reason to use rulesets rather than classic protection.

Your merge-gate evidence expires roughly twelve times sooner than HIPAA requires you to keep it. GitHub's organization audit log 'lists events triggered by activities that affect your organization within the last 180 days', while 45 CFR 164.316(b)(2)(i) requires documentation be retained 'for 6 years from the date of its creation or the date when it last was in effect, whichever is later'. Almost nobody notices this until an auditor asks for change-control evidence covering a period that has already aged out. The durable records are the pull requests themselves, the ruleset history endpoint (GET /repos/{owner}/{repo}/rulesets/{ruleset_id}/history), and a committed ruleset JSON plus a dated review log in your own repository - none of which are the audit log.

A pull request can weaken its own gate. For ordinary `pull_request` runs the workflow file is read from the PR branch, so a PR that edits .github/workflows/ci.yml runs the edited workflow as its own check - the required check name stays green while doing less. Two SDE 1s reviewing each other are unlikely to read a workflow diff as adversarially as they read application code. Relatedly and very recently: since 2025-12-08 pull_request_target takes its workflow file and checkout commit from the default branch regardless of the PR's base, and actions/checkout v7 (GA 2026-06-18, enforcement backported to v5/v6 on 2026-07-20) now 'refuses common pwn request patterns by default'. If your workflows pin @v4 or @v5 you received a behaviour change on 2026-07-20 without editing anything.

Most of the security merge gates GitHub advertises are unavailable to you on a private repository. 'You need to pay to use Advanced Security features in private repositories on GitHub.com' - that covers CodeQL code scanning and therefore the 'Require code scanning results' ruleset rule, secret scanning push protection, and dependency review. The ruleset editor will happily show you rules you cannot turn on. The free substitutes are genuinely good (NuGet Audit, yarn npm audit, gitleaks v8.30.1 released 2026-03-21) but you have to know to wire them yourself, and nothing in the GitHub UI tells you that.

.NET 10 silently changed your dependency-audit posture. NuGetAuditMode 'defaults to `all` when a project targets `net10.0` or higher. Otherwise NuGetAuditMode defaults to `direct`.' Your build is already auditing transitive dependencies and reporting NU1901-NU1904 as warnings you are almost certainly scrolling past. Turning the top two severities into errors in CI only - via Microsoft's documented `<WarningsAsErrors Condition=" '$(AuditPipeline)' == 'true' ">` pattern and `dotnet restore -p:AuditPipeline=true` - is about an hour of work and converts existing noise into a real gate without breaking anyone's local build.

The realistic decay mode for a two-person team is not bypass, it is a red main that stays red. The CI Theater study (1,270 projects, 534,417 builds) found 85% of projects had at least one build broken for more than four days, and that on the smallest projects those builds took an average of 40 days to fix. Nobody plans for this. The mitigations are cultural and cheap - a written rule that a red default branch outranks feature work, revert rather than fix-forward if it is not a few minutes' work, and keeping the whole required chain inside DORA's roughly 10-minute upper limit - and they matter more than any additional check you could add.

GitHub shipped a code-quality merge gate you have probably not seen. The 'Require code quality results' ruleset rule blocks merges at thresholds of 'Errors', 'Warnings and higher', 'Notes and higher' or 'All', and there is a separate 'Restrict code coverage' rule in public preview. Worth knowing these exist before you spend a week building your own coverage-threshold action - and worth knowing they sit behind the same private-repo licensing as the rest of code scanning.

Required status checks are matched by literal string, and the failure is asymmetric. Rename a job and the required check name never reports, which blocks every pull request repository-wide until someone with admin rights notices and edits the ruleset - and the fastest fix in the moment is an admin merge, which is precisely the bypass you built the gate to prevent. GitHub also warns that 'If a check and a commit status have the same name, both must pass when that name is required', so a name collision between an Action and a third-party app blocks silently. One required name, backed by an aggregator job, makes this entire class of incident impossible.

The cheapest gate on the list has the strongest compliance story and zero CI cost. 'Require all comments on the pull request to be resolved before it can be merged' is one checkbox, and it is the mechanism that makes SSDF PW.7.2 - 'record and triage all discovered issues and recommended remediations in the development team's workflow or issue tracking system' - true by construction rather than by assertion. Teams routinely skip it as trivial and then have no answer when asked how review findings are tracked to closure.
disagreements: Reviewer count: CIS Software Supply Chain Security Guide 1.1.3 requires 'approval of two strongly authenticated users', while NIST SSDF PW.7.1 explicitly declines to specify - 'Determine whether code review ... and/or code analysis ... should be used, as defined by the organization' - and DORA reports 'no evidence was found to support the hypothesis that a more formal, external review process was associated with lower change fail rates'. CIS is a prescriptive configuration checklist written for organisations with headcount; SSDF is risk-based; DORA is outcome-based research. For two developers the CIS control is not expensive, it is unsatisfiable, because GitHub forbids self-approval and two approvals therefore needs three people. I recommend one approval plus 'Require approval of the most recent reviewable push', and I recommend writing down that CIS 1.1.3 is a known, documented deviation rather than pretending it is met.

Branch currency: CIS 1.1.10 requires branches be up to date before merging, unconditionally. GitHub built merge queue precisely because that requirement serialises merges on active repositories, and DORA's trunk-based-development guidance points the other way (three or fewer active branches, branches lasting hours, merge to trunk daily) - at which point the requirement is largely moot. Since merge queue is unavailable on private repos outside Enterprise Cloud, following CIS 1.1.10 literally would cost you a full CI cycle per merge with no queue to absorb it. I recommend not enabling it and noting the deviation.

Scope of 'audit controls': HIPAA 164.312(b) is written about systems that contain ePHI - it requires mechanisms that 'record and examine activity in information systems that contain or use electronic protected health information'. A source-code repository containing no PHI is arguably outside it, and the honest reading is that your merge gate is a security measure selected under 164.308(a)(1)(ii)(B) risk management, with the PR and ruleset history as supporting documentation under 164.316. Vendors and consultancies frequently assert that 'HIPAA requires code review' or 'HIPAA requires change control'; no provision I read says either. Be careful not to over-claim in the other direction: the pending NPRM would remove the required/addressable distinction and require written documentation of all policies, procedures, plans and analyses, which would tighten the documentation obligation without ever naming a merge gate.

Feature availability: GitHub's documentation is internally inconsistent about where the plan-availability banners appear. Search snippets from docs.github.com consistently state that merge queue is available 'in any public repository owned by an organization, or in private repositories owned by organizations using GitHub Enterprise Cloud', and that rulesets are available on private repos only with Pro, Team or Enterprise Cloud - but neither banner rendered in the page bodies I fetched, so I could not quote them from a page I opened. I have marked both claims partial. Confirm against your own repository settings before designing around either, because whether merge queue exists for you changes the shape of the recommendation.

CI Theater vs the intuition that gates get bypassed: the empirical literature I could find does not establish a gate-count threshold at which teams begin bypassing - I searched for one and did not find it, so treat any specific number ('more than five checks and people start bypassing') as unsourced folklore. What the literature does establish is that small projects tolerate long-broken builds far worse than large ones. If someone cites a specific gate-count threshold at you, ask for the source.

research.area: Test strategy and depth for a .NET 10 / ABP Commercial 10.0.2 / Angular 20.3 multi-tenant (database-per-tenant) HIPAA line-of-business application
research.standard_summary: The 2026 standard is still pyramid-shaped, not trophy-shaped, and the two most authoritative published mixes agree: Software Engineering at Google targets "80% of our tests being narrow-scoped unit tests... 15% medium-scoped integration tests... and 5% end-to-end tests", and Microsoft's ASP.NET Core guidance says outright "If a behavior can be tested using either a unit test or an integration test, choose the unit test." What has genuinely changed since ~2022 is the database question: Microsoft's EF Core team now explicitly recommends "good test coverage of their application running against their actual production database system" and warns that SQLite-as-a-fake produces false passes (SQL Server is case-insensitive by default, SQLite is not; provider-specific translations and raw SQL do not survive the swap). This puts EF Core's own docs in direct conflict with the ASP.NET Core integration-testing page (which recommends SQLite in-memory) and with the ABP startup template (which ships SQLite in-memory). "Enough" is defined by credible sources as a *ratio and a rate of change*, not an absolute number: Sonar's default gate is 80% coverage on **new** code and ≤3% duplication on new code, while Microsoft explicitly refuses to name a number and warns "A high code coverage percentage isn't an indicator of success". For this specific stack the binding constraint is not proportion but *shape*: ABP's shipped integration tests resolve application services straight out of DI with `AddAlwaysAllowAuthorization()` pre-wired, so authorization, ASP.NET Core filters, model binding, routing and the multi-tenancy middleware — i.e. every mechanism that stops cross-tenant leakage on a Host-header-resolved tenancy model — are not exercised by the test shape the framework hands you.

standards.claim: Google's published target test mix is 80% narrow-scoped unit tests, 15% medium-scoped integration tests, and 5% end-to-end tests — not the 70/20/10 figure that circulates in blog posts.
standards.threshold: 80% small / 15% medium / 5% large
standards.source_name: Software Engineering at Google, Chapter 11 (Testing Overview), O'Reilly/abseil.io
standards.notes: Verbatim: "80% of our tests being narrow-scoped unit tests that validate the majority of our business logic; 15% medium-scoped integration tests that validate the interactions between two or more components; and 5% end-to-end tests". Same chapter defines small tests as single-process, no I/O, no sleeps; medium as multi-process, localhost network allowed; large as multi-machine. The often-quoted 70/20/10 traces to Google's 2010-era blog framing (https://testing.googleblog.com/2010/12/test-sizes.html, which I opened and which gives runtime targets of <60s / <300s / <900s but NO percentage split). Cite the book number, not the blog number. Fowler/Vocke corroborate the shape: "Write tests with different granularity. The more high-level you get the fewer tests you should have."

standards.claim: Microsoft's official ASP.NET Core guidance is to prefer the unit test whenever a behavior could be covered by either a unit or an integration test, and to limit integration tests to the most important infrastructure scenarios.
standards.threshold: n/a (explicit preference rule, no number)
standards.source_name: Microsoft Learn — Integration tests in ASP.NET Core
standards.notes: Page metadata: applies to ASP.NET Core 3.1–11.0, default moniker aspnetcore-10.0, last updated 2026-08-26. Verbatim: "Therefore, limit the use of integration tests to the most important infrastructure scenarios. If a behavior can be tested using either a unit test or an integration test, choose the unit test." Also verbatim: "Don't write integration tests for every permutation of data and file access with databases and file systems... a focused set of read, write, update, and delete integration tests are usually capable of adequately testing database and file system components." And: "Separate unit tests from integration tests into different projects."

standards.claim: Microsoft's EF Core team recommends testing against the real production database system, and states that SQLite used as a database fake produces divergent results versus SQL Server (case sensitivity, unsupported queries, provider-specific methods, raw SQL dialect).
standards.threshold: n/a (recommendation); EF Core's own suite is cited as >30,000 tests against SQL Server completing "in a few minutes"
standards.source_name: Microsoft Learn — Choosing a testing strategy (EF Core)
standards.notes: Page metadata updated_at 2026-06-26. Verbatim summary bullet: "We recommend that developers have good test coverage of their application running against their actual production database system." On SQLite: "SQL Server does case-insensitive string comparison by default, whereas SQLite is case-sensitive. This can make your tests pass against SQLite where they would fail against SQL Server (or vice versa)." And: "we recommend either writing your tests against your real database, or if using a test double is an absolute necessity, taking onboard the cost of a repository pattern". Names Testcontainers and SQL Server LocalDB as setup options. THIS CONTRADICTS the ASP.NET Core page — see the disagreements field.

standards.claim: The ASP.NET Core integration-testing page recommends the SQLite provider (not the EF Core in-memory provider) for in-memory testing, which is a weaker position than the EF Core team's own guidance on the same question.
standards.threshold: n/a
standards.source_name: Microsoft Learn — Integration tests in ASP.NET Core
standards.notes: Verbatim: "The EF-Core in-memory database provider can be used for limited and basic testing, however the SQLite provider is the recommended choice for in-memory testing." Sample code on that page (ASP.NET Core 10.0 sample) registers a singleton open SqliteConnection with DataSource=:memory: and UseSqlite. Both Microsoft pages agree on rejecting the EF in-memory provider; they disagree on whether SQLite is an acceptable destination or a trap.

standards.claim: EF Core's in-memory provider is explicitly discouraged by Microsoft for testing purposes and is described as supported only for legacy applications.
standards.threshold: n/a ("highly discouraged" / "Avoid")
standards.source_name: Microsoft Learn — Choosing a testing strategy (EF Core)
standards.notes: Verbatim: "Avoid the in-memory provider for testing purposes - this is discouraged and only supported for legacy applications." Listed limitations: transactions not supported, raw SQL completely unsupported, fewer query types than SQLite, slower than SQLite. ABP independently reaches the same conclusion: its docs say the EF in-memory provider "doesn't support transaction and rollback scenarios" whereas SQLite is "a real DBMS and supports the fundamental SQL database features."

standards.claim: EF Core ships a first-class way to assert that no migration has been forgotten, and Microsoft explicitly recommends turning it into a test: `dotnet ef migrations has-pending-model-changes` / `context.Database.HasPendingModelChanges()`.
standards.threshold: Feature added in EF Core 8.0; from EF Core 9 calling Migrate/MigrateAsync with pending model changes throws (event ID PendingModelChangesWarning)
standards.source_name: Microsoft Learn — Managing Migrations (EF Core)
standards.notes: Page metadata updated_at 2026-08-11. Verbatim: "You can also perform this check programmatically using `context.Database.HasPendingModelChanges()`. This can be used to write a unit test that fails when you forget to add a migration." This is the single cheapest high-value gate available to this team and it is Microsoft's own suggestion.

standards.claim: Microsoft publishes concrete isolation techniques for real-database tests: an xUnit class fixture that creates/seeds once, transaction-rollback for write tests, a separate database + collection fixture (parallelism disabled) for tests that manage their own transactions, and Respawn for efficient cleanup.
standards.threshold: n/a (technique catalogue); three named test categories: read-only, write, transactional
standards.source_name: Microsoft Learn — Testing against your Production Database System (EF Core)
standards.notes: Page metadata updated_at 2026-06-24. Verbatim summary: "Read-only tests are relatively simple, and can always execute in parallel against the same database... Write tests are more problematic, but transactions can be used to make sure they're properly isolated. Transactional tests are the most problematic, requiring logic to reset the database back to its original state, as well as disabling parallelization." Names https://github.com/jbogard/respawn: Respawn latest is 7.0.0, published 2025-11-30 per https://api.nuget.org/v3/registration5-gz-semver2/respawn/index.json — maintained within 12 months.

standards.claim: ABP's startup template creates five test projects mapped to layers — Domain.Tests, Application.Tests, EntityFrameworkCore.Tests, Web.Tests, and a shared TestBase — pre-wired with xUnit, NSubstitute and Shouldly, and runs them against SQLite in-memory with a fresh database per test case.
standards.threshold: 5 projects; xUnit + NSubstitute + Shouldly; one fresh SQLite in-memory DB per test case
standards.source_name: ABP.IO Documentation — Automated Testing (overall) and Integration Tests
standards.notes: Verbatim layer mapping: Domain.Tests "used to test your Domain Layer objects (like Domain Services and Entities)"; Application.Tests "used to test your Application Layer (like Application Services)"; EntityFrameworkCore.Tests "used to implement abstract test classes and test your custom repository implementations or EF Core mappings"; Web.Tests "used to test the UI Layer (like Pages, Controllers and View Components)". Integration tests use `AbpIntegratedTest<T>`, must run inside a unit of work (`IUnitOfWorkManager` / `WithUnitOfWorkAsync`), and the TestBase carries a `YourProjectTestDataSeedContributor`. NOTE: Web.Tests exists for MVC/Razor solutions; an Angular-UI ABP solution typically has no equivalent HTTP-pipeline test project, which is the gap addressed by the authz-contract-tests check.

standards.claim: ABP's startup template disables authorization in integration tests by default via AddAlwaysAllowAuthorization(), so permission and [Authorize] enforcement is not exercised by the shipped test shape.
standards.threshold: n/a — `context.Services.AddAlwaysAllowAuthorization();` present in the test module's ConfigureServices by default
standards.source_name: ABP.IO Documentation — Authorization (framework fundamentals)
standards.notes: Verbatim from ABP docs: AlwaysAllowAuthorizationService is used to "bypass the authorization service" and "is generally used in integration tests where you may want to disable the authorization system", registered via `AddAlwaysAllowAuthorization()` — and critically: "This is already done for the startup template integration tests." Corroborated by ABP's microservice testing guide, where tests obtain services via GetRequiredService<T>() rather than through the API authentication layer. This is the single highest-consequence finding in this area for an app about to accept anonymous internet traffic with four self-registering external roles.

standards.claim: Unit tests of ASP.NET Core controllers/actions deliberately do not exercise filters, routing or model binding; those must be covered by integration tests through the request pipeline.
standards.threshold: n/a (explicit scope boundary)
standards.source_name: Microsoft Learn — Test controller logic in ASP.NET Core
standards.notes: Page metadata: default moniker aspnetcore-10.0, updated_at 2026-07-22. Verbatim: "A controller unit test avoids scenarios such as filters, routing, and model binding. Tests that cover the interactions among components that collectively respond to a request are handled by integration tests." Directly load-bearing here: ABP implements authorization as filters and tenancy as middleware, so neither ABP unit tests nor ABP DI-level integration tests can cover them. Only a WebApplicationFactory/TestServer test can.

standards.claim: In Angular 20.3.x the Vitest-capable test builder exists but is marked EXPERIMENTAL, accepts runner values of exactly "karma" or "vitest", and pins an optional peer dependency of vitest ^3.1.1 — meaning Vitest 4.x is not compatible with Angular 20.3.
standards.threshold: @angular/build 20.3.35: builder `unit-test` described as "[EXPERIMENTAL] Run application unit tests"; schema runner enum ["karma","vitest"]; peerDependencies vitest ^3.1.1 (optional), karma ^6.4.0 (optional)
standards.source_name: npm registry package contents for @angular/build@20.3.35 (builders.json and src/builders/unit-test/schema.json)
standards.notes: Verified by downloading https://registry.npmjs.org/@angular/build/-/build-20.3.35.tgz and reading package/builders.json and the unit-test schema directly. 20.3.35 published 2026-08-26. Schema also exposes setupFiles, codeCoverage, browsers (jsdom when undefined) and watch (defaults false in non-TTY, i.e. CI-friendly). The v20 docs page corroborates the builder name and the experimental status verbatim: "The Angular CLI provides an experimental unit test system that can use Vitest as a test runner" and "This experimental unit testing system requires the use of the application build system." Practical consequence: `yarn add -D vitest` today installs 4.1.11 (published 2026-08-18) and will not satisfy the peer range.

standards.claim: Karma is deprecated by its own maintainers and accepts no new features or general bug fixes; Angular's current docs nonetheless still list Karma as supported while making Vitest the default for new projects.
standards.threshold: Karma: "deprecated... not accepting new features or general bug fixes"; security fixes continue "until 12 months after Angular CLI's Web Test Runner support is marked stable"
standards.source_name: karma-runner/karma repository README (deprecation notice)
standards.notes: Karma verbatim: "Karma is deprecated and is not accepting new features or general bug fixes." and "Critical security issues in Karma will still be triaged and fixed as necessary. This will continue until 12 months after Angular CLI's Web Test Runner support is marked stable." Angular never shipped Web Test Runner as the stable CLI runner — it shipped Vitest — so Karma's stated support horizon is anchored to an event that did not occur. Angular's current Karma page says only "While Vitest is the default test runner for new Angular projects, Karma is still a supported and widely used test runner." Two first-party sources, two different pictures.

standards.claim: ABP 10.0's Angular template ships Karma + Jasmine; ABP's current template ships Vitest with ABP-specific testing modules — so the runner migration is a supported ABP path, not a fork.
standards.threshold: ABP 10.0 docs: Karma + Jasmine, `npm test` / `npm test -- --prod`. ABP latest docs: Vitest, `yarn test` / `ng test --watch=false`
standards.source_name: ABP.IO Documentation — Unit Testing Angular UI (v10.0 and latest)
standards.notes: ABP 10.0 verbatim: "In Angular, unit tests use Karma and Jasmine by default. Although we like Jest more, we chose not to deviate from these defaults, so the application template you download will have Karma and Jasmine preconfigured." ABP latest: "The application template you download is preconfigured for unit testing. You can add a *.spec.ts file and run `yarn test`" — with Vitest. ABP-specific helpers in both: `CoreTestingModule.withConfig()` (which replaces PermissionService with MockPermissionService that GRANTS ALL POLICIES BY DEFAULT), `ThemeSharedTestingModule.withConfig()`, `clearPage()`, `wait()`. ABP also endorses @testing-library/angular as an alternative (latest 19.4.2, published 2026-08-07 per https://registry.npmjs.org/@testing-library/angular).

standards.claim: Angular 20's supported lifetime ends 2026-11-28 (LTS), roughly three months from today, and Angular's support policy is 12 months active + 12 months LTS per major.
