standards.source_name: Angular — Versioning and releases
standards.notes: Verbatim: "All major releases are typically supported for 24 months" — 12 months active, 12 months LTS ("Only critical fixes and security patches"). Page also notes "Until Angular v22, Angular had a 6-month major release cycle"; v22+ moves to a 12-month cycle. The CLI releases page confirms 20.3.x is still receiving patches (20.3.35 on 2026-08-26). Relevant to test strategy because it dictates whether to invest in Karma specs now or defer the suite build-out until after the v21/v22 upgrade.

standards.claim: The default credible definition of "enough" test coverage is a gate on NEW code, not on the whole codebase: Sonar's out-of-the-box quality gate requires ≥80.0% coverage on new code and ≤3.0% duplication on new code.
standards.threshold: Coverage on new code ≥ 80.0%; duplicated lines on new code ≤ 3.0%; no new issues; all new Security Hotspots reviewed
standards.source_name: SonarSource Documentation — Understanding quality gates (SonarQube Server)
standards.notes: The four Sonar way conditions verbatim: "No new issues are introduced", "All new Security Hotspots are reviewed", "New code test coverage is greater than or equal to 80.0%", "Duplication in the new code is less than or equal to 3.0%". Rationale verbatim: it "focuses on keeping high quality standards for new code, rather than spending a lot of effort remediating old code." Contrast with Microsoft, which names NO number and warns: "A high code coverage percentage isn't an indicator of success, and it doesn't imply high code quality" and "Setting an overly ambitious code coverage percentage goal can be counterproductive." Angular's v20 coverage page uses 80/80/80/80 only as an illustration ("suppose you want the code base to have a minimum of 80% code coverage"), not as a recommendation.

standards.claim: Flakiness has a published tolerance threshold: value degrades as a suite approaches 1% flaky tests, and Google operates at roughly 0.15%.
standards.threshold: ~1% flakiness = tests "begin to lose value"; Google's own rate ≈ 0.15%
standards.source_name: Software Engineering at Google, Chapter 11 (Testing Overview)
standards.notes: Verbatim: "as you approach 1% flakiness, the tests begin to lose value"; Google maintains "around 0.15%". Same chapter states the Beyoncé Rule ("If you liked it, then you shoulda put a test on it") and warns coverage "only measures that a line was invoked, not what happened as a result" and becomes "a goal unto itself". This is the number to hold a two-person team's E2E suite to — it is the reason to cap E2E at single digits rather than let it grow.

standards.claim: Thoughtworks' Technology Radar places broad integration tests (those requiring live versions of all run-time dependencies) in Hold, and in-memory component testing (jsdom) in Adopt.
standards.threshold: Broad integration tests = Hold, last appeared Vol 34 (April 2024). Component testing = Adopt (October 2024).
standards.source_name: Thoughtworks Technology Radar — Broad integration tests / Component testing
standards.notes: Broad integration tests verbatim definition: tests "that require live versions of all run-time dependencies"; criticised as "often fragile and unhelpful" with difficulty attributing failures. Recommended alternative: service virtualization plus contract tests. Component testing (Adopt) verbatim rationale: "test suites should be stable and run quickly"; browser-based tests are "slow, more flaky and harder to debug"; jsdom-based in-memory component tests are the balance point. Secondary-tier source (a consultancy radar) but a widely-cited industry one, and it independently corroborates the pyramid over the trophy. Directly supports running Angular tests in jsdom rather than a real browser.

standards.claim: Microsoft publishes first-party mutation-testing guidance naming Stryker.NET, and explicitly directs teams to scope it to risk rather than chase a score.
standards.threshold: "Don't chase a 100% mutation score. Instead, focus on high risk or business critical areas where undetected bugs would be most costly."
standards.source_name: Microsoft Learn — Mutation testing (.NET)
standards.notes: Page metadata updated_at 2026-04-03. Names `dotnet tool install -g dotnet-stryker`, the killed/survived/timeout taxonomy, stryker-config.json with `mutate` exclusions (their own example excludes `!**/Migrations/*` and `!**/*.Designer.cs`), and says Stryker "can be configured to run within your Azure Pipelines or GitHub Actions setup, allowing you to enforce quality thresholds". Maintenance verified: dotnet-stryker 4.16.0 published 2026-07-03 (https://api.nuget.org/v3/registration5-gz-semver2/dotnet-stryker/index.json).

standards.claim: In multi-tenant ABP with database-per-tenant, the IMultiTenant global query filter provides no cross-tenant protection — isolation comes entirely from connection-string resolution driven by ICurrentTenant.
standards.threshold: n/a (architectural constraint)
standards.source_name: ABP.IO Documentation — Multi-Tenancy
standards.notes: ABP verbatim: "ABP automatically filters entities for the current tenant when you query from database" — but also, regarding disabling the filter: "Note that this approach won't work if your tenants have separate databases since there is no built-in way to query from multiple database in a single database query." ABP documents built-in tenant resolvers reading user claims, query string, route, HTTP header and cookie (all `__tenant` by default) plus a domain/subdomain resolver. `using (CurrentTenant.Change(tenantId)) { ... }` is the documented scoping API and is the hook a tenant-isolation test uses. Consequence for testing: since isolation is connection-string-based, a test that asserts "tenant A cannot read tenant B's row" must go through tenant resolution (host header → tenant → connection string), which ABP's DI-level integration tests do not do.

standards.claim: OWASP WSTG defines the authorization-bypass test case that a multi-tenant portal's negative tests should be written against, covering unauthenticated, horizontal and vertical access.
standards.threshold: WSTG-ATHZ-02 — Testing for Bypassing Authorization Schema
standards.source_name: OWASP Web Security Testing Guide (latest) — 4.5.2
standards.notes: Test objective verbatim: "Assess if unauthenticated, horizontal, or vertical access is possible." Horizontal section tests "whether a user can access resources or conduct operations belonging to users with equivalent roles" — that is the cross-tenant / cross-patient case for this app. WSTG does not use the phrase multi-tenancy, so mapping tenant isolation to the horizontal-escalation case is my inference, not OWASP's wording. Useful because it gives the negative-test suite a citable requirement ID for HIPAA documentation without dragging in a full ASVS assessment.

standards.claim: `dotnet test` behaviour changed materially in the .NET 10 SDK: Microsoft.Testing.Platform is selected via global.json, runsettings is replaced by testconfig.json, and a test assembly containing zero tests now fails rather than passes.
standards.threshold: global.json: {"test": {"runner": "Microsoft.Testing.Platform"}}; zero-test assembly exits with code 8 under MTP (VSTest exited 0)
standards.source_name: .NET Blog — Enhance your CLI testing workflow with the new dotnet test
standards.notes: I opened and read the .NET Blog post (published 2025-08-21, author Mariam Abdullah) and confirmed the global.json snippet verbatim and the statement "MTP is designed to be the future of test execution in .NET". The exit-code-8 behaviour and the testconfig.json replacement for --settings came from the Microsoft Learn VSTest→MTP migration guide surfaced in search; I did NOT open that Learn page directly, so I am marking this entry partial rather than verified. Package maintenance is verified: Microsoft.Testing.Platform 2.3.3 published 2026-07-28, and xunit.v3 4.0.0 published 2026-08-15 (both via api.nuget.org registration index). Relevant because a CI job that passes today can begin failing for a non-test reason after an SDK bump.

standards.claim: NIST SP 800-218 (SSDF v1.1) is the current federal secure-development framework and locates executable-code testing under practice PW.8, but I could not extract the exact PW.8/PW.8.2 wording from the primary PDF.
standards.threshold: SP 800-218, SSDF Version 1.1, published February 2022; practice group PW; PW.8 concerns testing executable code
standards.source_name: NIST CSRC — SP 800-218 publication record
standards.notes: What I verified: the publication record confirms title "Secure Software Development Framework (SSDF) Version 1.1: Recommendations for Mitigating the Risk of Software Vulnerabilities", version 1.1, February 2022, DOI 10.6028/NIST.SP.800-218. The CSRC project page confirms 1.1 is current, that there is no v1.2, and that SP 800-218A exists as a GenAI community profile. What I could NOT verify: the exact wording of PW.8, PW.8.1 and PW.8.2 and their implementation examples. I downloaded https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/SpecialPublications/NIST.SP.800-218.pdf (739,891 bytes) but this environment has no working pdftotext/pypdf/poppler, and WebFetch could not extract the practice table from the PDF. The PW.8 title ("Test Executable Code to Identify Vulnerabilities and Verify Compliance with Security Requirements") appeared only in secondary search summaries. Do not quote a PW.8 requirement ID in a compliance document without opening the PDF yourself.

recommended_checks.what_it_does: Runs the ABP-shipped xUnit projects (Domain.Tests, Application.Tests, EntityFrameworkCore.Tests) on every PR against SQLite in-memory, exactly as the template configures them. Publishes a test-results summary. No coverage threshold attached.
recommended_checks.tool: dotnet test (.NET 10 SDK) + xUnit + Shouldly + NSubstitute, as shipped by the ABP 10.0.2 template; GitHub Actions ubuntu-latest
recommended_checks.tool_maintained_evidence: xunit.v3 4.0.0 published 2026-08-15 and Microsoft.Testing.Platform 2.3.3 published 2026-07-28 (https://api.nuget.org/v3/registration5-gz-semver2/xunit.v3/index.json, .../microsoft.testing.platform/index.json). NSubstitute 6.2.0 published 2026-08-11; Shouldly 4.3.0 stable published 2025-01-23 with 5.0.0-preview.2 on 2026-07-18 (.../nsubstitute/index.json, .../shouldly/index.json) — all released within 12 months.
recommended_checks.effort_hours: 3-6 (workflow YAML, caching, results summary; the test projects already exist)
recommended_checks.rationale_for_two_person_team: This is the zero-argument baseline: the projects already exist because ABP generated them, so the only work is CI wiring. It is also the fastest gate, so it should run first and fail fast. Deliberately no coverage gate here — Microsoft's own guidance is that "a high code coverage percentage isn't an indicator of success", and a percentage gate on 53k existing lines is exactly the kind of rule two people start bypassing.

recommended_checks.what_it_does: Fails the build if the EF Core model has changed without a corresponding migration, using Microsoft's own recommended pattern: an xUnit test asserting `context.Database.HasPendingModelChanges()` is false (or the `dotnet ef migrations has-pending-model-changes` CLI equivalent).
recommended_checks.tool: EF Core 10 CLI / DbContext API — `dotnet ef migrations has-pending-model-changes`, `context.Database.HasPendingModelChanges()`
recommended_checks.tool_maintained_evidence: First-party EF Core feature, added in EF Core 8.0 and documented on a page last updated 2026-08-11 (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/ef/core/managing-schemas/migrations/managing). Ships with the SDK — no third-party dependency to maintain.
recommended_checks.rationale_for_two_person_team: Highest value per hour of anything in this list. From EF Core 9 onward, Migrate() with pending model changes throws PendingModelChangesWarning at runtime — so a forgotten migration is a startup failure, and with database-per-tenant it is a startup failure repeated across 11 (headroom 33) databases at deploy time. One test file, no infrastructure, and Microsoft explicitly suggests writing it as a test.

recommended_checks.what_it_does: An HTTP-pipeline test project built on WebApplicationFactory/TestServer that deliberately does NOT call AddAlwaysAllowAuthorization(). For each externally reachable endpoint group it asserts: anonymous request returns 401 (or 200 only where anonymous access is intended — registration, login, password reset, upload); a caller in the wrong external role returns 403; the correct role returns 2xx. Includes tenant-resolution cases: a request with Host header for tenant A must not read data seeded for tenant B, and a request with an unknown/absent host must not silently resolve to the host (null-tenant) context.
recommended_checks.tool: Microsoft.AspNetCore.Mvc.Testing (WebApplicationFactory) + xUnit, layered over the ABP host project; ICurrentTenant.Change for seeding fixtures
recommended_checks.tool_maintained_evidence: Microsoft.AspNetCore.Mvc.Testing is first-party and ships with ASP.NET Core 10; the integration-testing guidance page carries an updated date of 2026-08-26 and an applies-to list that includes aspnetcore-10.0 and 11.0 (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/test/integration-tests).
recommended_checks.effort_hours: 20-32 initial (new project, factory that overrides tenancy + auth wiring, a token/role helper, first ~10 endpoint groups); then ~1 per new endpoint group
recommended_checks.rationale_for_two_person_team: This is the one thing on the list I would refuse to launch without, and it is the one thing the ABP template actively hides. ABP pre-wires AddAlwaysAllowAuthorization() into the startup template's integration tests, and ABP integration tests resolve application services from DI rather than over HTTP — so filters, model binding, routing and the multi-tenancy middleware never execute. Microsoft says the same thing from the other side: "A controller unit test avoids scenarios such as filters, routing, and model binding." On a portal where tenancy resolves from the Host header only and cross-tenant leakage is the stated top failure mode, no existing test in the solution can catch a tenancy or permission regression. Budget this as the single biggest item and cut something else — a table-driven [Theory] over (endpoint, role, expected status) keeps the marginal cost near zero afterwards. Maps to OWASP WSTG-ATHZ-02 for HIPAA documentation.

recommended_checks.what_it_does: Runs the migrations end-to-end against a real SQL Server container in CI, then executes a focused set of repository/query tests (read, write, update, delete plus every custom repository method and any raw SQL) against it. Uses transaction-rollback isolation for write tests per Microsoft's documented pattern.
recommended_checks.tool: GitHub Actions service container (mcr.microsoft.com/mssql/server, e.g. 2025-latest) + EF Core; Respawn only if transaction rollback proves insufficient. Testcontainers for .NET is the alternative if the team wants the same setup to run locally.
recommended_checks.tool_maintained_evidence: mcr.microsoft.com/mssql/server currently publishes 2025-latest and 2025-CU8-ubuntu-24.04 tags (https://mcr.microsoft.com/v2/mssql/server/tags/list). Testcontainers for .NET 4.14.0 published 2026-08-14 and Respawn 7.0.0 published 2025-11-30 (api.nuget.org registration indexes) — both released within 12 months. GitHub Actions service containers are documented and Linux-runner-only (https://docs.github.com/en/actions/tutorials/use-containerized-services/use-docker-service-containers).
recommended_checks.effort_hours: 12-20 initial; ~15 min per added repository test
recommended_checks.rationale_for_two_person_team: ABP's shipped EntityFrameworkCore.Tests run on SQLite in-memory, and Microsoft's EF Core team is explicit that this produces false results against SQL Server — most dangerously on case sensitivity (SQL Server default collation is case-insensitive, SQLite is case-sensitive), which is exactly how a duplicate-email or duplicate-username check passes in CI and fails in production. It also means migrations are never actually executed before deploy. Keep this suite small on purpose: Microsoft's own rule is "limit the use of integration tests to the most important infrastructure scenarios", which for this app means the migration run itself plus every custom repository method and anything with raw SQL or provider-specific EF.Functions. Prefer the GitHub Actions `services:` block over Testcontainers initially — it is ~10 lines of YAML versus a fixture abstraction to maintain. One line of infrastructure dependency, as permitted: whether you also get a pre-prod database to run these against is an infra decision outside this scope.

recommended_checks.what_it_does: Runs the Angular unit/component suite headlessly on every PR with `ng test --no-watch --code-coverage`, producing a coverage report artifact but not enforcing a threshold. Component tests run in jsdom, not a real browser.
recommended_checks.tool: Angular CLI 20.3.x. Stay on the shipped Karma/Jasmine setup for now; when the team upgrades past v20, switch to `@angular/build:unit-test` with runner "vitest" (which ABP's current template already uses).
recommended_checks.tool_maintained_evidence: Angular CLI 20.3.35 published 2026-08-26 (https://github.com/angular/angular-cli/releases). The `unit-test` builder in @angular/build@20.3.35 is labelled "[EXPERIMENTAL] Run application unit tests" with runner enum ["karma","vitest"] and optional peer vitest ^3.1.1 (verified by reading the published tarball). Karma itself is deprecated by its maintainers (https://github.com/karma-runner/karma) — hence the deliberate do-not-migrate-yet stance.
recommended_checks.effort_hours: 4-8 (CI wiring plus fixing whatever specs the template left broken)
recommended_checks.rationale_for_two_person_team: Cheap and it stops obvious breakage, but do not build a large Angular suite in the next quarter. Angular 20's LTS ends 2026-11-28 and the runner underneath these specs is deprecated, so specs written now are written twice. Thoughtworks puts in-memory component testing (jsdom) in Adopt and browser-based testing on the slow/flaky side of the ledger, so keep tests in jsdom. Concentrate the specs you do write on the four self-registration flows and any component that renders PHI, and let everything else wait for the Vitest migration.

recommended_checks.what_it_does: A hard-capped Playwright suite of 6-8 journeys run on PR to main and on deploy: register (each external role), login, password reset, document upload, view own record, and one negative cross-tenant journey (authenticate against tenant A's host, attempt to reach a tenant B resource, assert refusal). Uses getByRole/test-id locators and web-first assertions.
recommended_checks.tool: Playwright (@playwright/test for the Angular app, or Microsoft.Playwright from .NET if the team prefers one language)
recommended_checks.tool_maintained_evidence: @playwright/test 1.62.1 published 2026-07-30 (https://registry.npmjs.org/@playwright/test); Microsoft.Playwright 1.62.0 published 2026-08-11 (api.nuget.org). Best-practice guidance confirmed at https://playwright.dev/docs/best-practices — "Automated tests should verify that the application code works for the end users, and avoid relying on implementation details".
recommended_checks.effort_hours: 16-24 initial; treat the cap as a hard budget
recommended_checks.rationale_for_two_person_team: The hard cap is the recommendation. Google's published mix puts end-to-end at 5% and warns that value collapses as flakiness approaches 1%; Thoughtworks puts broad integration tests in Hold precisely because small teams cannot afford to debug them. Two SDE 1s with no QA and no DevOps will abandon a 40-test E2E suite within two months, and an abandoned suite is worse than none because it teaches the team to ignore red. Write the six journeys that are anonymous-reachable from the public internet, put a written rule in the repo that the suite may not exceed eight tests without deleting one, and quarantine (do not retry-loop) anything that flakes twice.

recommended_checks.what_it_does: Collects Coverlet/Cobertura output from backend-tests and Angular coverage from frontend-tests, merges, and posts a PR comment showing coverage of lines changed in that PR. Advisory only — it informs the reviewer, it does not block.
recommended_checks.tool: coverlet.collector + dotnet-reportgenerator-globaltool (ReportGenerator), rendered as a PR summary via the ReportGenerator GitHub Action or a markdown summary report
recommended_checks.tool_maintained_evidence: coverlet.collector 10.0.1 published 2026-05-18; dotnet-reportgenerator-globaltool 5.5.11 published 2026-07-27 (api.nuget.org registration indexes) — both within 12 months. Microsoft documents this exact pairing at https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/core/testing/unit-testing-code-coverage.
recommended_checks.rationale_for_two_person_team: Coverage on new code is the only coverage metric a credible source actually gates on — Sonar's default is ≥80.0% on new code, explicitly because it avoids "spending a lot of effort remediating old code". But start it advisory. Turn it into a required gate only after three months of data shows the team routinely clears the number without gaming it; flipping a gate on before then is how you get [ExcludeFromCodeCoverage] sprinkled through the domain layer. Note the alternative: SonarQube Cloud gives you this gate turnkey, but the repo is private, so that is a paid decision rather than a technical one.

recommended_checks.what_it_does: A weekly scheduled Stryker.NET run scoped to just the tenancy, authorization, and domain-invariant code paths — not the whole solution. Publishes an HTML report as an artifact for the team to read; no threshold enforced.
recommended_checks.tool: dotnet-stryker with a stryker-config.json restricting `mutate` to the relevant namespaces and excluding Migrations and generated files
recommended_checks.tool_maintained_evidence: dotnet-stryker 4.16.0 published 2026-07-03 (https://api.nuget.org/v3/registration5-gz-semver2/dotnet-stryker/index.json). Microsoft publishes first-party guidance for it at https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/core/testing/mutation-testing (updated 2026-04-03), including the config-file exclusion pattern.
recommended_checks.rationale_for_two_person_team: This answers the question coverage cannot: are the assertions in the tenancy and permission tests actually strong enough to fail when the logic is wrong. Scoped to a few namespaces it runs in minutes rather than hours, and Microsoft's own instruction is "Don't chase a 100% mutation score. Instead, focus on high risk or business critical areas." Weekly and advisory, read over coffee, never a gate — a mutation gate on a two-person team is a guaranteed bypass. Defer this until after authz-contract-tests exists; mutating code that has no tests tells you nothing you don't already know.

not_worth_it_here: Consumer-driven contract testing (Pact) between the Angular app and the .NET API. ABP already generates the TypeScript client proxies from the backend service signatures via `abp generate-proxy`. A CI step that regenerates the proxies and fails if `git diff` is non-empty gives you drift detection for roughly one hour of work; Pact would cost days and duplicate what the code generator already guarantees.

A whole-codebase coverage threshold (the classic '80% or the build fails'). Microsoft explicitly warns that "Setting an overly ambitious code coverage percentage goal can be counterproductive" and that a high percentage "doesn't imply high code quality". Applied retroactively to 53k lines of C# and 27k lines of TypeScript that were written without tests, this gate is unreachable, so it gets bypassed within a sprint — and the bypass habit then spreads to the gates that matter. Use new-code coverage advisory instead.

Broad integration tests that stand up SQL Server + Redis + MinIO + OpenIddict together on every PR. Thoughtworks places exactly this in Hold, defining it as tests "that require live versions of all run-time dependencies" and calling them "often fragile and unhelpful" because you cannot tell whether a failure came from your code, a version mismatch, or the environment. Two people cannot afford to triage that. Fake Redis and MinIO (ABP's own microservice guidance says "in the test environment, it's sufficient to use in-memory cache and in-memory event bus") and use a real database only.

Migrating the Angular suite from Karma/Jasmine to Vitest right now. It is genuinely the right destination — ABP's current template already ships Vitest, and Angular's default for new projects is Vitest — but on 20.3.x the `unit-test` builder is still labelled EXPERIMENTAL, the `refactor-jasmine-vitest` schematic is a v22 artifact that Angular itself calls experimental, and Angular's own migration page says "Migrating an existing project to Vitest is considered experimental." Do it as one deliberate task inside the v21/v22 upgrade, not as a separate project competing with the authorization tests.

Running the test suite once per tenant (an 11- or 33-way CI matrix). Tenant isolation in a database-per-tenant model is a property of connection-string resolution, not of per-tenant business logic. Two tenants plus one host-context case in the authz-contract-tests project proves the mechanism; eleven proves the same thing eleven times and multiplies your CI minutes and your flake surface by eleven.

Mutation testing or a mutation-score threshold as a merge gate. Even at Google scale this is a reporting tool, and Microsoft's own page says not to chase the score. As a required check on a two-person team it is a multi-hour PR wait for a signal nobody has time to act on.

Visual regression / screenshot-diff testing. Highest false-positive rate of any automated check, requires baseline curation every time a theme or ABP module updates, and this is an internal-facing LOB portal where a shifted button is not the failure mode anyone is worried about.

Load and performance tests as a merge gate. Performance budgets belong in a separate area, and a scheduling portal for eleven offices is not going to fall over on throughput before it falls over on a tenancy bug. Revisit after the first year of real traffic.

A formal test-plan / test-documentation regime (ISO/IEC 29119-style test specifications, traceability matrices, manual regression scripts). Real audit value exists, but for two SDE 1s it converts test-writing hours into document-writing hours. The cheaper equivalent: name the authz-contract-tests cases after their WSTG-ATHZ-02 objectives so the test names themselves are the traceability artifact.

Property-based testing (FsCheck / CsCheck) and fuzzing of the domain layer. High-quality technique, but it pays off in algorithmic or parsing-heavy code. A scheduling domain's invariants are better served by a handful of explicit [Theory] cases that a second developer can read in ten seconds.

Cross-browser E2E matrices. One Chromium project in Playwright. Adding Firefox and WebKit triples the runtime and the flake rate to defend against rendering differences that this application's user base will not encounter.
surprises: The ABP startup template ships integration tests with authorization switched off. `AddAlwaysAllowAuthorization()` is pre-wired into the test module's ConfigureServices — ABP's own docs say verbatim "This is already done for the startup template integration tests." So every green integration test in the solution today proves nothing whatsoever about whether a permission check exists, is correct, or was accidentally deleted. For an app that is about to let four external roles self-register over the public internet, this is the gap that matters most and it is invisible unless you go read ABP's Authorization page rather than its Testing page.

ABP's integration tests are not HTTP tests. `AbpIntegratedTest<T>` resolves application services straight out of the DI container. That means ASP.NET Core filters, model binding, routing and — decisively — ABP's multi-tenancy middleware never execute. Since tenancy on this system resolves from the Host header only, the mechanism that separates eleven offices' databases is literally not reachable from the test shape the framework provides. Microsoft states the same boundary from the other direction: "A controller unit test avoids scenarios such as filters, routing, and model binding."

Two first-party Microsoft doc sets give opposite answers on the same question, and both were updated in 2026. The ASP.NET Core integration-testing page (updated 2026-08-26) says "the SQLite provider is the recommended choice for in-memory testing" and "If a behavior can be tested using either a unit test or an integration test, choose the unit test." The EF Core testing pages (updated 2026-06-26) say "We recommend that developers have good test coverage of their application running against their actual production database system" and treat SQLite-as-a-fake as a trap that "tend[s] to eventually become problematic... even if they don't seem to be at the beginning." A team that reads only one page will build the wrong suite and have a Microsoft URL to justify it.

The SQLite/SQL Server divergence has a concrete, likely failure mode for this app. SQL Server's default collation is case-insensitive; SQLite is case-sensitive. A test asserting that a duplicate email or username is rejected can pass on SQLite and behave differently on SQL Server — and the direction of the error is the dangerous one for a registration endpoint open to anonymous traffic. Microsoft names this exact example: "This can make your tests pass against SQLite where they would fail against SQL Server (or vice versa)."

Migrations are never executed by ABP's test suite. The test database is created and seeded, not migrated. With database-per-tenant across 11 databases (headroom 33), the first execution of a new migration against SQL Server happens at deploy, against production data, eleven times. Meanwhile EF Core hands you the cheap half of the fix for free: Microsoft's Managing Migrations page says of `HasPendingModelChanges()`, verbatim, "This can be used to write a unit test that fails when you forget to add a migration" — and from EF Core 9, calling Migrate() with pending model changes throws at runtime rather than warning.

Angular 20 is about three months from end of support. Per Angular's own release policy page, v20 was released 2025-05-28, active support ended 2025-11-19, and LTS ends 2026-11-28. This is not a test-strategy fact on its face, but it determines the answer: any large Karma/Jasmine suite written this quarter is written against a runner Angular has already replaced, on a version that stops receiving security patches this year. It is the reason to cap frontend test investment rather than expand it.

Karma's own stated support horizon is anchored to an event that never happened. The karma-runner README says "Karma is deprecated and is not accepting new features or general bug fixes" and that critical security fixes continue "until 12 months after Angular CLI's Web Test Runner support is marked stable." Angular evaluated Web Test Runner and shipped Vitest instead — so the clock on Karma's security support has no defined start. Angular's own docs meanwhile still say "Karma is still a supported and widely used test runner." Two first-party sources, no clear answer.

The Vitest escape hatch already exists in 20.3.x, and the obvious way to reach for it breaks. `@angular/build@20.3.35` (published 2026-08-26) contains a builder described verbatim as "[EXPERIMENTAL] Run application unit tests" whose runner enum is exactly ["karma","vitest"], and its optional peer dependency is `vitest ^3.1.1`. Installing Vitest today gets you 4.1.11 (published 2026-08-18), which does not satisfy that range. A team that follows a 2026 blog post about 'Angular + Vitest' without checking the peer range spends an afternoon on an unexplained failure. The same builder schema, incidentally, already supports `setupFiles` and defaults `watch` to false in non-TTY environments — both limitations that early-v20 write-ups claim are missing.

The 70/20/10 test-mix number that everyone quotes is not the number Google publishes. Software Engineering at Google states "80% of our tests being narrow-scoped unit tests... 15% medium-scoped integration tests... and 5% end-to-end tests." The 70/20/10 figure comes from the 2010-era blog framing and was, by the account in circulation, roughly made up. Citing 70/20/10 pushes a team to build twice the integration layer the evidence supports — which for a two-person team is the difference between a suite they maintain and one they abandon.

Flakiness has a published tolerance and it is far tighter than intuition. Software Engineering at Google: "as you approach 1% flakiness, the tests begin to lose value"; Google runs at ~0.15% and still sees "thousands of flakes every day." A two-person team with an eight-test E2E suite gets exactly zero flaky-test budget in practice. This is the concrete argument for capping E2E and for quarantining rather than retrying — retry loops hide the 1% until it is 10%.

`dotnet test` semantics changed in the .NET 10 SDK. Microsoft.Testing.Platform is selected through a `global.json` `"test": {"runner": "Microsoft.Testing.Platform"}` block, `--settings`/runsettings is superseded by `testconfig.json`, and — the one that bites — a test assembly containing zero tests now fails with exit code 8, where VSTest exited 0. A CI job that is green today can turn red on an SDK bump for a reason that has nothing to do with the code. (Partly verified: I confirmed the global.json snippet on the .NET Blog directly; the exit-code and testconfig.json details came from search summaries of the Learn migration guide, which I did not open.)

The industry's most-cited radar has moved in the opposite direction from small-team instinct. Thoughtworks puts 'broad integration tests' in Hold and in-memory 'component testing' (jsdom) in Adopt. A team with no QA reasons 'we can't test manually, so test end-to-end.' The published position is the reverse: push toward fast in-memory component tests and away from anything requiring live run-time dependencies.

In database-per-tenant, ABP's multi-tenancy query filter gives you no protection at all — and ABP says so. `IMultiTenant` filtering is a shared-database mechanism; ABP's docs note "this approach won't work if your tenants have separate databases since there is no built-in way to query from multiple database in a single database query." Isolation is entirely a function of tenant resolution feeding connection-string selection. So the test that matters is not 'does the filter work' but 'does a request bearing tenant A's Host header ever obtain tenant B's connection string, and what happens when the host is unrecognised' — including the case where an unresolved tenant silently falls back to the host (null-tenant) context.

ABP quietly recommends the opposite of Microsoft on the unit-vs-integration question. ABP's docs say integration tests are "Easier to write since you don't work to establish mocking and dealing with the dependencies" and its unit-test page nudges you away from mocking ("It gets harder to setup the test objects and mock all the dependencies. See the Integration Tests section"). Microsoft says choose the unit test whenever either would do. Following ABP's grain gets you a suite that is integration-heavy — which is defensible on its own, except that ABP's integration tests are the ones with authorization disabled and no HTTP pipeline. The two facts compound.

ABP's Angular testing modules also grant all permissions by default. `CoreTestingModule.withConfig()` swaps `PermissionService` for a `MockPermissionService` that grants every policy. So the frontend mirror of the backend problem exists too: a component test cannot tell you whether a permission-gated element is correctly hidden from a role that should not see it. If any UI element gates PHI visibility by permission, that assertion has to be written against the real service or asserted in the E2E layer.
disagreements: Microsoft vs Microsoft on the test database. The ASP.NET Core integration-testing page (learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/test/integration-tests, updated 2026-08-26) recommends SQLite in-memory: "the SQLite provider is the recommended choice for in-memory testing." The EF Core testing pages (learn.microsoft.com/en-us/ef/core/testing/choosing-a-testing-strategy, updated 2026-06-26) recommend the opposite: "We recommend that developers have good test coverage of their application running against their actual production database system", and describe SQLite-as-fake limitations that "tend to eventually become problematic when testing EF Core applications, even if they don't seem to be at the beginning." Both are first-party, both current. I lean to the EF Core team here because they own the divergence and because SQL Server collation behaviour is directly load-bearing for a registration endpoint — but the disagreement is real and a reviewer can cite either page.

Microsoft vs ABP on which test type is the default. Microsoft: "If a behavior can be tested using either a unit test or an integration test, choose the unit test" and "limit the use of integration tests to the most important infrastructure scenarios." ABP: integration tests are "Easier to write since you don't work to establish mocking" and run "much closer to the real application test", with the caveat "Write unit or integration test where it is necessary and you find effective to write and maintain it." ABP's template embodies its preference by giving you five layer-mapped projects with an integration harness ready to go.

Pyramid vs trophy. The pyramid position has two strong sources: Google's book (80/15/5) and Fowler/Vocke ("the more high-level you get the fewer tests you should have"). The testing trophy — 'write tests, not too many, mostly integration' — originates in blog writing (Kent C. Dodds, Guillermo Rauch) and I found no primary-source empirical study supporting it over the pyramid; the 2025-26 commentary I saw was secondary (consultancy blogs) and converged on 'neither shape is universally correct; aim testing effort where your bugs come from.' Thoughtworks lands in between: component testing in Adopt (a trophy-ish middle layer) but broad integration tests in Hold (anti-trophy). I am labelling the trophy a secondary-source position, not an evidenced one.

The Google mix itself is quoted two ways. Software Engineering at Google (the book) states 80% small / 15% medium / 5% large. The widely-repeated 70/20/10 traces to Google's 2010-era blog-and-comment era; the Test Sizes post I opened gives runtime targets (<60s / <300s / <900s) but no percentage split at all, and secondary accounts of the 70/20/10 figure say the numbers were "essentially pulled out of a hat." Use 80/15/5 and cite the book.

Karma's status. karma-runner/karma's own README: "Karma is deprecated and is not accepting new features or general bug fixes." Angular's current Karma guide: "While Vitest is the default test runner for new Angular projects, Karma is still a supported and widely used test runner." Both first-party to their respective projects. Compounding it, Karma's stated security-support window runs "until 12 months after Angular CLI's Web Test Runner support is marked stable" — a milestone Angular abandoned in favour of Vitest, so the end date is undefined.

Coverage thresholds. Sonar ships a default gate of ≥80.0% coverage on new code and ≤3.0% duplication on new code. Microsoft names no number at all and warns against ambitious targets ("A high code coverage percentage isn't an indicator of success"). Angular's v20 coverage page shows 80/80/80/80 but frames it as an illustration ("suppose you want the code base to have a minimum of 80%"), not a recommendation. Google's book warns coverage "only measures that a line was invoked, not what happened as a result" and that targets get treated "like a ceiling." These reconcile only if you distinguish new-code coverage (where 80% is a defensible default) from whole-codebase coverage (where no credible source names a number).

material_errors: Claim 17: the Thoughtworks Radar volume number is wrong. The 'Broad integration tests' blip page shows 'Published: Apr 03, 2024' and blipUpdatedDate 'Apr 03, 2024' — the April 2024 edition is Volume 30, not Volume 34. 'Component testing' (Adopt) is 'Published: Oct 23, 2024' (Vol 31). The blip pages do not print volume numbers at all, so 'Vol 34' is unsupported by the cited source and is a superseded/incorrect version label.

Claim 19: the cited ABP multi-tenancy page does NOT say the IMultiTenant filter provides no cross-tenant protection under database-per-tenant. It says the opposite about the filter in general ('ABP automatically filters entities for the current tenant', 'a tenant can not access to data of another tenant by default'). The sentence the claim leans on — 'this approach won't work if your tenants have separate databases' — refers to the preceding example of DISABLING the filter (_dataFilter.Disable<IMultiTenant>()) to query across tenants, not to the filter's protective effect. The architectural conclusion is an inference the page does not state.

Claim 21: the cited devblog supports only the global.json snippet. It contains nothing about testconfig.json replacing runsettings, and nothing about zero-test assemblies failing or exit code 8. Both are documented elsewhere, and the exit-code-8 framing is misleading: 'test session ran zero tests' = exit code 8 is a Microsoft.Testing.Platform behavior (documented on the MTP troubleshooting page), not a .NET 10 SDK change; and .runsettings is not wholesale 'replaced' — the docs give a partial mapping table with several settings moving to CLI options instead, and VSTest mode still honors runsettings.

Claim 11: the conclusion 'Vitest 4.x is not compatible with Angular 20.3' overstates what the registry shows. @angular/build 20.3.35 declares vitest ^3.1.1 as an OPTIONAL peer dependency — that makes Vitest 4.x an undeclared/unsupported combination (npm peer warning or ERESOLVE), not a demonstrated runtime incompatibility. Also, the '[EXPERIMENTAL] Run application unit tests' description and the runner enum ["karma","vitest"] are in the package's builders.json / unit-test schema.json, not in the cited registry metadata document.

results.claim: In ABP database-per-tenant, the IMultiTenant global query filter provides no cross-tenant protection; isolation comes entirely from connection-string resolution driven by ICurrentTenant
results.evidence_quote: ABP automatically filters entities for the current tenant when you query from database ... Note that this approach won't work if your tenants have separate databases since there is no built-in way to query from multiple database in a single database query. You should handle it yourself if you need it.
results.correction: The page does not state this. "This approach" in the quoted note refers to DISABLING the IMultiTenant filter (_dataFilter.Disable<IMultiTenant>()) in order to query across tenants — i.e. cross-tenant querying is what breaks under separate databases, not the filter's protection. Supportable restatement: "ABP applies an automatic IMultiTenant query filter so a tenant cannot read another tenant's rows by default; under database-per-tenant the effective boundary is which connection string ICurrentTenant resolves, and ABP provides no built-in way to query across tenant databases in one query." Do not assert "the filter provides no protection" from this page.

Corrected and re-sourced: (a) MTP mode of dotnet test is new in the .NET 10 SDK and enabled by that global.json block — https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/core/testing/unit-testing-with-dotnet-test; (b) .runsettings is not simply "replaced": MTP uses [appname].testconfig.json and the docs give a partial migration mapping in which several runsettings features (loggers, blame/dump, coverage, MaxCpuCount) map to CLI options rather than JSON — https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/core/testing/microsoft-testing-platform-config; VSTest mode still consumes runsettings; (c) exit code 8 = "the test session ran zero tests" is a Microsoft.Testing.Platform exit code, not a .NET 10 SDK behavior change — https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/core/testing/microsoft-testing-platform-troubleshooting — and it can be suppressed with --ignore-exit-code 8.
