research.area: End-to-end browser testing (2026 standard) — tool selection, test count, OIDC auth patterns, GitHub Actions execution, merge-gate policy, and in-test accessibility assertions
research.standard_summary: In 2026 the defensible default for a new E2E suite on an Angular SPA is Playwright (@playwright/test 1.62.1, published 2026-07-30), and the margin over Cypress has widened rather than narrowed: 57.9M weekly npm downloads vs 7.6M, free built-in sharding vs sharding that Cypress's own GitHub Actions doc gates behind Cypress Cloud, and native cross-origin navigation vs Cypress's mandatory cy.origin() wrapper — which matters here because ABP's Angular client redirects to a separate OpenIddict auth-server host for the authorization-code+PKCE flow. Cypress is emphatically not dead (15.21.1, 2026-08-25) and Angular lists it first among five integrated e2e packages, but nothing about it wins on this app's specific shape. On count, no authority gives an absolute number: Google's canonical guidance is a 70/20/10 unit/integration/E2E mix, Fowler says "reduce the number of end-to-end tests to a bare minimum" around "one or two more crucial user journeys," and Microsoft Learn goes further — "Discourage the use of UI tests, because they tend to be unreliable." The binding constraint for two developers is DORA's "feedback from automated tests in less than ten minutes," which on a private-repo GitHub runner (2 vCPU / 8 GB, half the public-repo machine) caps a PR gate at roughly 8-14 tests; everything else belongs in a nightly job. Authentication follows Playwright's documented setup-project + storageState + dependencies pattern, never the OAuth password grant, which RFC 9700 (BCP 240) §2.4 now prohibits outright: "The resource owner password credentials grant MUST NOT be used." Accessibility assertions inside E2E are a first-party, actively maintained pattern — Playwright's own accessibility-testing doc is built on @axe-core/playwright (4.13.0, published 2026-08-11, 9.5M weekly downloads).

standards.claim: Playwright is actively maintained and is the current-generation default E2E runner: @playwright/test stable is 1.62.1, published 2026-07-30, with a steady ~5-6 week stable cadence through 2026 (1.59.0 2026-04-01, 1.60.0 2026-05-11, 1.61.0 2026-06-15, 1.62.0 2026-07-24) and nightly 1.63.0-alpha builds still shipping as of 2026-08-28.
standards.threshold: @playwright/test 1.62.1 (2026-07-30); next alpha 1.63.0-alpha-2026-08-28
standards.source_name: npm registry API (registry.npmjs.org, first-party npm metadata)
standards.notes: Fetched the full packument and sorted by publish time. Cross-checked against playwright.dev/docs/release-notes, whose newest documented release is Version 1.62 (new component-testing stories/galleries model, AbortSignal on operations, WebP screenshots, Reporter.preprocess(), retryStrategy). The GitHub API was blocked by this session's proxy, so release dates come from npm rather than GitHub Releases.

standards.claim: Cypress is also actively maintained — 15.21.1 published 2026-08-25, on a roughly two-week cadence (15.17.0 2026-06-09 through 15.21.1 2026-08-25) — but adoption has diverged sharply: @playwright/test draws 57,911,488 weekly npm downloads and the playwright package 86,996,936, against 7,569,177 for cypress, for the week 2026-08-21 to 2026-08-27.
standards.threshold: cypress 15.21.1 (2026-08-25); 57.9M vs 7.6M weekly downloads, week ending 2026-08-27
standards.source_name: npm registry API + npm downloads API (api.npmjs.org, first-party)
standards.notes: Pulled both packuments and the weekly download counts directly from npm's own APIs rather than relying on the 2026 comparison blog posts, which are secondary and disagree with each other (one claimed 33M weekly for Playwright, another 78M). Do not read the download gap as a quality verdict — Playwright's number is inflated by transitive use as a scraping/automation library. The maintenance evidence is what matters: both tools clear the 12-month bar comfortably.

standards.claim: Angular's official CLI documentation lists exactly five integrated E2E packages, offered by `ng e2e` when no e2e target exists: Cypress (ng add @cypress/schematic), Nightwatch (ng add @nightwatch/schematics), WebdriverIO (ng add @wdio/schematics), Playwright (ng add playwright-ng-schematics), Puppeteer (ng add @puppeteer/ng-schematics). Protractor is not mentioned anywhere on the page. Angular states there is nothing special about any of them: "The ng e2e command is really just running the e2e builder under the hood."
standards.threshold: 5 packages; ng e2e is a thin builder wrapper — no Angular-specific E2E coupling
standards.source_name: Angular (angular.dev) — CLI End-to-End Testing
standards.notes: Because ng e2e is just a builder shim, the Angular schematic is optional for Playwright. That matters: playwright-ng-schematics is a community package (not Microsoft), its current 22.1.0 pins @angular-devkit/core ^22.0.0, and the last release on the Angular-20 line was 20.0.2 on 2025-12-11. On Angular 20.3.19 you should skip the schematic and run `yarn create playwright` — Playwright's own installer, which also offers to write the GitHub Actions workflow. By contrast Cypress's @cypress/schematic 6.0.0 shipped 2026-08-26 and @cypress/angular 5.0.0 the same day, so Cypress's Angular integration is the better-maintained one; it just isn't needed for E2E.

standards.claim: Playwright's official GitHub Actions CI guidance is a single ubuntu-latest job with `timeout-minutes: 60`, actions/checkout@v6, actions/setup-node@v6 at `node-version: lts/*`, `npm ci`, `npx playwright install --with-deps`, `npx playwright test`, and actions/upload-artifact@v5 uploading `playwright-report/` with `retention-days: 30` under `if: ${{ !cancelled() }}`. A container variant uses `image: mcr.microsoft.com/playwright:v1.62.0-noble` with `options: --user 1001`.
standards.threshold: timeout-minutes: 60; checkout@v6; setup-node@v6; upload-artifact@v5; retention-days: 30; container mcr.microsoft.com/playwright:v1.62.0-noble
standards.source_name: Playwright — Continuous Integration
standards.notes: Fetched and text-stripped the page directly to read the literal YAML rather than trusting a summariser. The same page documents `--only-changed=origin/$GITHUB_BASE_REF` as a fail-fast preliminary run on pull requests, with the explicit caveat that it is a heuristic and "it's important that you always run the full test suite after the preliminary test run." Playwright's system requirements are Node.js latest 22.x, 24.x or 26.x — check this against whatever Node the Angular 20 build pins.

standards.claim: Playwright's own documentation contradicts itself on CI worker count. /docs/ci states: "We recommend setting workers to '1' in CI environments to prioritize stability and reproducibility" with `workers: process.env.CI ? 1 : undefined`. /docs/test-parallel shows `workers: process.env.CI ? 2 : undefined` under "Limit the number of workers on CI, use default locally." The generated default config in /docs/test-configuration uses 1.
standards.threshold: workers: process.env.CI ? 1 : undefined (CI doc + generated config) vs ? 2 : undefined (parallelism doc)
standards.source_name: Playwright — Continuous Integration / Parallelism / Configuration
standards.notes: I opened all three pages and read the literal code blocks. Resolve it in favour of 1 for this app: GitHub-hosted ubuntu-latest is 2 vCPU / 8 GB for private repositories (4 vCPU / 16 GB only for public), and that budget is already shared with a .NET 10 API, SQL Server, Redis and MinIO. `workers` also accepts a percentage of logical cores, e.g. '50%'. Note separately that every Playwright benchmark blog post you will read assumes the public-repo runner.

standards.claim: Playwright's generated default configuration encodes the CI hardening defaults: `fullyParallel: true`, `forbidOnly: !!process.env.CI`, `retries: process.env.CI ? 2 : 0`, `workers: process.env.CI ? 1 : undefined`, `use.trace: 'on-first-retry'`. Per-test timeout defaults to 30000 ms and web-first `expect()` assertions to 5000 ms.
standards.threshold: retries 2 on CI, 0 locally; trace 'on-first-retry'; test timeout 30000 ms; expect timeout 5000 ms
standards.source_name: Playwright — Configuration
standards.notes: Retries plus trace-on-first-retry is the whole flakiness strategy for a small team: the HTML reporter categorises results as passed / flaky (failed then passed on retry) / failed, so 'flaky' becomes a first-class signal you can triage weekly without building any tooling. `forbidOnly` on CI stops a stray `test.only` from silently reducing your gate to one test — a failure mode that is invisible in a green check.

standards.claim: Playwright 1.62 added `testConfig.retryStrategy`. The default 'immediate' retries a failed test as soon as a worker is free; 'isolated' "runs all retries at the end, one by one in a single worker, to minimize interference with the rest of the suite."
standards.threshold: retryStrategy: 'isolated' — new in Playwright 1.62 (2026-07-24)
standards.source_name: Playwright — Release notes, Version 1.62
standards.notes: This is the single highest-leverage flakiness knob for a resource-starved runner, and it is two months old, so it appears in no tutorial. On a 2 vCPU box shared with SQL Server, most flakes are contention, not app bugs; retrying in an otherwise idle worker at the end of the run converts a large share of them into passes without any test changes. Combine with `retries: 2`.

standards.claim: Playwright's documented authentication pattern is a `setup` project matched by `testMatch: /.*\.setup\.ts/` that authenticates once and calls `page.context().storageState({ path: authFile })`, with test projects declaring `dependencies: ['setup']` and `use.storageState: 'playwright/.auth/user.json'`. The docs call this "the recommended approach for tests without server-side state", require the auth directory be gitignored, and warn: "The browser state file may contain sensitive cookies and headers that could be used to impersonate you or your test account. We strongly discourage checking them into private or public repositories." For tests that mutate shared server state, the documented pattern is one account per parallel worker keyed on `testInfo.parallelIndex`; API-based auth uses `APIRequestContext` and `request.storageState({ path: authFile })`.
standards.threshold: setup project + storageState + testProject.dependencies; playwright/.auth in .gitignore; per-worker accounts via testInfo.parallelIndex when state is mutated
standards.source_name: Playwright — Authentication
standards.notes: For an ABP booking wizard that writes appointments, you are in the state-mutating case: either use the per-worker account fixture or keep workers at 1 on CI (recommended here — it solves both problems at once). The docs also warn that UI Mode does not run the setup project by default, so local runs go stale until you manually re-run auth.setup.ts.

standards.claim: Playwright's saved authentication state covers cookies, local storage, IndexedDB and WebAuthn passkeys, but NOT sessionStorage: "Playwright does not provide API to persist session storage" — the docs give a manual `page.evaluate(() => JSON.stringify(sessionStorage))` save plus `context.addInitScript()` restore snippet instead.
standards.threshold: storageState = cookies + localStorage + IndexedDB + credentials; sessionStorage excluded, manual workaround only
standards.source_name: Playwright — Authentication, "Session storage" section
standards.notes: Load-bearing for this stack specifically. ABP's Angular client uses angular-oauth2-oidc, whose default OAuthStorage implementation is sessionStorage (see abpframework/abp issue #13073, which is titled exactly that; ABP also ships an AbpLocalStorageService alternative). If your app is on the sessionStorage default, the canonical setup-project pattern will hand your tests a browser holding the auth cookie but no access token, and the app will look logged-out or silently re-run the code flow. Verify OAuthStorage in your own Angular providers before writing a single test — 10 minutes now, a lost day later. I could not confirm ABP 10.0.2's shipped default from first-party docs, so treat that half as unverified.

standards.claim: The OAuth 2.0 resource owner password credentials (ROPC / password) grant is prohibited by current IETF Best Current Practice. RFC 9700, "Best Current Practice for OAuth 2.0 Security" (BCP 240, January 2025), §2.4: "The resource owner password credentials grant [RFC6749] MUST NOT be used." §2.1.2 additionally states clients "SHOULD NOT use the implicit grant (response type token)."
standards.threshold: RFC 9700 / BCP 240 §2.4 — MUST NOT (normative prohibition), published January 2025
standards.source_name: IETF — RFC 9700, Best Current Practice for OAuth 2.0 Security
standards.notes: This kills the most common E2E auth shortcut. The usual trick is to have the setup project POST grant_type=password to /connect/token and skip the browser login entirely. Doing that requires leaving the password flow enabled on your OpenIddict server, which becomes an unthrottled internet-facing credential-stuffing endpoint the day you leave the office LAN. OpenIddict enables authorization code, hybrid, implicit, password, client credentials, refresh token, device and token exchange flows only when explicitly opted in — confirm the password flow is off in your production configuration, and drive login through the real authorization-code+PKCE flow once in the setup project instead.

standards.claim: Playwright cannot override the HTTP Host header from a browser context. The Route API documentation warns: "Some request headers are forbidden and cannot be overridden (for example, Cookie, Host, Content-Length and others...). If an override is provided for a forbidden header, it will be ignored and the original request header will be used." `testOptions.extraHTTPHeaders` (added v1.10) sets additional headers on every request but is subject to the same browser restriction.
standards.threshold: Host is a forbidden request header — overrides silently ignored, no error raised
standards.source_name: Playwright — API: class Route (route.continue / route.fallback)
standards.notes: This is the most consequential finding in this area for your app. Tenancy resolves from the Host header only, so a naive cross-tenant isolation test that tries to spoof Host via extraHTTPHeaders will be silently ignored, hit the default tenant, and PASS — a false green on your highest-consequence failure mode. The only correct approach is real distinct hostnames: add one /etc/hosts line per test tenant in the workflow (`echo '127.0.0.1 tenant-a.test tenant-b.test' | sudo tee -a /etc/hosts`) and define one Playwright project per tenant with its own `use.baseURL`. Cross-referenced against MDN's forbidden-header-name glossary, which Playwright's warning links to.

standards.claim: Cypress requires `cy.origin()` to drive any cross-origin login and gates CI parallelization behind its paid cloud. The cross-origin doc states: "With the exception of cy.origin, Cypress requires that the URLs navigated to have the same origin for the entirety of a single test... Cypress commands will timeout after the navigation and will eventually error." The GitHub Actions doc states: "Using parallelization with the Cypress GitHub Action requires setting up recording to Cypress Cloud." Playwright's `--shard=x/y` is built in and free.
standards.threshold: cy.origin() mandatory for cross-origin; Cypress Cloud account required for GH Actions parallelization; Playwright --shard=x/y free
standards.source_name: Cypress — Cross origin testing / GitHub Actions
standards.notes: Decisive for this app. ABP's Angular client performs an authorization-code+PKCE redirect to a separate OpenIddict auth-server host rendering an MVC/Razor Pages login — cross-origin by construction, so every authenticated Cypress test pays the cy.origin tax. Cypress additionally documents that "Navigating from HTTPS to HTTP will error" and "Cypress requires that the URLs navigated to have the same port", both of which bite in a local multi-host setup. None of this makes Cypress unusable; it makes Playwright the lower-friction choice for exactly your shape.

standards.claim: No credible source gives an absolute E2E test count; three primary sources converge on 'as few as possible.' Google's testing blog recommends a 70/20/10 unit/integration/end-to-end mix. Martin Fowler's Practical Test Pyramid: "Due to their high maintenance cost you should aim to reduce the number of end-to-end tests to a bare minimum" and "Maybe you'll find one or two more crucial user journeys that you can translate into end-to-end tests." Microsoft Learn goes furthest: "Discourage the use of UI tests, because they tend to be unreliable."
standards.threshold: 70/20/10 (Google); "bare minimum" / "one or two more crucial user journeys" (Fowler); "discourage the use of UI tests" (Microsoft)
standards.source_name: Google Testing Blog — Just Say No to More End-to-End Tests
standards.notes: Fowler's stated reason is the one that will actually bite two people: "High maintenance effort and lots of false positives will slow you down and cause you to lose trust in your tests, sooner rather than later." The 70/20/10 ratio is a proportion, not a count — it only yields a number once you know your unit-test total, which for a greenfield suite you don't. Use the time budget in the next entry as the real cap.

standards.claim: DORA's test-automation capability sets the binding time budget: "Developers should be able to get feedback from automated tests in less than ten minutes both on local workstations and from the continuous integration system", "Tests should be reliable: that is, when the tests pass we should be confident the software is releasable, and test failures should indicate a real defect", and "don't tolerate flaky tests." Microsoft Learn's L0-L4 taxonomy meanwhile expects "a pull request automatically fails if the L3 test run fails", where L3 = functional tests against a deployed service.
standards.threshold: < 10 minutes for CI test feedback (DORA); PR fails on L3 failure (Microsoft Learn)
standards.source_name: DORA — Test automation capability
standards.notes: These two collide for this app: a full E2E run that boots SQL Server, migrates a tenant database, builds Angular 20 and drives a nine-step wizard cannot both gate every PR and finish in ten minutes on a 2 vCPU runner. Resolve by gating a smoke subset (L3-lite) and pushing the rest nightly. Microsoft Learn also gives the specific L2 isolation rule that governs your auth setup: legacy tests calling external auth providers violate isolation and break on provider flakiness — "Consider preventing these issues by investing in identity support within the test framework", which is precisely Playwright's setup-project pattern.

standards.claim: Flakiness is a permanent operating cost, not a defect to eliminate once. Google reports "a continual rate of about 1.5% of all test runs reporting a 'flaky' result", "Almost 16% of our tests have some level of flakiness associated with them", and "about 84% of the transitions we observe from pass to fail involve a flaky test." Google's documented mitigations are re-running only failing tests, marking a test flaky so it reports failure only after 3 consecutive failures, and automated quarantine: "if the flakiness is too high, it automatically quarantines the test... removes the test from the critical path and files a bug."
standards.threshold: 1.5% of test runs flaky; ~16% of tests have some flakiness; 84% of pass→fail transitions are flakes
standards.source_name: Google Testing Blog — Flaky Tests at Google and How We Mitigate Them
standards.notes: Fetched the page and read the numbers in the original text — the figures are in the article body, not a secondary summary. Calibration point for two SDE 1s: these rates come from Google's engineers and infrastructure, so 'we'll just write non-flaky tests' is not a plan. The cheap version of quarantine for a two-person team is `test.fixme()` plus a line in a markdown file, reviewed once a month. Google's own warning against the 3-strikes rule applies: it "encourages developers to ignore flakiness in their own tests."

standards.claim: Accessibility assertions inside Playwright are a first-party, actively maintained pattern. Playwright's own accessibility-testing guide is written against @axe-core/playwright, which is at 4.13.0 published 2026-08-11 (monorepo release v4.13.0, 11 August), MPL-2.0, peer-dependency `playwright-core >= 1.0.0`, 9,519,206 weekly downloads. The documented WCAG scoping call is `new AxeBuilder({ page }).withTags(['wcag2a','wcag2aa','wcag21a','wcag21aa']).analyze()` asserted with `expect(results.violations).toEqual([])`, with `.include()`, `.exclude()` and `.disableRules()` for known issues. axe-core also defines a `wcag22aa` tag for WCAG 2.2 Level AA.
standards.threshold: @axe-core/playwright 4.13.0 (2026-08-11); tags wcag2a, wcag2aa, wcag21a, wcag21aa, wcag22aa; assert violations == []
standards.source_name: Playwright — Accessibility testing
standards.notes: Two traps. First, the official Playwright snippet omits `wcag22aa`, so copy-pasting it silently skips every WCAG 2.2 rule even though WCAG 2.2 has been a W3C Recommendation since 12 December 2024 — add it. Second, Deque's own study across 2,000+ audits, 13,000+ pages and ~300,000 issues found automated testing "completely covered" 57 percent of accessibility issues, so a green axe run is not a WCAG 2.2 AA conformance claim; Playwright's doc says the same ("many accessibility problems can only be discovered through manual testing"). The Cypress equivalent, cypress-axe, was last published 1.7.0 on 2025-08-29 — just inside 12 months, but a year behind the axe-core release line.

standards.claim: GitHub Actions economics constrain E2E frequency for a private repo. Included minutes per month: GitHub Free 2,000, Pro 3,000, Free for organizations 2,000, Team 3,000, Enterprise Cloud 50,000. Linux 2-core (x64) bills at $0.006/minute beyond quota. Artifact storage is 500 MB (Free) / 2 GB (Team) and is shared with GitHub Packages. Standard runners are free only for public repositories. GitHub-hosted ubuntu-latest is 2 CPU / 8 GB / 14 GB SSD for private repositories versus 4 CPU / 16 GB for public, both on ubuntu-24.04.
standards.threshold: 2,000 min (Free) / 3,000 (Pro, Team) private-repo minutes; $0.006/min Linux 2-core; private ubuntu-latest = 2 vCPU / 8 GB
standards.source_name: GitHub Docs — About billing for GitHub Actions
standards.notes: Do the arithmetic before you design the gate. A run that boots SQL Server, migrates a tenant DB, builds Angular 20 and drives ~12 tests is realistically 12-18 minutes on that runner. At 120 runs/month that is ~1,800 minutes — most of a Team plan, before the build, unit-test and static-analysis jobs. Mitigations that cost nothing: trigger on `pull_request` only (not `push`), and add `concurrency: { group: ${{ github.ref }}, cancel-in-progress: true }`, which GitHub documents as cancelling in-progress runs on the same ref. Also note Playwright reports and traces land in that 500 MB / 2 GB artifact allowance, so keep `retention-days` low and upload only on failure.

standards.claim: Playwright explicitly advises against caching browser binaries in CI: "Caching browser binaries is not recommended, since the amount of time it takes to restore the cache is comparable to the time it takes to download the binaries. Especially under Linux, operating system dependencies need to be installed, which are not cacheable." Browsers occupy a few hundred MB each (~281 MB chromium, ~187 MB firefox, ~180 MB webkit).
standards.threshold: Do not cache ms-playwright; if you must, key the cache on a hash of the Playwright version
standards.source_name: Playwright — Continuous Integration, "Caching browsers"
standards.notes: Directly contradicts the standard CI-optimization advice in almost every blog post, and it is worth obeying because a stale browser cache produces failures that look like app bugs. The supported alternative if you want to skip the download is the pinned container image mcr.microsoft.com/playwright:v1.62.0-noble. Install only the browser you gate on — `npx playwright install --with-deps chromium` — rather than all three.

standards.claim: Playwright ships first-party AI test-authoring agents: planner, generator and healer, installed with `npx playwright init-agents --loop=claude` (also vscode, codex, opencode). The planner "explores the app and produces a Markdown test plan", the generator "transforms the Markdown plan into the Playwright Test files", and the healer "executes the test suite and automatically repairs failing tests." The docs state agent definitions "should be regenerated whenever Playwright is updated."
standards.threshold: npx playwright init-agents --loop=<vscode|claude|codex|opencode>; three agents (planner, generator, healer)
standards.source_name: Playwright — Playwright Test Agents
standards.notes: Relevant precisely because you have zero E2E tests and a nine-step wizard that exists only in someone's head. The planner takes an optional seed test that sets up fixtures and global setup, so you write the auth setup project by hand once (which you must, given the OIDC and Host-header specifics above) and let the planner explore the wizard from an authenticated state. Treat generated tests as drafts to review, not output to trust — but for a first suite this is the cheapest entry point available and it is a Microsoft-maintained feature, not a third-party add-on.

recommended_checks.what_it_does: Runs 8-12 Playwright specs against a locally composed stack (SQL Server + .NET API + built Angular app started via Playwright's `webServer` option) on every pull request to main. Chromium only, `workers: 1`, `retries: 2`, `retryStrategy: 'isolated'`, `trace: 'on-first-retry'`, `forbidOnly: true`. Two Playwright projects — tenant-a and tenant-b — each with its own `use.baseURL` pointing at a real hostname added to /etc/hosts in the workflow, plus a `setup` project that performs the real authorization-code+PKCE login once and saves storageState. Uploads playwright-report and traces on failure only.
recommended_checks.tool: @playwright/test 1.62.1 (Node 22/24/26), installed via `yarn create playwright` — not the Angular schematic
recommended_checks.effort_hours: 24-32 h initial (harness, docker-compose for SQL Server, auth setup project, /etc/hosts wiring, CI workflow, first 3 specs); +2-3 h per additional spec; ~2 h/month upkeep
recommended_checks.rationale_for_two_person_team: This is the only new required gate worth adding in this area, and it is the one that buys back the manual regression pass you currently run by hand before every release. Keep it to 8-12 specs so it lands inside DORA's ten-minute feedback rule on a 2 vCPU private runner. Concretely: (1) tenant-A user completes the OIDC login and lands on the dashboard; (2) tenant-A storageState against tenant-B's host is refused — asserted both in the UI and via APIRequestContext; (3) tenant-B login page rejects tenant-A credentials; (4) anonymous self-registration for the highest-volume external role; (5) password reset request → token → new password → login; (6) the nine-step wizard, one happy path, asserting a persisted appointment; (7) back-navigation from a late step to an early step preserves entered data; (8) mid-wizard reload resumes state; (9) anonymous document upload rejects a disallowed content type; (10) authenticated upload succeeds and the file is invisible from the other tenant. Tests 2, 3 and 10 are the highest-value tests in the entire suite — they are the only automated proof you will have that Host-header tenancy holds, and they must use real distinct hostnames because the Host header cannot be spoofed. Trigger on `pull_request` only, never `push`, with `concurrency: cancel-in-progress: true`.
recommended_checks.tool_maintained_evidence: @playwright/test 1.62.1 published 2026-07-30; 1.62.0 2026-07-24; 1.61.0 2026-06-15; nightly 1.63.0-alpha-2026-08-28 still shipping. https://registry.npmjs.org/@playwright/test and https://playwright.dev/docs/release-notes

recommended_checks.what_it_does: Scheduled run (weeknights) of the entire E2E suite — the smoke specs plus the remaining three external-role registrations, per-step wizard validation branches, the role/permission matrix, and a second Playwright project running the smoke subset on WebKit. Same workflow file as the gate, selected by tag with `--grep` or a separate project list. Posts failures to whatever channel the two of you actually read.
recommended_checks.tool: @playwright/test 1.62.1 with `schedule:` cron trigger and `workflow_dispatch`
recommended_checks.effort_hours: 4-6 h once the smoke job exists (reuse the workflow, change the trigger and the grep tags)
recommended_checks.rationale_for_two_person_team: This is where the count grows without the gate slowing down. Ceiling of roughly 25 E2E tests total — past that you are contradicting Fowler's 'bare minimum' and Microsoft's 'discourage the use of UI tests', and you will start bypassing the gate. A nightly failure that neither of you looks at is worse than no nightly, so wire the notification before you wire the schedule. WebKit belongs here rather than in the gate: it is the only browser that catches Safari-specific layout and date-input bugs, which a workers' comp portal on the public internet will hit, but it triples PR cost for a defect class that shows up weekly, not hourly.

recommended_checks.what_it_does: Runs `new AxeBuilder({ page }).withTags(['wcag2a','wcag2aa','wcag21a','wcag21aa','wcag22aa']).analyze()` at 6-8 key states reached inside the existing smoke specs — the anonymous login page, the registration form, the dashboard, and three or four of the nine wizard steps — asserting `violations` equals a checked-in baseline rather than an empty array on day one.
recommended_checks.tool: @axe-core/playwright 4.13.0 (MPL-2.0, depends on axe-core ~4.13.0, peer playwright-core >= 1.0.0)
recommended_checks.effort_hours: 4-6 h (install, one shared AxeBuilder fixture, capture the baseline, wire the assertion)
recommended_checks.rationale_for_two_person_team: Nearly free because it rides inside tests you are already writing and already have an authenticated page for — no separate job, no extra app boot, no extra CI minutes. Start advisory against a frozen baseline so the existing violation backlog does not block every PR on day one, then flip to required-gate on the no-new-violations delta once the baseline is green-ish (realistically 60-90 days post-launch). Add `wcag22aa` explicitly: Playwright's own documented example omits it, so the copy-paste version silently skips every WCAG 2.2 rule. Be honest internally about what green means — Deque's own study puts automated coverage at 57% of issues by volume, so this is a floor, not a conformance claim, and a California-facing public portal will eventually need a manual assessment too.

recommended_checks.what_it_does: Weekly scheduled job running the gated smoke suite with `--repeat-each=3 --retries=0` and publishing the HTML report. Any spec that does not pass 3/3 is triaged: fixed, or marked `test.fixme()` with a line in a one-page markdown quarantine list reviewed monthly.
recommended_checks.tool: @playwright/test 1.62.1 (`--repeat-each`, HTML reporter's passed/flaky/failed categorisation)
recommended_checks.effort_hours: 2-3 h to stand up; ~1 h/month triage
recommended_checks.rationale_for_two_person_team: Google measures 1.5% of test runs flaky and ~16% of its tests carrying some flakiness, with 84% of pass-to-fail transitions being flakes — with far better engineers and infrastructure than you have. Without an explicit flake signal, a two-person team's failure mode is predictable: the gate goes red, someone re-runs it, it goes green, and within two months nobody believes the check. This is the cheapest possible version of Google's automated quarantine — a cron job and a markdown file, not a service. Run it against the merged main so the results are attributable to the tests rather than to whatever is on someone's branch.

recommended_checks.what_it_does: Runs a 3-4 spec subset (login, tenant isolation, one wizard happy path) against the actually deployed environment, triggered by `on: deployment_status` with `if: github.event.deployment_status.state == 'success'` and `PLAYWRIGHT_TEST_BASE_URL: ${{ github.event.deployment_status.target_url }}` — the pattern Playwright documents for exactly this.
recommended_checks.tool: @playwright/test 1.62.1 with the `deployment_status` trigger
recommended_checks.effort_hours: 3-4 h once a deployed environment with seeded synthetic tenants exists
recommended_checks.rationale_for_two_person_team: The composed CI stack does not exercise the thing you are actually about to change: real hostnames, real TLS, real per-tenant database routing. This subset is the cheapest check that the Host-header tenancy you assert in CI still holds against the deployment. Keep it to 3-4 read-mostly specs and run it against synthetic tenants only — it must never write test data into a tenant that will later hold PHI. One infrastructure dependency, stated once and not designed here: this requires a non-production deployed environment with seeded synthetic tenant hostnames, which the separate infrastructure exercise must provide.

not_worth_it_here: Cross-browser matrix on every PR (chromium + firefox + webkit). Playwright makes it a three-line config change, which is exactly why teams do it reflexively. It triples your gate's wall clock and CI minutes on a 2 vCPU private runner for a defect class that surfaces on a weekly cadence, not a per-PR one. Chromium on the gate, WebKit nightly. Revisit only if a real Safari bug reaches a user.

Sharding across multiple runners (`--shard=x/y` + blob reporter + `merge-reports`). This is the standard scaling answer and it is actively counterproductive below roughly a 15-minute suite: each shard re-boots SQL Server, re-runs migrations, re-builds Angular and re-downloads browsers, so fixed startup cost gets multiplied by N while only the test-execution slice gets divided. At 12 tests your run is mostly startup. Playwright's sharding doc also notes balanced shards require `fullyParallel: true`, which conflicts with the `workers: 1` you want on a 2 vCPU box.

Visual regression / screenshot snapshot testing (`toHaveScreenshot`, including 1.62's new WebP snapshots). Golden-image tests need a pinned rendering environment or they fail on font-hinting and antialiasing differences between a developer's machine and ubuntu-24.04. That means running everything in the pinned container and re-baselining on every intentional UI change. Two people shipping features will disable it within a month, and a disabled check is worse than an absent one because it teaches you that red is negotiable.

Cypress Cloud, Microsoft Playwright Testing / Playwright Service, or a third-party analytics layer (Currents, TestDino). These sell test-run history, flake analytics and parallel orchestration. At 12-25 tests, Playwright's free HTML reporter already gives you the passed/flaky/failed split that is 90% of the value, and the weekly `--repeat-each=3` job gives you the rest. Revisit at 100+ tests or when a third engineer joins.

A formal Page Object Model layer. Playwright documents POM and it is genuinely standard at scale, but at 12 tests the page objects are more code than the tests, and they add an indirection layer between a failing check and the line that broke. Cypress's own best-practices page even lists 'sharing page objects' as an anti-pattern. Use Playwright fixtures for shared setup and `getByRole` locators inline; extract a helper only on the third repetition.

GitHub merge queue. GitHub documents it as providing 'the same benefits as the Require branches to be up to date before merging branch protection, but does not require a pull request author to update their pull request branch.' That benefit only materialises when concurrent merges contend for the same base — which needs more than two developers. Just enable required status checks with 'Require branches to be up to date' off, and skip the queue.

Automated flaky-test quarantine tooling. Google's automatic quarantine service is the right answer at Google's scale; building or buying one for a 12-test suite is pure overhead. `test.fixme()` plus a one-page markdown list reviewed monthly does the same job. Also skip Google's 3-consecutive-failures rule — Google itself warns it 'encourages developers to ignore flakiness in their own tests.'

A BDD/Cucumber layer (playwright-bdd, cucumber-js) over the suite. Gherkin earns its keep when a non-engineer writes or reads the specs. You have two SDE 1s and no product owner writing scenarios, so it is an extra translation layer that will drift out of sync with the tests.

Playwright's new 1.62 component testing (the stories/galleries model). It is two months old, it replaces the previous component-testing model, and its API will move again. Angular component tests belong in TestBed/Angular Testing Library within the unit-test tier anyway — do not let a brand-new E2E-adjacent feature pull component testing into this area's budget.

Contract testing between the Angular client and the .NET API (Pact or similar). Justified when client and server ship on independent cadences owned by different teams. Yours are in one repo, deployed together, by the same two people. ABP's generated API proxies plus TypeScript already catch the shape mismatches that contract tests would.

One E2E test per wizard step (nine tests just for the wizard). Tempting because the wizard has nine steps, but eight of those tests would be asserting per-step field validation, which is an Angular reactive-forms unit test costing seconds instead of minutes. One happy path through all nine, plus back-navigation and mid-wizard resume — the two things only a browser can prove — and push the rest down the pyramid.
surprises: You cannot fake the Host header from a browser, and the failure is silent. Playwright's Route documentation states plainly that Host is a forbidden header and "If an override is provided for a forbidden header, it will be ignored and the original request header will be used." Since tenancy resolves from Host only, the obvious cross-tenant isolation test — set `extraHTTPHeaders: { Host: 'tenant-b.example' }` and assert you get denied — will hit the default tenant, get denied for the wrong reason, and PASS. You would ship a green check that proves nothing about your highest-consequence failure mode. The only correct construction is real distinct hostnames resolving to the runner (one /etc/hosts line per tenant in the workflow) plus one Playwright project per tenant with its own baseURL. Almost nobody discovers this before writing the tests.

Playwright's storageState does not include sessionStorage, and ABP's Angular OIDC client may store your token there. The auth docs say saved state covers "cookies, local storage, IndexedDB and passkey (WebAuthn) based authentication" and that "Playwright does not provide API to persist session storage." angular-oauth2-oidc — the library ABP's Angular UI uses — defaults its OAuthStorage to sessionStorage (abpframework/abp issue #13073 is titled exactly that). If your app is on that default, the canonical setup-project pattern hands every test a browser with the auth cookie but no access token: the app looks logged-out or silently re-runs the code flow, and you will spend a day blaming Playwright. Check your `OAuthStorage` provider before writing a line of test code.

The E2E auth shortcut everyone reaches for is now formally prohibited. RFC 9700 (BCP 240, January 2025) §2.4: "The resource owner password credentials grant MUST NOT be used." The classic move — have the setup project POST `grant_type=password` to /connect/token to mint a token and skip the browser login — requires leaving the password flow enabled on OpenIddict. On an office LAN that was a testing convenience. The week you go public it is an unthrottled credential-stuffing endpoint against accounts that will hold PHI. Your E2E convenience choice quietly becomes production attack surface, and no E2E tutorial mentions this.

Your CI runner is half the machine every tutorial assumes. GitHub-hosted ubuntu-latest is 4 CPU / 16 GB for public repositories but 2 CPU / 8 GB for private ones. Every Playwright benchmark, every 'we run 200 tests in 4 minutes' post, and most of the parallel-worker tuning advice online was measured on the public-repo runner. Your numbers will be worse than everything you read, and the correct response is fewer workers, not more.

E2E on every push will exhaust your Actions quota before it exhausts your patience. Private repos get 2,000 included minutes/month on Free and 3,000 on Pro or Team, with overage at $0.006/min for Linux 2-core. A run that boots SQL Server, migrates a tenant database, builds Angular 20 and drives ~12 tests is realistically 12-18 minutes. At 120 runs/month that is ~1,800 minutes — most of a Team plan — before build, unit-test and static-analysis jobs touch it. Two free mitigations: trigger on `pull_request` only, and set `concurrency: { group: ${{ github.ref }}, cancel-in-progress: true }`. Also remember Playwright reports and traces consume the 500 MB / 2 GB artifact allowance, which is shared with GitHub Packages.

Playwright's own documentation contradicts itself on CI worker count. /docs/ci says "We recommend setting workers to '1' in CI environments" with `workers: process.env.CI ? 1 : undefined`; /docs/test-parallel shows `? 2 :`. Neither page acknowledges the other. On a 2 vCPU runner already hosting a .NET API and SQL Server, 1 is the right read — but the more important point is that Playwright's docs are not internally consistent, so verify config advice against the specific page rather than assuming a single house position.

Caching Playwright browsers is explicitly discouraged by Playwright, contradicting the standard CI-optimization advice. "Caching browser binaries is not recommended, since the amount of time it takes to restore the cache is comparable to the time it takes to download the binaries. Especially under Linux, operating system dependencies need to be installed, which are not cacheable." Nearly every CI-speedup blog post tells you to cache ~/.cache/ms-playwright. Obey Playwright instead — a stale browser cache produces failures that look exactly like app bugs.

Microsoft ships AI test-authoring agents inside Playwright itself, as of 2026. `npx playwright init-agents --loop=claude` installs a planner (explores the app, emits a Markdown test plan), a generator (turns the plan into spec files) and a healer (runs the suite and repairs failures). For a team with zero E2E tests and a nine-step wizard that is documented nowhere, seeding the planner with a hand-written authenticated seed test is the cheapest possible start — and it is a first-party Microsoft feature, not a third-party add-on. It appears in almost no 2026 Playwright-vs-Cypress comparison.

`retryStrategy: 'isolated'`, added in Playwright 1.62 (July 2026), will fix more of your flakiness than any amount of 'add explicit waits' advice. It runs all retries at the end, one at a time in a single worker. On a resource-starved runner most flakes are contention with SQL Server and the Angular build, not app bugs, so retrying in a quiet worker converts a large share of them into passes with zero test changes. It is two months old and therefore absent from every guide.

Cypress's parallelization is paywalled and its own best-practices page contradicts Playwright's. Cypress's GitHub Actions doc: "Using parallelization with the Cypress GitHub Action requires setting up recording to Cypress Cloud." Playwright's `--shard=x/y` is free and built in. Separately, Cypress lists "using your UI to log in" as an outright anti-pattern, while Playwright's auth docs present UI login as the primary recommended pattern with API login relegated to "Advanced scenarios." There is no industry consensus here — pick per-app, and for you UI login once in the setup project is right because it is the only thing that proves the OIDC redirect chain across two hosts actually works.

A green axe run is not a WCAG claim, and the official Playwright snippet is incomplete. Deque's own study across 13,000+ pages found automated testing covered 57% of issues — and Deque notes that measuring by WCAG Success Criteria instead of issue volume gives a materially lower number, so even the vendor's headline figure is contested within its own source. Worse, Playwright's documented example uses `withTags(['wcag2a','wcag2aa','wcag21a','wcag21aa'])` and omits `wcag22aa`, so copy-pasting it silently skips every WCAG 2.2 rule despite WCAG 2.2 having been a W3C Recommendation since 12 December 2024.

The Angular ecosystem's E2E integration story mildly favours Cypress, which is the opposite of the overall verdict. `@cypress/schematic` 6.0.0 and `@cypress/angular` 5.0.0 both shipped 2026-08-26; `playwright-ng-schematics` is a community package whose current 22.1.0 pins Angular 22 devkit and whose last Angular-20-line release was 20.0.2 on 2025-12-11. This does not change the recommendation — `ng e2e` is, per Angular's docs, "really just running the e2e builder under the hood" — but it means you should install Playwright with `yarn create playwright` rather than `ng add`, and you should not read Angular's alphabetically-first listing of Cypress as an endorsement.
disagreements: Playwright contradicts itself on CI workers: https://playwright.dev/docs/ci says `workers: process.env.CI ? 1 : undefined` ("We recommend setting workers to '1' in CI environments to prioritize stability and reproducibility"), while https://playwright.dev/docs/test-parallel shows `workers: process.env.CI ? 2 : undefined`. The generated default config on /docs/test-configuration uses 1. Resolved here in favour of 1 because private-repo ubuntu-latest is 2 vCPU / 8 GB and is shared with SQL Server and the .NET API — but flagged because it means Playwright has no single house position.

Cypress and Playwright disagree on whether to log in through the UI. Cypress's best-practices page lists it as an anti-pattern outright ("Anti-Pattern: ...using your UI to log in"; "Best Practice: ...programmatically log into your application"). Playwright's authentication doc leads with a UI-driven setup project as the recommended approach and files API-based auth under "Advanced scenarios." Both are defensible; the disagreement is real and unacknowledged by either vendor.

No authority agrees on an E2E test count, and the three primary sources are not reconcilable into a number. Google gives a proportion (70/20/10) but no absolute count. Fowler gives neither, only "a bare minimum" and "one or two more crucial user journeys." Microsoft Learn gives no ratio at all and instead says "Discourage the use of UI tests, because they tend to be unreliable." Anyone quoting you a specific number of E2E tests is extrapolating, not citing.

Microsoft's PR-gate rule and DORA's feedback-time rule cannot both be satisfied here. Microsoft Learn's taxonomy expects "a pull request automatically fails if the L3 test run fails" (L3 = functional tests against a deployed service, i.e. your E2E tier). DORA requires "feedback from automated tests in less than ten minutes" from CI. On a 2 vCPU private runner that also boots SQL Server and builds Angular, a full E2E suite cannot do both. Resolved by gating a smoke subset and scheduling the remainder — but this is a genuine tension between two primary sources, not a settled practice.

Deque's own 57% automated-coverage figure is contested inside Deque's own article. The study measured "total volume of issues detected by severity and impact" and explicitly notes that measuring "based on WCAG Success Criteria downplays the effectiveness of automated testing" — i.e. the SC-based number is materially lower. Playwright's accessibility doc separately warns that "many accessibility problems can only be discovered through manual testing." Do not let anyone cite 57% as a coverage guarantee.

Angular's official documentation and the actual maintenance record point in different directions for Angular integration specifically. angular.dev lists Cypress first and Cypress's Angular schematics are current (2026-08-26), while the Playwright Angular schematic is a community package that has not shipped an Angular-20-compatible release since 2025-12-11. The CI, auth, cost and cross-origin evidence all favour Playwright decisively; the Angular-schematic evidence mildly favours Cypress. The resolution is to note that `ng e2e` is only a builder shim, so the schematic is not load-bearing — but the surface-level signal genuinely conflicts.
