research.area: Code coverage — defensible targets, measurement (Angular/TypeScript + .NET 10), diff vs absolute coverage, and CI enforcement for a two-person team on a HIPAA-regulated multi-tenant portal
research.standard_summary: The honest answer is that there is no universal number, and the most authoritative sources say so explicitly. Google's testing organisation states "There is no 'ideal code coverage number' that universally applies to all products" and offers 60/75/90% as acceptable/commendable/exemplary while refusing to mandate any of them; the largest empirical study (Inozemtseva & Holmes, ICSE 2014, 31,000 suites over 724k LoC) concludes coverage "should not be used as a quality target because it is not a good indicator of test suite effectiveness." What HAS converged by 2026 is the shape of enforcement rather than the number: gate on the diff (new/changed lines), trend the absolute number without gating it. Sonar's default "Sonar way" gate is coverage on new code >= 80.0% and duplication on new code <= 3.0%, and Sonar's rationale is that this "focuses on keeping high quality standards for new code, rather than spending a lot of effort remediating old code"; Codecov's `patch` status "only measures lines adjusted in the pull request" with default `target: auto, threshold: 0%`; Google says "While project wide goals above 90% are most likely not worth it, per-commit coverage goals of 99% are reasonable, and 90% is a good lower threshold." No healthcare regulation names a number: the HIPAA Security Rule text (45 CFR 164 Subpart C) contains the word "coverage" zero times, OWASP ASVS 5.0.0 has no coverage requirement, NIST SSDF PW.8 has none, and FDA's guidance — which does not apply to a non-device scheduling portal anyway — is explicitly risk-based ("Validation coverage should be based on the software's complexity and safety risk — not on firm size or resource constraints"). For this stack the mechanics are settled: coverlet 10.0.1 emits Cobertura/LCOV/OpenCover in one `dotnet test` pass, Angular v20 emits LCOV via `ng test --code-coverage`, and diff-cover 10.5.1 (Apache-2.0, released 2026-08-16) reads both formats and enforces `--fail-under` against `--compare-branch=origin/main` with no paid service and no data leaving GitHub.

standards.claim: Google's official testing guidance states there is no universal coverage number and refuses to mandate one, offering 60% as 'acceptable', 75% as 'commendable' and 90% as 'exemplary' as guidelines only. Verbatim: "Although there is no 'ideal code coverage number,' at Google we offer the general guidelines of 60% as 'acceptable', 75% as 'commendable' and 90% as 'exemplary.' However we like to stay away from broad top-down mandates and encourage every team to select the value that makes sense for their business needs." It also warns "Be mindful that engineers may start treating your target like a checkbox and avoid increasing coverage beyond the target, even if doing so would be prudent."
standards.threshold: 60% acceptable / 75% commendable / 90% exemplary (whole-project, non-binding)
standards.source_name: Google Testing Blog — 'Code Coverage Best Practices' (Bender, Arguelles, Ivanković, 7 Aug 2020)
standards.notes: WebFetch's markdown conversion dropped the post body, so I curled the page and extracted the post-body div directly; quotes above are byte-exact from that HTML. Cross-checked against the googblogs.com mirror, which reproduces the same sentences. This is the single most useful citation for the 'we are not picking 80% because someone said so' conversation.

standards.claim: Google explicitly separates project-wide goals from per-change goals and says the per-change bar should be much higher than the project bar: "While project wide goals above 90% are most likely not worth it, per-commit coverage goals of 99% are reasonable, and 90% is a good lower threshold." It also names mutation testing, not more coverage, as the way to tell whether covered lines are actually tested: "A better technique to assess whether you're adequately exercising the lines your tests cover, and adequately asserting on failures, is mutation testing." And on the asymmetry of the metric: "a low code coverage number does guarantee that large areas of the product are going completely untested by automation on every single deployment."
standards.threshold: per-commit/diff: 90% lower threshold, 99% reasonable; project-wide: >90% not worth it
standards.source_name: Google Testing Blog — 'Code Coverage Best Practices'
standards.notes: This is the clearest primary-source statement of the diff-coverage-over-absolute-coverage model, predating Sonar's marketing of it. Note the direction of the asymmetry: coverage is a valid lower bound (low number proves untested code exists) but not an upper bound (high number proves nothing).

standards.claim: The largest empirical study of the coverage/effectiveness relationship concludes coverage should not be used as a quality target. Abstract, verbatim: "We found that there is a low to moderate correlation between coverage and effectiveness when the number of test cases in the suite is controlled for. In addition, we found that stronger forms of coverage do not provide greater insight into the effectiveness of the suite. Our results suggest that coverage, while useful for identifying under-tested parts of a program, should not be used as a quality target because it is not a good indicator of test suite effectiveness." Study scale: 31,000 generated test suites across five Java systems up to 724,000 lines of source, evaluated by mutation testing.
standards.threshold: n/a — the finding is that no threshold is defensible as a quality target
standards.source_name: Inozemtseva & Holmes, 'Coverage Is Not Strongly Correlated with Test Suite Effectiveness', ICSE 2014 (ACM Distinguished Paper)
standards.notes: I downloaded the UBC-hosted author PDF (2.3 MB) but could not extract its text in this environment (no pdftotext, pypdf broken by a native-binding failure). The abstract quoted above is reproduced verbatim on neverworkintheory.org, a research-summary site run by Greg Wilson; ACM DL returned 403. Confidence 'verified' applies to the abstract text and the study's scale, which are consistent across both the summary and the search-result snippets from ACM and Semantic Scholar. Cite the DOI 10.1145/2568225.2568271 in any internal document.

standards.claim: Martin Fowler's position, still the most-cited practitioner statement: coverage is a tool for finding untested code, not a management metric. Specific bands he gives: below 50% is 'a sign of trouble'; 'upper 80s or 90s' is what thoughtful testing tends to produce as a by-product; 100% is 'suspicious', suggesting tests written to satisfy the metric. He explicitly warns against mandates of the form 'you can't go into production with less than 87% coverage', quoting Brian Marick: "I expect a high level of coverage. Sometimes managers require one. There's a subtle difference."
standards.threshold: <50% = trouble; upper 80s-90s = expected by-product; 100% = suspicious
standards.source_name: martinfowler.com — TestCoverage (bliki, 17 April 2012)
standards.notes: Fourteen years old and still the reference point. It is a practitioner opinion, not a standard — but it is the piece most reviewers will have read, and it is where the 'high coverage is an effect of good testing, not a cause' framing comes from. Fowler and Google agree on the shape and disagree slightly on the top of the band (see disagreements).

standards.claim: SonarQube's default, read-only, built-in quality gate ('Sonar way') applies four conditions to NEW code only: no new issues are introduced; all new Security Hotspots are reviewed; new code test coverage is greater than or equal to 80.0%; and duplication in the new code is less than or equal to 3.0%.
standards.threshold: Coverage on New Code >= 80.0%; Duplicated Lines on New Code <= 3.0%
standards.source_name: Sonar Documentation — Understanding quality gates (SonarQube Server)
standards.notes: This is the origin of the '80% is the industry standard' folklore — but note the denominator: it is 80% of NEW code, not 80% of the repository. Quoting it as an absolute-coverage target misrepresents the source. The doc page is unversioned ('latest').

standards.claim: Sonar's published rationale for the new-code model ('Clean as You Code') is cost avoidance on legacy, not a claim that 80% is intrinsically correct: the gate "focuses on keeping high quality standards for new code, rather than spending a lot of effort remediating old code," and "Analyzing and cleaning new code allows you to fix issues in your old code and gradually improve the overall quality of your codebase." The mechanism is that files you touch become 'new code', so the legacy codebase is remediated incrementally by ordinary feature work rather than by a coverage sprint.
standards.threshold: n/a — model, not number
standards.source_name: Sonar Documentation — Quality standards and new code / Understanding quality gates
standards.notes: For a two-person team inheriting an ABP Commercial codebase with low existing coverage, this is the whole argument: a new-code gate costs you nothing on day one and cannot generate a backlog you can't clear. An absolute gate at any meaningful number is unachievable on day one and therefore gets bypassed, which is precisely the failure mode the brief warns about.

standards.claim: Sonar shipped a distinct built-in gate for AI-assisted development in 2026, 'Sonar way for agentic AI', with six conditions on new code — no new bugs at severity >= Minor, no new vulnerabilities at severity >= Minor, no new code smells at severity >= Major, no dependency risks at severity >= Low, "Coverage on new code is greater or equal to 80%", and "Duplication on new code is less or equal to 3%". It replaces the legacy 'Sonar way for AI code' gate. The coverage bar is unchanged at 80% of new code.
standards.threshold: Coverage on new code >= 80%; duplication on new code <= 3%
standards.source_name: Sonar Documentation — Quality gate for agentic AI (SonarQube Cloud)
standards.notes: Relevant because AI-generated code is a live 2026 concern for small teams shipping fast. Note the vendor did NOT raise the coverage bar for AI-written code — it added issue-severity and dependency conditions instead. The Dependency Risks condition requires an Advanced Security subscription on the Enterprise plan, so the gate is not fully usable below that tier.

standards.claim: Codecov distinguishes two status checks with different defaults. `patch` "only measures lines adjusted in the pull request or single commit, if the commit is not in a pull request" and defaults to `target: auto`, `threshold: 0%`, `base: auto`, `if_ci_failed: error`. `project` measures whole-repository coverage against the base commit with an example `threshold: 5`. Either can be made non-blocking with `informational: true`, which makes "the resulting status will pass no matter what the coverage is or what other settings are specified."
standards.threshold: patch: target auto, threshold 0%; project: target auto, threshold 5
standards.source_name: Codecov Documentation — Commit status (project vs patch)
standards.notes: `informational: true` is the underrated setting: it lets you run the full gate configuration in shadow mode for a few sprints and collect real data on what your PRs actually achieve before you make anything blocking. That is the correct way for a two-person team to pick its number rather than copying 80% off a blog.

standards.claim: The free tiers of the two managed services do not fit this codebase. SonarQube Cloud's Free plan allows unlimited public projects but private projects only "Up to 50k LOC", a maximum of 5 organization members, "Only main branch analysis", and pull request analysis "Only if the target branch is the main branch". This repository is roughly 53k lines of C# plus 27k lines of TypeScript (~80k LoC), so it exceeds the free private-project cap. Self-hosting does not rescue it: SonarQube Server Community Build excludes branch and pull request analysis and PR decoration — "A significant addition in the Developer Edition is the capability for branch and pull request analysis and pull request decoration."
standards.threshold: SonarQube Cloud Free: 50k LoC private, 5 members, main-branch only. Branch/PR analysis on self-hosted: Developer Edition minimum.
standards.source_name: Sonar Documentation — Subscription plans (SonarQube Cloud); Sonar blog — Compare SonarQube editions (27 Oct 2025)
standards.notes: Both sources are first-party Sonar. Also confirmed on https://www.sonarsource.com/plans-and-pricing/ ("explore SonarQube with your private project up to a maximum size of 50k LoC"). This is the single most consequential practical finding in this area: every 'just enable Clean as You Code' recommendation you will read assumes a tier this project does not qualify for. Codecov's free Developer plan does cover private repos but at 1 user and 250 private uploads/month (Team is $5/user/month, 2,500 uploads) per https://about.codecov.io/pricing/ — 250 uploads/month is roughly 6 PR pushes a day across two devs and two languages, i.e. tight but not impossible. Cost is out of scope, so treat these as tool-availability facts, not a budget recommendation.

standards.claim: Sonar requires different coverage report formats for the two halves of this stack, and will silently report 0% if you feed it the wrong one. For C#: `sonar.cs.opencover.reportsPaths` (OpenCover, incl. coverlet OpenCover output), `sonar.cs.cobertura.reportsPaths` (coverlet or dotnet-coverage Cobertura), `sonar.cs.vscoveragexml.reportsPaths` (Visual Studio / dotnet-coverage XML), `sonar.cs.dotcover.reportsPaths`; `sonar.cs.ncover3.reportsPaths` is deprecated. For TypeScript: LCOV only — "SonarQube Cloud directly supports all coverage tools that produce reports in the LCOV format" via `sonar.javascript.lcov.reportPaths`, and "The parameter `sonar.typescript.lcov.reportPaths` was formerly used for TypeScript coverage. This parameter has been deprecated." Generated code is removed from the denominator with `sonar.coverage.exclusions`, which "excludes specific files from code coverage calculations" while still analysing them for quality issues.
standards.threshold: C#: opencover|cobertura|vscoveragexml reportsPaths. TS: sonar.javascript.lcov.reportPaths (LCOV only).
standards.source_name: Sonar Documentation — .NET test coverage; JavaScript/TypeScript test coverage; Analysis parameters
standards.notes: Two traps here. (1) LCOV is NOT accepted for C# and Cobertura is NOT accepted for TypeScript, so one CI run must produce two formats. (2) Much community advice from 2020-2022 insists OpenCover is the only option for C#; `sonar.cs.cobertura.reportsPaths` is now documented and supported, so following old advice wastes a day. The monorepo warning on the JS page also applies: "file paths inside each report must be unique across the whole repository."

standards.claim: Microsoft Learn documents coverlet plus ReportGenerator as the supported cross-platform coverage path for .NET. The canonical command is `dotnet test --collect:"XPlat Code Coverage"`, which emits `coverage.cobertura.xml` into the `TestResults` directory: "This is a cross-platform option that relies on the .NET CLI, and it is great for build systems where MSBuild isn't available." Microsoft also documents its own built-in collector (`--collect:"Code Coverage"`), which "generates a binary .coverage file" that "isn't human-readable, and it must be converted to a human-readable format before it can be used to generate reports outside of Visual Studio", with `dotnet-coverage` as the converter. Report generation is documented via `dotnet tool install -g dotnet-reportgenerator-globaltool`.
standards.threshold: n/a — `dotnet test --collect:"XPlat Code Coverage"` → coverage.cobertura.xml
standards.source_name: Microsoft Learn — Use code coverage for unit testing (.NET), ms.date 2026-03-04, updated 2026-04-02
standards.notes: The page carries `ai-usage: ai-assisted` in its front matter but is the official dotnet/docs article and was refreshed four months ago. It is the citation to use if anyone asks 'is coverlet a real Microsoft-sanctioned choice' — Microsoft's own docs teach it in preference to their binary collector for CI.

standards.claim: coverlet can emit every format this project needs from a single test run and can fail the build on a threshold without any external service. Formats: "The supported formats are lcov, opencover, cobertura, teamcity, json (default coverlet proprietary format)", combinable — `dotnet test --collect:"XPlat Code Coverage;Format=json,lcov,cobertura"`. Threshold enforcement: `dotnet test /p:CollectCoverage=true /p:Threshold=80` "will automatically fail the build if the line, branch or method coverage of any of the instrumented modules falls below 80%", narrowable with `/p:ThresholdType=line`. Exclusions: `ExcludeFromCoverageAttribute` and `ExcludeFromCodeCoverageAttribute` "are always excluded" by default; additional attributes via `ExcludeByAttribute` (e.g. `GeneratedCodeAttribute,CompilerGeneratedAttribute`), files via `ExcludeByFile` globs, and `SkipAutoProps` to drop auto-implemented properties.
standards.threshold: /p:Threshold=80 with /p:ThresholdType=line|branch|method; Format=lcov,opencover,cobertura,teamcity,json
standards.source_name: coverlet — VSTestIntegration.md and MSBuildIntegration.md (master)
standards.notes: `SkipAutoProps=true` matters disproportionately on an ABP codebase: DTOs and entities are mostly auto-properties, and leaving them in the denominator makes the absolute number a measure of how many DTOs you have rather than how well you test. Note the Threshold check is per-module, not per-solution, which makes it awkward as a repo-wide gate but excellent as a floor on one or two critical assemblies.

standards.claim: On .NET 10 / Microsoft Testing Platform the coverage story changes and one common setup breaks. Microsoft's own MTP coverage extension (`Microsoft.Testing.Extensions.CodeCoverage`) supports only `coverage`, `xml`, and `cobertura` for `--coverage-output-format` — it cannot emit LCOV. Version compatibility is pinned: CodeCoverage 18.1.x ↔ MTP 2.0.x, 18.0.x ↔ MTP 1.8.x, 17.14.x ↔ MTP 1.6.2. Its `IncludeTestAssembly` default flipped to `false` "while it used to be `true` in VSTest". To get LCOV under MTP you need `coverlet.MTP`, a native MTP extension run as `dotnet test --coverlet` with `--coverlet-output-format` supporting `json`, `lcov`, `opencover`, `cobertura`, `teamcity`. `coverlet.msbuild` relies on VSTest MSBuild targets that MTP does not invoke, so it collects nothing under MTP.
standards.threshold: Microsoft.Testing.Extensions.CodeCoverage 18.1.x ↔ MTP 2.0.x; MTP built-in formats: coverage|xml|cobertura (no lcov)
standards.source_name: Microsoft Learn — Microsoft.Testing.Platform (MTP) code coverage, ms.date 2026-02-25, updated 2026-04-27
standards.notes: ABP Commercial 10.0.2 test projects are xUnit-on-VSTest today, so this is a future-dated hazard rather than a current break — but it is exactly the kind of thing that silently zeroes a coverage gate during an SDK bump. The coverlet.msbuild incompatibility is stated in the coverlet/MS docs and in the MTP migration guidance; I did not reproduce it, so treat that specific sub-claim as documented rather than tested.

standards.claim: `dotnet-coverage` is the documented cross-platform way to merge many per-project coverage files into one report, which a multi-project ABP solution needs. Install: `dotnet tool install --global dotnet-coverage`. Merge with globbing: `dotnet-coverage merge -o merged.cobertura.xml -f cobertura **\*.coverage`. Supported merge/collect output formats are `coverage`, `xml`, `cobertura` (default `coverage`, the Visual Studio binary format). Applies to ".NET 8 SDK and later versions". Note: "Starting with version 18.10.0, the `dotnet-coverage` tool collects telemetry data" recording which commands and options you run, with an opt-out.
standards.threshold: dotnet-coverage merge -o merged.cobertura.xml -f cobertura; formats coverage|xml|cobertura; telemetry from 18.10.0
standards.source_name: Microsoft Learn — dotnet-coverage code coverage tool, ms.date 2026-08-05, updated 2026-08-13
standards.notes: coverlet's own docs recommend the same merge command. The telemetry note is three weeks old and worth a five-minute read for a team that will eventually have to answer 'what does your build tooling send outbound' in a security questionnaire — it records commands and options, not source, and can be disabled.

standards.claim: Angular v20 (this project's version) generates coverage with `ng test --no-watch --code-coverage`, or `"codeCoverage": true` in angular.json, with `--code-coverage-exclude` globs. The default test system in v20 is Karma: "The project you create with the CLI is setup to use the `karma` test system by default." Angular's own v20 docs give 80 as the threshold example across all four metrics via karma-coverage `check.global`: `statements: 80, branches: 80, functions: 80, lines: 80`, framed as a scenario where "the team has decided on a minimum of 80% code coverage". The Vitest-based `@angular/build:unit-test` builder exists in v20 but is explicitly experimental with no SemVer guarantees.
standards.threshold: karma-coverage check.global statements/branches/functions/lines = 80 (Angular's documented example)
standards.source_name: Angular v20 documentation — Code coverage; ng test; Experimental unit testing system
standards.notes: Important nuance: Angular presents 80 as an illustrative team decision, not as a recommendation. It is nonetheless the number most Angular teams end up with because it is the number in the docs. Note karma-coverage's `check.global` fails the whole test command, so it is an absolute gate, not a diff gate.

standards.claim: The Angular coverage toolchain is mid-migration and the flags are being renamed, which will invalidate coverage scripts written today. Karma itself is deprecated by its maintainers — "Karma is deprecated and is not accepting new features or general bug fixes" — with karma 6.4.4 last published 2024-07-29 and karma-coverage 2.2.1 last published 2023-06-23. Angular's current (post-v20) docs default `ng test` to Vitest, replace `--code-coverage` with `--coverage`, replace `codeCoverageExclude` with `--coverage-exclude`/`--coverage-include`, add `--coverage-reporters` (allowed values: `cobertura`, `html`, `json`, `json-summary`, `lcov`, `lcovonly`, `text`, `text-summary`), require `@vitest/coverage-v8`, and move thresholds into a `coverageThresholds` block (`statements/branches/functions/lines: 80`).
standards.threshold: v20: --code-coverage. Current: --coverage, --coverage-reporters (lcov|cobertura|json-summary|...), coverageThresholds {80,80,80,80}
standards.source_name: Angular documentation (current) — Code coverage and ng test; npm registry metadata for karma and karma-coverage
standards.notes: The Karma deprecation text is from the karma package README as served by registry.npmjs.org (https://registry.npmjs.org/karma), which mirrors the GitHub README; publish dates are from the same registry metadata. Practical consequence: write the CI step so the coverage-file path and format are the contract and the ng invocation is a one-line variable, so the Karma→Vitest move is a one-line change rather than a pipeline rewrite.

standards.claim: No US healthcare regulation or security standard in scope for this application specifies a code coverage number. The HIPAA Security Rule as currently in force (45 CFR Part 164 Subpart C, text retrieved for 2026-08-01) contains zero occurrences of 'coverage', 'unit test' or 'source code'; its only uses of 'testing' concern contingency-plan testing (§164.308(a)(7)(ii)(D)) and physical control of "access to software programs for testing and revision" (§164.310(a)(2)(iii)). OWASP ASVS 5.0.0 contains no code-coverage requirement — the five occurrences of 'coverage' in its English source refer to validation coverage, penetration-test coverage and SAST/DAST tool coverage, none as a metric or threshold. NIST SP 800-218 (SSDF v1.1) practice PW.8 and tasks PW.8.1/PW.8.2 name no coverage metric: PW.8.2 requires only to "Scope the testing, design the tests, perform the testing, and document the results, including recording and triaging all discovered issues and recommended remediations in the development team's workflow or issue tracking system."
standards.threshold: none — zero numeric coverage requirements in HIPAA Security Rule, ASVS 5.0.0, or SSDF PW.8
standards.source_name: eCFR (45 CFR Part 164 Subpart C, current text); OWASP ASVS v5.0.0 source; NIST SP 800-218 SSDF v1.1 (machine-readable practice text)
standards.notes: Method, so you can re-run it: I pulled the eCFR XML for Part 164 Subpart C via the versioner API and grepped the stripped text (27,401 chars, 0 hits for 'coverage'); I cloned OWASP/ASVS at tag v5.0.0_release (tagged 2025-05-30) and grepped 5.0/en (5 hits, all non-metric); and I pulled the CycloneDX machine-readable SSDF v1.1 standard (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CycloneDX/official-3rd-party-standards/main/standards/NIST/SSDF/nist_secure-software-development-framework_1.1.cdx.json — 0 hits for 'coverage' across all practice and task text). Caveat: the CycloneDX file carries practice/task text, and I could not reliably extract the SSDF PDF's 'Notional Implementation Examples' column (my zlib/regex extraction of https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/SpecialPublications/NIST.SP.800-218.pdf recovered only front matter), so a coverage mention buried in a notional example is not fully excluded. Also note the current eCFR text still uses the Required/Addressable distinction, indicating the January 2025 HIPAA Security Rule NPRM has not been finalised as of this text.

standards.claim: FDA is the one US regulator with substantive published guidance on structural coverage, and it prescribes a risk-based approach with no percentage. Verbatim from §4.8: "Validation coverage should be based on the software's complexity and safety risk – not on firm size or resource constraints." On structural testing: "The amount of structural coverage should be commensurate with the level of risk posed by the software." It also defines the vocabulary in a way that differs from industry usage: "Use of the term 'coverage' usually means 100% coverage. For example, if a testing program has achieved 'statement coverage,' it means that 100% of the statements in the software have been executed at least once." And it ranks the criteria: decision/branch coverage "is considered to be a minimum level of coverage for most software products, but decision coverage alone is insufficient for high-integrity applications." This guidance governs medical device software; a workers' compensation examination-scheduling portal is not a device software function, so it does not apply here.
standards.threshold: no percentage — risk-commensurate; branch/decision coverage named as the minimum criterion for most products
standards.source_name: FDA — General Principles of Software Validation; Final Guidance for Industry and FDA Staff (January 2002, v2.0), §4.8 and §5.2.5
standards.notes: Quotes extracted by downloading the FDA PDF and decompressing its content streams (154,711 chars recovered; 'software validation' appears 116 times, confirming a good extraction). I include this because teams in healthcare reflexively reach for FDA guidance and then either over-apply it or mis-cite it. The correct use here is rhetorical: the strictest healthcare software regulator in the country declines to name a number and ties the bar to risk — which is exactly the policy you should write.

standards.claim: HITRUST CSF is the one framework commonly cited in US healthcare vendor questionnaires whose control text I could not inspect, so I cannot confirm or deny that it names a coverage figure.
standards.threshold: unknown
standards.source_name: HITRUST Alliance — HITRUST CSF (control text not publicly available)
standards.notes: What I tried: targeted search for HITRUST CSF control text naming a code-coverage percentage; the public materials I could reach (framework overview page, the publicly posted CSF v11.2.0 Introduction PDF, and third-party control summaries) discuss SA-11 'Developer Testing and Evaluation' and system acceptance testing but expose no coverage metric. The full CSF requirement statements are licensed and paywalled. Practical read: no third-party summary I found alleges a coverage percentage, and HITRUST derives heavily from NIST/ISO sources that contain none — but treat this as unverified. If a customer contract references HITRUST, get the control text from them rather than guessing.

recommended_checks.what_it_does: Runs the .NET test suite with coverage, merges the per-project Cobertura files, then computes coverage of ONLY the lines this PR added or changed and fails if that number falls below a threshold. Concretely: `dotnet test --collect:"XPlat Code Coverage;Format=cobertura,opencover"` → `dotnet-coverage merge -o merged.cobertura.xml -f cobertura **/coverage.cobertura.xml` → `diff-cover merged.cobertura.xml --compare-branch=origin/main --fail-under=<N> --format markdown:patch-backend.md`. Requires `fetch-depth: 0` on actions/checkout so the merge-base exists.
recommended_checks.tool: coverlet.collector 10.0.1 + dotnet-coverage 18.10.0 + diff-cover 10.5.1
recommended_checks.tool_maintained_evidence: coverlet.collector 10.0.1 published 2026-05-18 (NuGet flat-container + registration API: https://api.nuget.org/v3-flatcontainer/coverlet.collector/index.json); dotnet-coverage 18.10.0 published 2026-08-12 (https://api.nuget.org/v3-flatcontainer/dotnet-coverage/index.json), documented on Microsoft Learn with ms.date 2026-08-05; diff-cover 10.5.1 published 2026-08-16, Apache-2.0, requires Python >=3.10 (https://pypi.org/pypi/diff-cover/json) with five releases in the last five weeks.
recommended_checks.rationale_for_two_person_team: This is the whole 2026 standard in one check, and it costs nothing per month. Start it ADVISORY and set no threshold for the first four to six weeks — just print the number on every PR. You will then have real data on what your PRs actually achieve, and you can set the threshold at roughly your observed median rather than importing Sonar's 80% or Google's 90%. Flip it to required-gate only after two consecutive weeks where it would have passed unmodified. A gate you cannot pass on the day you enable it is a gate you will start bypassing, which is the exact failure the brief warns about. Before you set any number, add coverage exclusions for generated code: ABP's Angular proxies live under `src/app/proxy/**`, and on the C# side EF Core migrations and ABP-generated DTOs should be excluded via `ExcludeByFile` globs plus `SkipAutoProps=true` — otherwise you are measuring how many DTOs you have.

recommended_checks.what_it_does: Same mechanism for Angular: `ng test --no-watch --code-coverage` produces `coverage/lcov.info`, then `diff-cover coverage/lcov.info --compare-branch=origin/main --fail-under=<N> --format markdown:patch-frontend.md`. diff-cover reads LCOV natively, so one tool covers both stacks.
recommended_checks.tool: Angular CLI 20.3.24 karma-coverage + diff-cover 10.5.1
recommended_checks.tool_maintained_evidence: diff-cover 10.5.1 published 2026-08-16 (https://pypi.org/pypi/diff-cover/json). Caveat, stated plainly: karma-coverage 2.2.1 last published 2023-06-23 and karma 6.4.4 last published 2024-07-29, and karma's own README says "Karma is deprecated and is not accepting new features or general bug fixes" (https://registry.npmjs.org/karma). The LCOV file it emits is fine; the runner underneath it is on a dead path.
recommended_checks.rationale_for_two_person_team: Deliberately identical in shape to the backend check so there is one mental model, one tool, one threshold conversation — not two. Write the workflow step so the coverage FILE PATH and FORMAT are the contract and the `ng test` invocation is a single variable. When you move to the `@angular/build:unit-test` Vitest builder (experimental in v20, default in current Angular), the flags rename from `--code-coverage` to `--coverage` and you add `--coverage-reporters lcov` plus `@vitest/coverage-v8`; if the path/format is the contract, that upgrade is a one-line change instead of a pipeline rewrite. Expect the frontend number to be lower than the backend number and do not force them to match — Angular component specs and C# application-service tests have genuinely different cost curves.

recommended_checks.what_it_does: Renders the merged coverage into a GitHub-flavoured markdown summary and posts/updates a single sticky comment on the PR, plus uploads the full HTML report as a workflow artifact. `reportgenerator -reports:merged.cobertura.xml -targetdir:coveragereport -reporttypes:Html;MarkdownSummaryGithub;MarkdownDeltaSummary` then `gh pr comment $PR_NUMBER --edit-last --create-if-none --body-file coveragereport/SummaryGithub.md`.
recommended_checks.tool: ReportGenerator 5.5.11 (dotnet-reportgenerator-globaltool) + gh CLI
recommended_checks.tool_maintained_evidence: dotnet-reportgenerator-globaltool 5.5.11 published 2026-07-27 (NuGet registration API); the author's own danielpalme/ReportGenerator-GitHub-Action last commit 2026-07-27 tagged 5.5.11 (verified by shallow clone). Report types confirmed from the upstream README (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/danielpalme/ReportGenerator/main/README.md): Html, Cobertura, MarkdownSummaryGithub, MarkdownDeltaSummary, TextSummary and others. Microsoft Learn documents ReportGenerator as the report step for the coverlet path.
recommended_checks.rationale_for_two_person_team: Do NOT use a third-party PR-comment action for this. The `gh pr comment --edit-last --create-if-none` pattern is straight out of the ReportGenerator author's own action README, needs no marketplace action, no external service, and no additional token scope beyond the default GITHUB_TOKEN. That matters more than convenience here: the most widely recommended action for exactly this job, irongut/CodeCoverageSummary, has had no commit since 2022-10-20 (verified by shallow clone), and an unmaintained third-party action with write access to a PHI-adjacent private repo is a supply-chain exposure, not just a staleness annoyance. Visibility is the point of this check — with two devs, a number on the PR does most of the behavioural work that a blocking gate would do, without the bypass pressure.

recommended_checks.what_it_does: A small, explicitly named test suite (10-25 tests) asserting the failure mode that actually ends this company: that a request resolving to tenant A can never read, write or enumerate tenant B's data. Covers Host-header tenant resolution including missing/unknown/spoofed hosts, connection-string selection per tenant, repository queries executed under an impersonated tenant, and the anonymous-reachable endpoints (registration, login, password reset, document upload). Gated on the suite existing and passing — plus a coverlet floor scoped to just those assemblies (`/p:Threshold=<high> /p:ThresholdType=line`), since coverlet's threshold is evaluated per module.
recommended_checks.tool: xUnit (ABP test host) + coverlet.msbuild 10.0.1 threshold, scoped to tenant-resolution and authorization projects only
recommended_checks.tool_maintained_evidence: coverlet.msbuild 10.0.1 published 2026-05-18 (https://api.nuget.org/v3-flatcontainer/coverlet.msbuild/index.json). Threshold semantics confirmed in coverlet's MSBuildIntegration.md: `/p:Threshold=80` "will automatically fail the build if the line, branch or method coverage of any of the instrumented modules falls below 80%", narrowable with `/p:ThresholdType=line`. Forward-compatibility note: coverlet.msbuild depends on VSTest MSBuild targets and does not function under Microsoft Testing Platform (per Microsoft Learn's MTP coverage page); if you ever migrate test projects to MTP, switch to coverlet.MTP 10.0.1 or use `Microsoft.Testing.Extensions.CodeCoverage`.
recommended_checks.effort_hours: 12-20 (one-off) + ~1/month
recommended_checks.rationale_for_two_person_team: This is the only coverage-adjacent item I would block launch on, and note carefully what is being gated: the existence and passing of a named suite over your highest-consequence code path, with a high coverage floor on two or three assemblies — NOT a repository-wide percentage. The brief states cross-tenant leakage is the highest-consequence failure mode and that tenancy resolves from the Host header alone; a global 80% number gives you no assurance whatsoever about that specific path, because the metric averages your riskiest code together with your CRUD. This is also the one place where the 'no data yet, destructive testing is safe' window is a genuine asset — write the tests that deliberately try to cross the boundary while there is no real PHI to leak. If you only do one thing from this entire area before going public, do this one and skip the percentages.

recommended_checks.what_it_does: A nightly or weekly scheduled workflow on main that produces the absolute coverage number for both stacks, publishes the HTML report as an artifact and writes a one-line summary to the job summary. Never blocks anything. Optionally uses ReportGenerator's `MarkdownDeltaSummary` with a `-historydir` so you can see direction over time.
recommended_checks.tool: ReportGenerator 5.5.11 with -historydir, on a GitHub Actions schedule trigger
recommended_checks.tool_maintained_evidence: dotnet-reportgenerator-globaltool 5.5.11 published 2026-07-27; history/delta report types documented in the upstream README. Runs on .NET 8/9/10.
recommended_checks.rationale_for_two_person_team: Absolute coverage is worth KNOWING and not worth GATING — this is precisely Google's position ("a low code coverage number does guarantee that large areas of the product are going completely untested") combined with Inozemtseva & Holmes' finding that it is not a valid quality target. Running it on a schedule rather than per-PR also keeps it off your critical path: it never makes a PR slower and it never fails a merge, so there is nothing to bypass. The trend line is what you show a customer's security reviewer or a future auditor; the number itself is not a promise you have to keep.

recommended_checks.what_it_does: Weekly Stryker.NET run scoped to the tenant-resolution, authorization and file-upload projects only. Mutation testing modifies the code (flipping comparisons, removing statements) and reports which mutants your tests failed to kill — i.e. which covered lines are covered but not actually asserted on. Advisory report only; triage findings into normal backlog.
recommended_checks.tool: dotnet-stryker 4.16.0 (Stryker.NET)
recommended_checks.tool_maintained_evidence: dotnet-stryker 4.16.0 published 2026-07-03, with 4.15.0 on 2026-06-23 and 4.14.2 on 2026-05-18 — three releases in the last three months (https://api.nuget.org/v3-flatcontainer/dotnet-stryker/index.json). Sibling project @stryker-mutator/core 10.0.0 published 2026-08-14 (npm registry) confirms the wider project is active.
recommended_checks.effort_hours: 6-8 (one-off) + ~2/quarter
recommended_checks.rationale_for_two_person_team: Google names this directly as the answer to the question coverage cannot answer: "A better technique to assess whether you're adequately exercising the lines your tests cover, and adequately asserting on failures, is mutation testing." It is also the single strongest defence against the gaming your patch-coverage gate will otherwise incentivise — a test that executes a line without asserting anything scores 100% patch coverage and kills zero mutants. The reason this is scoped and scheduled rather than a gate: mutation runs are slow (they re-run the suite once per mutant) and the report needs human triage. Point it at two or three assemblies, run it Sunday night, spend thirty minutes on Monday. Do not point it at the whole solution and do not put it in the PR path. If you are short on time this is the first check to defer — it is the highest-value optional item, not a required one.

not_worth_it_here: A repository-wide absolute coverage gate at 80% (or any meaningful number). At a larger company this is a standard merge requirement backed by a platform team who spent a quarter getting the codebase there first. Here it is unachievable on day one on an inherited ABP Commercial codebase, so it would be set to whatever you happen to have today (say 34%), which gates nothing, or set aspirationally, which blocks every PR until someone adds `continue-on-error` and everyone stops looking. Inozemtseva & Holmes give you the citation to decline it; Sonar's own Clean-as-You-Code rationale gives you the alternative.

Buying SonarQube Cloud Team or SonarQube Server Developer Edition purely for the coverage gate. The Clean-as-You-Code new-code model is genuinely the right model and Sonar's tooling for it is excellent, but this codebase (~80k LoC) exceeds the free plan's 50k-LoC private-project cap and Community Build has no PR analysis at all, so adopting it means a paid tier. `diff-cover` implements the same gating idea for free, on both stacks, with no data leaving GitHub. If you later buy Sonar it should be for the taint analysis and SAST on a public-internet PHI app, not for the coverage number — evaluate that as a security decision in the SAST workstream, not this one.

Codecov's `project` status as a required gate (as opposed to `patch`). Larger orgs run both and treat a project-coverage drop as a blocking regression. With two devs and a codebase whose baseline is about to move a lot, project status with `target: auto` will fail PRs for reasons unrelated to the PR — a refactor that deletes well-covered code lowers the ratio and blocks the merge. If you adopt Codecov at all, run `patch` only and set `project` to `informational: true`.

Mutation testing as a pull-request gate. Standard at companies with dedicated test-infrastructure engineers and a build farm. Here the runtime alone (a full suite re-run per mutant) makes it a non-starter in the PR path, and the output needs human triage rather than a pass/fail. Scheduled, scoped to two or three assemblies, is the version that survives contact with a two-person team.

100% branch coverage, MC/DC, or path coverage. These are real standards — MC/DC is mandated by DO-178C for Level A avionics, and FDA's guidance catalogues condition, multi-condition, loop and path coverage as criteria. None of them apply to a scheduling portal, and FDA itself notes that "Because of the very large number of possible paths through a software program, path coverage is generally not achievable." Do not let a HIPAA conversation drift into aerospace-grade structural coverage; the regulator that comes closest to caring says the amount should be commensurate with risk.

Per-file or per-directory coverage policies, CODEOWNERS-scoped coverage rules, and coverage-based review routing. These solve a coordination problem that appears at maybe fifteen engineers. With two people who both touch everything, the config is pure overhead and will drift out of date within a month.

Merging unit, integration and E2E coverage into one aggregate figure. Google says the aggregate view across the pipeline "is paramount" and they are right in principle — but instrumenting a running ASP.NET Core host for E2E coverage collection, merging it with unit coverage across two languages, and keeping the source-path mapping correct is multi-week work that breaks on every upgrade. Revisit when you have a third engineer.

Standing up your own SonarQube Server instance to dodge the licensing. Community Build cannot do PR analysis, so you would get an absolute-coverage dashboard you already decided not to gate on, plus a server to patch and back up. That is infrastructure work, which is out of scope here anyway, in exchange for less capability than the free `diff-cover` path.

A coverage badge in the README. Zero engineering value, non-trivial plumbing on a private repo, and it invites exactly the 'what's our number' conversation you want to replace with 'what's our patch coverage and what isn't tested'.
surprises: The obvious plan — 'enable SonarCloud free, turn on Clean as You Code' — fails on day one at your size, and nothing in the documentation says so up front. SonarQube Cloud's Free plan caps PRIVATE projects at 50k LoC with a 5-member limit and only main-branch analysis; you are at roughly 80k LoC across C# and TypeScript. Self-hosting does not rescue it, because SonarQube Server Community Build has no branch or pull request analysis at all — that starts at Developer Edition, per Sonar's own edition comparison. Every '80% coverage on new code is the 2026 standard' article assumes a tier this project does not qualify for.

The '80% industry standard' is two different numbers wearing the same label. Sonar's 80.0% is coverage of NEW CODE ONLY. Google's 60/75/90 is WHOLE-PROJECT. Angular's 80 is a whole-project karma-coverage `check.global` example. Anyone who quotes '80%' without naming the denominator is silently conflating a demanding per-PR bar with a moderate repo-wide bar. When you write your policy, state the denominator in the first sentence — that one clause is the difference between a rule you can keep and one you will bypass.

Sonar cannot read LCOV for C# and cannot read Cobertura for TypeScript. C# needs `sonar.cs.opencover.reportsPaths`, `sonar.cs.cobertura.reportsPaths` or `sonar.cs.vscoveragexml.reportsPaths`; TypeScript accepts LCOV only, via `sonar.javascript.lcov.reportPaths` (the old `sonar.typescript.lcov.reportPaths` is deprecated). Worse, plenty of 2020-2022 advice still insists OpenCover is the ONLY valid C# input; Cobertura is now documented as supported. Configure the wrong parameter and you do not get an error — you get 0% coverage and a green build, which is the most dangerous possible outcome for a gate. Emit both formats in one pass with `dotnet test --collect:"XPlat Code Coverage;Format=cobertura,opencover"`.

Microsoft's own next-generation coverage collector cannot emit LCOV. Under Microsoft Testing Platform, `Microsoft.Testing.Extensions.CodeCoverage` supports only `coverage`, `xml` and `cobertura`. And `coverlet.msbuild` does not work under MTP at all, because MTP does not invoke the VSTest MSBuild targets it depends on — it collects nothing, quietly. There is also a hard version-pinning table (CodeCoverage 18.1.x ↔ MTP 2.0.x, 18.0.x ↔ MTP 1.8.x) and `IncludeTestAssembly` flipped its default from true to false versus VSTest, which will move your number when you migrate. ABP 10 is on VSTest today so nothing is broken now, but this is precisely how a coverage gate silently zeroes itself during an SDK bump.

The most widely recommended GitHub Action for .NET coverage PR comments, irongut/CodeCoverageSummary, has had no commit since 20 October 2022 — nearly four years. For a private repo about to hold PHI, an unmaintained third-party action holding a token with write access to your pull requests is a supply-chain finding, not a staleness annoyance. The maintained alternative is better anyway and needs no marketplace action at all: ReportGenerator's `MarkdownSummaryGithub` report type plus `gh pr comment --edit-last --create-if-none --body-file`, which is the pattern in the ReportGenerator author's own action README. (For contrast: danielpalme/ReportGenerator-GitHub-Action last committed 2026-07-27, davelosert/vitest-coverage-report-action 2026-08-25, codecov/codecov-action 2026-06-06.)

Your Angular test runner is formally dead and the coverage flags are being renamed under you. Karma's own README says "Karma is deprecated and is not accepting new features or general bug fixes"; karma-coverage's last release was 2023-06-23. Angular 20 still defaults to Karma, but Angular's current docs have moved to Vitest and renamed everything: `--code-coverage` becomes `--coverage`, `codeCoverageExclude` becomes `--coverage-exclude`, `--coverage-reporters` appears with lcov/cobertura/json-summary values, and karma-coverage's `check.global` block becomes `coverageThresholds`. Any coverage scripting you write against Karma today gets rewritten at the v21/v22 upgrade — so make the output file path and format the CI contract, and keep the `ng test` invocation to one substitutable line.

ABP will make your absolute number meaningless in both directions if you do not tune the denominator. Generated Angular service proxies land in `src/app/proxy/**`; EF Core migrations, ABP-generated DTOs and the entity layer are almost entirely auto-properties. coverlet excludes `[ExcludeFromCodeCoverage]` and `ExcludeFromCoverage` by default and NOTHING else, so all of that generated bulk sits in your denominator. `SkipAutoProps=true`, `ExcludeByAttribute=GeneratedCodeAttribute,CompilerGeneratedAttribute`, `ExcludeByFile` globs for migrations, and `sonar.coverage.exclusions` for the proxies are prerequisites for the number meaning anything — configure exclusions BEFORE you pick a threshold, or you will pick a number calibrated to noise.

FDA's definition of 'coverage' is not the industry's. Verbatim: "Use of the term 'coverage' usually means 100% coverage. For example, if a testing program has achieved 'statement coverage,' it means that 100% of the statements in the software have been executed at least once." So in a regulated-language document, 'we have statement coverage' asserts something far stronger than 'our statement coverage is 78%'. If you ever produce a validation or assurance document for a customer, that wording distinction is a real liability — say 'statement coverage of 78%', never 'we have statement coverage'.

The number you write down becomes the number you are audited against, and no regulator supplies one. The HIPAA Security Rule text contains the word 'coverage' zero times; ASVS 5.0.0 has no coverage requirement; SSDF PW.8 has none. So the auditable artifact is not compliance with an external threshold — it is your own written policy plus evidence you actually follow it. That inverts the usual instinct: picking a high number to look rigorous creates an obligation you will visibly fail, while picking a modest number you genuinely hold every single PR is the stronger evidentiary position. Write down the number you can keep.

Diff coverage has a blind spot nobody mentions: it says nothing about code you did not touch. A PR at 100% patch coverage can still ship on top of a completely untested Host-header tenant-resolution path, because that path is not in the diff. This is the structural reason the tenant-isolation suite has to be its own separate, deliberately-written check rather than something you expect a percentage gate to produce as a side effect. Relatedly, a PR that only deletes code or only touches non-instrumented files has no new lines to measure and passes trivially — correct behaviour, but do not mistake a green diff-coverage check for evidence that anything was tested.

`dotnet-coverage` started collecting telemetry in version 18.10.0 (published 2026-08-12), recording which commands you run and which options you set, with an opt-out documented by Microsoft. Harmless in itself — it does not transmit source — but it is the kind of question that lands in a customer security questionnaire ('what build tooling transmits data outbound?'), and knowing the answer before you are asked is worth the five minutes. `coverlet` has no equivalent.

There is a genuinely free tool that does the whole 2026 diff-coverage standard across both your stacks, and almost nobody recommends it because it looks like a Python-ecosystem tool. `diff-cover` (Apache-2.0) reads Cobertura, Clover, JaCoCo XML AND LCOV, takes `--compare-branch=origin/main` and `--fail-under=80`, and emits `--format markdown:report.md` for a PR comment. Version 10.5.1 shipped 2026-08-16, with five releases in the preceding five weeks. One tool, both languages, no account, no per-seat cost, and no source code or coverage data leaving GitHub — which for a PHI-adjacent private repo is a security property, not just a convenience.
disagreements: Fowler vs Google on the top of the range. Fowler expects "upper 80s or 90s" as the natural by-product of thoughtful testing and treats 100% as suspicious. Google says project-wide goals "above 90% are most likely not worth it" but that "per-commit coverage goals of 99% are reasonable". These are reconcilable once you notice they are talking about different denominators (whole-project vs per-change), but the headline numbers look contradictory and are frequently quoted against each other. If someone cites 'Fowler says 90%' at you, ask which denominator.

Academic finding vs vendor default, and it is a real conflict. Inozemtseva & Holmes conclude coverage "should not be used as a quality target because it is not a good indicator of test suite effectiveness." Sonar ships an 80% coverage target as the default condition of its default quality gate, and has done so for years. Sonar's implicit defence is that the target applies to new code only and is paired with issue, hotspot and duplication conditions — a scope the 2014 study did not examine. I do not think either side is wrong, but nobody should present '80% on new code' as evidence-backed; it is a vendor default that has become a convention, and the strongest empirical evidence available argues against coverage targets in general. Say that out loud in your policy doc rather than pretending the research endorses the number.

Google's 60% 'acceptable' vs the near-universal 80% convention. This is a 20-point spread between the largest published corporate guidance and the de facto default, and it is almost entirely a denominator artefact — Google's 60/75/90 is whole-project, the 80% convention is Sonar's new-code condition. But note that even on new code Google would put the bar HIGHER than Sonar (90% lower threshold, 99% reasonable). So depending on which source you cite and which denominator you mean, 'the standard' is anywhere from 60% to 99%. There is no reconciling this into a single number, which is itself the answer to the question the brief asked.

Whether Cobertura is a valid Sonar input for C#. Current Sonar documentation lists `sonar.cs.cobertura.reportsPaths` as supported and shows a coverlet `-f=cobertura` example. A large body of community advice and older documentation states that OpenCover is required and that Cobertura will not be read. Both were true at different times. The failure mode is silent (0% coverage, green build), so verify empirically on your first run by checking that Sonar reports a non-zero figure for a file you know is tested — do not trust either source blind.

Whether coverage thresholds belong in the test runner or in CI. coverlet (`/p:Threshold`) and karma-coverage (`check.global`) both enforce absolute thresholds by failing the test command itself; Sonar, Codecov and diff-cover enforce at the CI/PR layer against a diff. Both approaches are documented as normal by their respective first-party sources. They pull in opposite directions: runner-level thresholds are absolute and fail locally (good feedback, wrong metric), CI-level gates are diff-based and only fail in the pipeline (right metric, later feedback). My recommendation splits them deliberately — runner-level thresholds ONLY as a high floor on the two or three tenant-isolation and authorization assemblies, diff-based gating for everything else — but be aware that is a judgement call reconciling two legitimate conventions, not a settled standard.

verification.area: Code coverage thresholds, coverage tooling, and regulatory coverage requirements for a 2026 CI/security standard
material_errors: CLAIM 12 IS A MATERIAL ERROR. The claim says coverlet 'can emit every format this project needs from a single test run AND can fail the build on a threshold', citing VSTestIntegration.md for both. That page explicitly contradicts the threshold half twice: 'At the moment VSTest integration **doesn't support all features** of msbuild and .NET tool, for instance show result on console, report merging and threshold validation' and 'Feature parity with other modes is partial (for example, threshold validation and built-in merge are not provided by this integration mode).' The /p:CollectCoverage=true /p:Threshold=80 quote is from a DIFFERENT document (MSBuildIntegration.md). The two capabilities belong to two mutually exclusive coverlet integration modes and cannot be obtained from one `dotnet test --collect:"XPlat Code Coverage"` run. Any CI design built on this claim will silently not enforce its threshold.

CLAIM 9 LOC METHODOLOGY IS WRONG AND THE CONCLUSION MAY REVERSE. The claim compares a raw ~80k line count against Sonar's 50k cap. The cited page states Sonar's LOC calculation EXCLUDES 'Test code. Files excluded from analysis. Code in unsupported languages. Comments or blank lines.' A raw wc-style count typically overstates Sonar LOC by 40-60%, so ~80k raw lines may well fall UNDER the 50k cap. The cap also applies only to PRIVATE projects ('Analysis of public projects: unlimited number of projects'). The claim's headline conclusion 'it exceeds the free private-project cap' is not established.

CLAIM 12/9/10/15/16/17 CITATION HYGIENE: six claims attach quotes to URLs that do not contain them. Most consequential: claim 17 cites an eCFR HIPAA API endpoint as the source for assertions about OWASP ASVS 5.0.0 and NIST SP 800-218 (it can support neither); claim 9 cites a SonarQube CLOUD subscription page for a quote about self-hosted SonarQube SERVER Community Build vs Developer Edition, and that verbatim sentence does not appear on the current editions page either.

CLAIM 8 CITES A DEPRECATED PARAMETER AS A CURRENT DEFAULT. The claim lists `base: auto` among Codecov's patch/project defaults. The cited page annotates that parameter '[Deprecated as of July 2020 -- Codecov's product roadmap includes a novel way to manually pick base of pull requests]'. It should not appear in a 2026 standard.

results.claim: Google testing guidance: no ideal coverage number; 60% acceptable / 75% commendable / 90% exemplary as non-binding guidelines; plus the 'checkbox' warning
results.evidence_quote: Although there is no "ideal code coverage number," at Google we offer the general guidelines of 60% as "acceptable", 75% as "commendable" and 90% as "exemplary." However we like to stay away from broad top-down mandates and encourage every team to select the value that makes sense for their business needs. ... Be mindful that engineers may start treating your target like a checkbox and avoid increasing coverage beyond the target, even if doing so would be prudent.
results.correction: none

results.claim: Google separates project-wide from per-commit goals: >90% project-wide not worth it, 99% per-commit reasonable, 90% a good lower threshold; names mutation testing; low coverage DOES guarantee untested areas
results.evidence_quote: While project wide goals above 90% are most likely not worth it, per-commit coverage goals of 99% are reasonable, and 90% is a good lower threshold. ... A better technique to assess whether you're adequately exercising the lines your tests cover, and adequately asserting on failures, is mutation testing. ... But a low code coverage number does guarantee that large areas of the product are going completely untested by automation on every single deployment.
results.correction: none

results.claim: Largest empirical study concludes coverage should not be used as a quality target; 31,000 suites, five Java systems, up to 724,000 LOC, mutation-tested
results.evidence_quote: we generated 31,000 test suites for five systems consisting of up to 724,000 lines of source code ... Our results suggest that coverage, while useful for identifying under-tested parts of a program, should not be used as a quality target because it is not a good indicator of test suite effectiveness.
results.correction: none

results.claim: Fowler: <50% trouble; upper 80s/90s expected by-product; 100% suspicious; warns against '87% coverage' mandates; Marick quote
results.evidence_quote: Certainly low coverage numbers, say below half, are a sign of trouble. ... I would expect a coverage percentage in the upper 80s or 90s. ... I would be suspicious of anything like 100% ... "I expect a high level of coverage. Sometimes managers require one. There's a subtle difference."
results.correction: Cosmetic only: Fowler writes "below half", not the numeral "50%". Substance is exact.

results.claim: SonarQube default read-only built-in gate 'Sonar way' has four new-code-only conditions incl. coverage >= 80.0% and duplication <= 3.0%
results.evidence_quote: It is provided by Sonar, activated by default, and read-only. ... New code test coverage is greater than or equal to 80.0% ... Duplication in the new code is less than or equal to 3.0%
results.correction: none

results.claim: Sonar's published rationale for the new-code model ('Clean as You Code') is cost avoidance on legacy, per two verbatim quotes
results.evidence_quote: When you add new code to your projects, you usually touch a portion of the old code in the process. As a consequence, analyzing and cleaning new code allows you to fix issues in your old code and gradually improve the overall quality of your codebase.
results.correction: Only the SECOND quote is on this page (and it begins 'As a consequence, analyzing and cleaning...'). The first quote -- 'focuses on keeping high quality standards for new code, rather than spending a lot of effort remediating old code' -- does NOT appear anywhere on this page. The phrase 'Clean as You Code' also does not appear on this page; the page is titled 'Quality standards and new code'. Drop the first quote or find its real source. Also correct the stated mechanism: the page defines new code as 'code that you've recently added or modified' and the remediation effect comes from touching old code incidentally while adding new -- not from whole files flipping to 'new code' status.

results.claim: 'Sonar way for agentic AI' gate shipped 2026 with six new-code conditions; replaces 'Sonar way for AI code'; coverage >= 80%, duplication <= 3%
results.evidence_quote: The quality gate enforces six conditions on new code ... 5. Coverage on new code is greater or equal to 80%. 6. Duplication on new code is less or equal to 3% ... The Sonar way for agentic AI quality gate replaces the Sonar way for AI code quality gate.
results.correction: Thresholds and the replacement statement are exact. Two fixes: (a) the page carries NO ship date -- delete 'in 2026' or source it elsewhere; (b) the claim quotes only the legacy 'Type' phrasing and omits the primary software-quality phrasing, which uses different severity words: 'No new Reliability issues with severity greater or equal to Low', 'No new Security issues with severity greater or equal to Low', 'No new Maintainability issues with severity greater or equal to Medium'. Also note the Dependency Risks condition requires an Enterprise plan and is skipped (grayed out) otherwise, so on non-Enterprise plans the gate effectively enforces five conditions.

results.claim: Codecov patch vs project status checks with defaults target auto / threshold 0% / base auto / if_ci_failed error (patch) and threshold 5 (project); informational:true makes it non-blocking
results.evidence_quote: [Deprecated as of July 2020 -- Codecov's product roadmap includes a novel way to manually pick base of pull requests]
results.correction: The patch/project descriptions and the informational quote are verbatim correct. But: (1) `base` is documented on this very page as '[Deprecated as of July 2020]' -- remove it from a 2026 standard; (2) the values `threshold: 0%` (patch) and `threshold: 5` (project) appear only inside illustrative YAML blocks, not as documented defaults. Only `target: auto` ('This is the default') and `if_ci_failed` ('the default is error') are stated as defaults on the page. Restate as: 'example configuration shows patch threshold 0% and project threshold 5; documented defaults are target: auto and if_ci_failed: error.'

results.claim: SonarQube Cloud Free: 50k LOC private, 5 members, main-branch only; repo ~80k LoC exceeds cap; self-hosted Community Build lacks branch/PR analysis (Developer Edition minimum)
results.evidence_quote: Analysis of private projects: Up to 50k LOC | Maximum number of organization members: 5 | Branch analysis: Only main branch analysis | Pull request analysis: Only if the target branch is the main branch ... During calculation, the following are excluded from your LOC count: Test code. Files excluded from analysis. Code in unsupported languages. Comments or blank lines.
results.correction: The Free-plan limits are exactly right. Three errors: (1) The 'Developer Edition' sentence is NOT on this page -- this is a SonarQube CLOUD page and says nothing about self-hosted Community Build; the verbatim sentence quoted does not appear on the current SonarQube Server editions page either, which instead says Developer Edition 'Adds branch/PR analysis, more languages, and stronger security on top of SonarQube Community Build' (https://docs.sonarsource.com/sonarqube-server/discovering/sonarqube-server-editions.md). Substance holds; the quote does not. (2) The ~80k figure is not comparable to the 50k cap -- Sonar excludes test code, comments and blank lines, so a raw line count materially overstates Sonar LOC; recompute with those exclusions before concluding the cap is exceeded. (3) The cap applies to PRIVATE projects only; public projects are unlimited on Free. Separately, the ~53k C# / ~27k TS figures could not be checked: the working directory contains zero .cs and zero .ts/.tsx files.

results.claim: Sonar coverage report format params: C# opencover/cobertura/vscoveragexml/dotcover reportsPaths (ncover3 deprecated); TypeScript LCOV only via sonar.javascript.lcov.reportPaths; sonar.coverage.exclusions removes generated code from the denominator
results.evidence_quote: sonar.cs.opencover.reportsPaths ... sonar.cs.cobertura.reportsPaths ... sonar.cs.vscoveragexml.reportsPaths ... sonar.cs.dotcover.reportsPaths ... The parameter `sonar.cs.ncover3.reportsPaths` was formerly used for or NCover3 . This parameter has been deprecated.
results.correction: All C# parameter claims verified on this URL, including the ncover3 deprecation. But the TypeScript and exclusions material is not on this .NET page. Cite instead: the LCOV quotes ('SonarQube Cloud directly supports all coverage tools that produce reports in the LCOV format' and 'The parameter sonar.typescript.lcov.reportPaths was formerly used for TypeScript coverage. This parameter has been deprecated.') are at .../test-coverage/javascript-typescript-test-coverage.md. sonar.coverage.exclusions is documented at .../setting-analysis-scope/exclude-from-coverage-duplication.md, and its actual wording is 'Defines the source files to be excluded from the code coverage analysis' -- not the phrasing quoted in the claim.

results.claim: Microsoft Learn documents coverlet + ReportGenerator as the supported cross-platform .NET coverage path; dotnet test --collect:"XPlat Code Coverage" emits coverage.cobertura.xml to TestResults; built-in collector emits a binary .coverage needing dotnet-coverage conversion
results.evidence_quote: a resulting coverage.cobertura.xml file is output to the TestResults directory ... This is a cross-platform option that relies on the .NET CLI, and it is great for build systems where MSBuild isn't available. ... This data collector generates a binary .coverage file ... The binary file isn't human-readable, and it must be converted to a human-readable format before it can be used to generate reports outside of Visual Studio. ... dotnet tool install -g dotnet-reportgenerator-globaltool

results.claim: coverlet can emit every needed format from a single test run AND fail the build on a threshold (/p:Threshold=80, /p:ThresholdType=line), per VSTestIntegration.md
results.evidence_quote: :warning:At the moment VSTest integration **doesn't support all features** of msbuild and .NET tool, for instance show result on console, report merging and threshold validation. ... Feature parity with other modes is partial (for example, threshold validation and built-in merge are not provided by this integration mode).
results.correction: MATERIAL ERROR -- split the claim in two. VSTestIntegration.md (cited URL) supports ONLY the format half: 'The supported formats are lcov, opencover, cobertura, teamcity, json (default coverlet proprietary format)', `dotnet test --collect:"XPlat Code Coverage;Format=json,lcov,cobertura"`, and the exclusion options (ExcludeByAttribute -- 'Default is no additional attributes, but ExcludeFromCoverageAttribute and ExcludeFromCodeCoverageAttribute are always excluded' -- ExcludeByFile globs, SkipAutoProps). The SAME page states twice that this mode does NOT do threshold validation. The threshold text ('will automatically fail the build if the line, branch or method coverage of any of the instrumented modules falls below 80%', /p:ThresholdType=line|branch|method, /p:ThresholdStat=Minimum|Total|Average) lives in a different document: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/coverlet-coverage/coverlet/master/Documentation/MSBuildIntegration.md. Corrected claim: coverlet's VSTest/collector mode emits multiple formats but enforces no threshold; coverlet's MSBuild mode (coverlet.msbuild, /p:CollectCoverage=true) enforces thresholds. You cannot get both from one --collect run -- enforce the threshold in a separate step (e.g. ReportGenerator or a CI gate) if you stay on the collector.
