research.area: Static Application Security Testing (SAST) configuration and gating — SonarQube Cloud quality gates, GitHub CodeQL, in-compiler Roslyn analyzers, and suppression governance for a .NET 10 / Angular 20 multi-tenant PHI application
research.standard_summary: The 2026 standard is three-layered, not one-tool. Layer one is in-compiler analysis that is already paid for: .NET SDK Roslyn analyzers are on by default for .NET 5+ targets, but in `Default` analysis mode "only a small number of rules are enabled as build warnings" and the taint rules that matter here (CA3001 SQL injection, CA3002 XSS) are explicitly "Enabled by default in .NET 10: No". Layer two is a semantic whole-program SAST — CodeQL — where the meaningful configuration decision is `default` vs `security-extended` query suite; those suites are defined by a precision filter (`default` = precision high/very-high, security-extended adds precision medium, both filtered to `problem.severity` error/warning and `tags contain security`), and for C# that means 54 queries vs 64. Layer three is SonarQube Cloud, whose built-in read-only "Sonar way" gate applies four conditions to *new code only* — no new issues, 100% of new Security Hotspots reviewed, new-code coverage ≥ 80.0%, new-code duplication ≤ 3.0% — with a documented "fudge factor" waiving coverage and duplication until 20 new lines exist. On gating, no authority requires a hard block: NIST SSDF PW.7.2 requires that analysis be performed and that all discovered issues be "record[ed] and triage[d] ... in the development team's workflow or issue tracking system," and OWASP's DevSecOps Verification Standard DSOVS-CODE-004 Level 2 accepts "fail *or flag*" a build. SonarSource states the gate "can be used to block the merge of the pull request," and GitHub's code scanning check fails only on severity `error`, `critical` or `high` by default. Suppressions are the weak point: Sonar "ignores accepted issues in the quality reports and ratings," so a green gate is silent about suppressed risk, and Sonar's own docs say issue-ignore multicriteria should be configured in the UI and that the CI/CD-properties route "is not documented in this guide."

standards.claim: The built-in "Sonar way" quality gate contains exactly four conditions, all scoped to new code: no new issues are introduced; all new Security Hotspots are reviewed; new code test coverage >= 80.0%; duplication in new code <= 3.0%. It is provided by Sonar, activated by default, and read-only (not editable).
standards.threshold: 4 conditions; new-code coverage >= 80.0%; new-code duplicated lines <= 3.0%; new Security Hotspots reviewed = 100%
standards.source_name: Sonar Documentation — Understanding quality gates (SonarQube Server, current)
standards.notes: The two Sonar pages disagree on wording — see disagreements. The Cloud page still describes the older rating-based framing (Reliability A / Security A / Maintainability A) alongside the coverage and duplication numbers; the current Server page states the consolidated "No new issues are introduced". The numeric thresholds (80.0% / 3.0%) are identical on both.

standards.claim: The Sonar way gate applies a "fudge factor": duplication conditions are waived until at least 20 new lines are added, and coverage conditions are waived until at least 20 new lines to cover exist. Small pull requests therefore pass the coverage and duplication conditions without meeting them.
standards.threshold: 20 new lines (duplication); 20 new lines to cover (coverage)
standards.source_name: Sonar Documentation — Understanding quality gates (SonarQube Server, current)
standards.notes: Confirmed on the current Server docs page. I did not find the same paragraph restated on the SonarQube Cloud page, so I have not cross-verified that Cloud applies the identical 20-line threshold.

standards.claim: SonarQube Cloud supports four new code definitions: Previous version, Number of days, Specific version, Specific date (plus reference-branch comparison for branches). "Previous version" means the start date is the date of the first analysis performed for the current project version, as determined by the `sonar.projectVersion` property supplied at analysis time. Only Previous version and Number of days can be set at organization level; Specific version and Specific date are project-level or Web API only.
standards.threshold: Number of days default 30, maximum 90; Previous version keys off `sonar.projectVersion`
standards.source_name: Sonar Documentation — Quality standards and new code (SonarQube Cloud)
standards.notes: Practical consequence for this team: `previous_version` is a trap unless CI actually increments `sonar.projectVersion` on every release. If the version string never changes, the new-code window silently grows until it spans the whole project history and the gate stops meaning anything. For a team that does not cut versioned releases on a fixed cadence, reference-branch (compare to `main`) is the safer definition.

standards.claim: SonarSource's documented guidance is that quality gate conditions must use differential (new code) values, not absolute values, and that the recommended gate is the built-in Sonar way, which "focuses on keeping high quality standards for new code, rather than spending a lot of effort remediating old code." SonarSource states the gate result "can be used to block the merge of the pull request if the quality gate fails" and "can be used to fail your CI pipeline" — it is stated as a capability, not as a mandate.
standards.threshold: n/a — differential values only; blocking is described as optional
standards.source_name: Sonar Documentation — Quality gates (SonarQube Server 10.8)
standards.notes: Direct quote from the 10.8 page: "Quality gate conditions must use differential values. For example, there's no point in checking an absolute value such as: Number of Lines of Code is greater than 1000." I could not find any SonarSource page that says a gate SHOULD block a PR — only that it CAN. Anyone claiming SonarSource mandates blocking is overstating the source.

standards.claim: CodeQL's `default` and `security-extended` query suites are defined by metadata filters, not curated lists. `default` selects queries with `precision` in {high, very-high}, `problem.severity` in {error, warning}, and `tags contain security`. `security-extended` selects that same set PLUS queries with `precision` medium and `problem.severity` in {error, warning} tagged security. Both exclude deprecated and `experimental/` queries.
standards.threshold: default = precision high|very-high; security-extended adds precision medium; both require problem.severity error|warning and tag security
standards.source_name: github/codeql repository — misc/suite-helpers/code-scanning-selectors.yml and security-extended-selectors.yml
standards.notes: This is the actual mechanism, read from the source of truth in the CodeQL repo, and it makes the false-positive tradeoff quantifiable rather than vague: security-extended adds exactly the medium-precision tier. The language-level suite files (e.g. csharp/ql/src/codeql-suites/csharp-security-extended.qls) are two-line files that `apply` these shared selectors.

standards.claim: CodeQL's documented false-positive posture: "The queries in the `default` query suite are highly precise and return few false positive code scanning results." `security-extended` "consists of all the queries in the `default` query suite, plus additional queries with slightly lower precision and severity" and "may return a greater number of false positive code scanning results." The `@precision` metadata property "[i]ndicates the percentage of query results that are true positives," with allowed values low, medium, high, very-high.
standards.threshold: @precision allowed values: low | medium | high | very-high; @problem.severity: error | warning | recommendation; @security-severity: 0.0-10.0
standards.source_name: GitHub Docs — CodeQL query suites; CodeQL docs — Metadata for CodeQL queries
standards.notes: GitHub publishes no numeric false-positive rate. "Highly precise" and "few false positives" are the strongest claims made. Anyone quoting a percentage FP rate for CodeQL is not quoting GitHub.

standards.claim: For C#, CodeQL ships 64 built-in queries across both suites: 54 in `default`, with 10 additional queries available only in `security-extended`. The security-extended-only queries include Missing function level access control (CWE-285/284/862), Insecure Direct Object Reference (CWE-639), Use of file upload (CWE-434), Missing XML validation (CWE-112), Insecure SQL connection (CWE-327), Empty password in configuration file (CWE-258/862), Serialization check bypass (CWE-020), Value shadowing (CWE-348), and two thread-unsafe ICryptoTransform queries (CWE-362).
standards.threshold: 64 total C# queries; 54 in default; 10 security-extended-only
standards.source_name: GitHub Docs — CodeQL queries for C# (built-in queries reference)
standards.notes: This is the single most consequential finding in this area for this application. The three queries that map directly to the new risk surface — missing authorization on an endpoint, IDOR, and file upload — are ALL excluded from the default suite. Default setup uses `default`. Enabling CodeQL and leaving it on the default suite would miss exactly the class of bug that going public with anonymous registration, self-service roles and document upload creates.

standards.claim: Running CodeQL code scanning on a PRIVATE repository requires a paid GitHub Code Security / Advanced Security license. "To enable code scanning for private or internal repositories, you must upgrade to GitHub Team or GitHub Enterprise with GitHub Code Security." GitHub Free and GitHub Pro can use code scanning only on public repositories.
standards.threshold: GitHub Team or Enterprise + GitHub Code Security (Advanced Security) required for private repos
standards.source_name: GitHub Docs — Cannot enable CodeQL in a private repository
standards.notes: Licensing availability, not cost — I am flagging that the tool may simply not be switch-on-able, which is a tool-selection fact. If the org is on GitHub Team without Code Security purchased, every CodeQL recommendation in this report is blocked until that changes, and Semgrep CE becomes the fallback.

standards.claim: GitHub's code scanning pull request check fails only on high-severity findings by default: "If the code scanning results check finds any problems with a severity of `error`, `critical`, or `high`, the check fails." The check is named "Code scanning results". Alerts carry a level of Error, Warning or Note; CodeQL security alerts additionally carry a security severity of Critical, High, Medium or Low.
standards.threshold: Default check failure on: severity `error`, or security severity `critical` or `high`. Check name: "Code scanning results"
standards.source_name: GitHub Docs — Triage code scanning alerts in pull requests; Code scanning alerts
standards.notes: Cross-checked against the GHES 3.11 page, which words it as "the check fails only if one or more alerts of severity `error`, or security severity `critical` or `high` are detected". Medium and low findings are informational by default — which is the right default for a two-person team and should NOT be tightened.

standards.claim: GitHub code scanning merge protection via rulesets is explicitly NOT the same mechanism as a required status check: "Merge protection with rulesets is not related to status checks." A ruleset blocks a merge when a required tool finds an alert at or above a configured severity, when a required tool's analysis is still in progress, or when a required tool is not configured for the repository. Severity options are Alerts: None / Errors / Errors and Warnings / All; Security alerts: None / Critical / High or higher / Medium or higher / All. It does not apply to merge queue groups or to Dependabot pull requests analyzed by default setup.
standards.threshold: Ruleset option values — Alerts: None|Errors|Errors and Warnings|All; Security alerts: None|Critical|High or higher|Medium or higher|All
standards.source_name: GitHub Docs — Code scanning merge protection; Set merge protection
standards.notes: The "required tool is not configured" condition is the valuable one: it fails closed if someone deletes or renames the CodeQL workflow, which a plain required status check does not do (a deleted check just never reports and, depending on config, can leave the PR mergeable or permanently pending).

standards.claim: NIST SP 800-218 (SSDF v1.1, February 2022) locates static analysis in practice PW.7, "Review and/or Analyze Human-Readable Code to Identify Vulnerabilities and Verify Compliance with Security Requirements". Task PW.7.2 requires: "Perform the code review and/or code analysis based on the organization's secure coding standards, and record and triage all discovered issues and recommended remediations in the development team's workflow or issue tracking system." Notional Implementation Example 4 is "Use a static analysis tool to automatically check code for vulnerabilities and compliance with the organization's secure coding standards with a human reviewing the issues reported by the tool and remediating them as necessary"; Example 6 is "Use automated tools to identify and remediate documented and verified unsafe software practices on a continuous basis as human-readable code is checked into the code repository."
standards.threshold: Practice PW.7; tasks PW.7.1 and PW.7.2; PW.7.2 examples 4 and 6. Document: SP 800-218 SSDF v1.1, Feb 2022
standards.source_name: NIST SP 800-218, Secure Software Development Framework (SSDF) Version 1.1
standards.notes: Quotes extracted from the actual PDF text, not from memory. SSDF v1.1 (Feb 2022) is still the current final version; no Rev 1 / v1.2 is listed on the CSRC page, only the related SP 800-218A. Note what PW.7.2 does NOT say: it never requires that analysis block a merge. It requires that findings be recorded and triaged. A team that files every finding as an issue and triages it is SSDF-conformant even with an advisory-only scan.

standards.claim: NIST SSDF PW.6.2 Example 2 defines the "clean build" concept: "Implement the 'clean build' concept, where all compiler warnings are treated as errors and eliminated except those determined to be false positives or irrelevant." This is the SSDF basis both for treating analyzer warnings as build errors and for permitting suppressions — but only after a per-item determination.
standards.threshold: PW.6.2, Notional Implementation Example 2
standards.source_name: NIST SP 800-218, SSDF v1.1, practice PW.6 (Configure the Compilation, Interpreter, and Build Processes to Improve Executable Security)
standards.notes: The clause "except those determined to be false positives or irrelevant" is the governing standard for a suppression list. It permits suppressions and simultaneously requires that each one carry a determination. A 19-entry `sonar.issue.ignore.multicriteria` block with no recorded rationale does not meet this bar; the same 19 entries each with a one-line justification and a date would.

standards.claim: OWASP's DevSecOps Verification Standard defines requirement DSOVS-CODE-004 (Static Application Security Testing) with four maturity levels. Level 2 is "SAST scanning is implemented into the software build pipeline" with automated scans on each build, where "the pipeline can be configured to fail or flag a build when issues of a given severity are detected." Level 3 adds that all identified vulnerabilities are recorded in a centralised issue tracking system and "periodically reviewed to evaluate the effectiveness of the SAST tool," enabling teams to suppress false positives and confirm the analyser is keeping pace with the languages and frameworks in use.
standards.threshold: DSOVS-CODE-004; Level 2 = SAST in build pipeline (fail OR flag); Level 3 = centralised tracking + periodic review
standards.source_name: OWASP DevSecOps Verification Standard — CODE-004 Static Application Security Testing (SAST)
standards.notes: This is the closest thing to a citable OWASP position on SAST-in-CI. Two things matter for a two-person team: (a) OWASP treats "flag" as equally valid as "fail" at Level 2, so an advisory-first rollout is standard-conformant, not a shortcut; (b) Level 3's "periodically reviewed" is the OWASP hook for a suppression-review cadence. The OWASP DevSecOps Guideline page itself is thinner than its reputation — it names SAST and lists tools (SonarQube, Semgrep, Checkmarx, Fortify) but gives no gating or false-positive guidance.

standards.claim: .NET Roslyn code quality analysis is enabled by default for projects targeting .NET 5 or later, but in the default analysis mode "only a small number of rules are enabled as build warnings." The security taint rules are not among them: CA3001 (Review code for SQL injection vulnerabilities) is documented as "Enabled by default in .NET 10: No". Analysis mode is raised with `<AnalysisMode>` (None | Default | Minimum | Recommended | All) or the compound `<AnalysisLevel>` (e.g. `latest-Recommended`). Under `-warnaserror`, CA warnings become errors unless `CodeAnalysisTreatWarningsAsErrors` is set to false.
standards.threshold: AnalysisMode values: None|Default|Minimum|Recommended|All. CA3001 enabled by default in .NET 10 = No. AnalysisLevel default = `latest`.
standards.source_name: Microsoft Learn — Code analysis in .NET; CA3001
standards.notes: The .NET 10 default-enabled table on the overview page contains only Interoperability, Performance, Reliability and Usage rules — zero Security-category rules. CA3001 also carries a hard architectural caveat: "This rule can't track data across assemblies. For example, if one assembly reads the HTTP request input and then passes it to another assembly that executes the SQL command, this rule won't produce a warning." In a layered ABP solution (HttpApi / Application / Domain / EntityFrameworkCore projects) that is precisely where the flow goes, so CA3xxx is worth enabling but must not be treated as sufficient taint coverage.

standards.claim: Microsoft documents four suppression mechanisms for .NET analyzer warnings, of which only one carries a machine-readable rationale: `SuppressMessageAttribute` takes a `Justification` property and can be scoped in-source or in a per-project GlobalSuppressions.cs with `Scope` and `Target`. The alternatives — `dotnet_diagnostic.<rule-ID>.severity = none` in EditorConfig, and `#pragma warning disable` — carry no justification field and apply file- or project-wide.
standards.threshold: SuppressMessageAttribute(category, ruleId, Justification=..., Scope=..., Target=...); EditorConfig severity = none; #pragma warning disable/restore
standards.source_name: Microsoft Learn — Suppress code analysis warnings
standards.notes: This is the practical answer to "how should suppressions be reviewed": prefer the mechanism that forces a written reason next to the code, so the suppression shows up in the PR diff of the file it protects rather than in a central properties file nobody reads. CA3001's own page adds the correct standard for a security suppression: "It's safe to suppress a warning from this rule if you know that the input is always validated against a known safe set of characters" — i.e. suppression requires an affirmative safety argument, not just noise-fatigue.

standards.claim: Sonar's own documentation discourages the configuration pattern this repository uses. On advanced exclusions: "It is strongly advised to configure these features in SonarQube UI. The configuration on the CI/CD host which is very tedious and implies using a set of properties is not documented in this guide." On scope narrowing generally: "Inclusions and exclusions should not be part of the initial analysis configuration" — they are intended to resolve specific problems found during analysis. The `sonar.issue.ignore.multicriteria` property pairs a rule key pattern (`<repository>:<ruleKey>`, e.g. `java:S1195`, or a globbing pattern such as `java:*Naming*`) with a file path pattern.
standards.threshold: sonar.issue.ignore.multicriteria=<ids>; .<id>.ruleKey=<repo>:<S-number>; .<id>.resourceKey=<glob>
standards.source_name: Sonar Documentation — Applying advanced exclusions; Analysis scope (SonarQube Server 10.7)
standards.notes: Worth being precise about the tradeoff rather than repeating Sonar's advice uncritically. Properties-file suppressions ARE version-controlled, diffable and reviewable in a PR, which UI suppressions are not — that is a genuine governance advantage Sonar's docs ignore. The real risk is not the file; it is that `ruleKey` accepts globs and `resourceKey` accepts `**`, so a single entry can silently disable a rule across the entire codebase, and nothing in the gate reports how much is being suppressed.

standards.claim: Suppressed findings are invisible to the Sonar quality gate: "SonarQube ignores accepted issues in the quality reports and ratings" of the code, and likewise ignores false-positive issues. `//NOSONAR` on a line suppresses all issues on that line "now and in the future". Issues filtered by `sonar.issue.ignore.multicriteria` are never raised at all, so they do not even appear as suppressed.
standards.threshold: Accepted and False positive statuses excluded from quality reports and ratings; NOSONAR = permanent line-level suppression of all rules
standards.source_name: Sonar Documentation — Editing/managing issues (SonarQube Server)
standards.notes: This is the core risk of a 19-entry suppression list: the gate cannot go red because of it, by design. There is no built-in "suppression budget" condition. Sonar does expose accepted-issue and false-positive counts as metrics, so the count can be tracked, but a filter-based multicriteria suppression is not even counted — the issue is suppressed before it is created. The only durable control is reviewing the properties file itself.

standards.claim: SonarQube Cloud's Free plan does not fit this codebase: private-project analysis is capped at 50k lines of code, the organization is capped at 5 members, custom quality gates and custom quality profiles are Team/Enterprise only, and pull request analysis on Free works "[o]nly if the target branch is the main branch" (unlimited on Team and Enterprise). Advanced Security (Advanced SAST + SCA + malware detection) is a separate subscription available from the Team plan and covers JavaScript/TypeScript, Java and C#/.NET.
standards.threshold: Free plan: 50k LOC private, 5 members, no custom quality gates, PR analysis only when target branch is main. Advanced Security = separate subscription, Team plan and up.
standards.source_name: Sonar Documentation — Subscription plans (SonarQube Cloud); Advanced Security introduction
standards.notes: This repo is roughly 53k lines of C# plus 27k of TypeScript, so it exceeds the 50k private-LOC Free cap on the backend alone. I am reporting the plan boundary as a tool-availability constraint, not making a cost recommendation. The practical consequence: on Free you cannot author a custom gate, so you get Sonar way or nothing — which, given Sonar way is the right gate anyway, is less painful than it sounds; the LOC cap is the real blocker.

standards.claim: SonarQube Cloud's GitHub status check is still literally named `SonarCloud Code Analysis` despite the product rename to SonarQube Cloud, and it is added to a branch ruleset or branch protection rule as a required status check. The check name only appears in GitHub's status-check search after at least one successful analysis has run.
standards.threshold: Status check name (literal): `SonarCloud Code Analysis`
standards.source_name: Sonar Documentation — Configuring GitHub project binding (SonarQube Cloud)
standards.notes: Verified on the Sonar Cloud GitHub-binding doc. I did not find a second primary source confirming the name survived the rebrand unchanged, so treat the exact string as needing a one-minute confirmation in the repo's own settings after the first analysis. The ordering constraint (must run once before it is selectable) is the part that trips teams up on day one.

standards.claim: CodeQL supports this exact stack. Supported C# frameworks include .NET 5 through .NET 10, ASP.NET Core, and Entity Framework Core; supported TypeScript versions are 2.6-7.0 and supported frameworks include Angular (modern) and angular.js (legacy). Support for .NET 10 and C# 14 shipped in CodeQL 2.24.0 on 29 January 2026.
standards.threshold: .NET 5-10 supported; TypeScript 2.6-7.0; .NET 10 + C# 14 support added in CodeQL 2.24.0 (2026-01-29)
standards.source_name: CodeQL docs — Supported languages and frameworks; GitHub Changelog — CodeQL 2.24.0
standards.notes: TypeScript 5.8 sits comfortably inside the 2.6-7.0 range. Both halves of the stack are first-class; there is no version-compatibility excuse for not running CodeQL here (only the private-repo licensing constraint).

standards.claim: For C#, CodeQL default setup automatically selects `build-mode: none` (buildless analysis), which has documented accuracy caveats: when multiple versions of the same NuGet dependency exist CodeQL can use only one (typically the newer); when multiple .NET target frameworks are referenced only a single version is used; and colliding class names may cause "missing method call targets, impacting dataflow analysis."
standards.threshold: C# build modes: none | autobuild | manual. Default setup sets build-mode: none for C# automatically.
standards.source_name: GitHub Docs — CodeQL build options and steps for compiled languages
standards.notes: Directly relevant to a multi-project ABP solution with a private NuGet feed for ABP Commercial packages. Degraded dataflow is silent — there is no banner on the alerts page saying "taint analysis was incomplete." If the ABP Commercial feed is not reachable from the CodeQL job, dependency restore partially fails and the taint queries quietly under-report. Building explicitly (`build-mode: manual`) removes this class of doubt at the cost of a slower job.

standards.claim: NIST's own multi-tool study found low overlap between static analysis tools: "As Figure 4 shows, tools mostly find different weaknesses. This is partly due to the fact that tools often look for different weakness types." In the Dovecot test case, of 23 weaknesses reported by multiple tools, 21 were reported by exactly 2 tools and only 2 by 3 tools, with 7 tools analysed; for the Pebble test case one tool's warnings "did not overlap with the warnings from other tools at all."
standards.threshold: Dovecot: 21 of 23 multi-tool weaknesses found by exactly 2 of 7 tools; 2 found by 3 tools; none by 4+
standards.source_name: NIST SP 500-283, Report on the Third Static Analysis Tool Exposition (SATE 2010)
standards.notes: This is the best primary evidence I could find for the "is running two SAST tools redundant?" question, and it says no — tools mostly do not overlap. But it is dated: SP 500-283 was published in 2011 on SATE 2010 data, long before CodeQL existed and before Sonar's current taint engine. I am marking it partial because the finding is directionally sound and primary, but the specific tools studied are not the tools being recommended. I found no modern equivalent study from NIST or OWASP.

standards.notes: NuGet and npm publish dates were read from the registry APIs directly (machine-readable `published` fields), not from a rendered page — GitHub's release list renders current-year dates without a year, which is easy to misread. Counter-example worth recording: SecurityCodeScan.VS2019, still widely recommended in .NET security blog posts, last published 5.6.7 on 2022-09-05 — nearly four years stale. Do not adopt it.

standards.claim: Sonar ships a dedicated rule for the Angular XSS-bypass pattern: S6268 "Disabling Angular built-in sanitization is security-sensitive", raised as a Security Hotspot (requiring manual review) rather than a vulnerability, covering the DomSanitizer bypass APIs such as bypassSecurityTrustHtml.
standards.threshold: Rule S6268 (typescript/javascript), type: Security Hotspot
standards.source_name: SonarSource rules catalogue (rspec-6268) — reached via SonarSource blog on bypassing front-end sanitization
standards.notes: Marked unverified deliberately. rules.sonarsource.com did not resolve from this environment (DNS failure on the direct rule page), so I could not open the canonical rule page and read the rule text, CWE mapping or default-profile membership myself. The rule ID and its Security-Hotspot classification come from search результаты and the SonarSource blog, which is a first-party but secondary source. Verify at rules.sonarsource.com/javascript/RSPEC-6268 before relying on it. It matters here because the Sonar way gate requires 100% of NEW hotspots to be reviewed, so if S6268 is in the profile, every new DomSanitizer bypass becomes a mandatory human review — which is exactly the control you want on a PHI app.

recommended_checks.what_it_does: One `dotnet build` with (a) the .NET security analyzer rules explicitly turned on in a repo-root .editorconfig — the CA3xxx taint family (CA3001 SQL injection, CA3002 XSS, CA3003 file path, CA3006 command, CA3012 regex) and the CA5xxx crypto/config family raised to `error`, since none are enabled by default in .NET 10 — and (b) Microsoft.CodeAnalysis.BannedApiAnalyzers (RS0030) with a BannedSymbols.txt that bans the ABP tenancy-escape APIs (IDataFilter.Disable<IMultiTenant>, ICurrentTenant.Change, and raw-SQL entry points such as FromSqlRaw/ExecuteSqlRaw) outside a short reviewed allowlist. Build runs with -warnaserror.
recommended_checks.tool: .NET 10 SDK Roslyn analyzers (Microsoft.CodeAnalysis.NetAnalyzers) + Microsoft.CodeAnalysis.BannedApiAnalyzers
recommended_checks.tool_maintained_evidence: BannedApiAnalyzers 5.6.0 published 2026-07-02 (https://api.nuget.org/v3/registration5-gz-semver2/microsoft.codeanalysis.bannedapianalyzers/5.6.0.json). NetAnalyzers ship in the SDK; docs page last updated 2026-05-28 (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/fundamentals/code-analysis/overview). Latest NetAnalyzers package on NuGet 11.0.100-preview.7.26381.103, 2026-08-11.
recommended_checks.rationale_for_two_person_team: Highest value per hour available anywhere in this area, because it adds zero new CI minutes, zero new dashboards and zero new logins — it is the build they already run. It is also the only control on this list that speaks to the highest-consequence failure mode: no SAST product on the market has a rule for host-header-resolved cross-tenant leakage, but a banned-API list makes every deliberate tenant-filter bypass a compile error that must be justified in a PR. Do NOT set AnalysisMode=All; enumerate the ~20 security rules you want and leave everything else alone, or the first build will produce hundreds of style warnings and the team will turn -warnaserror off within a week.

recommended_checks.what_it_does: CodeQL advanced setup (a committed workflow, not default setup) with a language matrix of `csharp` and `javascript-typescript`, `queries: security-extended`, triggered on pull_request to main, push to main, and a weekly cron. security-extended is non-negotiable here: the three C# queries that map to this launch — Missing function level access control (CWE-285/284/862), Insecure Direct Object Reference (CWE-639), and Use of file upload (CWE-434) — are all excluded from the `default` suite.
recommended_checks.tool: github/codeql-action with the security-extended query suite
recommended_checks.tool_maintained_evidence: codeql-action v4.37.9 released 2026-08-26, bundling CodeQL 2.26.4 released 2026-08-26 (https://github.com/github/codeql-action/releases). .NET 10 / C# 14 support added in CodeQL 2.24.0, 2026-01-29.
recommended_checks.rationale_for_two_person_team: Advanced setup rather than default setup costs about an extra hour and buys the two things default setup cannot give you: the security-extended suite selection, and control over build mode. Budget most of the effort for the first triage pass, not the YAML. Expect security-extended to surface medium-precision findings that default would not — that is the point, and with 80k lines the initial queue is a one-time cost of maybe half a day, not an ongoing tax, because subsequent runs only surface new alerts on the PR. Hard prerequisite: this repo is private, so it needs a GitHub Code Security licence; if that is not in place, substitute Semgrep CE (LGPL 2.1, free, no repo limits) and accept that Semgrep CE is single-file and will not follow taint across files.

recommended_checks.what_it_does: A branch ruleset on main with `Require code scanning results`, CodeQL added as a required tool, Security alerts set to `High or higher` and Alerts set to `Errors`. This blocks a merge on a qualifying alert, on analysis still running, AND on the required tool not being configured for the repository — the last condition fails closed if someone deletes or renames the workflow, which a plain required status check does not do.
recommended_checks.tool: GitHub repository rulesets — code scanning merge protection
recommended_checks.tool_maintained_evidence: Current GitHub Docs, retrieved 2026-08-28 (https://docs.github.com/en/code-security/concepts/code-scanning/merge-protection and .../how-tos/find-and-fix-code-vulnerabilities/manage-your-configuration/set-merge-protection). Feature GA'd from the 2024-04-30 beta changelog.
recommended_checks.rationale_for_two_person_team: An hour of clicking that converts CodeQL from a dashboard nobody opens into an actual gate. Keep the threshold at High or higher — GitHub's own default for the PR check is error/critical/high, and tightening to Medium or All on a 2-person team is the single most reliable way to make them start using admin bypass. Note explicitly that this is NOT the same as adding a required status check; GitHub documents that "merge protection with rulesets is not related to status checks," and teams routinely configure one while believing they have the other.

recommended_checks.what_it_does: SonarScanner for .NET wrapping the build, plus SonarJS on the Angular app, publishing to SonarQube Cloud with the built-in read-only Sonar way gate (no new issues; 100% of new Security Hotspots reviewed; new-code coverage >= 80.0%; new-code duplication <= 3.0%), new code defined as reference branch `main`. Reported back to GitHub as the status check literally named `SonarCloud Code Analysis` and added to the branch ruleset as required.
recommended_checks.tool: SonarQube Cloud + dotnet-sonarscanner + SonarSource/sonarqube-scan-action
recommended_checks.tool_maintained_evidence: dotnet-sonarscanner 11.2.1 published 2026-04-02 (https://api.nuget.org/v3/registration5-gz-semver2/dotnet-sonarscanner/11.2.1.json). SonarAnalyzer.CSharp 10.33.0.1635 published 2026-08-21 (NuGet registration API). sonarqube-scan-action v8.2.1, GitHub renders the date as 15 Jul with no year, which it does only for the current year (https://github.com/SonarSource/sonarqube-scan-action/releases/tag/v8.2.1).
recommended_checks.rationale_for_two_person_team: Set new code to reference-branch `main`, not `previous_version`. previous_version keys off `sonar.projectVersion` at analysis time, so if CI does not bump that string on every release the new-code window silently widens until the gate is meaningless — a failure mode with no error message. Two constraints to settle before starting, both licensing not cost: the Free plan caps private analysis at 50k LOC (this backend alone is ~53k), and Free restricts PR analysis to PRs targeting main and forbids custom quality gates. The last part is fine — Sonar way is the gate you want and it is read-only anyway. Not launch-blocking because a new-code gate says nothing about the 80k lines already written; the launch-relevant Sonar work is a one-time full scan and Security Hotspot triage, which is a different activity from the gate.

recommended_checks.what_it_does: ESLint over the Angular workspace with typescript-eslint in type-checked mode, @angular-eslint (including the template plugin so .component.html is parsed at all), and eslint-plugin-security, run with --max-warnings=0. Covers the frontend layer that neither CodeQL's C# analysis nor Roslyn touches, and is the only tool in this set that reads Angular template binding expressions.
recommended_checks.tool: ESLint + typescript-eslint + @angular-eslint + eslint-plugin-security
recommended_checks.tool_maintained_evidence: typescript-eslint 8.68.0 published 2026-08-24; @angular-eslint/eslint-plugin 22.1.0 published 2026-07-12; eslint-plugin-security 4.0.1 published 2026-06-12 — all read from the npm registry API on 2026-08-28 (https://registry.npmjs.org/typescript-eslint).
recommended_checks.rationale_for_two_person_team: Cheap, fast, and it is the only check that sees Angular templates. Adopt it in two steps or it will not stick: land the config with `--max-warnings` unbounded and a committed baseline, fix or explicitly disable the existing violations in one sitting, then flip to --max-warnings=0 in a second PR. Type-checked linting roughly triples lint time on 27k lines of TS — still under a minute, but run it as its own job so a slow lint never masks a build failure.

recommended_checks.what_it_does: A ~40-line script that inventories every suppression across the repo — sonar.issue.ignore.multicriteria entries, //NOSONAR comments, SuppressMessageAttribute occurrences, #pragma warning disable, EditorConfig `severity = none` lines, and eslint-disable comments — writes the count to a committed baseline file, and fails the PR if the count rises without a matching line in a SUPPRESSIONS.md giving rule ID, scope, reason and date. Directly targets the existing 19 sonar.issue.ignore.multicriteria entries.
recommended_checks.tool: Custom shell/Python script in GitHub Actions (grep + a checked-in baseline)
recommended_checks.tool_maintained_evidence: No third-party tool; the mechanisms it counts are documented by their vendors — SuppressMessageAttribute Justification and GlobalSuppressions.cs (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/fundamentals/code-analysis/suppress-warnings, retrieved 2026-08-28) and Sonar's multicriteria/NOSONAR behaviour (https://docs.sonarsource.com/sonarqube-server/project-administration/adjusting-analysis/setting-analysis-scope/advanced-exclusions).
recommended_checks.rationale_for_two_person_team: This is the missing instrument, not a nice-to-have. Sonar explicitly "ignores accepted issues in the quality reports and ratings," and multicriteria-filtered issues are never raised at all — so no gate on this list can ever go red because of suppression growth. Without a counter, a suppression list only moves one direction. Launch-blocking specifically because the existing 19 entries must be read once before anonymous traffic arrives: NIST SSDF PW.6.2 permits suppressing warnings "except those determined to be false positives or irrelevant," and a determination that was never written down has not been made. Realistic outcome of that first review: most will be legitimate (generated ABP code, migrations, test fixtures), one or two will be a rule that was globbed off across the whole codebase, and that one is why you do the review.

recommended_checks.check_name: Quarterly SAST suppression and dismissal review (calendar, not CI)
recommended_checks.what_it_does: A 2-3 hour recurring session, once a quarter, that re-reads SUPPRESSIONS.md, re-opens every CodeQL alert dismissed as 'false positive' or "won't fix" in the period, and re-checks Sonar issues marked Accepted. Each entry is either re-justified with a date or deleted. Output is a dated one-page note in the repo.
recommended_checks.tool: GitHub code scanning alert list (filtered to dismissed) + SonarQube Cloud issue list filtered to Accepted/False positive + SUPPRESSIONS.md
recommended_checks.tool_maintained_evidence: Practice, not a tool. The requirement is OWASP DSOVS-CODE-004 Level 3, which requires findings be "periodically reviewed to evaluate the effectiveness of the SAST tool" (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/OWASP/www-project-devsecops-verification-standard/main/document/CODE-004-Static-Application-Security-Testing-SAST.md, retrieved 2026-08-28), and NIST SSDF PW.7.2, which requires discovered issues be recorded and triaged (NIST SP 800-218 v1.1).
recommended_checks.effort_hours: 3 per quarter (12/year)
recommended_checks.rationale_for_two_person_team: Quarterly, not monthly, and deliberately so — 12 hours a year out of roughly 96 available for this work. This is the cheapest way to reach OWASP DSOVS-CODE-004 Level 3 and it is the only item that catches the slow failure where suppressions added under deadline pressure are never revisited. Put it on the calendar attached to an existing ritual (the sprint after each quarter's release) rather than as a standalone reminder, or it will be skipped. If only one of the last two items survives contact with reality, keep this one and drop the CI script — a human reading the list quarterly beats a counter nobody investigates.

not_worth_it_here: A third SAST engine (Semgrep, Checkmarx, Veracode, Snyk Code) on top of CodeQL and Sonar. NIST SP 500-283 shows tools mostly find different weaknesses, so a third would genuinely add findings — but findings are not the constraint here, triage capacity is. Two SDE 1s with one developer-week per month cannot absorb a third alert queue. Semgrep CE is the exception ONLY as a substitute if the private repo cannot get a GitHub Code Security licence, and even then note that Semgrep CE is single-file and will not follow taint across files.

CodeQL's `security-and-quality` suite, or AnalysisMode=All / AnalysisLevel=latest-all for the Roslyn analyzers. Both add large volumes of maintainability and style findings on top of the security set. GitHub's current docs list only `default` and `security-extended` as built-in suites for code scanning, and Microsoft documents that AnalysisMode=All enables ALL rules as build warnings. On 80k lines this produces a queue in the thousands and the predictable response from a two-person team is to disable the whole thing. Enumerate ~20 security rules instead.

Writing custom CodeQL queries for the tenancy invariant. This is the technically correct answer to 'no SAST rule covers host-header tenant resolution', and at a larger company with an AppSec engineer it is exactly what you would build. QL is a real language with a real learning curve, and a query that models ABP's IMultiTenant/IDataFilter abstractions is a multi-week project for someone who has never written QL. A BannedApiAnalyzers BannedSymbols.txt gets 80% of the protection in an afternoon. Revisit this only after a security hire.

A vulnerability-management platform (DefectDojo, ThreadFix) aggregating SARIF from all tools into one queue with per-severity remediation SLAs. NIST SSDF PO.4.1 examples 2 and 6 describe exactly this — KPIs, KRIs, severity scores, analysing collected data to improve the SDLC. It is correct at 50 engineers. At two, GitHub's own alert list plus SonarQube Cloud IS the tracking system, and PW.7.2 only requires that issues be recorded and triaged in 'the development team's workflow or issue tracking system' — GitHub Issues satisfies that literally.

SonarQube Advanced Security (Advanced SAST + SCA add-on) at launch. It is a separate subscription from the Team plan and its differentiator is following taint into third-party dependency code. Real value, wrong sequencing: buy it after the base gates are running and being acted on, not while the team is still learning to triage the standard injection rules. Same reasoning for Sonar's AI CodeFix.

A formal SAST tool evaluation or bake-off (OWASP Benchmark runs, precision/recall measurement on your own codebase). This is standard procurement practice at scale and it would consume most of a month here. CodeQL and Sonar are both first-party-supported for .NET 10 and Angular 20 and both are actively released; that is sufficient basis for a two-person decision.

Self-hosting SonarQube Community Build to avoid the Cloud LOC cap. It looks like the frugal option and it is a trap for this team: Community Build has no injection/taint rules (Sonar documents security-injection rules as supported by SonarQube Cloud and SonarQube Server, i.e. the commercial editions), so you would inherit a server to patch and back up in exchange for the weaker half of the product. Note that whether self-hosting is even viable touches infrastructure, which is out of scope for this exercise.

Blocking merges on Medium or Low severity code scanning alerts, or a zero-suppression policy. GitHub's documented default is to fail the PR check only on error/critical/high, and that default exists because it is the line at which developers keep trusting the tool. Tightening it is the most common way small teams end up routinely using admin bypass — at which point every gate on this list becomes decorative.

SecurityCodeScan (SecurityCodeScan.VS2019). Still recommended in a lot of .NET security writing; last published 5.6.7 on 2022-09-05 per the NuGet registration API — nearly four years stale, predating .NET 8, 9 and 10. Named here specifically so it gets rejected on evidence rather than adopted on reputation.
surprises: CodeQL's default suite omits precisely the queries that match this launch. Missing function level access control (CWE-285/284/862), Insecure Direct Object Reference (CWE-639) and Use of file upload (CWE-434) are all security-extended-only for C#. Default setup uses `default`. So the obvious move — click 'enable default setup', see a green check — leaves out the three queries most aligned with going public with anonymous registration, four self-registering external roles, and document upload. 54 of 64 C# queries in default, 10 held back, and those are the 10.

The suites are precision filters, not curated lists. Reading the actual selector files in github/codeql: `default` = precision high|very-high, security-extended = that plus precision medium, both gated to problem.severity error|warning and tags containing security. 'security-extended has more false positives' is therefore a bounded, knowable statement — you are adding the medium-precision tier, not an open-ended pile. That reframes it from a scary unknown into a decision you can actually make.

CodeQL is not free on a private repo. Free and Pro plans can only run code scanning on public repositories; private needs GitHub Team or Enterprise WITH GitHub Code Security. Two developers who have only ever seen CodeQL running on open-source repos will reasonably assume it is a free GitHub feature, plan around it, and discover the block on the day they try to turn it on.

SonarQube Cloud's Free plan does not fit this codebase, and the reason is not the one people expect. The 50k private-LOC cap is exceeded by the C# alone (~53k). But the sharper limits are that Free forbids custom quality gates entirely and restricts PR analysis to pull requests whose target branch is main. The gate restriction turns out not to matter — Sonar way is the right gate and it is read-only anyway — but the LOC cap is a hard stop.

The GitHub status check is still literally named `SonarCloud Code Analysis` after the rename to SonarQube Cloud, and it does not appear in GitHub's required-status-check picker until at least one successful analysis has run on a PR. Day one goes: configure Sonar, go to branch protection, search for 'SonarQube', find nothing, conclude the integration is broken.

The .NET taint rules are off by default and structurally weak for this architecture — a double surprise. CA3001 (SQL injection) is documented as 'Enabled by default in .NET 10: No', and the .NET 10 default-enabled rule table contains zero Security-category rules. Worse, CA3001's own page states it 'can't track data across assemblies' — and in a layered ABP solution the HTTP request is read in one project and the SQL executes in another, which is exactly the flow it cannot follow. Free in-compiler taint analysis here is both switched off AND, once switched on, unable to see the shape of your code.

A green Sonar gate is structurally incapable of reporting suppression risk. Sonar 'ignores accepted issues in the quality reports and ratings', and multicriteria-filtered issues are never raised at all, so they do not even show up as suppressed. There is no built-in suppression-budget condition. The 19 existing entries could be hiding a rule globbed off across the entire codebase and every dashboard would stay green. This is not a bug — it is the documented design — which is why an external counter is the only control that works.

Sonar's own documentation says the repo's configuration approach is unsupported. On advanced exclusions: 'It is strongly advised to configure these features in SonarQube UI. The configuration on the CI/CD host ... is not documented in this guide.' And: 'Inclusions and exclusions should not be part of the initial analysis configuration.' Worth arguing with, though — a properties file is version-controlled, diffable and reviewable in a PR, which UI suppressions are not. The real hazard is not the file; it is that `ruleKey` accepts globs like `csharp:*Naming*` and `resourceKey` accepts `**`, so one line can disable a rule everywhere, and nothing anywhere reports how much is being suppressed.

Merge protection rulesets and required status checks are two different mechanisms, and GitHub says so in one sentence: 'Merge protection with rulesets is not related to status checks.' Only the ruleset can block on alert severity, and only the ruleset fails closed when a required tool is not configured — meaning it catches a deleted or renamed CodeQL workflow, which a required status check does not. Teams commonly configure one, believe they have the other, and never find out.

CodeQL C# defaults to build-mode: none, and its documented failure modes are silent. It picks one NuGet version when several exist, one target framework when several are referenced, and colliding class names cause 'missing method call targets, impacting dataflow analysis'. On an ABP Commercial solution pulling from a private NuGet feed, a partial restore degrades taint analysis with no banner, no warning, and a green check. Fewer alerts looks like good news.

The Sonar way gate silently waives its own coverage and duplication conditions on any change under 20 new lines — the documented 'fudge factor'. A team that ships small PRs, which two people under time pressure will, can pass the 80% coverage condition for weeks without ever meeting it.

No SAST tool on this list has a rule for the highest-consequence failure mode in this system. Host-header-resolved tenancy with database-per-tenant is an application-specific invariant; CodeQL's C# suites and Sonar's rule set contain nothing that models 'this query ran without a tenant filter'. The whole SAST layer is silent on cross-tenant leakage. The affordable substitute is not a SAST rule at all — it is a banned-API list that turns every deliberate tenant-filter bypass into a compile error requiring a written justification.

The evidence for running two SAST tools is real but old. NIST SP 500-283 states outright that 'tools mostly find different weaknesses' — in one test case, of 23 weaknesses reported by multiple tools, 21 were found by exactly two of seven tools and none by four or more. That is the answer to 'is CodeQL plus Sonar redundant?' and it is no. But it was published in 2011 on SATE 2010 data, before CodeQL existed. I could not find a modern primary replacement, which is itself worth knowing: the standard justification for defence-in-depth SAST rests on a fifteen-year-old study.
disagreements: Sonar's own documentation contradicts itself on what the Sonar way gate contains. The current SonarQube Server page lists four conditions with the first as 'No new issues are introduced'; the SonarQube Cloud page describes the older rating-based framing — 'No new bugs are introduced (Reliability rating is A)', 'No new vulnerabilities are introduced (Security rating is A)', 'New code has limited technical debt (Maintainability rating is A)'. Both are first-party Sonar docs, both current, and they describe different gates. The numeric conditions (coverage >= 80.0%, duplication <= 3.0%, hotspots reviewed) are consistent across both. Treat the four-condition Server version as current and verify in the actual organisation's gate view before quoting either.

GitHub's documentation and the CodeQL product disagree on which query suites exist. Both the Enterprise Cloud and GHES 3.16 docs pages list only `default` and `security-extended` as built-in suites, while the github/codeql repository still ships `security-and-quality` and `code-quality` suite files per language. Most likely the docs describe what default setup exposes while the CLI retains more. Anyone reading only the docs will conclude security-and-quality was removed; anyone reading only the repo will assume it is supported.

There is no authoritative source that says SAST must be a hard merge gate, and the sources lean the other way. OWASP DSOVS-CODE-004 Level 2 accepts 'fail OR flag' as equivalent. NIST SSDF PW.7.2 requires only that findings be recorded and triaged in the team's workflow or issue tracker; it never mentions blocking. SonarSource says the gate 'can be used to block the merge', framing it as a capability. Only GitHub ships an opinionated default (fail on error/critical/high) and even that is configurable to None. So an advisory-first rollout is standards-conformant, not a compromise — which matters for a team that cannot absorb a hard gate on day one.

Sonar is ambiguous about where standard taint analysis ends and the paid Advanced SAST add-on begins. The security-related-rules page says security-injection rules are 'supported only by SonarQube Cloud and SonarQube Server' with no plan qualification, implying taint is included in the base product. The Advanced Security page says Advanced SAST is a separate subscription starting at Team plan that covers 'the unknown parts of the code that are in the open-source dependencies'. The most consistent reading is that first-party taint is included and cross-dependency taint is the add-on, but Sonar does not state that boundary in one place and I would confirm it with Sonar before budgeting.

Secondary sources disagree with Sonar's own docs on the Free plan. Third-party pricing write-ups describe the free tier as covering private repos up to 50k LOC as though PR analysis came with it; Sonar's own subscription-plans page adds that on Free, PR analysis works 'only if the target branch is the main branch' and that custom quality gates and profiles are Team/Enterprise only. The vendor page is stricter than the summaries. Use the vendor page.

material_errors: [7] C# CodeQL query counts are wrong. The cited page lists 55 built-in C# queries, 44 in `default`, 11 security-extended-only — not 64/54/10. The claim's own list of extended-only queries also omits 'Value shadowing: server variable' (CWE-348), which is the 11th.

[5] security-extended is NOT 'the default set plus precision medium'. In misc/suite-helpers/security-extended-selectors.yml the high/very-high-precision include block has NO `problem.severity` filter at all (so it also admits `recommendation`-severity security queries), and it omits kinds `alert`/`path-alert` that the default selectors include. The stated threshold 'both require problem.severity error|warning' is false for security-extended. The cited URL contains only the default selectors and documents nothing about security-extended.

[4] Two of the three quoted strings do not appear on the cited page. Grepping the fetched page: 'block the merge' = 0 hits, 'pull request' = 0 hits, 'CI pipeline' = 0 hits. The Sonar way sentence is also misquoted — the page says the gate 'focuses on keeping new code clean, rather than spending a lot of effort remediating old code', not 'keeping high quality standards for new code'. The page is additionally an archived 10.8 version banner-marked 'no longer maintained'.

[20] CodeQL 2.24.0 shipped 2026-01-26, not 29 January 2026 (changelog title: 'CodeQL 2.24.0 (2026-01-26)'). It also states only 'Basic extractor support for .NET 10' and a narrow C# 14 item (implicit span conversions), not blanket 'support for .NET 10 and C# 14'. None of this appears on the cited supported-languages page.
[15] Microsoft documents THREE suppression mechanisms on the cited page (Disable the rule via EditorConfig severity=none; #pragma warning / #Disable; SuppressMessageAttribute), not four.

[24] The cited SonarSource blog never mentions rule S6268 — no rule ID appears anywhere in it. The rule ID and its Security Hotspot classification are unsupported by this citation, and rules.sonarsource.com was unreachable for independent confirmation.

results.claim: Sonar way quality gate: exactly 4 conditions, all new-code; coverage >= 80.0%; duplication <= 3.0%; provided by Sonar, default-activated, read-only
results.evidence_quote: The Sonar way quality gate has four conditions: No new issues are introduced; All new Security Hotspots are reviewed; New code test coverage is greater than or equal to 80.0%; Duplication in the new code is less than or equal to 3.0% ... It is provided by Sonar, activated by default, and read-only.
results.correction: none

results.claim: Sonar way 'fudge factor': duplication conditions waived until >= 20 new lines; coverage conditions waived until >= 20 new lines to cover

research.area: Supply chain and dependency management (SBOM, SLSA, GitHub Actions pinning, Dependabot semantics, lockfile policy, NIST SSDF third-party practices)
research.standard_summary: In 2026 the honest answer for a private healthcare SaaS is: SBOM is good practice, not law. FDA §524B does not reach this app because 21 U.S.C. §360j(o)(1)(A) explicitly excludes software for "appointment schedules" from the definition of a device; the current HIPAA Security Rule has no SBOM requirement and the January 2025 NPRM does not contain the words "bill of materials" anywhere in its 1.07 MB of text (final action now projected July 2027); and the federal procurement mandate that once forced SBOMs was dismantled — EO 14306 (11 June 2025) struck EO 14144's subsection 2(c) and contains zero mentions of SBOM or attestation, and OMB then rescinded M-22-18/M-23-16. What has actually hardened since 2025 is the CI layer: after tj-actions/changed-files (CVE-2025-30066, CVSS 8.6) attackers moved tags to a malicious commit and dumped runner memory into public logs, so GitHub shipped a repository/org policy checkbox on 15 August 2025 that flatly refuses to run any action not pinned to a full-length commit SHA — pinning is now a setting, not a linter. The current baseline is therefore: every action SHA-pinned by policy; lockfiles committed and enforced (`RestoreLockedMode` for NuGet, `--immutable` for Yarn, which is already the CI default); vulnerability scanning wired into restore/install rather than bolted on (NuGetAudit defaults to `NuGetAuditMode=all` on net10.0, so this .NET 10 solution is already auditing transitive packages and almost certainly emitting unread NU1902/NU1903 warnings); and Dependabot security updates left ungated. Current spec versions are CycloneDX 1.7 (ECMA-424 2nd ed., December 2025), SPDX 3.0.1 released with 3.1 still in RC, SLSA v1.2, and NIST SSDF v1.1 (SP 800-218) with v1.2 sitting as an unfinalised initial public draft. For two SDE 1s, SLSA Build L2 is not even purchasable — GitHub artifact attestations require GitHub Enterprise Cloud on a private repo — so the realistic target is SLSA Build L1 plus rigorous L2-adjacent hygiene, and the highest-value work is not producing an SBOM artifact but closing three specific, cheap, invisible gaps in Dependabot, Yarn and NuGet configuration.

CycloneDX 2.0 is announced for fall 2026 with Ecma ratification targeted for December 2026.

standards.claim: SBOM is NOT a legal requirement for this application. FDA section 524B of the FD&C Act only binds 'cyber devices', and 21 U.S.C. §360j(o)(1)(A) removes from the statutory definition of 'device' any software function intended 'for administrative support of a health care facility, including the processing and maintenance of financial records, claims or billing information, appointment schedules, business analytics, ... practice and inventory management ...'. A workers' comp examination scheduling portal is squarely inside that exclusion.

This is the cleanest single citation for 'FDA SBOM rules do not apply to us' — keep it in the compliance file, because auditors and prospective customers will ask about FDA SBOM in a healthcare context.
