At one dev-week per month, a 246-requirement checklist (253 minus WebRTC) is roughly a two-year project, and the exercise of grading yourself against every requirement produces a spreadsheet rather than a defence. Do this instead: adopt L2 as the stated target, and formally verify only the ~35 requirements the four merge-gate checks above cover. Write down the other ~210 as accepted-and-untested with a date. A dated, honest gap list is a better artefact for an eventual HIPAA conversation than a half-finished self-assessment.

The ASVS 'documentation defines...' requirements as a document set (V8.1.1, V8.1.2, V2.1.1-2.1.3, V5.1.1, V6.1.1-6.1.3, V13.1.x, V14.1.1-14.1.2, V16.1.1). A larger company staffs these as security-architecture deliverables with review cycles. Two SDE 1s should not. But do not skip them entirely, because V8.2.x is untestable without V8.1.1: the authorization matrix in check 1 IS your V8.1.1 documentation, and a permitted-types/max-size constant in the upload validator IS your V5.1.1. Let the code be the document. Budget one page total, not a doc set.

CodeQL / GitHub code scanning. It genuinely covers C# and TypeScript well, but 'If you want to use code scanning on private repositories, you need a GitHub Code Security license', and the tuning burden on a 53k-line ABP codebase (which generates a lot of code) lands on two people who have no security background to judge the findings. The built-in .NET analyzers plus Semgrep OSS (LGPL 2.1, free on private and commercial repos; latest v1.175.0, 26 Aug 2026) cover the realistic subset at zero licence cost. Revisit when there is a third engineer.

A ZAP full active scan, or any DAST, as a per-PR required gate. Active scanning is slow, order-of-magnitude noisier than baseline, and needs a live environment per PR. On a two-person team the first time it flakes it gets marked continue-on-error and never looked at again, which is worse than not having it. Weekly and non-blocking is the sustainable shape.

SBOM generation plus a Dependency-Track server. A03:2025 recommends both, and at a company with a platform team they are correct. Here it means standing up and patching a Java web application and its database purely to display information that `dotnet list package --include-transitive` already prints. Revisit when a customer contract demands an SBOM — which for California workers' comp offices is unlikely soon.

Per-feature threat modelling, a security champions programme, and a formal secure-SDLC attestation exercise. These are how a 50-person engineering org distributes security knowledge. With two people the knowledge is already distributed. One 90-minute whiteboard session on the tenancy boundary before launch delivers most of the value; the ceremony delivers none.

A hand-maintained cross-reference from every ASVS 5.0 requirement to CWE and to HIPAA safeguards. ASVS 5.0.0 shipped without the CWE and NIST 800-63B mappings that 4.0.3 had, so you would be building that mapping yourself. Unless a specific auditor asks for it in writing, this is pure paperwork with no effect on whether an office can read another office's data.

Thirty required checks. The eight above are already at the outer edge of what one dev-week per month sustains, and only five are proposed as blocking gates. If something new has to become a gate, something existing should stop being one — treat the gate count as a fixed budget, not a growing list.
surprises: The premise 'tenancy resolves from the HTTP Host header ONLY' is very likely false in the running application. ABP registers CurrentUser, QueryString (?__tenant=), Route, Header (__tenant) and Cookie (__tenant) resolvers by default, and AddDomainTenantResolver INSERTS the domain resolver into that chain rather than replacing it. Unless someone explicitly cleared AbpTenantResolveOptions.TenantResolvers, an anonymous request to a registration or upload endpoint carrying ?__tenant=<other-office-guid> may resolve to a different office's database. This is a five-minute thing to check in startup configuration and it is the highest-value five minutes in this whole analysis. Related: ASVS V14.2.1 is an L1 requirement that sensitive data must not appear in the query string — ABP's default puts the tenant selector exactly there.

ASP.NET Core will not validate the Host header for you. Microsoft's own words: Kestrel 'largely ignores the host name... Host headers aren't validated', and 'Host-filtering middleware is disabled by default.' The default project template ships "AllowedHosts": "*", which accepts anything. For an app whose entire tenant boundary is the Host header, going public with the template default means the boundary is enforced only by whatever the reverse proxy happens to do — and if the proxy rewrites Host, you need ForwardedHeadersOptions.AllowedHosts instead, which is a different setting. (This is the one place in this area where the answer genuinely depends on the hosting exercise; assert AllowedHosts != "*" in CI either way.)

ASVS 5.0 has essentially nothing to say about Host headers. Grepping all 345 requirements for 'host header' returns exactly one hit — V4.1.3, about intermediary-set headers. And 'tenant' appears exactly once, at V8.4.1. So the two things that define this application's risk profile are covered by two requirements in the entire standard. The real guidance lives in WSTG-INPV-17, not ASVS. Anyone planning to justify the security posture by citing ASVS coverage should know there is almost no ASVS coverage to cite here.

Password reset poisoning is the concrete way Host-header tenancy bites, and WSTG-INPV-17 names it first: if the reset link is built from the inbound Host header, an attacker sets Host to their own domain, the victim receives a genuine email from your system, clicks, and hands over the token. Worse, WSTG says the standard bypass for naive Host validation is to move the payload to X-Forwarded-Host — so a check that only validates Host is incomplete. Password reset goes anonymous-facing on day one.

ASVS 5.0 V16 Security Logging and Error Handling contains ZERO Level 1 requirements — 16 at L2 and 1 at L3. V13 Configuration has exactly one L1 requirement. So a team that says 'we'll start at L1 and work up' has, by ASVS's own structure, committed to no logging requirements and almost no configuration requirements at all. For a HIPAA-regulated system that needs an audit trail of who accessed which patient record, starting at L1 is not a conservative choice, it is an empty one. Target L2 or the level label means nothing.

CA2100 — the .NET analyzer that reviews SQL queries for injection — is documented as 'Enabled by default in .NET 10: No'. Teams routinely assume the SDK's built-in analyzers cover SQL injection out of the box. They do not. It costs one .editorconfig line to turn on.

NuGetAuditMode changed its default in .NET 10: it is now 'all' (audits transitive dependencies) for projects targeting net10.0 or higher, where it was 'direct' before. Expect a sudden increase in NU1901-NU1904 warnings that has nothing to do with any code you wrote. Also: those are warnings, and warnings do not fail a build — an audit that is 'running' in CI may be reporting into a log nobody reads.

ZAP is not an OWASP project any more. Per zaproxy.org's own ownership page it left OWASP in September 2023 and is now 'an independent Open Source project controlled by the ZAP Core Team and supported by Checkmarx'; the site states plainly that references to 'OWASP ZAP' indicate outdated sources. Separately, OWASP Dependency-Check's long-standing repository (jeremylong/DependencyCheck) was archived on 27 Sep 2025 and moved to dependency-check/DependencyCheck. Both tools are alive and maintained, but any policy document, blog post or LLM answer that says 'run OWASP ZAP and OWASP Dependency-Check' is citing names and URLs that have moved — and a pinned GitHub Action pointing at an archived repo rots silently.

SSRF is no longer its own OWASP Top 10 category. It was absorbed into A01:2025 Broken Access Control (CWE-918 is now listed there). Any internal checklist derived from the 2021 list has an A10 that no longer exists, and A10:2025 is now something entirely different — Mishandling of Exceptional Conditions. Similarly, A06:2021 Vulnerable and Outdated Components has become the much broader A03:2025 Software Supply Chain Failures. Checklists copied from 2021 will silently miss two whole categories.

OWASP itself says the automation you are being asked to build will not be sufficient, and says why: 'testable using automation != running an off the shelf tool', and automated tools are 'unable entirely to verify many of the more complicated ASVS requirements or those that relate to business logic and access control'. The practical consequence is counter-intuitive and worth stating to whoever is funding this: money spent on scanners will not reduce cross-tenant risk, and days spent writing your own boring cross-tenant integration tests will. The one thing CI genuinely cannot substitute for, per ASVS, is source-code-led human testing before the first real patient record exists.

ASVS 5.0.0 shipped without the CWE and NIST SP 800-63B mappings that 4.0.3 carried — the only such files in the repo are archived exports of the pre-release v5.0.be. If anyone intends to build a HIPAA traceability story of the form 'ASVS requirement -> CWE -> safeguard', that chain does not exist for the current version and would have to be hand-built. Conversely, mapping files between 4.0.3 and 5.0.0 DO exist in both directions, so an older 4.0.3 checklist can be migrated mechanically rather than redone.

The scope of the multi-tenancy problem is much smaller than it feels. ASVS V8 Authorization is 13 requirements total, 7 at L1+L2, and only one of those is specifically about tenancy. The reason this work feels enormous is not the number of requirements — it is that the one requirement has to hold across every endpoint. That reframing is what makes it tractable for two people: you are not implementing a standard, you are building one table-driven test harness and then adding a row per endpoint forever.
disagreements: ASVS 4.0.3 and ASVS 5.0.0 conflict on which level a PHI application needs. 4.0.3 says Level 2 is 'typically appropriate for applications that handle significant business-to-business transactions, including those that process healthcare information' — but also says Level 3 is for applications that 'contain sensitive medical data'. A workers' comp medical-examination portal is arguably both. ASVS 5.0.0 removed the healthcare wording entirely and replaced it with generic risk guidance (startup -> L1, bank -> L3, 'Most applications should be striving' for L2). So OWASP's current text does not answer 'which level for PHI', and OWASP's previous text answers it two different ways. My read, stated as a judgement rather than a citation: target L2, and treat the L3 authorization requirements specifically (V8.3.2 immediate effect of permission changes, V8.3.3 originating-subject permissions, V8.4.2 layered admin access) as a deliberate, dated deferral — because for this app the authorization chapter is where the L3 arguments actually have force, and the rest of L3 does not.

Release status of the OWASP Top 10:2025 is inconsistently presented. Search engines still index owasp.org/Top10/ with the title 'OWASP Top 10:2025 RC1', and third-party write-ups variously date the release to November 2025 (announced at Global AppSec USA, Washington DC) or January 2026 (final). I resolved this by fetching primary sources: owasp.org/Top10/ now simply redirects to the 2025 edition with no RC1 text; www-project-top-ten states 'The most current released version is the OWASP Top Ten 2025'; and the OWASP/Top10 repository README says 'OWASP Top 10 2025 - RELEASED' and 'We have released the OWASP Top 10:2025 (Final)'. Treat it as final. No OWASP primary page I opened states a calendar release date, so I have not asserted one.

OWASP's A03:2025 prevention guidance recommends 'OWASP Dependency Track and Dependency Check' for continuous dependency inventory, while Microsoft's first-party guidance points .NET teams at NuGet audit built into restore. For a .NET 10 + Yarn 4 stack these are not equivalent in effort: Dependency-Check needs an NVD API key, a large local cache, and has weaker NuGet and Yarn-Berry support, whereas NuGet audit is already running on every restore. I have recommended the first-party path and am flagging that this diverges from OWASP's named tooling. The divergence is about tooling, not about the requirement — both satisfy A03's intent.

OWASP is not internally consistent about how much a scanner buys you. The Top 10:2025 programme guidance says to 'Give your developers security tools... especially static analysis, software composition analysis, secret, and Infrastructure-as-Code (IaC) scanners' and to 'Create regular scanning schedules', which reads as tool-first. ASVS 5.0's assessment chapter pushes hard the other way: 'Merely running an automated tool without thorough testing is insufficient' and 'testable using automation != running an off the shelf tool'. For a two-person team these point at different budgets. I have weighted toward ASVS, because the failure mode that matters here (cross-tenant data access) is precisely the class ASVS says tools cannot verify.

material_errors: Claim 14 states A03:2025 has 'the highest average incidence rate of any 2025 category at 5.72%'. The A03 page's own prose says 'this category has the highest average incidence rate at 5.19%' while its factors table says 5.72% Avg Incidence Rate. The claim welds the 'highest' sentence to the wrong number. Additionally, OWASP's own Introduction page says A03 has 5 CWEs while the A03 page table says 6 CWEs Mapped — the '6 CWEs' figure is defensible but OWASP contradicts itself, so it should not be asserted as settled.

Claim 2 says '246 excluding the 7 non-applicable WebRTC L1/L2 requirements'. V17 WebRTC contains ZERO L1 requirements: its 12 requirements are 7x L2 and 5x L3. The arithmetic (253-7=246) is right but the 'L1/L2' framing is wrong — all 7 excluded are L2.

Six claims (1, 2, 7, 11, 12, 14) cite a URL that does not actually contain the stated threshold. The numbers are correct but are sourced from a different page than the one cited: ASVS counts are in the CSV not the Frontispiece; the 4.0.3 healthcare wording is in 4.0/en/0x03-Using-ASVS.md not the 5.0 file; Top 10 methodology stats are in 0x00_2025-Introduction not the /Top10/2025/ index; 'AllowedHosts: *' in the default template is not on the Kestrel host-filtering page; ABP's Insert-vs-Clear behavior is not in the ABP docs; NuGet audit defaults are not on the A03 page. Each needs its citation swapped before this goes into a standard.

Claim 11's example AllowedHosts value 'office1.example.com;office2.example.com' does not appear on the cited Kestrel page — that page's example is 'example.com;localhost'. The format rule (semicolon-delimited hostnames without ports) IS verbatim on the page; only the example is imported from elsewhere.

Claim 12 asserts AddDomainTenantResolver works by 'TenantResolvers.Insert(1, ...) — Insert, not Clear'. The ABP docs page shows only options.AddDomainTenantResolver("{0}.mydomain.com") and options.TenantResolvers.Add(...) for custom resolvers; it never shows Insert or documents the internal implementation. This is a source-code fact stated as a documented one.

results.claim: ASVS current release is 5.0.0, May 2025; 345 requirements, 17 chapters (V1 Encoding/Sanitization - V17 WebRTC); L1=70 / L2=183 / L3=92
results.evidence_quote: Version 5.0.0, May 2025
results.correction: Every number is CORRECT — I parsed the official CSV: 345 rows, Counter({'2':183,'3':92,'1':70}), 17 chapters V1 Encoding and Sanitization ... V17 WebRTC. But the cited Frontispiece contains ONLY 'Version 5.0.0, May 2025'; it has no requirement count, chapter count, or level distribution. Cite https://raw.githubusercontent.com/OWASP/ASVS/master/5.0/docs_en/OWASP_Application_Security_Verification_Standard_5.0.0_en.csv for the counts.

results.claim: ASVS 5.0 does not name healthcare in level definitions; L2 is what most apps should target (~70% incl. L1); 4.0.3 named healthcare at L2 and sensitive medical data at L3; L2 target = 253 reqs, 246 excluding 7 WebRTC L1/L2
results.evidence_quote: Most applications should be striving to achieve this level of security. Around 50% of the requirements in the ASVS are L2 meaning that an application needs to implement around 70% of the requirements in the ASVS (all of the L1 and L2 requirements) in order to comply with L2.
results.correction: 5.0 half confirmed: L1 'contains around 20% of the ASVS requirements', L1+L2 ~70%, and no healthcare/medical/industry mention anywhere on the page. 70+183=253 is right. TWO fixes: (a) V17 WebRTC has 0 L1 and 7 L2 requirements, so say 'the 7 non-applicable WebRTC L2 requirements', not 'L1/L2'; (b) the 4.0.3 healthcare evidence is NOT on this URL — cite https://raw.githubusercontent.com/OWASP/ASVS/master/4.0/en/0x03-Using-ASVS.md, which says L2 is 'typically appropriate for applications that ... process healthcare information' and L3 is for apps that 'contain sensitive medical data'.

results.claim: OWASP warns that 'automatable' ASVS requirements still need custom application-specific tests; automated tools cannot verify business logic or access control
results.evidence_quote: testable using automation != running an off the shelf tool ... [tools] will be unable entirely to verify many of the more complicated ASVS requirements or those that relate to business logic and access control.
results.correction: none

results.claim: ASVS V8 Authorization is 13 requirements, 7 at L1/L2 (L1=4, L2=3, L3=6); V8.4.1 (L2) is the single explicit multi-tenancy requirement in all of ASVS 5.0
results.evidence_quote: **8.4.1** | Verify that multi-tenant applications use cross-tenant controls to ensure consumer operations will never affect tenants with which they do not have permissions to interact. | 2
results.correction: none — I counted the chapter: V8.1 (4) + V8.2 (4) + V8.3 (3) + V8.4 (2) = 13. L1 = 8.1.1, 8.2.1, 8.2.2, 8.3.1 (4). L2 = 8.1.2, 8.2.3, 8.4.1 (3). L3 = 8.1.3, 8.1.4, 8.2.4, 8.3.2, 8.3.3, 8.4.2 (6). A grep of all 345 requirements for 'tenan' returns V8.4.1 and nothing else, so the uniqueness claim holds. Quoted wording is verbatim.

results.claim: Automatable authz requirements are V8.2.1 (L1), V8.2.2 (L1), V8.2.3 (L2), V8.3.1 (L1), V8.4.1 (L2), with V8.1.1 (L1) and V8.1.2 (L2) as documentation prerequisites
results.evidence_quote: **8.2.2** | Verify that the application ensures that data-specific access is restricted to consumers with explicit permissions to specific data items to mitigate insecure direct object reference (IDOR) and broken object level authorization (BOLA). | 1
results.correction: none — all seven IDs exist with exactly the stated levels: 8.1.1=L1, 8.1.2=L2, 8.2.1=L1, 8.2.2=L1 (IDOR/BOLA verbatim), 8.2.3=L2 (BOPLA verbatim), 8.3.1=L1 (trusted service layer verbatim), 8.4.1=L2. The 'you cannot test 8.2.x without them' framing is the researcher's judgement, not text on the page, but it is not contradicted.

results.claim: OWASP API Security says 'Write tests to evaluate the vulnerability of the authorization mechanism. Do not deploy changes that make the tests fail.'; current edition is still 2023 (API1:2023 BOLA), no 2025/2026 edition
results.evidence_quote: Write tests to evaluate the vulnerability of the authorization mechanism. Do not deploy changes that make the tests fail.
results.correction: none — quote is verbatim in How To Prevent, and the category is API1:2023 Broken Object Level Authorization. I separately checked https://owasp.org/API-Security/: only the 2023 and 2019 editions exist, so 'no 2025/2026 edition' holds as of Aug 2026.

results.claim: OWASP Top 10:2025 is FINAL not an RC; the ten categories as listed; SSRF absorbed into A01; ~175k CVE records (up from 125k in 2021); 12 categories ranked from data, 2 promoted by survey
results.evidence_quote: Welcome to the OWASP Top 10:2025 Release. ... This is the 2025 version of the OWASP Top 10.
results.correction: All substance is CORRECT but the cited index page carries only the ten category names and the 'Release' wording. The methodology thresholds are on https://owasp.org/Top10/2025/0x00_2025-Introduction/, which says 'There are approximately 175k records (up from 125k in 2021) of CVEs mapped to CWEs' and 'We ranked 12 categories based on the data contributed, and allowed two to be promoted or highlighted by responses from the community survey', and 'Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) has been rolled into this category [A01]'. Note that same Introduction later says 'we only pick eight of the ten categories from the data ... The other two categories are from the Top 10 community survey' — OWASP's own text is loose here, so quote the Methodology paragraph specifically. Also use OWASP's exact A09 name: 'Security Logging & Alerting Failures'.

results.claim: A01:2025 Broken Access Control is #1, owns multi-tenant authz/IDOR/SSRF; 40 CWEs, 3.74% avg incidence, 1,839,701 occurrences, 32,654 CVEs, '100% of the applications tested', CWE-918 and CWE-352 under A01
results.evidence_quote: 40 CWEs Mapped | 20.15% Max Incidence Rate | 3.74% Avg Incidence Rate | 1,839,701 Total Occurrences | 32,654 Total CVEs; '100% of the applications tested were found to have some form of broken access control'
results.correction: none — every figure matches the page's factors table, and CWE-918 (SSRF) and CWE-352 (CSRF) are both called out in the background text and appear in the 40-CWE list. Minor: the Introduction page rounds avg incidence to 3.73%; the 3.74% used here is the A01 page's own table value, so it is the right one to cite.

results.claim: A07:2025 Authentication Failures governs self-registration and password reset; 36 CWEs, 15.80% max / 2.92% avg incidence, 1,120,673 occurrences, 7,147 CVEs, rank unchanged from #7; CWE-287/384/798/259 named; identical error messages named as the anti-enumeration control
results.evidence_quote: Ensure registration, credential recovery, and API pathways are hardened against account enumeration attacks by using the same messages for all outcomes ('Invalid username or password.').
results.correction: none — factors table confirms 36 CWEs Mapped, 15.80% Max Incidence Rate, 2.92% Avg Incidence Rate, 1,120,673 Total Occurrences, 7,147 Total CVEs; the page states A07 'maintains its position at #7 with a slight name change' (from 'Identification and Authentication Failures'); CWE-287, CWE-384, CWE-798 and CWE-259 are all named.

results.claim: ASVS 5.0 has no Host-header requirement (closest is V4.1.3 L2); Host-header attacks covered by WSTG-INPV-17, which names password reset poisoning, cache poisoning, unintended virtual hosts and X-Forwarded-Host; related IDs WSTG-ATHZ-02/03/04, WSTG-BUSL-08/09
results.evidence_quote: In the event that Host header injection is mitigated by checking for invalid input injected via the Host header, you can supply the value to the `X-Forwarded-Host` header.
results.correction: none — WSTG-INPV-17 'Testing for Host Header Injection' covers password reset poisoning, web cache poisoning and access to unintended virtual hosts, and names X-Forwarded-Host as the bypass. I grepped all 345 ASVS requirements: nothing addresses the Host request header, and V4.1.3 (L2) is indeed the closest ('any HTTP header field ... set by an intermediary layer ... cannot be overridden by the end-user. Example headers might include X-Real-IP, X-Forwarded-*, or X-User-ID'). All five related WSTG IDs verified: ATHZ-02 Testing for Bypassing Authorization Schema, ATHZ-03 Testing for Privilege Escalation, ATHZ-04 Testing for Insecure Direct Object References, BUSL-08 Test Upload of Unexpected File Types, BUSL-09 Test Upload of Malicious Files.

results.claim: ASP.NET Core does not validate the Host header by default; Kestrel 'largely ignores the host name', 'Host headers aren't validated', host-filtering middleware disabled by default, default template ships "AllowedHosts": "*"; AllowedHosts must be semicolon-delimited hostnames without ports
results.evidence_quote: Kestrel largely ignores the host name ... `Host` headers aren't validated. ... Host-filtering middleware is disabled by default. To enable the middleware, define an `AllowedHosts` key in `appsettings.json`/`appsettings.{Environment}.json`. The value is a semicolon-delimited list of host names without port numbers
results.correction: The Kestrel behaviour and the AllowedHosts format rule are verbatim on the page. TWO unsupported bits: (a) the page never says the default project template ships "AllowedHosts": "*" — that is true but must be cited to the ASP.NET Core configuration/app-startup docs or the template's appsettings.json, not here; (b) the page's own example is "AllowedHosts": "example.com;localhost", not "office1.example.com;office2.example.com" — use the page's example or drop the quotation marks around yours.

results.claim: ABP does not resolve tenancy from Host by default; defaults are CurrentUser, QueryString, Route, Header, Cookie (all __tenant); DomainTenantResolveContributor not registered by default and is added via Insert into the existing chain, not Clear
results.evidence_quote: Configure<AbpTenantResolveOptions>(options => { options.AddDomainTenantResolver("{0}.mydomain.com"); });
results.correction: Confirmed on the page: the five default resolvers in order are CurrentUserTenantResolveContributor, QueryStringTenantResolveContributor, RouteTenantResolveContributor, HeaderTenantResolveContributor, CookieTenantResolveContributor, all keyed on __tenant, and DomainTenantResolveContributor is NOT registered by default. NOT supported: the 'TenantResolvers.Insert(1, new DomainTenantResolveContributor(...)) — Insert, not Clear' detail. The docs show only AddDomainTenantResolver(...) usage and TenantResolvers.Add(...) for custom contributors, and explicitly do not document the internal implementation. Either verify against the AbpTenantResolveOptionsExtensions source in the abp repo and cite that, or restate as 'AddDomainTenantResolver adds the domain resolver without removing the query-string/header/cookie resolvers, so those remain live attack surface — confirm against source.'

results.claim: ASVS 5.0 V5 File Handling gives 4 L1 and 5 L2 requirements; L1 core is 5.2.1 size, 5.2.2 extension+content/magic bytes, 5.3.1 no execution, 5.3.2 internally generated paths; plus 5.2.3, 5.4.1, 5.4.2, 5.4.3, 5.1.1 at L2
results.evidence_quote: checking the initial 'magic bytes', performing image re-writing, and using specialized libraries for file content validation. For L1, this can focus just on files which are used to make specific business or security decisions. For L2 and up, this must apply to all files being accepted.
results.correction: none — V5 has 13 requirements: L1 = 5.2.1, 5.2.2, 5.3.1, 5.3.2 (exactly 4); L2 = 5.1.1, 5.2.3, 5.4.1, 5.4.2, 5.4.3 (exactly 5); L3 = 5.2.4, 5.2.5, 5.2.6, 5.3.3. Every ID/level pairing in the threshold is right, including the quoted L1-vs-L2 scoping sentence in 5.2.2, RFC 6266 in 5.4.2, and antivirus in 5.4.3.

results.claim: A03:2025 Software Supply Chain Failures is new and was ranked #1 by 50% of survey respondents; NuGet audit on by default with NuGetAuditMode defaulting to 'all' for net10.0+; A03 has highest avg incidence at 5.72%, 6 CWEs, 215,248 occurrences
results.evidence_quote: This was top-ranked in the Top 10 community survey with exactly 50% respondents ranking it #1. ... when tested and reported in the contributed data, this category has the highest average incidence rate at 5.19%.
results.correction: Three problems. (1) The '5.72%' and 'highest average incidence rate' come from two different places: the factors table reads '6 CWEs Mapped | 9.56% Max Incidence Rate | 5.72% Avg Incidence Rate | 215,248 Total Occurrences | 11 Total CVEs', while the prose says the highest average incidence rate is 5.19%. State it as 'the highest average incidence rate of any 2025 category; the factors table reports 5.72% Avg Incidence Rate (the narrative text cites 5.19%)'. (2) The CWE count is contested inside OWASP's own docs — the A03 page says 6, the Introduction says 'This category has 5 CWEs'. (3) The NuGet half of the threshold is not on this page at all; it is correct and should be cited to https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/nuget/concepts/auditing-packages, which gives NuGetAudit default true, NuGetAuditLevel default low, and the footnote 'NuGetAuditMode defaults to all when a project targets net10.0 or higher. Otherwise NuGetAuditMode defaults to direct', with NU1901 low / NU1902 moderate / NU1903 high / NU1904 critical / NU1905 audit source provides no vulnerability database.

results.claim: ASVS 5.0 gives byte-assertable header/cookie thresholds (V3.4.1, V3.4.3, V3.4.4, V3.4.6, V3.3.1, V3.3.3, V14.3.2, V14.2.1, V16.5.1, V13.4.2) and A02:2025 asks for 'an automated process to verify the effectiveness of the configurations and settings in all environments'
results.evidence_quote: V3.4.1 (L1): 'A maximum age of at least 1 year must be defined, and for L2 and up, the policy must apply to all subdomains as well.' V3.4.3 (L2): 'a global policy must be used which includes the directives object-src 'none' and base-uri 'none' and defines either an allowlist or uses nonces or hashes.'
results.correction: none — I pulled all ten IDs from the cited CSV and every ID exists at the stated level with the stated substance: 3.4.1 L1 HSTS >=1yr + subdomains at L2+; 3.4.3 L2 CSP with object-src 'none' and base-uri 'none'; 3.4.4 L2 'X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff' on all responses; 3.4.6 L2 frame-ancestors every response with X-Frame-Options called 'obsolete'; 3.3.1 L1 Secure + __Host-/__Secure- prefix; 3.3.3 L2 __Host- prefix; 14.3.2 L2 'Cache-Control: no-store'; 14.2.1 L1 no sensitive data in URL/query string; 16.5.1 L2 generic message, no stack traces; 13.4.2 L2 debug modes disabled. The A02 quote is verbatim in the How to Prevent list at https://owasp.org/Top10/2025/A02_2025-Security_Misconfiguration/ (a second URL that should be cited alongside the CSV).

results.claim: ASVS 5.0 dropped 4.0.3's CWE and NIST SP 800-63B mappings; no official ASVS-to-Top-10 mapping exists; the only CWE/NIST files are archived exports of pre-release v5.0.be
results.evidence_quote: just-in-case exports before deleted from v5.0.be — nist.md: v5.0.be requirement ids and mapping to NIST 800-63B identifiers before those were removed; v5.0.be_cwe_mapping.json: v5.0.be requirement ids and mapping to CWE identifiers before those were removed
results.correction: none, though the researcher's own 'partial' confidence flag was appropriate and the listing should be stated exactly. The directory holds README.md plus mapping_v4.0.3_to_v5.0.0.yml, mapping_v4.0.3_to_v5.0.be.yml, mapping_v5.0.0_to_v4.0.3.yml, mapping_v5.0.be_to_v4.0.3.yml, mapping_v5.0.be_to_v5.0.0.yml, nist.md and v5.0.be_cwe_mapping.json — the claim's file list is complete except it omits README.md. No Top-10 mapping file is present, and the README confirms the CWE/NIST files are v5.0.be-era archives, not 5.0.0 mappings.

research.area: Performance — Core Web Vitals thresholds, Lighthouse CI enforcement, and Angular bundle budgets
research.standard_summary: As of August 2026 the Core Web Vitals set is unchanged and stable: LCP ≤ 2.5s, INP ≤ 200ms, CLS ≤ 0.1, each assessed at the 75th percentile of page loads, segmented across mobile and desktop. FID is fully retired (removed from the web-vitals library in v5.0.0, May 2025). The load-bearing 2026 reality for CI is that field measurement and lab measurement have diverged further, not converged: Google's own guidance says field data (CrUX/RUM) is what you prioritise on, but a login-gated portal is permanently ineligible for CrUX (which requires publicly indexable, sufficiently-visited pages), so field data for this app will exist only if the team ships the web-vitals library themselves. On the lab side, Lighthouse's performance score does not score INP at all (weight 0 in Lighthouse 13.4.1's default config) and Lighthouse 12.0.0 deleted budget.json/LightWallet support outright, while web.dev's article recommending it is still live and undated-as-deprecated. Lighthouse CI is real but quietly aging — @lhci/cli 0.15.1 shipped 2025-06-25 with no release since, pinning Lighthouse 12.6.1 while Lighthouse itself is at 13.4.1. The sustainable 2026 standard for a small team is therefore: gate merges on deterministic byte-count budgets (Angular's built-in budgets, plus LHCI resource-summary assertions), treat every timing-derived number as an advisory trend, and collect real field data from your own users rather than pretending a CI runner is a user.

standards.claim: The Core Web Vitals metric set in 2026 is exactly three metrics — Largest Contentful Paint (LCP), Interaction to Next Paint (INP), Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS) — and all three are assessed at the 75th percentile of page loads, segmented across mobile and desktop devices.
standards.threshold: LCP ≤ 2.5s; INP ≤ 200ms; CLS ≤ 0.1; all at p75
standards.source_name: web.dev — Web Vitals
standards.notes: web.dev/articles/vitals shows last-updated 2024-10-31 and states INP became a stable Core Web Vital in 2024. Cross-checked against the CrUX release notes through July 2026 (published 2026-08-11), which continue to track LCP/CLS/INP as the Core Web Vitals with no new metric and no threshold change. The percentile wording is verbatim: 'the 75th percentile of page loads, segmented across mobile and desktop devices.'

standards.claim: LCP bands: 'good' is 2.5 seconds or less; 'needs improvement' is between 2.5 and 4.0 seconds; 'poor' is greater than 4.0 seconds.
standards.threshold: good ≤ 2500ms; needs-improvement 2500–4000ms; poor > 4000ms
standards.source_name: web.dev — Largest Contentful Paint (LCP)
standards.notes: Page last updated 2025-09-04, i.e. still actively maintained. Same thresholds restated on web.dev/articles/vitals.

standards.claim: INP bands: 'good' is 200ms or below; 'needs improvement' is above 200ms and at or below 500ms; 'poor' is above 500ms. INP has fully replaced FID — FID was deprecated and removed from the web-vitals library in v5.0.0 (May 2025).
standards.threshold: good ≤ 200ms; needs-improvement 200–500ms; poor > 500ms
standards.source_name: web.dev — Interaction to Next Paint (INP)
standards.notes: INP article last updated 2025-09-02. The FID removal is confirmed in the web-vitals CHANGELOG at v5.0.0 (May 2025); the library today exposes LCP, FCP, CLS, INP, TTFB and no FID. There is no residual FID anywhere in the current metric set.

standards.claim: CLS bands: 'good' is 0.1 or less; 'needs improvement' is between 0.1 and 0.25; 'poor' is greater than 0.25.
standards.threshold: good ≤ 0.1; needs-improvement 0.1–0.25; poor > 0.25
standards.source_name: web.dev — Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS)
standards.notes: The CLS article itself shows last-updated 2023-04-12 — the oldest of the three metric pages — but the threshold is restated unchanged on the currently-maintained web.dev/articles/vitals and in the 2026 CrUX release notes, so the staleness is cosmetic, not substantive.

standards.claim: The web-vitals JavaScript library is the recommended way to collect Core Web Vitals from real users, and it is actively maintained: latest is v6.2.1 published 2026-08-26, with v6.0.0 adding soft-navigation support.
standards.source_name: npm registry — web-vitals (verified directly via registry.npmjs.org) and GoogleChrome/web-vitals CHANGELOG
standards.notes: Registry shows six releases in the five weeks to 2026-08-26 (6.0.0 on 2026-07-21 through 6.2.1) — unambiguously maintained. web.dev's field-measurement guidance (last updated 2022-05-11) explicitly names the library and states you need the metric 'at the 75th percentile' in your own reporting.

standards.claim: Core Web Vitals do not measure client-side route changes in a Single Page Application by default. Soft-navigation measurement is a separate opt-in capability, shipping unflagged from Chrome 151, and requires the site to explicitly observe soft-navigation entries (via the Performance Observer API or the web-vitals library) to slice LCP/CLS/INP per route change.
standards.threshold: Chrome 151 (unflagged); requires explicit instrumentation
standards.source_name: Chrome for Developers — Measuring soft navigations
standards.notes: Page updated 2026-07-21. Verbatim: 'The popular Single Page Application architecture has never been fully supported by the Core Web Vitals metrics.' web-vitals v6.0.0 CHANGELOG confirms 'Soft Navigation support for the Web Vitals metrics when supported by the browser.' The CrUX release notes through July 2026 make no mention of soft-navigation data entering the public dataset, so this is currently self-collected-only.

standards.claim: A page is only eligible for the Chrome UX Report if it is publicly discoverable/indexable and sufficiently popular (a minimum, undisclosed number of visitors), and only from opted-in Chrome users who enable usage-statistic reporting, sync browser history and have no sync passphrase.
standards.threshold: Public indexability required; undisclosed minimum visitor count; four user opt-in conditions
standards.source_name: Chrome for Developers — CrUX methodology
standards.notes: Excludes pages served with non-200 status, X-Robots-Tag: noindex, or noindex meta. Directly load-bearing for this app: a login-gated scheduling portal serving 11 offices will never meet either the indexability or the popularity bar, so PageSpeed Insights field data, Search Console CWV reports and CrUX-based dashboards will be permanently empty for it. Cross-check: CrUX tracked 18.06M origins in July 2026 out of the whole web — it is a long way from universal coverage.

standards.claim: Field data (CrUX/RUM) is what you should prioritise optimisation work on because it represents real users; lab data (Lighthouse) is for identifying optimisation opportunities and testing lower-end devices. Neither substitutes for the other.
standards.threshold: n/a
standards.source_name: web.dev — Why lab and field data can be different (and what to do about it)
standards.notes: Verbatim: 'field data is what you should use to prioritize your efforts'; and 'if you're only using one you may be missing an opportunity.' Article last updated 2022-07-18. This is the guidance that determines what CI can legitimately enforce: CI runs lab data only, so CI can enforce opportunity/byte-level facts but cannot certify user experience.

standards.claim: In Lighthouse 13.4.1 the performance category weights are FCP 10, LCP 25, Total Blocking Time 30, CLS 25, Speed Index 10 — and Interaction to Next Paint carries a weight of 0, i.e. INP does not contribute to the Lighthouse performance score at all.
standards.threshold: FCP 10 / LCP 25 / TBT 30 / CLS 25 / SI 10 / INP 0
standards.source_name: GoogleChrome/lighthouse — core/config/default-config.js at tag v13.4.1 (fetched raw)
standards.notes: Read directly from source at lines 408–413. The same weight-0 INP entry is present in v12.6.1 and v13.0.0, so this is not a 13.4.1 quirk. The Chrome docs page on performance scoring lists the same five weighted metrics but is stamped last-updated 2019-09-19 and does not mention INP at all — the source file is the authority. Score bands from the docs page: 90–100 good, 50–89 needs improvement, 0–49 poor.

standards.claim: Lighthouse removed budget.json support entirely in v12.0.0 — the performance-budget audit, the timing-budget audit, core/config/budget.js and the lighthouse CLI's --budget-path (LightWallet) flag no longer exist.
standards.threshold: Removed in Lighthouse 12.0.0; present through 11.7.1
standards.source_name: GoogleChrome/lighthouse v12.0.0 release notes
standards.notes: Release notes carry the literal line 'remove budgets (#15950)'. Verified independently by listing package file trees: lighthouse@10.4.0 and @11.7.1 contain /core/audits/performance-budget.js, /core/audits/timing-budget.js and /core/config/budget.js; lighthouse@12.0.0, @12.6.1 and @13.4.1 contain zero files matching 'budget'. Also verified the CLI flag: 'budget-path' is present in lighthouse@11.7.1/cli/cli-flags.js and absent from lighthouse@13.4.1/cli/cli-flags.js. Same release also removed the entire PWA category, which makes the lighthouse:no-pwa preset vestigial.

standards.claim: Lighthouse CI (@lhci/cli) still exists but has had no release in over 12 months: latest is 0.15.1 published 2025-06-25, last commit to main 2025-06-26, and it pins lighthouse at exactly 12.6.1 while Lighthouse itself has moved to 13.4.1 (2026-07-20).
standards.threshold: @lhci/cli 0.15.1 (2025-06-25); pins lighthouse 12.6.1; upstream lighthouse 13.4.1 (2026-07-20)
standards.source_name: npm registry — @lhci/cli (queried directly) and GoogleChrome/lighthouse-ci commit history
standards.notes: Release cadence has historically been roughly annual (0.13.0 Dec 2023, 0.14.0 Jun 2024, 0.15.0 Jun 2025), so 14 months is a slip rather than clear abandonment — no archive notice, no deprecation on the repo. But it is a real risk to name: the 0.15.1 dependency tree pins yargs ^15, inquirer ^6, uuid ^8, tmp ^0.1 and express ^4, all several majors behind, which will surface in whatever dependency scanning the team stands up. Recommendation: pin @lhci/cli@0.15.x, treat it as a CI-only devDependency, and re-evaluate at the next Lighthouse major.

standards.claim: Lighthouse CI assertion syntax: assertions are keyed by Lighthouse audit ID in an eslint-style 'level | [level, options]' form; levels are 'off', 'warn' (prints, does not fail the build) and 'error' (prints, causes non-zero exit); checkable options are minScore, maxLength and maxNumericValue; aggregationMethod is one of median, optimistic, pessimistic, median-run; and when no options are given the defaults are {aggregationMethod: 'optimistic', minScore: 1}.
standards.threshold: levels off|warn|error; minScore/maxLength/maxNumericValue; aggregationMethod median|optimistic|pessimistic|median-run; defaults {aggregationMethod:'optimistic', minScore:1}
standards.source_name: GoogleChrome/lighthouse-ci — docs/configuration.md
standards.notes: Read the rendered doc and then re-read the raw markdown to confirm exact strings. Presets are exactly three: lighthouse:all, lighthouse:recommended, lighthouse:no-pwa. Category assertions use 'categories:<categoryId>' e.g. 'categories:performance': ['warn', {minScore: 0.9}]. Note the default aggregationMethod is 'optimistic' — 'the value most likely to pass' — so out-of-the-box LHCI is deliberately lenient across runs.

standards.claim: budget.json still works under Lighthouse CI despite Lighthouse dropping it, because @lhci/utils converts budget.json client-side into LHCI-native resource-summary assertions; but assert.budgetsFile cannot be combined with any other assert option, and resource-summary sizes are transfer size in kilobytes while LHCI-native maxNumericValue is in bytes.
standards.threshold: budgetsFile is mutually exclusive with other assert options; budget.json sizes in KB (transfer size), maxNumericValue in bytes
standards.source_name: @lhci/utils 0.15.1 — src/budgets-converter.js (fetched source)
standards.notes: Source confirms convertBudgetsToAssertions() maps resourceSizes → 'resource-summary:<type>:size' with maxNumericValue: budget * 1024, resourceCounts → 'resource-summary:<type>:count', and timings → the metric audit id, all at 'error' level, scoped by matchingUrlPattern derived from budget.path. Because it uses the resource-summary audit (still present and weight 0 in both LH 12.6.1 and 13.0.0) rather than the deleted performance-budget audit, it survives. Practical consequence: prefer writing resource-summary:* assertions directly in lighthouserc so you can mix them with other assertions and control the level per-assertion. The upstream budget.json spec repo GoogleChrome/budget.json was archived 2022-12-29 and is read-only.

standards.claim: Lighthouse CI's default numberOfRuns is 3, and the documented posture is that failing the build on assertions is optional and should be skipped by teams new to performance measurement or with a lot of room for improvement.
standards.threshold: numberOfRuns default 3; 5 runs in the 'complete experience' recipe
standards.source_name: GoogleChrome/lighthouse-ci — docs/configuration.md and docs/getting-started.md
standards.notes: getting-started.md verbatim: 'If you're new to performance measurement or your site has a lot of room for improvement, we recommend skipping this step for now' (referring to assertions), alongside 'failing the build based on the audit results is even better!'. This is the primary-source basis for gate-vs-advisory: the tool's own maintainers do not recommend a hard perf gate as a starting position. The docs are showing age — the sample workflow still uses actions/checkout@v3 and Node 16.

standards.claim: The maintained GitHub Actions integration is treosh/lighthouse-ci-action, currently 12.6.2 tagged 2026-03-12 (running on node24 and bundling @lhci/cli 0.15.1), with inputs including urls, configPath, budgetPath, runs, uploadArtifacts and temporaryPublicStorage. temporaryPublicStorage uploads the full Lighthouse report to a publicly readable URL.
standards.threshold: treosh/lighthouse-ci-action 12.6.2 (2026-03-12); v12 floating tag
standards.source_name: treosh/lighthouse-ci-action — releases and tags
standards.notes: Tags page shows 12.6.2 and the v12 floating tag both dated Mar 12, 2026, i.e. a release within the last 6 months — this action is more current than @lhci/cli itself. The public-storage risk is stated by LHCI's own docs: 'This is temporary and public storage. If you're uncomfortable with the idea of your Lighthouse reports being stored on a public URL for anyone to see, skip to the add assertions or Lighthouse CI server steps.' For a HIPAA-regulated portal, set temporaryPublicStorage: false and use uploadArtifacts instead.

standards.claim: Angular 20.3's application builder accepts exactly seven budget types — all, allScript, any, anyScript, anyComponentStyle, bundle, initial — with properties type (required), name, baseline, maximumWarning, maximumError, minimumWarning, minimumError, warning, error and no others (additionalProperties: false).
standards.threshold: 7 types; 9 properties; additionalProperties false
standards.source_name: angular/angular-cli 20.3.x — packages/angular/build/src/builders/application/schema.json (fetched raw)
standards.notes: Read the definitions.budget enum directly from the 20.3.x schema. The Angular docs source markdown lists the identical set with descriptions: initial = 'The size of JavaScript and CSS needed for bootstrapping the application. This corresponds to the Initial Total value shown in the build output summary'; allScript = 'The size of all scripts'; anyScript = 'The size of any one script'; anyComponentStyle = 'This size of any one component stylesheet'.

standards.claim: Lazy-chunk budgets ARE supported in Angular 20, but only by naming each bundle individually: 'To configure a budget for a lazy-loaded bundle, use type: "bundle" and set name to that bundle's name.' The name matches the builder-reported bundle name, not the emitted filename, and wildcards/regex such as admin.*.js are not supported. A bundle budget whose name matches no chunk evaluates to 0 bytes and silently passes.
standards.threshold: type: 'bundle' + exact name; no wildcard support; unmatched name → 0 bytes → always passes
standards.source_name: Angular docs source — adev/src/content/tools/cli/build.md (fetched raw) and angular-cli bundle-calculator.ts
standards.notes: Docs verbatim at lines 99 and 114. The silent-pass behaviour is read from source: BundleCalculator.calculate() does chunks.filter(c => c?.names?.includes(budgetName)).map(...).reduce((l,r)=>l+r, 0) and returns [{size, label}] — with no match the reduce seed yields 0 and every maximumError comparison passes. Chunk names come from budget-stats.ts as initialRecord?.name ?? getChunkNameFromMetafile(metafile, file), and getChunkNameFromMetafile only returns a name when metafile.outputs[file].entryPoint is set, so esbuild-produced shared/split chunks can carry no name at all. Practical read: per-lazy-chunk budgets are supported on paper and fragile in practice — use allScript and anyScript for coverage instead.

standards.claim: Angular budgets are evaluated against RAW uncompressed output bytes, not the 'Estimated transfer size' column printed beside them in the same build summary — that column is brotli-compressed. Angular's kb/mb units are decimal (1 kb = 1000 bytes, 1 mb = 1,000,000 bytes), not binary.
standards.threshold: Raw bytes; BYTES_IN_KILOBYTE = 1000; transfer-size column uses brotliCompress
standards.source_name: angular/angular-cli 20.3.x — tools/esbuild/budget-stats.ts, tools/esbuild/utils.ts, utils/bundle-calculator.ts (fetched raw)
standards.notes: generateBudgetStats() populates stats.assets from outputFiles' raw `size`; the separate calculateEstimatedTransferSizes() calls Node's brotliCompress and feeds only the display table. bundle-calculator.ts line 15 defines BYTES_IN_KILOBYTE = 1000 and calculateBytes multiplies by it for 'kb'/'mb'/'gb' (case-insensitive). Consequence for this repo: the existing 2.5MB error means 2,500,000 raw bytes, which for typical Angular/ABP output is roughly 500–700 KB over the wire with brotli. The scary-looking number is not as scary as it reads, and conversely a raw budget cannot be compared directly against 'ship under 170 KB' compressed guidance without dividing by ~4.

standards.claim: Angular CLI 20.3.x generates budgets of initial 500kB warn / 1MB error and anyComponentStyle 4kB warn / 8kB error under --strict, and initial 2MB warn / 5MB error with anyComponentStyle 6kB warn / 10kB error when not strict. Budgets are emitted only into the production configuration.
standards.threshold: strict: initial 500kB/1MB, anyComponentStyle 4kB/8kB. non-strict: initial 2MB/5MB, anyComponentStyle 6kB/10kB
standards.source_name: angular/angular-cli 20.3.x — packages/schematics/angular/application/index.ts (fetched raw)
standards.notes: Read the literal budget arrays at lines 227–254 and their placement under configurations.production at line 278. This directly diagnoses the repo's current 2MB warn / 2.5MB error: it is the NON-STRICT scaffold default (2MB/5MB) with only the error value lowered. It was almost certainly never chosen on evidence. Also note the docs and the code disagree on anyComponentStyle defaults — see disagreements.

standards.claim: For an enterprise SPA there is no published authoritative initial-bundle number; the defensible practice is to set the error threshold from the measured current build plus a small headroom and ratchet down, using web.dev's ~170 KB compressed critical-path figure as the long-term target (≈700–850 KB raw at typical brotli ratios) and Angular's strict default of 500kB warn / 1MB error raw as the aspirational ceiling.
standards.threshold: Target: ≤1MB raw initial (Angular strict error). Interim: maximumWarning = measured current, maximumError = measured × 1.10, never above 2MB raw. Legacy anchor: <170 KB compressed critical path, <5s TTI on 3G
standards.source_name: web.dev — Performance budgets 101, cross-referenced with Angular CLI strict defaults
standards.notes: Marked partial deliberately. The 170 KB / 5s-TTI figures come from a web.dev article last updated 2018-11-05, and its headline metric (TTI) was dropped from the Lighthouse performance score in Lighthouse 10 and is now a hidden weight-0 audit in 13.4.1 — so the article is directionally useful but numerically dated, and I found no current first-party replacement number for 'enterprise SPA initial bundle'. I could not measure this repo's actual initial bundle: the working directory available to me (/home/user/Aditya-gam) contains only a personal README and PDFs, not the portal source, so the 'measured current' input must be filled in by the team from one `ng build --configuration production` run.

recommended_checks.what_it_does: Runs `ng build --configuration production` in CI and fails the job on Angular's built-in size budgets. Replace the current single `initial` budget with four entries: `initial` (maximumWarning = today's measured initial total, maximumError = measured × 1.10, capped at 2MB raw), `allScript` (total JS across the whole app including every lazy chunk — this is the entry that actually catches 'someone added a 3 MB PDF library to a lazy route'), `anyScript` (set ~15% above today's largest single emitted chunk, to catch a runaway individual chunk), and keep `anyComponentStyle`.
recommended_checks.tool: Angular CLI 20.3 / @angular-devkit/build-angular:application — built in, no new dependency
recommended_checks.tool_maintained_evidence: Budget implementation read directly from angular/angular-cli branch 20.3.x: packages/angular/build/src/utils/bundle-calculator.ts and tools/esbuild/budget-stats.ts. Angular 20.3.x is the version the repo is already on. https://raw.githubusercontent.com/angular/angular-cli/20.3.x/packages/angular/build/src/utils/bundle-calculator.ts
recommended_checks.rationale_for_two_person_team: Zero new tooling, zero new failure modes, and it is the only performance check here that is fully deterministic — the same commit produces the same bytes on any runner, so it will never flake and therefore will never be bypassed. It also fixes a live defect rather than adding ceremony: the current 2MB/2.5MB is the Angular non-strict scaffold default, so the team has an unowned number guarding nothing, and no coverage at all for lazy chunks. Do NOT try to write per-lazy-chunk `type: bundle` budgets — the names are builder-derived, unwildcardable, and a mistyped name silently passes; `allScript` + `anyScript` gets 90% of the value for 10% of the maintenance.

recommended_checks.what_it_does: On every PR that touches the Angular app, builds production, serves dist statically, and runs `lhci autorun` against the four anonymous routes that are about to face the public internet (login, registration, password reset, and the public document-upload entry). Sets `error`-level assertions ONLY on deterministic byte and count facts (`resource-summary:script:size`, `resource-summary:total:size`, `resource-summary:third-party:count`), and `warn`-level on everything score- or timing-derived (`categories:performance`, `largest-contentful-paint`, `cumulative-layout-shift`). numberOfRuns: 3, aggregationMethod: median. temporaryPublicStorage MUST be false; use uploadArtifacts instead.
recommended_checks.tool: treosh/lighthouse-ci-action@12.6.2 (bundles @lhci/cli 0.15.1 / Lighthouse 12.6.1)
recommended_checks.tool_maintained_evidence: treosh/lighthouse-ci-action 12.6.2 and the v12 floating tag both dated 2026-03-12 (https://github.com/treosh/lighthouse-ci-action/tags) — a release within the last 6 months. Caveat to accept knowingly: the underlying @lhci/cli is 0.15.1 from 2025-06-25 with no release in 14 months (https://registry.npmjs.org/@lhci/cli), pinning Lighthouse 12.6.1 while upstream Lighthouse is 13.4.1 (2026-07-20).
recommended_checks.rationale_for_two_person_team: The split is what makes this survivable: the job is a required check, but the only things that can turn it red are byte counts, which are as reproducible as the bundle budget. Timing metrics still get measured and printed on every PR — the team sees the trend — but a noisy GitHub-hosted runner cannot block a merge. This is exactly the posture LHCI's own docs recommend for teams new to performance measurement, and it means the check earns trust instead of being routinely overridden. Scope it to anonymous routes only: those are the pages going public for the first time, they need no auth setup, and they are the ones a stranger will actually load.

recommended_checks.what_it_does: A scheduled workflow (nightly or weekly, on a cron) running the same LHCI config against the deployed non-production environment with numberOfRuns: 5 and aggregationMethod: median, uploading the HTML reports as workflow artifacts with ~90-day retention. Nothing fails; it exists purely to give a trend line that PR-level runs cannot.
recommended_checks.tool: treosh/lighthouse-ci-action@12.6.2 with uploadArtifacts: true
recommended_checks.tool_maintained_evidence: Same action as above, 12.6.2 dated 2026-03-12. LHCI's documented default numberOfRuns is 3 and its 'complete experience' recipe uses 5 (https://github.com/GoogleChrome/lighthouse-ci/blob/main/docs/configuration.md).
recommended_checks.rationale_for_two_person_team: Reuses the lighthouserc.json already written for the PR job, so the marginal cost is a cron block and an artifact upload. It is the cheap substitute for a self-hosted LHCI server: five runs on a quiet schedule against a stable environment produce a far more meaningful number than three runs on a contended PR runner, and artifacts give you month-over-month comparison without operating a database. Two people can look at this once a month and be done.

recommended_checks.what_it_does: A documented one-liner — `ng build --configuration production --stats-json`, then drop dist/stats.json into https://esbuild.github.io/analyze/ — run by hand whenever the bundle-budget check goes red or a large dependency is proposed. Written into CONTRIBUTING.md so it is not tribal knowledge.
recommended_checks.tool: Angular CLI `statsJson` option (built in) + esbuild's own analyzer
recommended_checks.tool_maintained_evidence: `statsJson` confirmed present in the Angular 20.3.x application builder schema with description 'Generates a stats.json file which can be analyzed with https://esbuild.github.io/analyze/' (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/angular/angular-cli/20.3.x/packages/angular/build/src/builders/application/schema.json). Deliberately NOT recommending source-map-explorer: its latest release is 2.5.3 from 2022-09-26 (https://registry.npmjs.org/source-map-explorer), roughly four years stale.
recommended_checks.rationale_for_two_person_team: A size gate without a diagnosis tool is a gate people disable. This costs an hour, adds no CI minutes, no dependency and no maintenance, and turns 'the budget check is red and I don't know why' — the single most common reason budgets get raised instead of fixed — into a two-minute answer.

recommended_checks.what_it_does: Extends the LHCI config with a puppeteerScript that logs into a seeded synthetic tenant and audits two or three of the real post-login screens (the scheduling grid, an examination detail page). Runs on the same nightly schedule, advisory only, never on PRs.
recommended_checks.tool: @lhci/cli puppeteerScript + puppeteer (installed separately)
recommended_checks.tool_maintained_evidence: puppeteerScript documented in LHCI docs/configuration.md, which notes puppeteer must be installed independently and that 'the browser is kept open across all URLs, so if you're keeping auth in cookies then everything should be remembered between runs' (https://github.com/GoogleChrome/lighthouse-ci/blob/main/docs/configuration.md).
recommended_checks.rationale_for_two_person_team: This is honestly the phase-2 item — do it in the second or third month, not before launch. It matters because the anonymous routes are the pages nobody spends time on: real users log in once and then live inside data grids for an hour, which is precisely where an ABP/Angular admin app goes slow. But it is also the most expensive and most fragile thing on this list (auth flow drift, tenant seeding, host-header tenancy resolution making the login URL non-obvious), so it must never be a gate. Defer it consciously rather than half-building it now.

not_worth_it_here: Standing up a self-hosted Lighthouse CI server (the Node app plus its Postgres/SQLite store) for historical trending, build diffing and GitHub status checks. This is what a larger org does and it genuinely gives better reporting, but it is a service two SDE 1s would have to operate, patch and back up for the rest of the product's life — and @lhci/cli itself has had no release since 2025-06-25, so you would be operating an unmaintained service. Nightly `uploadArtifacts` retained for 90 days gets you the trend line for a cron block and zero operational surface.

Gating merges on `categories:performance` with a minScore threshold. Lighthouse's score is 30% Total Blocking Time and 10% Speed Index, both of which swing materially on shared GitHub-hosted runners depending on what else is on the box; Chrome's own scoring documentation advises thinking of performance as 'a distribution of scores, rather than a single number'. A team of two who see a red check they cannot reproduce locally will start merging past it within about three weeks, and the habit generalises to the checks that DO matter. Keep the score visible and advisory.

Per-lazy-route `type: "bundle"` budgets for every feature area. Angular supports them, but the `name` is the builder-reported bundle name with no wildcard support, esbuild-produced shared/split chunks may carry no name at all, and a budget whose name matches nothing silently computes 0 bytes and always passes. You would be maintaining a list of fragile strings that fail open. `allScript` plus `anyScript` covers the same failure mode with two lines and no rot.

Commercial synthetic + RUM platforms (SpeedCurve, Calibre, DebugBear and similar) and real-device labs. These are the correct answer at 30 engineers. Setup, dashboard curation and alert tuning are recurring work you do not have, and the specific value they add — cross-device field distributions — is muted for an app whose entire population is ~11 offices of staff on managed desktops.

A full INP/soft-navigation attribution pipeline with a metrics backend, dashboards and alerting before launch. Ship the minimal thing instead: web-vitals v6 with a beacon to one endpoint, so that six months from now you have data. The attribution build, per-route slicing and dashboards are a month of work to analyse a population that does not exist yet.

Server-side rendering or hydration to improve first-paint metrics. This is a large architectural change to an ABP Angular app, aimed at a metric (LCP on cold navigation) that each user experiences roughly once per working session on a portal they are contractually obliged to use. The payoff structure that justifies SSR — anonymous visitors who bounce — does not apply here.

Backend/API load and latency testing (k6, NBomber, Gatling) as a merge gate. It is real work and it should happen, but with database-per-tenant across 11 to 33 SQL Server databases the interesting performance questions are connection-pool, per-tenant-DB and hosting-shaped, which is the separate infrastructure exercise. A merge gate on API latency measured on a CI runner would measure the runner.

Chasing a green Lighthouse accessibility or best-practices score inside the performance job. Keep the perf workflow doing one thing; accessibility has its own gate and its own owner, and bundling them means one flaky metric holds the other hostage.
surprises: Lighthouse's performance score does not include INP at all. In Lighthouse 13.4.1's default-config.js the entry is literally `{id: 'interaction-to-next-paint', weight: 0, ...}` — same in 12.6.1 and 13.0.0. So a green Lighthouse performance score is silent about the one Core Web Vital most likely to be bad in an ABP data-grid admin app. Total Blocking Time (weight 30, the largest single weight) is the lab proxy, and it is measured during page load only. If the team's mental model is 'Lighthouse 90+ means we're fine on Core Web Vitals', that model is wrong by one whole metric.

budget.json is dead upstream. Lighthouse 12.0.0's release notes say, verbatim, 'remove budgets (#15950)'; I confirmed by file listing that /core/audits/performance-budget.js, /core/audits/timing-budget.js and /core/config/budget.js exist in lighthouse@11.7.1 and are absent from 12.0.0 onward, and that the `--budget-path` CLI flag is present in 11.7.1 and gone in 13.4.1. Meanwhile web.dev's own article 'Use Lighthouse for performance budgets' — which walks you through exactly this — is still live, still shows no deprecation notice, and is stamped last-updated 2019-06-14. Any tutorial-following attempt to add budget.json via the plain Lighthouse CLI produces a silent no-op. It survives only inside @lhci/cli, which converts budget.json client-side into its own resource-summary assertions. The spec repo GoogleChrome/budget.json was archived 2022-12-29.

Angular budgets measure RAW uncompressed bytes, while the 'Estimated transfer size' column printed immediately beside them in the same build table is brotli-compressed (Node's brotliCompress, in tools/esbuild/utils.ts). The two numbers differ by roughly 4x and it is very easy to read the wrong one. Their 2.5MB error is ~2.5 MB on disk, likely 500–700 KB over the wire — so the budget is looser than the raw number makes it sound relative to shipping advice, and it cannot be compared to any 'ship under N KB compressed' guidance without converting.

Their current budget was never chosen. Angular CLI 20.3.x's schematic emits `initial: 2MB warn / 5MB error` for a non-strict `ng new`, and `500kB / 1MB` for `--strict`. The repo's 2MB warn / 2.5MB error is the non-strict scaffold with only the error value nudged down. It is scaffold residue that has been passing for the life of the project, not a threshold anyone defended.

A `type: "bundle"` budget that matches no chunk fails OPEN. BundleCalculator reduces the filtered chunk list with a seed of 0 and returns `[{size: 0, ...}]`, so a misspelled or drifted bundle name yields 0 bytes and passes every maximumError forever. The budget appears in angular.json, shows up in code review as 'we have lazy budgets', and enforces nothing. This is the worst failure mode on the list because it is invisible.

This app will never appear in CrUX — ever. CrUX requires pages that are publicly discoverable and indexable AND meet an undisclosed minimum visitor count, plus opted-in Chrome users. A login-gated portal for 11 offices fails on every axis. That means PageSpeed Insights' field-data panel, Search Console's Core Web Vitals report and every CrUX-backed dashboard will be permanently blank for this origin. Field data is not something the team will 'get later'; it exists only if they instrument it themselves with the web-vitals library. Most teams discover this the week after launch when they open PSI and see nothing.

Core Web Vitals barely apply to a SPA after the first page load. Chrome's own soft-navigations documentation states plainly: 'The popular Single Page Application architecture has never been fully supported by the Core Web Vitals metrics.' LCP and CLS are scoped to hard navigations, so on a portal where a user logs in once and works for an hour, essentially one navigation out of dozens is measured. Soft-navigation measurement only ships unflagged from Chrome 151 and still requires explicit instrumentation (Performance Observer or web-vitals v6). This is genuinely new — the doc was updated 2026-07-21 — and it changes what 'measuring Core Web Vitals' even means for this app.

`temporaryPublicStorage: true` is the copy-paste default in nearly every Lighthouse CI tutorial, and it uploads the complete Lighthouse report — including a full-page screenshot and every network request URL — to a publicly readable address. LHCI's own docs warn: 'This is temporary and public storage. If you're uncomfortable with the idea of your Lighthouse reports being stored on a public URL for anyone to see, skip to the add assertions or Lighthouse CI server steps.' On a HIPAA-regulated portal this is a data-egress path that is harmless today with synthetic data and will still be there, unnoticed, the day real PHI arrives. Set it false at the moment the workflow is written, not later.

Lighthouse CI is quietly aging and nobody announces it. @lhci/cli 0.15.1 shipped 2025-06-25, the last commit to main is 2025-06-26, and it pins `lighthouse: "12.6.1"` exactly — while Lighthouse itself is at 13.4.1 (2026-07-20) with daily dev builds. There is no archive banner and no deprecation notice, so it looks healthy. Its dependency tree also pins yargs ^15, inquirer ^6, uuid ^8, tmp ^0.1 and express ^4, which will generate audit noise the moment the team turns on dependency scanning — worth deciding in advance that this is an accepted CI-only devDependency rather than re-litigating it in a PR.

LHCI's default aggregationMethod is `optimistic` — documented as 'the value most likely to pass'. Combined with the default numberOfRuns of 3, the out-of-the-box behaviour is deliberately lenient, and a team assuming they are asserting against a median is measuring something meaningfully more forgiving than they think. Set `aggregationMethod: 'median'` explicitly.

The `lighthouse:no-pwa` preset is now pointless — Lighthouse 12.0.0 removed the entire PWA category. Copying the `lighthouse:no-pwa` recipe from a 2023 blog post is harmless but signals the recipe is stale in other ways too.

Angular's `kb` and `mb` are decimal, not binary: bundle-calculator.ts defines `BYTES_IN_KILOBYTE = 1000`. So `2.5MB` means 2,500,000 bytes, not 2,621,440. A ~5% discrepancy, which matters only when a budget is set right at the edge — which is exactly where a ratcheting budget lives.
disagreements: Angular's documentation contradicts the Angular CLI's own code on default budget values. The docs source (adev/src/content/tools/cli/build.md) states anyComponentStyle 'Defaults to warning at 2kb and erroring at 4kb' and initial 'Defaults to warning at 500kb and erroring at 1mb'. The 20.3.x application schematic actually generates anyComponentStyle 4kB/8kB and initial 500kB/1MB under --strict, and anyComponentStyle 6kB/10kB with initial 2MB/5MB when not strict. The initial value matches only in the strict case; the anyComponentStyle value matches neither. Treat the schematic source as authoritative for what you will actually get, and the docs as a statement of intent.

web.dev actively recommends a feature Lighthouse deleted. 'Use Lighthouse for performance budgets' (web.dev/articles/use-lighthouse-for-performance-budgets, last updated 2019-06-14) walks through budget.json and LightWallet with no deprecation notice, while the Lighthouse v12.0.0 release notes say 'remove budgets (#15950)' and the audit files are verifiably gone from the package from 12.0.0 onward. Google's guidance site and Google's tool disagree, and the guidance site is the one that is wrong. Resolved in favour of the release notes and the package contents.

Chrome's 'Lighthouse performance scoring' page (developer.chrome.com/docs/lighthouse/performance/performance-scoring) is stamped last-updated 2019-09-19 and presents the weights as 'Lighthouse 10'. The weights it lists happen to still match Lighthouse 13.4.1's default-config.js (FCP 10 / LCP 25 / TBT 30 / CLS 25 / SI 10), but the page never mentions INP, whose weight-0 entry is the single most consequential fact about the score for a 2026 reader. Resolved by reading default-config.js at tag v13.4.1 directly.

Guidance on whether performance budgets should break the build is genuinely split, including within one document. LHCI's getting-started.md says both 'failing the build based on the audit results is even better!' and 'If you're new to performance measurement or your site has a lot of room for improvement, we recommend skipping this step for now.' web.dev's 'Performance budgets 101' (last updated 2018-11-05) recommends wiring budgets into the build but stops short of saying they should fail it. There is no single authoritative answer; my recommendation — gate on deterministic bytes, advise on timings — is a synthesis, not a citation.

The most widely-cited concrete budget number, web.dev's '<170 KB of critical-path resources, <5s Time to Interactive on 3G' (2018), is anchored to a metric that no longer exists in the scoring model: TTI was dropped from the Lighthouse performance score in Lighthouse 10 and is a hidden weight-0 audit in 13.4.1. The byte figure remains a reasonable directional target; the timing figure should not be quoted as a current standard.

Angular's docs and Angular's code do not agree on whether lazy-chunk budgets are practically usable. The docs say plainly 'To configure a budget for a lazy-loaded bundle, use type: "bundle" and set name to that bundle's name' — presented without caveat. The implementation resolves chunk names via metafile entryPoints and fails open (0 bytes, always passes) when no chunk matches, which the docs never mention. Both statements are true; the docs are incomplete in a way that matters.

material_errors: [7] The claim enumerates only three CrUX user opt-in conditions but its own THRESHOLD field says 'four'; the page lists four — the omitted one is 'Use a supported platform.'

[14] The cited getting-started.md contains NEITHER 'numberOfRuns' NOR any 'complete experience' recipe with 5 runs. numberOfRuns default 3 is documented in docs/configuration.md, not the cited page. The '5 runs in the complete experience recipe' threshold is unsupported by any page I could find.

[17] The final sentence ('a bundle budget whose name matches no chunk evaluates to 0 bytes and silently passes') does not appear on the cited Angular build.md. It is true, but only verifiable from bundle-calculator.ts source.

[18] The cited budget-stats.ts contains neither BYTES_IN_KILOBYTE = 1000 nor brotliCompress. The claim's substance is correct but needs two additional citations (utils/bundle-calculator.ts and tools/esbuild/utils.ts).

[13] The cited budgets-converter.js proves only the KB→bytes (×1024) conversion. 'budgetsFile cannot be combined with any other assert option' is in lighthouse-ci docs/configuration.md, and 'transfer size' is from the budget.json spec README — neither is in the cited file.

The claim's prose names only three and omits the fourth: 'Use a supported platform' (desktop Chrome or Android Chrome) — its own THRESHOLD field already says 'four user opt-in conditions', so claim text and threshold disagree.
