results.claim: Lazy-chunk budgets are supported only by naming each bundle individually via type:'bundle' + name; name matches the builder-reported bundle name not the emitted filename; no wildcards/regex; an unmatched name evaluates to 0 bytes and silently passes.
results.evidence_quote: To configure a budget for a lazy-loaded bundle, use `type: "bundle"` and set `name` to that bundle's name. ... The `name` field matches the bundle name, not the emitted filename, so it does not use wildcard or regular expression patterns such as `admin.*.js`.
results.correction: First three sub-claims are verbatim-correct on this page. The fourth — 'unmatched name → 0 bytes → silently passes' — is NOT documented anywhere on this page; it is an inference from source. I verified it holds: BundleCalculator in packages/angular/build/src/utils/bundle-calculator.ts does `this.chunks.filter(chunk => chunk?.names?.includes(budgetName)).map(...).reduce((l, r) => l + r, 0)`, so a non-matching name yields size 0 and any maximumError passes. Cite bundle-calculator.ts for that sentence, and flag it as source-derived rather than documented. Separately, be aware this same build.md is stale on defaults — it claims anyComponentStyle 'Defaults to warning at 2kb and erroring at 4kb', which contradicts the actual schematic (see claim 19).

results.claim: Angular budgets are evaluated against raw uncompressed bytes, not the brotli-compressed 'Estimated transfer size' column; kb/mb are decimal (1 kb = 1000 bytes).
results.evidence_quote: stats.assets.push({ name: file, size });  // size taken directly from BuildOutputFile, no compression applied
results.correction: Claim substance is correct but the cited file supports only the 'raw bytes' half. budget-stats.ts contains no BYTES_IN_KILOBYTE and no brotli reference. Add two citations: (a) packages/angular/build/src/utils/bundle-calculator.ts line 15, `export const BYTES_IN_KILOBYTE = 1000;` with 'mb' computed as BYTES_IN_KILOBYTE * BYTES_IN_KILOBYTE — confirms decimal units; (b) packages/angular/build/src/tools/esbuild/utils.ts, which does `import { brotliCompress } from 'node:zlib'` and stores `result.byteLength` per output file — confirms the transfer-size column is brotli.

results.claim: Angular CLI 20.3.x generates initial 500kB/1MB and anyComponentStyle 4kB/8kB under --strict, and initial 2MB/5MB with anyComponentStyle 6kB/10kB when not strict; budgets emitted only into the production configuration.
results.evidence_quote: if (options.strict) { budgets = [{type:'initial', maximumWarning:'500kB', maximumError:'1MB'}, {type:'anyComponentStyle', maximumWarning:'4kB', maximumError:'8kB'}]; } else { budgets = [{type:'initial', maximumWarning:'2MB', maximumError:'5MB'}, {type:'anyComponentStyle', maximumWarning:'6kB', maximumError:'10kB'}]; }
results.correction: none — all eight numbers exact, and `configurations: { production: { budgets, outputHashing: 'all' } }` confirms production-only emission. Worth flagging that Angular's own adev build.md is stale here, stating anyComponentStyle 'Defaults to warning at 2kb and erroring at 4kb'; the schematic source is authoritative.

results.claim: No published authoritative initial-bundle number for enterprise SPAs; ratchet from measured build, using web.dev's ~170 KB compressed critical-path figure (<5s TTI on 3G) as long-term target and Angular strict 500kB/1MB raw as ceiling.
results.evidence_quote: Under 5 s Time to Interactive ... Under 170 KB of critical-path resources (compressed/minified) ... These numbers are calculated based on real-world baseline devices and 3G network speed.
results.correction: The 170 KB compressed / <5s TTI on 3G anchor is confirmed verbatim, including the 3G basis. The rest of the claim is not from this page and should be labelled as such: the ≈700–850 KB raw equivalent is an unsourced brotli-ratio extrapolation by the author (real brotli ratios on Angular bundles vary roughly 3.5–5×, so the range is a guess, not a derivation), and the Angular strict 500kB/1MB ceiling comes from the schematics source in claim 19. Also note the page frames 170 KB / 5s TTI as a legacy 2019-era default, and TTI is no longer a Core Web Vital and carries weight 0 in Lighthouse 13.4.1 — so present it as a directional anchor, not a current standard. 'partial' confidence is the right label.

research.area: Accessibility — WCAG conformance target, US/California legal exposure for a private healthcare-adjacent portal, and sustainable CI enforcement for a two-person Angular 20 team
research.standard_summary: Build to WCAG 2.2 Level A + AA. WCAG 2.2 is still the current W3C Recommendation (REC 5 Oct 2023, republished 12 Dec 2024); WCAG 3.0 got a fresh Working Draft on 3 March 2026 but W3C says it "is not expected to be a completed W3C standard for a few more years," so it is not a build target. Level AA is the operative level — every US regulation that names a technical standard names Level A+AA (DOJ Title II and HHS both name WCAG 2.1 AA; Section 508 still names WCAG 2.0 AA), and WCAG 2.2 AA is backward-compatible with all of them. Legally, nothing in the federal web-accessibility rulebook binds this private company directly: the DOJ's April 2024 rule (28 CFR 35.200) covers public entities only, Section 508 covers federal agencies and federal procurement, and Section 1557/504's web rule (45 CFR 84.84, 92.204) covers recipients of HHS federal financial assistance — which a workers' comp IME scheduling vendor almost certainly is not. What does bind it is ADA Title III (its customers' medical offices are enumerated public accommodations under 42 U.S.C. 12181(7)(F), giving the portal a Robles-style nexus) plus California's Unruh Act, which converts any ADA violation into a state claim carrying a $4,000 statutory minimum per offense plus attorney's fees — and going onto the public internet is precisely the event that makes an anonymous tester able to reach the registration page. Two indirect routes matter more than the direct ones: both 28 CFR 35.200 and 45 CFR 84.84 cover content a covered organization provides "directly or through contractual, licensing, or other arrangements," and Cal. Gov. Code 7405 binds "any entity that contracts with a state or local entity subject to Section 11135" to Section 508 — so a single California city, county, school district or state-agency office as a tenant pulls a dated WCAG conformance obligation into the contract. For CI, the sustainable shape is one linter gate with a banked baseline (angular-eslint's templateAccessibility config plus ESLint bulk suppressions) and one axe-core run over the six anonymous-reachable pages, backed by a short manual keyboard/screen-reader pass per release — because axe-core 4.13 carries exactly one rule tagged wcag22aa, and five of WCAG 2.2's six new A/AA criteria are undetectable by any scanner.

standards.claim: WCAG 2.2 is the current W3C Recommendation and is the correct build target in 2026; WCAG 3.0 remains a Working Draft and is not a conformance target. WCAG 2.2 was published as a W3C Recommendation on 5 October 2023 and republished 12 December 2024; a new WCAG 3.0 Working Draft was published 3 March 2026, and W3C states WCAG 3 'is not expected to be a completed W3C standard for a few more years' and 'will not supersede WCAG 2.'
standards.threshold: WCAG 2.2 (W3C Recommendation, 2024-12-12 republication of the 2023-10-05 REC)
standards.source_name: W3C — Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.2, W3C Recommendation
standards.notes: Opened the TR document (status: 'This document was published by the Accessibility Guidelines Working Group as a Recommendation... W3C recommends the wide deployment of this specification as a standard for the Web'), the WAI WCAG overview page, the WAI WCAG 3 intro page, and the WAI news item at https://www.w3.org/WAI/news/2026-03-03/wcag3 confirming the 3 March 2026 Working Draft. W3C also confirms WCAG 2.0/2.1/2.2 all remain valid Recommendations — later versions do not deprecate earlier ones — and that content conforming to 2.2 also conforms to 2.1 and 2.0. Ignore the trade-press '174 requirements / Candidate Recommendation Q4 2027' timeline chatter: W3C itself publishes no date.

standards.claim: Level AA is the operative conformance level for a public-facing service. WCAG defines three levels — A (lowest), AA, AAA (highest) — and AAA is not a general policy target. Every US regulation that adopts a technical standard adopts 'Level A and Level AA success criteria and conformance requirements.'
standards.threshold: WCAG 2.2 Level A + AA (not AAA)
standards.source_name: W3C — WCAG 2.2 Conformance section
standards.notes: WCAG 2.2 conformance text: 'three levels of conformance are defined: A (lowest), AA, and AAA (highest).' Cross-checked against 28 CFR 35.200 (DOJ) and 45 CFR 84.84 (HHS), both of which adopt 'Level A and Level AA success criteria and conformance requirements specified in WCAG 2.1.' Building to 2.2 AA satisfies 2.1 AA and 2.0 AA by W3C's backward-compatibility statement.

standards.claim: The DOJ's April 2024 ADA Title II web rule (28 CFR 35.200) applies to PUBLIC entities — state and local governments, special purpose districts, Amtrak, commuter authorities — and does NOT apply to a private company. It requires WCAG 2.1 Level A and AA. Its compliance dates were extended by one year on 20 April 2026: 26 April 2027 for public entities serving 50,000+ people, and 26 April 2028 for smaller entities and special district governments.
standards.threshold: WCAG 2.1 A+AA; 2027-04-26 (pop. ≥50,000) / 2028-04-28 [sic: 2028-04-26] (pop. <50,000 and special districts); amendment cite 91 FR 20912, Apr. 20, 2026 (AG Order No. 6742-2026), amending 89 FR 31337, Apr. 24, 2024 (AG Order No. 5919-2024)
standards.source_name: 28 CFR 35.200 (Cornell LII, current text with amendment citations)
standards.notes: Both dates are 26 April (2027 and 2028). ada.gov's own fact sheet carries the extension notice and confirms scope is 'state and local governments... special purpose districts, Amtrak, and other commuter authorities' — it does not address Title III. I could not open federalregister.gov directly: every FR URL 302-redirected to unblock.federalregister.gov through the agent proxy, so I used the current CFR text (which carries the FR amendment citations) plus ada.gov instead.

standards.claim: The Title II rule reaches private vendors indirectly by contract. 28 CFR 35.200(a) covers '(1) Web content that a public entity provides or makes available, directly or through contractual, licensing, or other arrangements; and (2) Mobile apps that a public entity provides or makes available, directly or through contractual, licensing, or other arrangements.' A California city, county, school district or other self-insured public employer using this portal to administer its workers' comp program makes the portal its web content for this purpose.
standards.threshold: 'directly or through contractual, licensing, or other arrangements' — 28 CFR 35.200(a)(1)-(2)
standards.source_name: 28 CFR 35.200 (Cornell LII)
standards.notes: 45 CFR 84.84(a) uses word-for-word the same 'directly or through contractual, licensing, or other arrangements' construction for HHS recipients. The regulation text is verified; the inference that a public-agency tenant triggers it for this specific portal is a fact-dependent legal conclusion, not something I can cite. This is not legal advice.

standards.claim: ADA Title III imposes no technical web standard. DOJ has never issued a Title III web regulation; its 2010 ANPRM and 2016 SANPRM were withdrawn in 2017, and Title III rulemaking remains shelved. DOJ's current public guidance says businesses 'can currently choose how they will ensure that the programs, services, and goods they provide online are accessible to people with disabilities' and that 'The Department of Justice does not have a regulation setting out detailed standards.'
standards.threshold: No mandated technical standard for Title III; WCAG named only as 'helpful guidance'
standards.source_name: ADA.gov — Guidance on Web Accessibility and the ADA (last updated March 18, 2022)
standards.notes: The second source is Seyfarth Shaw's ADA Title III blog (SECONDARY, law firm) dated 20 April 2026, which states Title III regulations are 'now paused indefinitely.' The absence of a DOJ standard is not a defense: courts supply WCAG as the remedy (see next entry).

standards.claim: ADA Title III very likely does apply to this portal. 42 U.S.C. 12181(7)(F) enumerates as public accommodations 'a laundromat, dry-cleaner, bank, barber shop, beauty shop, travel service, shoe repair service, funeral parlor, gas station, office of an accountant or lawyer, pharmacy, insurance office, professional office of a health care provider, hospital, or other service establishment.' In the Ninth Circuit, Robles v. Domino's Pizza (No. 17-55504, filed January 15, 2019) held the ADA applies to a website and app that 'connected customers to the goods and services of Domino's physical restaurants,' that 'the ADA applies to the services of a public accommodation, not services in a place of public accommodation,' and that 'the lack of specific regulations, not yet promulgated by the Department of Justice, did not eliminate Domino's statutory duty.'
standards.threshold: Nexus test (9th Cir.); 42 U.S.C. 12181(7)(F) covers 'professional office of a health care provider' and 'insurance office'
standards.source_name: Robles v. Domino's Pizza, LLC, 9th Cir. No. 17-55504 (Jan. 15, 2019), slip opinion
standards.notes: I downloaded and extracted the slip opinion text directly. A portal that schedules medical examinations at physical examiner offices has a stronger nexus than Domino's did. California is in the Ninth Circuit. Counter-authority exists for website-only businesses in California state court (Martinez v. Cot'n Wash, Cal. Ct. App. 2022) — I could not open it (WebSearch budget exhausted; only a Mintz summary title was visible), and it is likely irrelevant here because this portal has a physical-office nexus. Not legal advice.

standards.claim: ADA Title III itself yields no money damages to private plaintiffs — only injunctive relief plus discretionary attorney's fees. 42 U.S.C. 12188(a)(1) provides that 'The remedies and procedures set forth in section 2000a-3(a) of this title are the remedies and procedures this subchapter provides,' and 42 U.S.C. 2000a-3(a) authorizes 'a civil action for preventive relief, including an application for a permanent or temporary injunction, restraining order, or other order,' while 2000a-3(b) lets the court 'in its discretion... allow the prevailing party, other than the United States, a reasonable attorney's fee.'
standards.threshold: Injunctive relief + discretionary attorney's fees; $0 statutory damages under Title III
standards.source_name: 42 U.S.C. 12188 and 42 U.S.C. 2000a-3 (Cornell LII)
standards.notes: This is why California web-accessibility complaints are almost always pleaded as ADA + Unruh: the ADA count supplies the violation, the Unruh count supplies the money.

standards.claim: California's Unruh Civil Rights Act converts any ADA violation into a state-law claim with a $4,000 statutory minimum per offense plus attorney's fees. Cal. Civ. Code 51(f): 'A violation of the right of any individual under the federal Americans with Disabilities Act of 1990 (Public Law 101-336) shall also constitute a violation of this section.' Cal. Civ. Code 52(a) makes a violator 'liable for each and every offense for the actual damages, and any amount that may be determined by a jury, or a court sitting without a jury, up to a maximum of three times the amount of actual damage but in no case less than four thousand dollars ($4,000), and any attorney's fees.'
standards.threshold: $4,000 statutory minimum per offense, up to 3x actual damages, plus attorney's fees (Cal. Civ. Code 52(a))
standards.source_name: California Civil Code sections 51 and 52 (California Legislative Information)
standards.notes: This is the single largest legal exposure created by moving off the office LAN. The driver of filing volume is fee-shifting under 52(a), not the $4,000 itself. Civ. Code 52(f) also permits a complaint to the California Civil Rights Department. Not legal advice — have counsel confirm before relying on any of this.

standards.claim: California has NO private-sector web accessibility statute. AB 1757 (2023-2024 session), which would have required 'business establishments' and their third-party developers and vendors to meet WCAG 2.1 AA and created a private right of action against developers, died — last action 'From Senate committee without further action' on 11/30/24, status 'Inactive Bill - Died.' It was never enacted.
standards.threshold: No California statutory WCAG mandate for private businesses as of 2026-08-28; AB 1757 died 2024-11-30
standards.source_name: California Legislative Information — AB-1757 bill status (2023-2024 session)
standards.notes: Verified that AB 1757 died. I could NOT verify whether a successor bill exists in the 2025-2026 session — my WebSearch budget was exhausted before I could search the current session, and leginfo's search is form-driven and not fetchable. Treat 'no successor bill' as unverified; check leginfo for the 2025-26 session before relying on this. Note what AB 1757 would have done: extend liability to third-party developers. That is a two-person dev team.

standards.claim: California Government Code 7405 extends Section 508 obligations to private contractors of state and local entities. It requires that 'state governmental entities, in developing, procuring, maintaining, or using electronic or information technology, either indirectly or through the use of state funds by other entities, shall comply with the accessibility requirements of Section 508 of the federal Rehabilitation Act of 1973, as amended (29 U.S.C. Sec. 794d)' and extends to 'any entity that contracts with a state or local entity subject to Section 11135.' Gov. Code 11135(a) reaches 'any program or activity that is conducted, operated, or administered by the state or by any state agency, is funded directly by the state, or receives any financial assistance from the state.'
standards.threshold: Section 508 / 36 CFR Part 1194 — i.e. WCAG 2.0 Level A+AA — flowed down by contract to entities contracting with California state/local entities
standards.source_name: California Government Code section 7405 (California Legislative Information)
standards.notes: California workers' comp is full of public self-insured employers (cities, counties, school districts, CSU/UC, State Fund). This is the most likely route by which a hard, dated WCAG obligation lands in a contract. Note the awkward result: 7405 points at Section 508, which is still WCAG 2.0 AA, while 28 CFR 35.200 points at WCAG 2.1 AA — a public-sector contract can impose two different WCAG versions at once. Building to 2.2 AA satisfies both.

standards.claim: Section 508 does not reach this application directly. The Revised 508 Standards (36 CFR Part 1194, finalized January 2017) incorporate WCAG 2.0 Level A and AA — E205.4: 'Electronic content shall conform to Level A and Level AA Success Criteria and Conformance Requirements in WCAG 2.0' — and apply to federal agencies developing, procuring, maintaining or using ICT. They bind a private company only through federal procurement, which does not describe this portal.
standards.threshold: WCAG 2.0 Level A+AA (36 CFR Part 1194, E205.4 / 501); federal agencies and federal procurement only
standards.source_name: U.S. Access Board — Information and Communication Technology (Section 508 / 255) standards
standards.notes: Verified the standard, the WCAG 2.0 A+AA level and the federal-agency scope. I found NO evidence of a pending Access Board refresh to WCAG 2.1/2.2 on the page I opened, but I could not affirmatively confirm the absence of one (search budget exhausted) — treat 'no refresh pending' as unverified. Section 508 matters here only via the California Gov. Code 7405 flow-down above.

standards.claim: Section 1557 of the ACA applies only to recipients of HHS federal financial assistance, HHS-administered health programs, and Title I entities — not to vendors as such. 45 CFR 92.2 applies the rule to 'Every health program or activity, any part of which receives Federal financial assistance, directly or indirectly, from the Department', 'Every health program or activity administered by the Department', and 'Every health program or activity administered by a title I entity.' Its ICT provision, 45 CFR 92.204(b), does not itself name WCAG: it says 'A recipient or State Exchange shall ensure that its health programs and activities provided through websites and mobile applications comply with the requirements of section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act, as interpreted consistent with title II of the ADA.'
standards.threshold: Scope = recipients of HHS FFA / HHS programs / Title I entities. 92.204(b) defers to the Section 504 rule; no WCAG version stated in 92.204 itself
standards.source_name: 45 CFR 92.2 and 45 CFR 92.204 (Cornell LII)
standards.notes: IMPORTANT PRECISION: a lot of published commentary says '1557 requires WCAG 2.1 AA by May 2026.' The regulation does not say that. 92.204(b) routes to Section 504, whose technical standard and dates live in 45 CFR 84.84 (next entry). A workers' comp IME scheduling vendor is very unlikely to be an HHS FFA recipient — workers' compensation is state-regulated and is not HHS federal financial assistance — so 1557 most likely does not bind this company directly. That is a fact question for counsel, not something I can determine.

standards.claim: The HHS Section 504 web rule, 45 CFR 84.84, is the provision that actually carries WCAG 2.1 A+AA for health programs, and its compliance dates were extended by one year in May 2026. Current text: recipients with 15 or more employees must comply by May 11, 2027, and recipients with fewer than 15 employees by May 10, 2028. Coverage extends to '(1) Web content that a recipient provides or makes available, directly or through contractual, licensing, or other arrangements; and (2) Mobile apps...'
standards.threshold: WCAG 2.1 Level A+AA; 2027-05-11 (15+ employees) / 2028-05-10 (<15 employees); amendment cites 89 FR 40193 (May 9, 2024) and 91 FR 25507 (May 11, 2026)
standards.source_name: 45 CFR 84.84 (Cornell LII, current text with amendment citations)
standards.notes: HHS OCR's own press release confirms the new dates (May 11, 2027 / May 10, 2028) and the WCAG 2.1 AA standard, and states the extension aligns Section 504 with DOJ's parallel Title II action. The original dates were May 11, 2026 / May 10, 2027 — anyone working from 2024 or 2025 notes has the wrong dates. HHS also stated the delay 'does not relieve recipients of their other obligations under Section 504.' As with Title II, the 'through contractual, licensing, or other arrangements' language is what pulls a vendor in via its customers.

standards.claim: Most physician offices became Section 1557 covered entities in 2024 because HHS reclassified Medicare Part B as federal financial assistance, eliminating the long-standing Part B exception. Providers whose only federal funding was Part B were given until May 6, 2025 to come into compliance.
standards.threshold: Medicare Part B = federal financial assistance under the 2024 Section 1557 final rule (89 FR 37522, May 6, 2024)
standards.source_name: HHS — Section 1557 Final Rule FAQs (and the 2024 final rule at 89 FR 37522)
standards.notes: SECONDARY sourcing. I surfaced the HHS FAQ URL and the Bass Berry & Sims client alert through search but did not open either page directly before my WebSearch budget was exhausted, and federalregister.gov / govinfo were unreachable through the proxy for 89 FR 37522. Marked partial. Load-bearing implication if true: the examiner offices using this portal are themselves 1557 covered entities, which is how a WCAG obligation becomes a procurement question for this vendor even though the vendor is not itself covered.

standards.claim: WCAG 2.2 added six Level A/AA success criteria that land directly on the flows about to become publicly reachable, and removed 4.1.1 Parsing. New A/AA criteria: 3.2.6 Consistent Help (A), 3.3.7 Redundant Entry (A), 2.4.11 Focus Not Obscured (Minimum) (AA), 2.5.7 Dragging Movements (AA), 2.5.8 Target Size (Minimum) (AA), 3.3.8 Accessible Authentication (Minimum) (AA). 3.3.8 requires that 'Content does not rely on cognitive function test to authenticate unless an alternative authentication method is available.' 2.5.8 requires targets of at least 24 by 24 CSS pixels. 4.1.1 Parsing was 'obsolete and removed from WCAG 2.2.'
standards.source_name: W3C WAI — What's New in WCAG 2.2
standards.notes: Levels taken from the WAI 'What's New' page and cross-checked against the TR. Caution: the WCAG 2.2 Quick Reference rendering I fetched mis-reported 3.3.8 and 2.5.8 as Level A — the normative TR and the WAI page both say AA. Practical read for this app: a CAPTCHA on the public registration form with no non-cognitive alternative is a straight 3.3.8 AA failure, and a drag-and-drop-only document uploader is a straight 2.5.7 AA failure. Those are the two most likely public-internet hardening moves.

standards.claim: angular-eslint ships a dedicated accessibility rule set. The umbrella `angular-eslint` package exports the flat configs `tsRecommended`, `templateRecommended`, `tsAll`, `templateAll` and `templateAccessibility`. The accessibility preset in `@angular-eslint/eslint-plugin-template` contains 12 rules: alt-text, click-events-have-key-events, elements-content, interactive-supports-focus, label-has-associated-control, mouse-events-have-key-events, no-autofocus, no-distracting-elements, no-positive-tabindex, role-has-required-aria, table-scope, valid-aria. For an Angular 20.3.x app the correct pin is angular-eslint 20.7.0 (published 2025-11-22), whose peer range is eslint ^8.57.0 || ^9.0.0 (NOT ESLint 10).
standards.threshold: `angular.configs.templateAccessibility`; angular-eslint 20.7.0 for Angular 20; eslint ^8.57.0 || ^9.0.0
standards.source_name: angular-eslint — eslint-plugin-template README and configs README
standards.notes: Note the rule name is `label-has-associated-control`, NOT `label-for` (an older name that no longer appears in the rule list) — the task brief called it 'label-for-control'; that rule name does not exist in v20+. Peer ranges pulled from https://registry.npmjs.org/angular-eslint (20.7.0 peerDeps eslint ^8.57.0 || ^9.0.0; 21.4.0 adds ^10.0.0). Wiring: put `...angular.configs.templateRecommended, ...angular.configs.templateAccessibility` in the `files: ['**/*.html']` block of eslint.config.js. Project is actively maintained — latest is 22.1.0 (2026-07-12).

standards.claim: axe-core carries exactly ONE rule tagged wcag22aa (`target-size`), so automated scanning covers almost none of WCAG 2.2's new criteria. Available filter tags are wcag2a, wcag2aa, wcag2aaa, wcag21a, wcag21aa, wcag22aa, best-practice, ACT, section508, EN-301-549, RGAAv4 and experimental. The WCAG 2.0/2.1 A+AA rule set is roughly 60 rules; 'experimental' rules (css-orientation-lock, focus-order-semantics, hidden-content, label-content-name-mismatch, p-as-heading, table-fake-caption, td-has-header) are disabled by default.
standards.threshold: 1 rule tagged wcag22aa (target-size); ~60 rules across wcag2a/wcag2aa/wcag21a/wcag21aa
standards.source_name: axe-core rule descriptions (dequelabs/axe-core, develop branch)
standards.notes: Filter with `.withTags(['wcag2a','wcag2aa','wcag21a','wcag21aa','wcag22aa'])` and deliberately EXCLUDE 'best-practice' from the gate — best-practice rules (landmark-*, region, heading-order, page-has-heading-one, tabindex...) are not WCAG failures and will inflate the 253 number with things you are not legally obliged to fix.

standards.claim: Automated tools cannot establish WCAG conformance. W3C WAI states: 'Web accessibility evaluation tools can not determine accessibility, they can only assist in doing so', 'Tools cannot check all accessibility aspects automatically. Human judgement is required', and 'Sometimes evaluation tools can produce false or misleading results.' Lighthouse's accessibility score is a weighted average of axe-based audits ('Weighting is based on axe user impact assessments') and excludes manual checks entirely.
standards.threshold: No automated tool output constitutes a conformance claim; manual evaluation required
standards.source_name: W3C WAI — Selecting Web Accessibility Evaluation Tools
standards.notes: Directly relevant to how you should word any accessibility statement or ACR: 'axe reports zero violations' is not 'WCAG 2.2 AA conformant', and claiming the latter without a manual audit is itself a liability-creating statement.

standards.claim: ESLint has a first-party bulk-suppressions mechanism designed exactly for the 'enable the rule, don't fix 253 things today' problem. Introduced in ESLint v9.24.0 (April 4, 2025), it provides `--suppress-all`, `--suppress-rule <rule>`, `--prune-suppressions` and `--pass-on-unpruned-suppressions`, writing to `eslint-suppressions.json` in the project root (relocatable via `--suppressions-location`). Only rules configured as 'error' are suppressed; new violations of a suppressed rule still fail.
standards.threshold: ESLint >= 9.24.0; default file `eslint-suppressions.json`
standards.source_name: ESLint documentation — Suppressions
standards.notes: Compatibility check for this stack: angular-eslint 20.7.0 requires eslint ^8.57.0 || ^9.0.0, and ESLint 9.x is still maintained (9.39.5, published 2026-07-10, per https://registry.npmjs.org/eslint). So pin ESLint ^9.39 — that gives you bulk suppressions AND angular-eslint v20. Do not jump to ESLint 10 until you move to angular-eslint 21+.

standards.claim: Both axe-core and pa11y are actively maintained in 2026; Lighthouse CI is effectively dormant. axe-core 4.13.0 published 2026-08-05 (canary builds daily through 2026-08-25); @axe-core/playwright and @axe-core/cli 4.13.0 published 2026-08-11; pa11y 10.0.0 published 2026-08-28 and pa11y-ci 4.1.1 published 2026-05-12; IBM equal-access accessibility-checker 4.0.31 published 2026-08-21. By contrast @lhci/cli's latest release is 0.15.1 from 2025-06-25 and the last commit on GoogleChrome/lighthouse-ci main is 2025-06-26 — over 14 months stale — even though Lighthouse core itself is at 13.4.1 (2026-07-20).
standards.source_name: npm registry metadata (registry.npmjs.org) for each package
standards.notes: I queried the npm registry directly via curl and read the `time` object, so these dates are publication timestamps, not blog claims. Also verified pa11y 10.0.0 requires 'an even numbered version of Node.js 22.13.0 or above'. GitHub's REST API and releases.atom feeds were blocked through the agent proxy, so lighthouse-ci commit dates come from the rendered commits page via WebFetch — treat the exact commit date as approximate, but the 0.15.1 npm date is hard.

standards.claim: Two first-party baseline/ratchet mechanisms exist for a11y scanning, so a pre-existing violation count never needs to break the build. pa11y-ci's `threshold` option 'permit[s] this number of errors, warnings, or notices, otherwise fail with exit code 2' (default 0), settable globally under `defaults` or per URL. IBM's accessibility-checker supports a baseline directory natively: 'Baselines are a helpful feature of accessibility-checker' where tests fail only when results differ from the established baseline, configured via `baselineFolder` (default 'baselines'), `failLevels` (default ['violation','potentialviolation']), `reportLevels`, `policies` (default ['IBM_Accessibility']) and `ruleArchive` (default 'latest').
standards.threshold: pa11y-ci `threshold` (default 0); accessibility-checker `baselineFolder` (default 'baselines'), `failLevels` default ['violation','potentialviolation']
standards.source_name: pa11y-ci README and IBM equal-access accessibility-checker configuration README
standards.notes: @axe-core/playwright has NO built-in baseline — its API is AxeBuilder({page}).withTags([...]).include(...).exclude(...).disableRules(...).analyze(). With axe you implement the ratchet yourself: assert zero violations at impact 'serious'/'critical', and snapshot the sorted list of remaining violation rule-ids per page so a NEW rule id fails but the known set passes. That is ~20 lines and is what I recommend over adopting a second engine. Caution on pa11y: its default runner is HTML_CodeSniffer and its `standard` values are only WCAG2A/WCAG2AA/WCAG2AAA — that is WCAG 2.0, not 2.1 or 2.2. If you use pa11y at all, set runners to ['axe'].

recommended_checks.what_it_does: Runs ESLint over *.ts and *.html with `...angular.configs.templateRecommended` plus `...angular.configs.templateAccessibility` in the HTML block — 12 accessibility rules including label-has-associated-control, valid-aria, click-events-have-key-events, interactive-supports-focus, role-has-required-aria and alt-text — all set to 'error'. The 253 pre-existing violations are banked once with `npx eslint --suppress-all` into a committed `eslint-suppressions.json`, so CI fails only on NEW violations. A monthly `--prune-suppressions` run ratchets the baseline down as files get touched.
recommended_checks.tool: angular-eslint 20.7.0 (`angular.configs.templateAccessibility`) on ESLint ^9.39; bulk suppressions from ESLint 9.24.0
recommended_checks.tool_maintained_evidence: angular-eslint latest 22.1.0 published 2026-07-12; the v20 line's last release is 20.7.0 on 2025-11-22 and is the correct pin for Angular 20.3.x (peer eslint ^8.57.0 || ^9.0.0) — https://registry.npmjs.org/angular-eslint . ESLint 9.x still maintained: 9.39.5 published 2026-07-10 — https://registry.npmjs.org/eslint . Suppressions feature docs: https://eslint.org/docs/latest/use/suppressions
recommended_checks.rationale_for_two_person_team: Highest value per hour in the whole area. It is one config block plus one command, it runs in the lint job they almost certainly already have, it adds no new CI service, no browser, no flakiness, and zero runtime. Bulk suppressions mean day one is green — nobody is asked to fix 253 things — while every new template written from now on is held to WCAG-relevant rules. Crucially it is a *prevention* gate: at ~27k lines of TS growing weekly, the cheapest a11y strategy is to stop the bleeding rather than remediate. Do NOT also turn on templateAll; that adds stylistic noise and the team will start bypassing.

recommended_checks.what_it_does: A Playwright spec that visits the six anonymous-reachable pages — tenant landing, registration (each of the four external roles if the form differs), login, forgot-password, reset-password, document upload — and runs `new AxeBuilder({page}).withTags(['wcag2a','wcag2aa','wcag21a','wcag21aa','wcag22aa']).analyze()`. Fails the build on any violation with impact 'critical' or 'serious'. For 'moderate'/'minor', it compares the sorted set of violation rule-ids against a committed per-page JSON baseline and fails only when a NEW rule id appears. 'best-practice' tag is deliberately excluded.
recommended_checks.tool: @axe-core/playwright 4.13.0 + @playwright/test 1.62.1
recommended_checks.tool_maintained_evidence: @axe-core/playwright 4.13.0 published 2026-08-11 with release-candidate builds as recent as 2026-08-28; axe-core 4.13.0 published 2026-08-05 with daily canaries — https://registry.npmjs.org/axe-core and https://registry.npmjs.org/@axe-core/playwright . @playwright/test 1.62.1 published 2026-07-30 — https://registry.npmjs.org/@playwright/test . API confirmed at https://github.com/dequelabs/axe-core-npm/blob/develop/packages/playwright/README.md
recommended_checks.rationale_for_two_person_team: Scope it to the pages an anonymous plaintiff-side tester can reach, because those are the only pages that generate an Unruh demand letter, and there are about six of them. Six pages is a half-day of test authoring, not a program. The critical/serious-only gate plus a rule-id baseline means the build does not turn red over pre-existing moderate findings, which is the failure mode that gets a11y gates disabled. If they already run Playwright for e2e, this is an additional spec file, not new infrastructure. Deliberately excluding 'best-practice' keeps the finding list to things that are actually WCAG failures.

recommended_checks.what_it_does: Same axe configuration run on a scheduled workflow against a broader page list — the 10-15 highest-traffic authenticated screens (scheduling calendar, appointment detail, document list, admin user management) — reporting all impact levels to a job summary and opening/updating a single tracking issue. Never blocks a PR. Because tenancy resolves from the Host header, it runs against at least two tenant hosts so that per-office theming (colour contrast especially) is covered.
recommended_checks.tool: @axe-core/playwright 4.13.0 in a GitHub Actions `schedule` workflow
recommended_checks.tool_maintained_evidence: Same as above: @axe-core/playwright 4.13.0, 2026-08-11 — https://registry.npmjs.org/@axe-core/playwright
recommended_checks.rationale_for_two_person_team: Authenticated screens are behind a login, so they carry far lower drive-by-litigation risk than the public pages and do not justify a merge gate. A nightly advisory run gives visibility and a work queue they can pull from during the one dev-week per month, without ever being the reason a PR is stuck at 6pm. The multi-tenant-host detail matters and costs almost nothing once the first spec exists: contrast failures introduced by one office's theme are literally invisible if you only ever scan one Host header.

recommended_checks.what_it_does: A written 60-90 minute checklist run by one developer before each release, covering only the six public flows: full keyboard-only traversal (no mouse) checking visible focus and no keyboard traps; one screen reader pass (NVDA on Windows or VoiceOver on macOS) through registration and login; and explicit checks of the WCAG 2.2 criteria no scanner can see — 3.3.8 Accessible Authentication (is there a non-cognitive alternative to any CAPTCHA?), 2.5.7 Dragging Movements (is there a click/keyboard alternative to drag-and-drop upload?), 3.3.7 Redundant Entry, 3.2.6 Consistent Help, 2.4.11 Focus Not Obscured (does a sticky header or toast cover the focused field?).
recommended_checks.tool: Keyboard + NVDA/VoiceOver + a checklist file in the repo; no CI tooling
recommended_checks.tool_maintained_evidence: Not a tool. Justified by W3C WAI: 'Web accessibility evaluation tools can not determine accessibility, they can only assist in doing so' — https://www.w3.org/WAI/test-evaluate/tools/selecting/ ; and by axe-core carrying only one wcag22aa-tagged rule (target-size) — https://github.com/dequelabs/axe-core/blob/develop/doc/rule-descriptions.md
recommended_checks.effort_hours: 6-8 to write the checklist, then 2-3 per release
recommended_checks.rationale_for_two_person_team: This is the only check that catches the failures most likely to be introduced by going public. Hardening a public registration form usually means adding a CAPTCHA; hardening document upload usually means adding drag-and-drop. Both are WCAG 2.2 Level AA failures that every scanner in this list will report as green. A single keyboard-only pass over six pages also finds focus traps in ABP/Angular Material modals faster than any automated rule. It is deliberately NOT a CI gate — a two-person team cannot automate screen-reader testing sustainably, and pretending otherwise produces a flaky job that gets deleted in three weeks.

recommended_checks.what_it_does: Optional Lighthouse run on the public landing and login pages asserting `"categories:accessibility": ["error", {"minScore": 0.9}]` in lighthouserc, with `numberOfRuns: 3` and median aggregation. Advisory only — reports to the PR, never blocks.
recommended_checks.tool: @lhci/cli 0.15.1 (or lighthouse 13.4.1 invoked directly)
recommended_checks.tool_maintained_evidence: FAILS THE FRESHNESS BAR: @lhci/cli latest is 0.15.1 published 2025-06-25 (14 months old) — https://registry.npmjs.org/@lhci/cli — and the last commit on GoogleChrome/lighthouse-ci main is 2025-06-26 — https://github.com/GoogleChrome/lighthouse-ci/commits/main . Lighthouse core itself is healthy at 13.4.1, published 2026-07-20 — https://registry.npmjs.org/lighthouse . Config syntax verified at https://github.com/GoogleChrome/lighthouse-ci/blob/main/docs/configuration.md
recommended_checks.rationale_for_two_person_team: Include this ONLY if a Lighthouse job already exists for performance budgets — then the accessibility category is a free extra assertion. Do not stand it up solely for accessibility. Its engine is axe-core under the hood ('Weighting is based on axe user impact assessments'), so it finds a strict subset of what check #2 already finds, and the runner is 14 months stale. A score of 100 is not a conformance claim and should never be reported to a customer as one.

recommended_checks.what_it_does: A public /accessibility page stating the conformance target (WCAG 2.2 Level AA), the known gaps, and a monitored contact address for accessibility problems; plus a completed VPAT 2.5Rev (WCAG or INT edition) held internally, ready to hand to procurement. The statement must describe conformance honestly — 'we target WCAG 2.2 AA and test with axe and manual review' — not claim conformance the manual pass has not established.
recommended_checks.tool: ITI VPAT 2.5Rev (April 2025), WCAG or INT edition
recommended_checks.tool_maintained_evidence: VPAT 2.5Rev released April 2025; the WCAG edition covers 'WCAG 2.0 or ISO/IEC 40500..., WCAG 2.1, and WCAG 2.2'; a completed VPAT is an Accessibility Conformance Report (ACR) — https://www.itic.org/policy/accessibility/vpat
recommended_checks.rationale_for_two_person_team: Not a CI check, but it is the artifact that actually gets asked for, and the moment it gets asked for it is urgent. Both indirect legal routes run through procurement — 28 CFR 35.200(a) and 45 CFR 84.84(a) both cover content a covered organization provides 'through contractual, licensing, or other arrangements', and Cal. Gov. Code 7405 binds 'any entity that contracts with a state or local entity subject to Section 11135'. With 11 offices at launch and headroom to 33, the first California city, county, school district or state-agency tenant will send a VPAT request. Writing it after check #4 exists is a day's work; writing it under a contract deadline with no test evidence is a scramble. Have counsel review the wording — an overstated conformance claim is itself a liability.

not_worth_it_here: A commissioned third-party WCAG 2.2 AA audit with a signed VPAT/ACR (typically $15-40k and 4-8 weeks of remediation follow-up). This is what a larger company does annually. Do it ONCE, and trigger it on a business event — the first public-agency or large-carrier contract that demands an ACR — not on a calendar. Until then the money buys a document nobody has asked for, at the cost of roughly two months of the team's entire discretionary capacity.

Running more than one scan engine. Standard enterprise practice is axe + HTML_CodeSniffer (pa11y) + Lighthouse for coverage breadth. For two people this triples the triage load for heavily overlapping findings, and the engines disagree, which turns every red build into a research task. Pick axe-core and only axe-core. (Extra reason to skip pa11y specifically: its default HTML_CodeSniffer runner's `standard` values are WCAG2A/WCAG2AA/WCAG2AAA — WCAG 2.0 — so it silently tests an older standard than the one you are targeting.)

Automated screen-reader testing in CI (Guidepup, W3C AT Driver, or Deque's paid axe DevTools Watcher tier). Genuinely valuable and genuinely the direction the industry is heading, but the harnesses are slow, OS-pinned, and flaky enough that a two-person team will end up disabling the job. The manual 90-minute pass in check #4 gets most of the same signal at a fraction of the maintenance cost.

Scanning every page. Enterprise programs crawl the whole app and track a site-wide violation count. Here that turns 253 findings into 900 and produces a number nobody can act on. Scan six public pages as a gate and ~15 authenticated pages nightly; that is where the risk and the traffic are.

A hosted Lighthouse CI server with historical dashboards and per-PR performance-plus-a11y trend graphs. This is infrastructure to run, and the accessibility signal it produces is a subset of what axe already gives you. It also depends on hosting decisions that are explicitly out of scope for this exercise.

Component-level a11y unit tests (jest-axe / karma-accessibility-checker) across the shared component library. Sound practice at scale, but for ~27k lines of TS built largely on ABP's supplied Angular components it duplicates the page-level axe run while adding a second set of fixtures to maintain. Revisit only if the team starts authoring genuinely custom interactive widgets (a custom combobox, tree, or date picker) — those are the components page-level scanning covers worst.

Targeting WCAG Level AAA. No US or California legal instrument requires it, W3C does not recommend AAA as a general policy for entire sites, and several AAA criteria (e.g. 3.3.9 Accessible Authentication (Enhanced)) are in direct tension with the security hardening this app needs for public exposure.

Usability testing with disabled users, an accessibility persona program, or a named a11y champion role. All are real practices at companies with an accessibility function. With no QA, no DevOps and one developer-week per month, adopting any of them means dropping the merge gates that actually prevent regressions.

Turning on `angular.configs.templateAll`, or including axe's `best-practice` tag in the merge gate. Both expand the finding count with items that are not WCAG failures (landmark-*, region, heading-order, page-has-heading-one, stylistic template rules). The whole design of this recommendation is to keep the gated rule set small enough that nobody wants to bypass it.
surprises: The DOJ Title II rule you were told doesn't apply to you can apply to you by contract. 28 CFR 35.200(a) covers web content a public entity provides 'directly or through contractual, licensing, or other arrangements'. California workers' comp is unusually public-sector-heavy: cities, counties, school districts, special districts, CSU and UC are large self-insured employers. The moment one of them is an 'office' on this platform, its injured workers use your portal to access its workers' comp program, and WCAG 2.1 AA by 26 April 2027 (or 2028 for entities under 50,000 population) becomes a contract term. 45 CFR 84.84(a) uses word-for-word the same 'through contractual, licensing, or other arrangements' language for HHS recipients. Both indirect routes are far more likely to bind this company than any direct obligation.

California Gov. Code 7405 explicitly names contractors, and it points at an OLDER standard. It binds 'any entity that contracts with a state or local entity subject to Section 11135' to Section 508 — which is still WCAG 2.0 Level A+AA under 36 CFR Part 1194 E205.4, finalized in 2017 and never refreshed. So a single public-sector contract can impose WCAG 2.0 AA (via 7405/508) and WCAG 2.1 AA (via 28 CFR 35.200) simultaneously, with different dates. Building to WCAG 2.2 AA satisfies both because W3C's versions are backward-compatible — but the VPAT has to say which one you are claiming against.

Both federal deadlines moved in 2026, and almost every guide still online has the old dates. DOJ extended Title II by one year on 20 April 2026 (91 FR 20912): now 26 April 2027 / 26 April 2028. HHS extended the Section 504 web rule on 11 May 2026 (91 FR 25507): now 11 May 2027 (15+ employees) / 10 May 2028 (under 15). If anyone on the team read a 2024 or 2025 article, they have 'April 2026' and 'May 2026' in their heads — dates that have already passed. This buys roughly twelve months of headroom on the procurement-driven routes, and it is the single most useful correction in this whole area.

The ADA is not where the money is — Unruh is, and going public is the event that switches it on. ADA Title III provides only injunctive relief plus attorney's fees (42 U.S.C. 12188(a)(1), incorporating 42 U.S.C. 2000a-3(a)-(b)); it has no damages. California Civil Code 51(f) makes any ADA violation an Unruh violation, and 52(a) sets a floor of $4,000 per offense plus fees. On an office LAN, no anonymous tester could reach a page. From the day registration, login and password reset are on the public internet, a tester with a screen reader can, and the fee-shifting — not the $4,000 — is what drives filing volume in California.

axe-core has exactly ONE rule tagged wcag22aa: `target-size`. Five of WCAG 2.2's six new Level A/AA criteria are undetectable by any scanner, and they land squarely on the flows going public. The two most likely public-internet hardening moves both CREATE new AA failures while every scanner stays green: adding a CAPTCHA to the registration form breaks 3.3.8 Accessible Authentication (Minimum) unless a non-cognitive alternative is offered, and adding a drag-and-drop document uploader breaks 2.5.7 Dragging Movements unless there is a click/keyboard path. Also watch 2.4.11 Focus Not Obscured — a sticky header or a toast notification covering the focused form field is an AA failure that looks fine in a screenshot.

Lighthouse CI is effectively abandoned even though half the '2026 CI accessibility' guides still lead with it. @lhci/cli's last release is 0.15.1 from 25 June 2025 and the last commit on GoogleChrome/lighthouse-ci main is 26 June 2025 — 14 months stale as of today — while Lighthouse core has moved on to 13.4.1 (20 July 2026). The tools that ARE moving are the ones you'd probably assume were legacy: pa11y shipped 10.0.0 today (28 August 2026) and IBM's equal-access accessibility-checker shipped 4.0.31 a week ago.

ESLint has a first-party answer to the exact '253 pre-existing violations' problem, and most teams have never heard of it. Bulk suppressions landed in ESLint 9.24.0 (4 April 2025): run `eslint --suppress-all` once, commit `eslint-suppressions.json`, and every existing violation is banked while new ones fail. It beats the usual improvisations — `--max-warnings 253`, or a scatter of eslint-disable comments — because `--prune-suppressions` makes the baseline ratchet down automatically as files get touched, and the count can never silently drift upward. Compatibility trap for this stack: angular-eslint 20.7.0 (the right pin for Angular 20.3.x) peers on eslint ^8.57.0 || ^9.0.0, so pin ESLint ^9.39, not ESLint 10.

The rule the brief called 'label-for-control' does not exist. In angular-eslint v20 it is `@angular-eslint/template/label-has-associated-control`; the older `label-for` name is gone. If anyone wired a config from a pre-v15 blog post, that rule is silently doing nothing right now — ESLint does not error on an unknown rule inside a plugin namespace in every configuration path, so a dead a11y rule can sit in the config looking like coverage.

Database-per-tenant plus Host-header tenancy makes contrast failures invisible to a single-host scan. If any of the 11 offices gets custom branding — a logo colour that becomes a button background, a themed link colour — axe's `color-contrast` rule will only catch it on the tenant host you happen to scan. This is the one place where the multi-tenant architecture creates an accessibility-specific blind spot rather than just a security one, and the fix costs nothing if you build the nightly job to loop over two or three tenant hosts from day one.

The '253 violations' number is probably not 253 problems. In an ABP Commercial / Angular Material application, axe findings are typically dominated by two rules — `color-contrast` (a theme token) and `target-size` (a component-library default). If that holds here, the remediation plan changes from 'fix 253 things over six months' to 'change two theme values and re-scan', which is a day, not a quarter. Before planning any remediation, group the existing violations by rule id and count. Also strip the `best-practice` tag from the count first: `region`, `landmark-*`, `heading-order` and `page-has-heading-one` are not WCAG failures and may be inflating the number substantially.

WCAG 2.2 deleted a criterion, so some old findings are no longer failures. 4.1.1 Parsing is 'obsolete and removed from WCAG 2.2'. Duplicate `id` attributes and unclosed tags are still real bugs that break assistive technology, but they are no longer a WCAG conformance failure — and older audit reports, older linters and some vendor scanners still report them as one. Do not spend the one dev-week per month on them.

No automated result is a conformance claim, and saying otherwise is itself a risk. W3C WAI is explicit: 'Web accessibility evaluation tools can not determine accessibility, they can only assist in doing so.' A green axe run or a Lighthouse accessibility score of 100 is evidence of diligence, not conformance. If an accessibility statement or a VPAT says 'Supports' for a criterion that was only ever checked by a scanner, that written statement becomes the document a plaintiff quotes back. Word the statement as a target plus a method, and have counsel read it.
disagreements: Which WCAG version is 'the standard' depends entirely on who is asking. W3C says WCAG 2.2 (Recommendation, republished 2024-12-12). DOJ's Title II rule (28 CFR 35.200) and HHS's Section 504 rule (45 CFR 84.84) both say WCAG 2.1 Level A+AA. Section 508 (36 CFR Part 1194, E205.4), reachable here via Cal. Gov. Code 7405, still says WCAG 2.0 Level A+AA. There is no single answer. Build to 2.2 AA — W3C states conformance to 2.2 also satisfies 2.1 and 2.0 — but a VPAT/ACR must name the specific version being claimed against, and different customers will demand different ones.

DOJ's own guidance and Ninth Circuit litigation reality point in opposite directions for Title III. ADA.gov (updated 2022-03-18) says businesses 'can currently choose how they will ensure' online accessibility and that 'The Department of Justice does not have a regulation setting out detailed standards' — and Title III rulemaking is now shelved indefinitely. But Robles v. Domino's (9th Cir. 2019) held that 'the lack of specific regulations, not yet promulgated by the Department of Justice, did not eliminate Domino's statutory duty', and courts routinely order WCAG 2.x AA as the equitable remedy. Reading DOJ's guidance as permission is a mistake; reading WCAG AA as legally mandated for Title III is also technically wrong. Both are true at once.

Published commentary on Section 1557 is widely inaccurate on the mechanics. Many law-firm alerts and vendor blogs say '1557 requires WCAG 2.1 AA by May 2026.' The regulation does not say that: 45 CFR 92.204(b) contains no WCAG citation at all and instead routes to 'the requirements of section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act, as interpreted consistent with title II of the ADA', with the technical standard and dates living in 45 CFR 84.84. The dates were also extended by one year in May 2026. When this matters for a contract, read 84.84 and 92.204 directly rather than a summary.

Whether a covered entity's web-accessibility obligation flows down to a software vendor is unsettled. Both 28 CFR 35.200(a) and 45 CFR 84.84(a) reach content provided 'through contractual, licensing, or other arrangements', which clearly obligates the covered entity for vendor-supplied content, but neither regulation makes the vendor itself a regulated party. Sources differ on how aggressively agencies will police flow-down. Practically, the exposure arrives as a contract clause and a VPAT request, not as an enforcement action against this company.

Whether a website standing alone is a 'public accommodation' splits federal and California state authority. The Ninth Circuit's nexus test (Robles) is favourable to plaintiffs where a physical place of public accommodation exists — which it does here, since 42 U.S.C. 12181(7)(F) enumerates 'professional office of a health care provider'. California's Court of Appeal reached a narrower result for website-only businesses in Martinez v. Cot'n Wash (2022), which I could NOT open (WebSearch budget exhausted; only a law-firm summary was surfaced) and which likely does not help this portal anyway given its physical-office nexus. Flagging the split rather than picking a side.

None of the above is legal advice. It is a research summary of primary regulatory and statutory text, assembled by an engineer for engineering planning. The applicability questions that actually decide this company's exposure — is it an HHS federal financial assistance recipient, will any tenant be a California public entity, does the Robles nexus attach — are fact-specific legal determinations. Get a California employment/civil-rights attorney to confirm before treating any of it as a compliance position.

material_errors: CLAIM 10 IS WRONG ON ITS CENTRAL POINT: Cal. Gov. Code 7405 does NOT flow Section 508 / WCAG 2.0 A+AA conformance down to private contractors. 7405(a) binds only 'state governmental entities'; 7405(b) requires a contracting entity merely to 'agree to respond to, and resolve any complaint regarding accessibility of, its products or services.' No conformance standard is imposed on the contractor. The stated threshold ('Section 508 / 36 CFR Part 1194 - i.e. WCAG 2.0 Level A+AA - flowed down by contract') is not in the statute.

CLAIM 16 STATES A RULE COUNT AND A RULE THAT DO NOT EXIST: the angular-eslint template accessibility preset contains 11 rules, not 12, and does NOT include `no-positive-tabindex`. Verified in packages/eslint-plugin-template/src/configs/accessibility.json at tag v20.7.0 and in the current README: alt-text, click-events-have-key-events, elements-content, interactive-supports-focus, label-has-associated-control, mouse-events-have-key-events, no-autofocus, no-distracting-elements, role-has-required-aria, table-scope, valid-aria. (The rest of claim 16 - config names, 20.7.0 published 2025-11-22, peer range eslint ^8.57.0 || ^9.0.0 - is correct.)

CLAIM 15 PRESENTS A FABRICATED QUOTE OF SC 3.3.8. The claim says 3.3.8 'requires that Content does not rely on cognitive function test to authenticate unless an alternative authentication method is available.' The actual normative text is: 'A cognitive function test (such as remembering a password or solving a puzzle) is not required for any step in an authentication process unless that step provides at least one of the following: Alternative, Mechanism, Object Recognition, Personal Content.' The claim collapses four exception paths into one and would understate what satisfies the criterion.

CLAIM 17 OMITS THE FACT THAT MAKES IT ACTIONABLE: axe-core's rule-descriptions.md says of the WCAG 2.2 section, 'These rules are disabled by default, until WCAG 2.2 is more widely adopted and required.' So the single wcag22aa rule (target-size) does not even run unless explicitly enabled. Also, the section counts are 60 (WCAG 2.0 A/AA) + 2 (WCAG 2.1 A/AA) = 62, and the tag list is incomplete - it omits `TTv5` and `wcag2a-obsolete`, and the authoritative tag table lives in doc/API.md, not the cited rule-descriptions.md.
CLAIM 3's THRESHOLD FIELD CARRIES A WRONG DATE: it states '2028-04-28'. 28 CFR 35.200(b)(2) reads 'Beginning April 26, 2028'. The claim body has it right; the threshold string does not.

CLAIM 14 CANNOT BE VERIFIED AT ITS CITED URL: https://www.hhs.gov/civil-rights/for-individuals/section-1557/faqs/index.html returns HTTP 403 to every fetch attempt. Separately, the operative regulation - 45 CFR 92.4's definition of 'Federal financial assistance' - does not name Medicare Part B anywhere in its text. The Part B position and any May 6, 2025 date live in the 2024 final rule preamble (89 FR 37522), which must be cited instead; as written the claim rests on an unreachable page.

CLAIM 6 OVERSTATES ITS OWN AUTHORITY: the Robles opinion itself distinguishes Weyer v. Twentieth Century Fox, where the Ninth Circuit held an insurance company administering an employer-provided policy was NOT a covered place of public accommodation, and rests its holding on a 'nexus between Domino's website and app and physical restaurants - which Domino's does not contest.' A standalone workers'-comp administration portal with no nexus to a physical place of public accommodation is exactly the Weyer fact pattern. 'Very likely does apply' is not supported; 'contested, nexus-dependent' is.

results.claim: WCAG 2.2 is the current W3C Recommendation (5 Oct 2023, republished 12 Dec 2024); WCAG 3.0 remains a Working Draft (3 Mar 2026) and W3C says it 'is not expected to be a completed W3C standard for a few more years' and 'will not supersede WCAG 2.'
results.evidence_quote: W3C Recommendation 12 December 2024 ... changes made to 2.2 since its original publication on 05 October 2023
results.correction: Threshold is correct as stated. But this page settles only the WCAG 2.2 half. The two WCAG 3 quotes are NOT on this page - the only supersession language here is 'The publication of WCAG 2.2 does not deprecate or supersede WCAG 2.0 or WCAG 2.1', which is a different statement about 2.0/2.1, not about WCAG 3. Cite https://www.w3.org/TR/wcag-3.0/ (verified: 'W3C Working Draft 03 March 2026', with 'It is inappropriate to cite this document as other than a work in progress') for the WD status/date, and the WAI WCAG 3 Introduction page for the 'not expected to be a completed W3C standard' / 'will not supersede WCAG 2' quotes.

results.claim: Level AA is the operative conformance level; WCAG defines A/AA/AAA and AAA is not a general policy target. Every US regulation that adopts a technical standard adopts 'Level A and Level AA success criteria and conformance requirements.'
results.evidence_quote: three levels of conformance are defined: A (lowest), AA, and AAA (highest) ... It is not recommended that Level AAA conformance be required as a general policy for entire sites because it is not possible to satisfy all Level AAA success criteria for some content.
results.correction: The A/AA/AAA and 'not recommended as a general policy' points are fully supported. The universal quantifier is not, and cannot be, settled by this page - drop 'Every US regulation' and say instead: 'the three federal standards checked here all adopt Level A + AA - 28 CFR 35.200(b), 45 CFR 84.84(b), and 36 CFR Part 1194 E205.4 (WCAG 2.0 A+AA).'

results.claim: DOJ's April 2024 ADA Title II web rule (28 CFR 35.200) applies to public entities only, requires WCAG 2.1 A+AA, dates extended one year on 20 Apr 2026 to 26 Apr 2027 / 26 Apr 2028.
results.evidence_quote: Beginning April 26, 2028, a public entity with a total population of less than 50,000 or any public entity that is a special district government ... [AG Order No. 5919-2024, 89 FR 31337, Apr. 24, 2024, as amended by AG Order No. 6742-2026, 91 FR 20912, Apr. 20, 2026]
results.correction: Correct threshold: WCAG 2.1 A+AA; 2027-04-26 (pop. >=50,000, other than special district governments) / 2028-04-26 (pop. <50,000 OR any special district government). The threshold field's '2028-04-28' is wrong - the regulation says April 26, 2028. Two other scope notes: (a) the 50,000+ tier expressly excludes special district governments ('a public entity, other than a special district government'); (b) 'Amtrak, commuter authorities' are not in 35.200 - they come from the definition of 'public entity' at 28 CFR 35.104, which should be the cite for that sentence.

results.claim: 28 CFR 35.200(a) covers web content and mobile apps a public entity provides 'directly or through contractual, licensing, or other arrangements', so a vendor portal used by a public employer is reached indirectly by contract.
results.evidence_quote: (1) Web content that a public entity provides or makes available, directly or through contractual, licensing, or other arrangements; and (2) Mobile apps that a public entity provides or makes available, directly or through contractual, licensing, or other arrangements.
results.correction: none. (Verbatim match, including the (b)(1)-(b)(2) repetition of the same 'directly or through contractual, licensing, or other arrangements' phrase inside the operative WCAG 2.1 requirement. Note the duty runs to the public entity, not to the vendor - the vendor's exposure is contractual/indemnity, not direct regulatory liability under Part 35.)

results.claim: ADA Title III imposes no technical web standard; DOJ never issued a Title III web regulation; 2010 ANPRM and 2016 SANPRM withdrawn 2017; businesses 'can currently choose how they will ensure' accessibility and DOJ 'does not have a regulation setting out detailed standards.'
results.evidence_quote: The Department of Justice does not have a regulation setting out detailed standards, but the Department's longstanding interpretation of the general nondiscrimination and effective communication provisions applies to web accessibility.
results.correction: Both quoted sentences and the 'helpful guidance' characterization of WCAG are on the page and accurate. The 2010 ANPRM / 2016 SANPRM withdrawal is NOT on this page - cite 82 FR 60932 (Dec. 26, 2017) for that (the Robles opinion itself quotes it: DOJ 'continue[s] to assess whether specific technical standards are necessary and appropriate'). Also flag that the page now carries a banner: 'The guidance on this page does not reflect requirements for state and local governments that were published in the Federal Register on April 24, 2024' - so it is Title III-only guidance and should be labeled as such.

results.claim: Title III very likely applies; 42 U.S.C. 12181(7)(F) covers 'professional office of a health care provider' and 'insurance office'; Robles v. Domino's (9th Cir., No. 17-55504, filed Jan. 15, 2019) applies the ADA to a website/app connecting customers to physical restaurants.
results.evidence_quote: Filed January 15, 2019 ... the ADA applies to the services of a public accommodation, not services in a place of public accommodation ... the lack of specific regulations, not yet promulgated by the Department of Justice, did not eliminate Domino's statutory duty.
results.correction: All three Robles quotations, the docket number (No. 17-55504, D.C. No. 2:16-cv-06599-SJO-FFM), and the filing date are verified verbatim in the PDF. Two corrections: (1) 12181(7)(F) is not in this document - verified separately at https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/42/12181, which does list 'pharmacy, insurance office, professional office of a health care provider' in (7)(F); cite that URL for the statutory element. (2) 'Very likely does apply' overstates the holding. Robles is expressly a nexus case ('This nexus between Domino's website and app and physical restaurants - which Domino's does not contest - is critical to our analysis'), and the same opinion reaffirms Weyer v. Twentieth Century Fox, 198 F.3d 1104, 1113-14 (9th Cir. 2000), which held an insurance company administering an employer-provided policy was NOT a covered place of public accommodation. Restate as: Title III coverage in the Ninth Circuit turns on a nexus to a physical place of public accommodation and is contested for a standalone administration portal.

results.claim: Title III yields no money damages to private plaintiffs - only injunctive relief plus discretionary attorney's fees, per 42 U.S.C. 12188(a)(1) incorporating 42 U.S.C. 2000a-3(a) and (b).
results.evidence_quote: The remedies and procedures set forth in section 2000a-3(a) of this title are the remedies and procedures this subchapter provides to any person who is being subjected to discrimination on the basis of disability in violation of this subchapter
results.correction: Threshold is correct. But the cited page carries only the 12188(a)(1) sentence; the 2000a-3(a) 'civil action for preventive relief' and 2000a-3(b) 'in its discretion, may allow the prevailing party, other than the United States, a reasonable attorney's fee' quotes are at https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/42/2000a-3 - both verified verbatim there. Add the caveat this page does show: 12188(b)(2)(B) authorizes monetary damages, but only in suits brought by the Attorney General, not by private plaintiffs.

results.claim: Unruh (Cal. Civ. Code 51(f) + 52(a)) converts an ADA violation into a state claim with a $4,000 statutory minimum per offense, up to 3x actual damages, plus attorney's fees.
results.evidence_quote: (f) A violation of the right of any individual under the federal Americans with Disabilities Act of 1990 (Public Law 101-336) shall also constitute a violation of this section.
results.correction: Threshold ($4,000 minimum per offense, up to 3x actual damages, plus attorney's fees) is correct and the 52(a) language is verbatim - but it is NOT on the cited page. Section 51 ends at subdivision (h); the damages text is at https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=52 ('is liable for each and every offense for the actual damages, and any amount ... up to a maximum of three times the amount of actual damage but in no case less than four thousand dollars ($4,000), and any attorney's fees'). Cite both sections. Note also the currency stamp on 51: 'Amended by Stats. 2024, Ch. 779, Sec. 2.5. (SB 1137) Effective January 1, 2025.'

results.claim: California has no private-sector web accessibility statute; AB 1757 (2023-24) would have required WCAG 2.1 AA of business establishments and their developers/vendors with a private right of action, and died 11/30/24 ('From Senate committee without further action', 'Inactive Bill - Died').
results.evidence_quote: Type of Measure Inactive Bill - Died ... 11/30/24 From Senate committee without further action.
results.correction: The death, the date, the exact last-action wording, and the absence of enactment are all confirmed on this page, as is the subject ('An act to amend the heading of Part 2.53 (commencing with Section 55.55) of Division 1 of, and to add Sections 55.565 and 55.566 to, the Civil Code, relating to accessibility'). What is NOT on this status page is the substantive description - the WCAG 2.1 AA standard, the reach to third-party developers/vendors, and the private right of action. That content changed materially across six versions (last amended 06/12/24), so cite the specific version text (the 06/12/24 Amended Senate version) rather than describing the bill from the status page. Stated confidence 'partial' is appropriate.

results.claim: Cal. Gov. Code 7405 extends Section 508 obligations to private contractors of state and local entities.
results.evidence_quote: (b) Any entity that contracts with a state or local entity subject to Section 11135 ... shall agree to respond to, and resolve any complaint regarding accessibility of, its products or services that is brought to the attention of the entity.
results.correction: MATERIAL ERROR. Section 7405 does not impose Section 508 / WCAG 2.0 A+AA conformance on contractors. 7405(a) directs 'state governmental entities' to comply with Section 508 and 36 CFR Part 1194 (the claim's quote also silently drops the trailing clause 'and regulations implementing that act as set forth in Part 1194 of Title 36 of the Federal Code of Regulations'). 7405(b) imposes on a contracting entity one obligation only: to agree to respond to and resolve accessibility complaints about its products or services. Corrected threshold: 'Gov. Code 7405(b) requires a vendor contracting with a Section 11135 entity to agree to respond to and resolve accessibility complaints - it does not itself impose a WCAG/508 conformance standard on the vendor. Conformance reaches the vendor only if the customer's own 7405(a)/11135 duty is written into the contract.' Separately, the Gov. Code 11135(a) quote is not on this page - cite GOV 11135.

results.claim: Section 508 does not reach this application directly; the Revised 508 Standards (36 CFR Part 1194, Jan 2017) incorporate WCAG 2.0 A+AA via E205.4 and bind private parties only through federal procurement.
results.evidence_quote: Electronic content shall conform to Level A and Level AA Success Criteria and Conformance Requirements in WCAG 2.0
results.correction: none. E205.4 verbatim, WCAG 2.0 Level A+AA, final rule January 18, 2017 (with a January 22, 2018 correction restoring TTY provisions) all confirmed. One note for the write-up: the Access Board standards still reference WCAG 2.0, not 2.1 - so a design targeting WCAG 2.2 AA is a superset and needs no separate 508 work, which is worth stating explicitly.

results.claim: ACA Section 1557 applies to HHS FFA recipients, HHS-administered programs, and Title I entities; 45 CFR 92.204(b) names no WCAG version and defers to Section 504 as interpreted consistent with ADA Title II.
results.evidence_quote: (b) A recipient or State Exchange shall ensure that its health programs and activities provided through websites and mobile applications comply with the requirements of section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act, as interpreted consistent with title II of the ADA (42 U.S.C. 12131 through 12165).
results.correction: The 92.204(b) quotation is verbatim and the 'no WCAG version in 92.204' point is confirmed. The scope quotation is from 45 CFR 92.2, not 92.204 - cite https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/45/92.2 (text verified: 'Every health program or activity, any part of which receives Federal financial assistance, directly or indirectly, from the Department'). Add one qualifier the claim omits: 92.204(a) imposes a general ICT accessibility duty on any 'covered entity' (subject to undue burden / fundamental alteration), so the rule is not limited to the 92.204(b) recipient/State-Exchange subset.

results.claim: 45 CFR 84.84 carries WCAG 2.1 A+AA for health programs; dates extended one year in May 2026 to May 11, 2027 (15+ employees) and May 10, 2028 (<15).
results.evidence_quote: Beginning May 11, 2027, a recipient with fifteen or more employees ... comply with Level A and Level AA success criteria and conformance requirements specified in WCAG 2.1 ... [89 FR 40193, May 9, 2024, as amended at 91 FR 25507, May 11, 2026]

results.claim: Most physician offices became Section 1557 covered entities in 2024 because HHS reclassified Medicare Part B as federal financial assistance; Part B-only providers had until May 6, 2025 to comply.
results.evidence_quote: none
results.correction: The cited URL is not fetchable - it returns HTTP 403 ('Access Denied ... Reference #18.8192117') to both WebFetch and direct curl, so nothing on it can be relied on as a citation. Independent check of the regulation text: 45 CFR 92.4's definition of 'Federal financial assistance' does NOT mention Medicare Part B anywhere; the closest text is '(2) Federal financial assistance the Department provides or otherwise makes available includes Federal financial assistance that the Department plays a role in providing or administering...'. The Part B position and the May 6, 2025 date, if they exist, are in the 2024 final rule preamble (89 FR 37522, May 6, 2024), not in the codified rule. Either cite the Federal Register document directly and quote it, or drop this claim - as written it rests on an unreachable page and is not corroborated by the CFR text. Stated confidence 'partial' is if anything too generous.

results.claim: WCAG 2.2 added six A/AA criteria (3.2.6 A, 3.3.7 A, 2.4.11 AA, 2.5.7 AA, 2.5.8 AA, 3.3.8 AA) and removed 4.1.1 Parsing; 3.3.8 requires that 'Content does not rely on cognitive function test to authenticate unless an alternative authentication method is available'; 2.5.8 requires 24x24 CSS px.
results.evidence_quote: 4.1.1 Parsing is obsolete and removed from WCAG 2.2. ... 2.5.8 Target Size (Minimum) (AA): The size of the target for pointer inputs is at least 24 by 24 CSS pixels, except where...
results.correction: The six new A/AA criteria, their levels, the 24x24 CSS pixel threshold, and the removal of 4.1.1 Parsing are all confirmed (the page also lists three new AAA criteria - 2.4.12, 2.4.13, 3.3.9 - which the claim correctly excludes from the A/AA count). The 3.3.8 'quote' is wrong. Actual text: 'A cognitive function test (such as remembering a password or solving a puzzle) is not required for any step in an authentication process unless that step provides at least one of the following: Alternative; Mechanism; Object Recognition; Personal Content.' Four exception paths, not one - a password field satisfies 3.3.8 if a password manager can fill it (Mechanism), which is materially different from requiring 'an alternative authentication method'.

results.claim: axe-core carries exactly one rule tagged wcag22aa (target-size); listed filter tags are wcag2a...RGAAv4/experimental; WCAG 2.0/2.1 A+AA is ~60 rules; 7 experimental rules disabled by default.

results.correction: Confirmed: exactly one wcag22aa rule (target-size), and the seven experimental rules are named exactly right and are 'disabled by default in axe-core and the axe browser extensions'. Three corrections. (1) The claim's own conclusion is understated: target-size is DISABLED BY DEFAULT, so out of the box axe-core covers ZERO of WCAG 2.2's new criteria unless the rule is explicitly enabled. (2) Counts are 60 WCAG 2.0 A/AA + 2 WCAG 2.1 A/AA = 62, not '~60 across wcag2a/wcag2aa/wcag21a/wcag21aa'. (3) The tag list is incomplete and mis-sourced: rule-descriptions.md does not enumerate filter tags; doc/API.md does, and it also lists `TTv5`, `wcag2a-obsolete`, `wcag***`, `section508.*.*`, `EN-9.*`, `RGAA-*.*.*` and `cat.*`. Cite https://github.com/dequelabs/axe-core/blob/develop/doc/API.md for the tag table.

results.claim: Automated tools cannot establish conformance - W3C WAI says tools 'can not determine accessibility', 'Human judgement is required', and can 'produce false or misleading results'; Lighthouse's a11y score is a weighted average of axe audits based on 'axe user impact assessments' and excludes manual checks.

results.correction: All three W3C quotations are verbatim on the page and fully support the threshold. The Lighthouse sentence is not on this page and needs its own citation - Google's Lighthouse accessibility scoring doc (developer.chrome.com/docs/lighthouse/accessibility/scoring) for the 'Weighting is based on axe user impact assessments' language. Split the claim so the W3C cite is not made to carry the Lighthouse assertion.

results.correction: Every mechanical detail is confirmed verbatim: all five flags, the default file name and project-root location, the error-only rule, and 'While the rule will be enforced for new code, the existing violations will not be reported.' The one thing the page does NOT state is the introducing version - verify it against the ESLint v9.24.0 release notes rather than this page (npm confirms eslint 9.24.0 published 2025-04-04T19:20:41Z, consistent with the claim).
