research.area: Multi-tenant isolation testing for a database-per-tenant, host-header-resolved PHI system (ABP Commercial 10.x / .NET 10 / EF Core / SQL Server / Redis / MinIO)
research.standard_summary: The 2026 standard is that tenant isolation is an *authorization* property that must be proven by executable tests, not by reading the ORM. OWASP ASVS 5.0.0 makes this an explicit, citable requirement: 8.4.1 "Verify that multi-tenant applications use cross-tenant controls to ensure consumer operations will never affect tenants with which they do not have permissions to interact" (Level 2), sitting on top of 8.2.1/8.2.2 (function-level access and BOLA, both Level 1). OWASP API Security Top 10 API1:2023 goes further and requires the tests be a merge gate: "Create tests evaluating authorization mechanism vulnerability; reject changes that cause test failures." Because tenancy here is derived from an attacker-supplied HTTP header, the standard also pulls in WSTG-INPV-17 (Host header injection) and the PortSwigger host-header bypass catalogue — Host, X-Forwarded-Host, X-Host, X-Forwarded-Server, X-HTTP-Host-Override, Forwarded, duplicate Host lines, absolute-form request targets, line wrapping and port injection — each of which must have a test asserting the *resolved tenant*, not just the HTTP status. Critically, an ABP unit or integration test proves almost none of this: the ABP startup template runs tests against a single in-memory SQLite database, so connection-string routing, cross-database leakage, Redis key scoping, background-job tenant context and token/claims-vs-host binding are all structurally untestable in the shipped harness. A rigorous standard therefore requires (a) at least two real, separate tenant databases in the test run, (b) HTTP-level tenant-resolution tests through the real middleware pipeline, (c) a static deny-list for the handful of one-line framework switches that disable isolation globally, and (d) out-of-band data-plane audits (per-database TenantId fingerprint, Redis key prefix audit) that catch misrouting the application itself reports as success.

standards.claim: OWASP ASVS 5.0.0 contains an explicit, dedicated multi-tenancy requirement: multi-tenant applications must use cross-tenant controls ensuring consumer operations never affect tenants they have no permission to interact with. It is a Level 2 requirement, so it applies to any application handling sensitive data such as PHI.
standards.threshold: ASVS 5.0.0 requirement 8.4.1, Level 2 (chapter V8 Authorization, section V8.4 'Other Authorization Considerations')
standards.source_name: OWASP Application Security Verification Standard 5.0.0, V8 Authorization (raw source in OWASP/ASVS repo)
standards.notes: Fetched the chapter file directly and read requirement 8.4.1 verbatim. The repo README confirms 'Latest Stable Version - 5.0.0 ... (dated May 2025)', so 5.0.0 is the current edition to verify against in 2026, not 4.0.3. Note the chapter's own References section points to WSTG Authorization Testing and the OWASP Authorization Cheat Sheet, which is the recommended chain for building the actual test cases. Companion Level 1 requirements that this system must also meet: 8.2.1 (function-level access restricted to consumers with explicit permissions) and 8.2.2 (data-specific access restricted, explicitly naming IDOR and BOLA), plus 8.3.1 (enforce authorization at a trusted service layer, not client-side). ASVS Level 3 items in this chapter (8.1.3, 8.1.4, 8.3.2, 8.3.3, 8.4.2) are out of proportion for this team.

standards.claim: OWASP API Security Top 10 requires that object-level authorization be covered by automated tests that block merges, not by manual review: prevention guidance explicitly says to create tests evaluating the authorization mechanism and reject changes that fail them. The companion function-level entry requires denial-by-default and warns that endpoints must not be assumed administrative based on URL path alone.
standards.threshold: API1:2023 Broken Object Level Authorization; API5:2023 Broken Function Level Authorization
standards.source_name: OWASP API Security Top 10 2023 (API1:2023 and API5:2023)
standards.notes: Both pages opened. API1 'How To Prevent' includes 'Create tests evaluating authorization mechanism vulnerability; reject changes that cause test failures' — this is the direct basis for making a tenant-isolation test suite a required CI gate rather than advisory. API5's 'Is the API Vulnerable?' questions map cleanly onto tenant tests: can a user from group X access a function scoped to group Y by guessing the endpoint; can they change HTTP method to reach a sensitive action. Neither page addresses whether scanners can find these flaws; in practice generic DAST cannot, because it has no model of which tenant owns which object.

standards.claim: OWASP publishes a specific test for Host header injection that requires substituting an attacker domain into the Host header and, when that is blocked, retrying with X-Forwarded-Host; a vulnerability is indicated when the application's behaviour or generated links reflect the attacker-supplied host. The named exploitation classes include accessing private/internal virtual hosts, password-reset poisoning and cache poisoning.
standards.threshold: WSTG-INPV-17 'Testing for Host Header Injection'
standards.source_name: OWASP Web Security Testing Guide (latest), Input Validation Testing
standards.notes: Test ID and How-to-Test steps read verbatim from the WSTG 'latest' branch. Caveat: I verified the ID in the 'latest' tree only; WSTG stable numbering has historically differed, so cite the version you test against. For this application the 'accessing private virtual hosts' scenario is the exact threat: an unmatched Host does not error, it silently selects the host/landlord context (see the ABP DomainTenantResolveContributor entry below). Password-reset poisoning is also directly in scope because password reset is one of the anonymous endpoints going public.

standards.claim: Host-header validation must be tested against a specific catalogue of bypasses, not just a single spoofed Host: override headers X-Forwarded-Host, X-Host, X-Forwarded-Server, X-HTTP-Host-Override and Forwarded; an absolute-form request target ('GET https://vulnerable-website.com/ HTTP/1.1' with a different Host line); duplicate Host header lines; space-indented line wrapping; and injecting into the port position ('Host: vulnerable-website.com:bad-stuff-here').
standards.threshold: 5 override header names, plus absolute-URI, duplicate-Host, line-wrapping and port-injection variants
standards.source_name: PortSwigger Web Security Academy — Exploiting HTTP Host header vulnerabilities (secondary/vendor source, but the canonical catalogue)
standards.notes: Labelled secondary per the evidence rules: PortSwigger is a vendor, not a standards body. I am citing it because it is the most complete public enumeration of the bypass techniques and OWASP WSTG covers only Host and X-Forwarded-Host. The prevention guidance on the parent page is the design rule to test for: 'Don't support Host override headers ... in particular X-Forwarded-Host', and validate Host against an allowlist of permitted domains.

standards.claim: An HTTP origin server MUST ignore the Host header entirely when the request-target is in absolute-form and use the authority from the request-target instead; and a server MUST return 400 to any HTTP/1.1 request lacking a Host field, containing more than one Host field line, or containing an invalid Host value. This means a tenant-resolution test suite must cover absolute-form and duplicate-Host requests, because the value the framework sees may not be the value a proxy or WAF inspected.
standards.threshold: RFC 9112 Section 3.2.2 (absolute-form) and Section 3.2 (Host field rules; 400 Bad Request)
standards.source_name: RFC 9112 — HTTP/1.1 (IETF)
standards.notes: Quoted from the RFC text. This is the specification-level reason the absolute-URI test case exists and is not paranoia: it is mandated divergent behaviour. I did not empirically verify how Kestrel 10 resolves absolute-form request targets into HttpContext.Request.Host — that is exactly why it belongs in the test suite as an assertion about the resolved tenant rather than as an assumption.

standards.claim: Kestrel does not validate the Host header at all, and ASP.NET Core's host-filtering middleware is disabled by default; it only activates when an AllowedHosts key is defined in configuration as a semicolon-delimited list of hostnames without ports. The default ASP.NET Core project template ships AllowedHosts set to a wildcard, which leaves filtering effectively off.
standards.threshold: AllowedHosts configuration key in appsettings.json, e.g. "AllowedHosts": "example.com;localhost"
standards.source_name: Microsoft Learn — Host filtering with ASP.NET Core Kestrel web server (aspnetcore-10.0)
standards.notes: Verified verbatim: 'Host headers aren't validated' and 'Host-filtering middleware is disabled by default. To enable the middleware, define an AllowedHosts key'. Marked partial because the specific claim that the current .NET 10 web template emits "AllowedHosts": "*" is from my own knowledge of the template, not from a page I opened — treat it as a thing to check in the repo rather than a cited fact. The actionable, fully-cited part is: filtering is off unless you explicitly set AllowedHosts, and this app's tenancy depends entirely on the Host value.

standards.claim: If forwarded-headers middleware is enabled with the XForwardedHost forwarder, HttpContext.Request.Host is overwritten from the client-supplied X-Forwarded-Host header. ForwardedHeadersOptions.AllowedHosts, which restricts acceptable X-Forwarded-Host values, defaults to an empty list meaning all hosts are allowed; ForwardedHeaders itself defaults to None so the middleware does nothing until explicitly configured. Microsoft links this behaviour to an elevation-of-privilege advisory where a proxy fails to restrict Host headers to known-good values.
standards.threshold: ForwardedHeadersOptions.AllowedHosts default = empty IList<string> (all hosts allowed); ForwardedHeadersOptions.ForwardedHeaders default = ForwardedHeaders.None; KnownNetworks default = loopback /8; KnownProxies default = IPv6 loopback; ForwardLimit default = 1; CVE-2018-0787
standards.source_name: Microsoft Learn — Configure ASP.NET Core to work with proxy servers and load balancers (aspnetcore-10.0)
standards.notes: Read the options table verbatim. Two traps worth a test each: (1) the same Microsoft page shows a sample that calls options.KnownNetworks.Clear(); options.KnownProxies.Clear(); which removes the only spoofing protection, and this snippet is very widely copy-pasted; (2) setting the environment variable ASPNETCORE_FORWARDEDHEADERS_ENABLED=true enables forwarding with cloud-oriented settings and, per the page, 'doesn't enable features such as the KnownProxies option to restrict which IPs forwarders are accepted from'. Whether a reverse proxy sits in front is an infrastructure decision and out of scope here; the in-scope, code-level control is that the app must not accept X-Forwarded-Host from an untrusted peer, and the test asserts the resolved tenant when that header is spoofed.

standards.claim: ABP registers the __tenant query-string, route, header and cookie tenant resolvers unconditionally in every ASP.NET Core application, and inserts the current-user (token claim) resolver at position 0. Adding a domain resolver does not remove them: AddDomainTenantResolver inserts the domain contributor immediately after the current-user contributor, leaving the four __tenant resolvers behind it in the chain.
standards.threshold: Resolver order: CurrentUserTenantResolveContributor (index 0), DomainTenantResolveContributor (inserted after it), QueryStringTenantResolveContributor, RouteTenantResolveContributor, HeaderTenantResolveContributor, CookieTenantResolveContributor. Default tenant key: '__tenant' (TenantResolverConsts.DefaultTenantKey)
standards.source_name: ABP Framework source — AbpAspNetCoreMultiTenancyModule.cs, AbpMultiTenancyModule.cs, AbpMultiTenancyOptionsExtensions.cs
standards.notes: Read all three source files directly. This directly contradicts the premise 'tenancy resolves from the HTTP Host header ONLY'. Unless the application explicitly clears AbpTenantResolveOptions.TenantResolvers, ?__tenant=<guid>, a __tenant header and a __tenant cookie are all live inputs. Whether they are *effective* depends on the Handled short-circuit described in the next entry — which is exactly why this must be asserted by a test rather than reasoned about. ABP's own documentation and its first-party AI skill file both list Domain as the LAST resolver (position 6), which is wrong; see the disagreements list.

standards.claim: ABP's domain tenant resolver reads httpContext.Request.Host.Value and sets context.Handled = true whenever the Host has any value at all — including when the host does not match the configured domain format. Because the resolver chain stops at the first contributor where Handled is true or a tenant was found, a request bearing an unrecognised Host is not rejected: it resolves to a null tenant, i.e. the host/landlord context, and the chain never reaches the __tenant resolvers.
standards.threshold: DomainTenantResolveContributor.GetTenantIdOrNameFromHttpContextOrNullAsync sets context.Handled = true unconditionally after the Host check; TenantResolveContext.HasResolvedTenantOrHost() returns 'Handled || TenantIdOrName != null'
standards.source_name: ABP Framework source — DomainTenantResolveContributor.cs, TenantResolveContext.cs, TenantResolver.cs
standards.notes: Read all three files. This is the single most important behaviour to test in this application. It means Host-header spoofing does not produce an error page — it produces a silent downgrade to the host context, where the tenant list, tenant connection strings and landlord admin identity live. Anonymous endpoints (registration, login, password reset, document upload) are the ones that will execute in that context. The correct assertion is not 'returns 400' but 'ICurrentTenant.Id for this request equals the expected tenant', which requires an HTTP-level test with an inspectable resolved-tenant signal (a test-only endpoint or a log/response header emitted in the test environment).

standards.claim: ABP's multi-tenancy middleware writes a persistent __tenant cookie whenever the tenant was resolved by the query-string resolver. A single crafted link therefore pins a victim's browser to a chosen tenant for subsequent requests, converting a one-shot parameter into a durable tenant-confusion condition.
standards.threshold: MultiTenancyMiddleware.InvokeAsync: if AppliedResolvers contains QueryStringTenantResolveContributor.ContributorName then AbpMultiTenancyCookieHelper.SetTenantCookie(context, CurrentTenant.Id, options.TenantKey)
standards.source_name: ABP Framework source — MultiTenancyMiddleware.cs
standards.notes: Read the middleware source directly. The AbpAspNetCoreMultiTenancyOptions default error-page builder also manipulates the tenant cookie and, when only the CurrentUser resolver applied, will sign the user out of cookie authentication — so tenant-resolution failures have session side effects. Test case: assert no Set-Cookie for __tenant is ever emitted in production configuration, and that a request carrying a forged __tenant cookie resolves to the host-derived tenant, not the cookie's.

standards.claim: ABP's multi-tenant connection-string resolver falls back silently to the application's Default connection string when the current tenant has no connection string configured. There is no exception and no warning: a tenant whose connection string is missing or blank reads and writes the shared/host database, and the EF Core tenant filter then makes the result look merely empty rather than wrong.
standards.threshold: MultiTenantConnectionStringResolver.ResolveAsync: 'if (tenant == null || tenant.ConnectionStrings.IsNullOrEmpty()) { //Tenant has not defined any connection string, fallback to default logic; return await base.ResolveAsync(connectionStringName); }'
standards.source_name: ABP Framework source — MultiTenantConnectionStringResolver.cs
standards.notes: Read the resolver source and the connection-strings doc, which confirms the resolver 'fallbacks to the base logic if no connection string specified for the current tenant'. With 11 offices at launch and headroom to 33, tenant onboarding is the highest-risk repeated operation in this system, and this is its failure mode. Compounding it: UnitOfWorkDbContextProvider.GetDatabaseApiKey keys cached DbContext instances as '{DbContextType.FullName}_{SHA256(connectionString)}', so two tenants that both fall back to Default share one DbContext inside a unit of work, leaving only the EF query filter between them. Also note ResolveConnectionStringAsync forces the HOST connection string for any DbContext type marked [IgnoreMultiTenancy].

standards.claim: Background job tenant context in ABP is opt-in per job-args class. The executor derives the tenant from the job arguments only if that args type implements IMultiTenant; otherwise it falls back to the ambient ICurrentTenant.Id, which in a background worker process is normally null — so the job executes in the host context and, under database-per-tenant, against the host database.
standards.threshold: BackgroundJobExecuter.GetJobArgsTenantId: 'jobArgs switch { IMultiTenant multiTenantJobArgs => multiTenantJobArgs.TenantId, _ => CurrentTenant.Id }', wrapped in using(CurrentTenant.Change(...))
standards.source_name: ABP Framework source — BackgroundJobExecuter.cs
standards.notes: Read the executor source verbatim. Cross-checked the second source and found the opposite of confirmation, which is itself the finding: ABP's background-jobs documentation page contains zero occurrences of the word 'tenant', as does the background-workers page. The framework behaviour is real but undocumented, so a developer adding a job has no prompt to implement IMultiTenant on the args class. This yields a two-hour reflection test with very high value: enumerate all IBackgroundJob<T>/IAsyncBackgroundJob<T> implementations in the solution and assert every T implements IMultiTenant.

standards.claim: Redis keys are tenant-scoped only when data goes through ABP's typed IDistributedCache<TCacheItem>, which prefixes 't:{tenantId},' via DistributedCacheKeyNormalizer. Injecting Microsoft's raw IDistributedCache bypasses the normalizer entirely and produces unprefixed, cross-tenant keys, and the [IgnoreMultiTenancy] attribute on a cache-item class deliberately removes the prefix. ABP's own tenant configuration cache — which carries each tenant's connection string — is marked [IgnoreMultiTenancy] and is therefore stored under a global, unprefixed key.
standards.threshold: Key format: 't:{CurrentTenant.Id},c:{CacheName},k:{KeyPrefix}{Key}'; prefix omitted when args.IgnoreMultiTenancy is true or CurrentTenant.Id is null. TenantConfigurationCacheItem is decorated [IgnoreMultiTenancy]; its cache name defaults to the type FullName minus the 'CacheItem' suffix, i.e. 'Volo.Abp.MultiTenancy.TenantConfiguration', with key format 'i:{id},n:{name}'.
standards.source_name: ABP Framework source — DistributedCacheKeyNormalizer.cs, TenantConfigurationCacheItem.cs, TenantConfiguration.cs, CacheNameAttribute.cs
standards.notes: Read all four source files plus the caching doc, which states ABP 'automatically adds the current tenant id to the cache key ... Define IgnoreMultiTenancy attribute on the cache item class to disable this'. TenantConfiguration carries a ConnectionStrings property and is serialised into the cache item, so every office's SQL Server connection string — credentials included — sits in Redis under a globally-readable, non-tenant-prefixed key. Redis hardening is infrastructure and out of scope; the in-scope controls are (a) an automated audit that every Redis key either carries a t:{guid} prefix or is on an explicit allowlist, and (b) a decision about encrypting tenant connection strings at rest in the tenant store.

standards.claim: Tenant isolation can be switched off globally or per-artifact by several single-line changes, each of which is invisible in a code review that is not looking for it: DataFilter.Disable<IMultiTenant>() in a using block; AbpDataFilterOptions.DefaultStates[typeof(IMultiTenant)] = new DataFilterState(isEnabled: false) which disables the filter application-wide; [IgnoreMultiTenancy] on a DbContext which forces the host connection string; and BlobContainerConfiguration.IsMultiTenant = false which shares stored documents across all tenants.
standards.threshold: Four deny-list constructs: DataFilter.Disable<IMultiTenant>(); AbpDataFilterOptions.DefaultStates[typeof(IMultiTenant)]; [IgnoreMultiTenancy]; container.IsMultiTenant = false
standards.source_name: ABP documentation — Data Filtering, Multi-Tenancy, and BLOB Storing
standards.notes: All read as raw doc source. ABP's strongest wording on Disable is hygiene, not security: 'Always use the Disable and Enable methods it inside a using block to guarantee that the filter is reset to its previous state', and on AbpDataFilterOptions merely 'Carefully change defaults for global filters'. The multi-tenancy page's only note on disabling the tenant filter is a *functionality* caveat — 'this approach won't work if your tenants have separate databases since there is no built-in way to query from multiple database in a single database query' — not a warning about leakage. In other words, ABP does not document DataFilter.Disable<IMultiTenant>() as a security-critical operation, so the guardrail has to come from your own CI. The BLOB page confirms IsMultiTenant = false makes blobs 'available to all the tenants' — for a PHI document store that is the highest-severity one-liner in the list.

standards.claim: ABP's shipped test infrastructure cannot test database-per-tenant isolation. The startup template configures integration tests against a single in-memory SQLite database, creating a fresh database per test case, and ABP's testing documentation contains no guidance on multi-tenancy: the words 'tenant'/'tenancy' appear zero times across its unit-test, integration-test and UI-test pages.
standards.threshold: 0 occurrences of 'tenant' in docs/en/testing/{unit-tests,integration-tests,ui-tests}.md; template test database = in-memory SQLite, one fresh database per test case
standards.source_name: ABP documentation — Integration Tests (docs/en/testing/integration-tests.md)
standards.notes: Downloaded all three testing docs and grep-counted 'tenant' — zero in each. Verified verbatim: 'The startup template is configured to use in-memory SQLite database for the EF Core ... It creates a new fresh database for each test case'. This is the crux of the brief's question about what unit tests cannot prove. With one SQLite database, CurrentTenant.Change() exercises only the EF Core global query filter; connection-string routing, cross-database queries, the DbContext-per-connection-string cache key and the Default-connection-string fallback are all invisible. Any tenant-isolation suite must therefore run against at least two genuinely separate databases.

standards.claim: The EF Core global query filter is the only in-database isolation control ABP applies, it is applied per entity type at model-build time, and its correctness depends on a compiled-query cache key that includes the current tenant id and the filter states. It is applied only to entities implementing IMultiTenant and only to LINQ queries — raw SQL execution paths are outside it.
standards.threshold: AbpDbContext.CreateFilterExpression: 'e => !IsMultiTenantFilterEnabled || EF.Property<Guid>(e, multiTenantPropertyName) == CurrentTenantId'; AbpDbContext.GetCompiledQueryCacheKey(): '{CurrentTenantId ?? "Null"}:{IsSoftDeleteFilterEnabled}:{IsMultiTenantFilterEnabled}'
standards.source_name: ABP Framework source — AbpDbContext.cs
standards.notes: The filter expression and cache-key code were read directly and are verified. Marked partial on one sub-claim: I did not open Microsoft's EF Core documentation on whether global query filters compose over FromSqlRaw, so treat 'raw SQL bypasses the filter' as the reason to test rather than as a cited fact — ExecuteSqlRaw and any Dapper usage certainly bypass it, FromSqlRaw composition is the uncertain case. Two testable consequences either way: (1) an entity that forgets to implement IMultiTenant gets no filter at all and ShouldFilterEntity will not flag it; (2) a row written while the tenant context is null lands with TenantId = null inside a tenant database and becomes permanently invisible to that tenant — silent data loss rather than a leak, which no exception will surface.

recommended_checks.what_it_does: HTTP-level xUnit tests through the real ASP.NET Core middleware pipeline (WebApplicationFactory) that fire a matrix of crafted requests at the four anonymous endpoints — registration, login, password reset, document upload — and assert the RESOLVED TENANT, not the status code. Matrix: valid Host for tenant A; Host for tenant B; unknown/attacker Host; no Host; duplicate Host lines; absolute-form request target with a conflicting Host; X-Forwarded-Host, X-Host, X-Forwarded-Server, X-HTTP-Host-Override and Forwarded set to tenant B while Host is tenant A; ?__tenant=<B guid>; __tenant header; __tenant cookie; and a tenant-A bearer token replayed against tenant B's hostname. Each case asserts an expected ICurrentTenant.Id, exposed in the Test environment only via a minimal diagnostic endpoint or a test-only response header. Also asserts no Set-Cookie for __tenant is ever emitted.
recommended_checks.tool: xUnit v3 + Microsoft.AspNetCore.Mvc.Testing (WebApplicationFactory), already present in the ABP template test stack
recommended_checks.tool_maintained_evidence: Microsoft.AspNetCore.Mvc.Testing 10.0.11 is current, and the 11.0.0-preview.7.26381.103 preview published 2026-08-11 (NuGet registration index, https://api.nuget.org/v3/registration5-gz-semver2/microsoft.aspnetcore.mvc.testing/page/10.0.11/11.0.0-preview.7.26381.103.json). xunit.v3 4.0.0 published 2026-08-15 (https://azuresearch-usnc.nuget.org/query?q=packageid:xunit.v3). Volo.Abp.TestBase 10.6.0 stable, 10.7.0-rc.3 published 2026-08-18 (https://api.nuget.org/v3/registration5-gz-semver2/volo.abp.testbase/page/10.0.0-rc.1/10.7.0-rc.3.json).
recommended_checks.effort_hours: 10-14 to build the harness and first 15 cases; ~1 per new case thereafter
recommended_checks.rationale_for_two_person_team: This is the highest value-per-hour check in the whole area and the only one that directly tests the stated top risk. It needs no Docker, no new tooling and no infrastructure decisions — it runs in the existing test project against the existing in-memory database, because it asserts tenant RESOLUTION, not tenant DATA. It is also the check most likely to fail immediately: ABP registers the __tenant query-string, route, header and cookie resolvers by default, so the premise 'tenancy resolves from the Host header only' is probably false in the running app right now. Fifteen assertions that take an afternoon to write will tell you that on day one.

recommended_checks.what_it_does: Integration tests running against TWO genuinely separate tenant databases plus a host database, proving the things a single-database ORM test cannot: that a query executed under tenant A's context physically hits A's database; that data written under A is absent from B's database at the SQL level (not merely filtered out); that a tenant configured with no connection string does NOT silently fall back to the Default/host database; that switching CurrentTenant inside one unit of work yields a different DbContext and a different physical connection; and that a DbContext marked [IgnoreMultiTenancy] is routed to the host. Assertions read the actual connection string and query the target database directly, so a wrong-database result cannot masquerade as an empty result.
recommended_checks.tool: Testcontainers.MsSql with xUnit (replacing the template's single in-memory SQLite for this one test project). Cheap fallback if Docker in CI proves painful: two SQLite FILE databases with per-tenant connection strings — this still proves routing, fallback and DbContext-cache-key behaviour, just not SQL Server semantics.
recommended_checks.tool_maintained_evidence: Testcontainers.MsSql 4.14.0 published 2026-08-14, 32.4M total downloads (https://azuresearch-usnc.nuget.org/query?q=packageid:Testcontainers.MsSql and https://api.nuget.org/v3/registration5-gz-semver2/testcontainers.mssql/index.json). Core Testcontainers 4.14.0, 109M downloads.
recommended_checks.effort_hours: 16-24 for the two-database harness and ~10 tests; the SQLite-file fallback is 4-6
recommended_checks.rationale_for_two_person_team: ABP's own testing docs are silent on multi-tenancy and its template gives you one in-memory SQLite database, so without this the team has literally zero coverage of the mechanism their entire isolation model rests on. Cap it hard: about ten tests, one test project, running on PR. Do NOT try to provision all 11 offices — two tenants plus the host proves every routing rule that 33 would. If Docker-in-Actions becomes a maintenance tax, take the two-SQLite-files version; it is worse fidelity but it still catches the silent Default-connection-string fallback, which is the specific bug most likely to bite during office onboarding.

recommended_checks.what_it_does: A single reflection-driven test that enumerates every IBackgroundJob<T> and IAsyncBackgroundJob<T> implementation in the solution and asserts each argument type T implements IMultiTenant with a non-null TenantId at enqueue time. Optionally extends to distributed event ETOs and to asserting that every periodic background worker explicitly establishes a tenant scope rather than inheriting the ambient (host) context.
recommended_checks.tool: xUnit + System.Reflection (no new dependency)
recommended_checks.tool_maintained_evidence: Uses only xunit.v3 4.0.0, published 2026-08-15 (https://azuresearch-usnc.nuget.org/query?q=packageid:xunit.v3) — no additional tool to maintain.
recommended_checks.rationale_for_two_person_team: Two hours of work that closes a failure mode the team cannot reasonably be expected to know about: ABP's BackgroundJobExecuter derives tenant from job args only when the args class implements IMultiTenant, and otherwise falls back to the ambient tenant, which in a worker is null — so the job runs against the host database. ABP's background-jobs documentation never mentions tenants, so nothing in the developer's normal workflow prompts them to get this right. A reflection test is self-maintaining: it automatically covers every job added in future without anyone remembering to write a test.

recommended_checks.what_it_does: Static deny-list scan for the small set of one-line changes that disable isolation: DataFilter.Disable<IMultiTenant>(); any write to AbpDataFilterOptions.DefaultStates for IMultiTenant; [IgnoreMultiTenancy] on entities, DbContexts or cache-item classes; BlobContainerConfiguration IsMultiTenant = false; constructor injection of Microsoft's raw IDistributedCache instead of ABP's IDistributedCache<T>; and FromSqlRaw/ExecuteSqlRaw/Dapper usage on multi-tenant entities. Findings require an inline allowlist annotation with a justification comment, so each one becomes a deliberate, reviewed decision.
recommended_checks.tool: Semgrep OSS with ~6 custom rules (C# support is Generally Available). A ripgrep-based shell step in the workflow is a legitimate 1-hour substitute if Semgrep feels heavy.
recommended_checks.tool_maintained_evidence: Semgrep 1.175.0 published 2026-08-26 (https://pypi.org/pypi/semgrep/json). C# is listed at the 'Generally available' maturity tier on https://docs.semgrep.dev/supported-languages. Note the page advertises 170+ C# 'Pro rules' behind the commercial product — your own custom rules run fine in the OSS CLI, which is all this check needs.
recommended_checks.effort_hours: 4-6 for the Semgrep rules; 1-2 for the ripgrep version
recommended_checks.rationale_for_two_person_team: With no senior reviewer on the team, code review will not reliably catch a single added line like container.IsMultiTenant = false — especially since ABP's documentation presents these as ordinary configuration options and never flags DataFilter.Disable<IMultiTenant>() as security-critical. Six rules over about six lines of forbidden syntax is the cheapest durable guardrail available, and the allowlist-with-justification pattern means it produces near-zero recurring noise: a clean repo stays green, and the only time it speaks is when someone is about to do the exact thing you are afraid of.

recommended_checks.what_it_does: Scheduled job that connects to each tenant database in turn and, for every table backing an IMultiTenant entity, asserts SELECT DISTINCT TenantId returns exactly one value equal to that tenant's id, with no NULLs and no foreign tenant ids. Also asserts each tenant's resolved connection string is non-empty, distinct from every other tenant's, and distinct from the Default connection string.
recommended_checks.tool: A small dotnet console tool or SQL script driven from a scheduled GitHub Actions workflow against the staging environment
recommended_checks.tool_maintained_evidence: No third-party dependency: plain ADO.NET/EF Core against SQL Server plus the existing GitHub Actions scheduler. Nothing to fall out of maintenance.
recommended_checks.rationale_for_two_person_team: This is the backstop for the failure mode the application reports as success. When MultiTenantConnectionStringResolver silently falls back to the Default connection string, or a row is written while the tenant context is null, no exception is thrown and no test fails — the data simply lands in the wrong database or becomes invisible. A fingerprint check inspects the outcome rather than the code path, so it catches misrouting regardless of cause. Mark it launch-blocking in the sense of running it once, manually, against a fully seeded staging environment before go-live; after that a nightly cron is enough and it should be silent, which keeps the alert meaningful. The connection-string-distinctness assertion is the part to run every single time an office is onboarded.

recommended_checks.what_it_does: Scheduled check that drives a synthetic two-tenant workload against staging, then SCANs Redis and asserts every key either begins with the t:{guid}, prefix or appears on an explicit allowlist of intentionally global keys. Separately asserts that no value in Redis contains a plaintext SQL Server connection string or credential.
recommended_checks.tool: redis-cli --scan plus a short script, run from a scheduled GitHub Actions workflow
recommended_checks.tool_maintained_evidence: redis-cli ships with the Redis server the application already runs; no additional tool is introduced or has to be kept alive.
recommended_checks.rationale_for_two_person_team: Only ABP's typed IDistributedCache<T> adds the tenant prefix; injecting Microsoft's raw IDistributedCache produces unprefixed keys that are shared across all 11 offices, and nothing in the compiler, the framework or code review will tell you. The key audit detects that empirically, including for cases the static deny-list misses (a third-party library, or ABP module code you did not write). It is scheduled rather than gating because it needs a running environment and a seeded workload. Not launch-blocking on the leak dimension, but do run it once before go-live specifically for the credential assertion: ABP's TenantConfigurationCacheItem is marked [IgnoreMultiTenancy], so every office's connection string sits in Redis under a global, unprefixed key — you want to know that with your own eyes before PHI arrives.

not_worth_it_here: A dedicated third-party tenant-isolation penetration test per release. A larger org buys one every quarter or before each major release. Buy exactly ONE, scoped tightly to tenant resolution and cross-tenant access, timed for the window when the app is on the public internet but still holds only synthetic data — that window is a genuine gift and it closes permanently the day real PHI lands. Recurring engagements are not defensible on two developers' budget or calendar.

Authenticated multi-tenant DAST in CI (OWASP ZAP or Burp Enterprise crawling as tenant A and diffing against tenant B). This is standard at a company with an AppSec team. Here it is the wrong tool: a generic scanner has no model of which object belongs to which office, so it will not recognise a cross-tenant read as a finding, and maintaining authenticated scan sessions for 11 tenants is a permanent part-time job. Targeted xUnit assertions on the resolved tenant find strictly more, for less.

A custom Roslyn analyzer NuGet package for the forbidden-construct rules. It is the 'proper' engineering answer and gives editor squiggles, but it is a separate project to build, version, publish and keep compiling against each .NET SDK bump. Six Semgrep rules — or six ripgrep patterns — get you the same CI enforcement this year for a tenth of the effort and no ongoing maintenance surface.

Property-based or fuzz testing of the tenant resolver (generating random Host values and header combinations). The interesting inputs here are a small, enumerable, well-documented set — the PortSwigger bypass catalogue is about a dozen cases. A hand-written table-driven test covers them exhaustively and readably. Fuzzing adds flaky runtime and a triage burden for no additional coverage.

Provisioning all 11 (or 33) tenant databases in the test environment. Isolation is a pairwise property: every routing and leakage rule that can be violated between 33 tenants can be violated between 2. Two tenants plus the host proves the mechanism; 11 just multiplies test runtime, fixture complexity and CI cost. Scale-out belongs in the onboarding runbook, not the test matrix.

Chaos or failure-injection testing on connection-string routing (killing a tenant database mid-request, corrupting the tenant cache). Valuable at a company with an on-call rotation that can act on what it learns. With two SDE 1s and no DevOps, the realistic outcome is a suite that breaks, gets muted, and teaches nothing.

Database-level Row-Level Security in SQL Server as defence in depth behind the EF Core filter. This is a common recommendation and it is genuinely strong — for SHARED-database multi-tenancy. You are database-per-tenant, so RLS defends against a threat your architecture has already eliminated, while adding migration complexity to 11 databases and a second place where isolation logic can drift out of sync with the first.

ASVS Level 3 authorization requirements (8.1.3, 8.1.4, 8.3.2, 8.3.3, 8.4.2) — documented environmental and contextual decision attributes, immediate propagation of authorization changes through self-contained tokens, delegated-identity token chaining, and layered device-posture controls on admin interfaces. Level 2 is the correct target for this application, and 8.4.1 (the multi-tenancy requirement) is itself Level 2. Reaching for L3 dilutes attention across requirements that will not be met rather than deepening the ones that must be.

Continuous production leak detection via per-tenant honeytoken records and alerting. This is real practice at scale and it is the right eventual answer, but it presumes someone is watching an alert channel and can respond. Build the nightly tenant-data-fingerprint check first; it is the same idea at a cadence two people can actually sustain, and it works without a monitoring stack.

A formal written threat model document satisfying ASVS 8.1.1/8.1.2's authorization-documentation requirements. The documentation requirements are Level 1 and you will eventually want them for HIPAA evidence anyway — but as a first move, a one-page table mapping each of the four external roles to what they may touch is worth more than a document nobody re-reads. Do not spend a developer-week on documentation before the spoofing tests exist.
surprises: The premise 'tenancy resolves from the HTTP Host header ONLY' is very likely false in the running application. ABP's AbpAspNetCoreMultiTenancyModule unconditionally registers QueryString, Route, Header and Cookie resolvers for __tenant, and AddDomainTenantResolver does not replace them — it inserts the domain resolver after the current-user resolver, leaving all four behind it. Unless the code explicitly clears AbpTenantResolveOptions.TenantResolvers, ?__tenant=<other office's guid> is a live input on every anonymous endpoint. This is the first thing to check in the repo and the first test to write.

A spoofed or unrecognised Host does not produce an error — it produces the HOST (landlord) context. DomainTenantResolveContributor sets context.Handled = true whenever Request.Host has any value, including when the domain format does not match, and the resolver chain stops at the first Handled contributor. So Host: attacker.com yields a null tenant, which under database-per-tenant means the host database: the tenant registry, the connection strings, the landlord admin identity. The endpoints most exposed to this are exactly the ones going public for the first time — registration, password reset, document upload.

One crafted link can pin a victim's browser to another office. MultiTenancyMiddleware writes a persistent __tenant cookie whenever the query-string resolver was the one that applied. That converts a one-shot ?__tenant= parameter into durable tenant confusion for that browser, and it is emitted by the framework with no application code involved.

A tenant with no connection string silently uses the shared/host database. MultiTenantConnectionStringResolver falls back to base resolution when tenant.ConnectionStrings is empty — no exception, no log. With 11 offices at launch and headroom to 33, tenant onboarding is the most-repeated high-risk operation in the system, and its failure mode is invisible: the EF Core filter makes wrong-database results look merely empty. Assert connection-string distinctness on every onboarding.

Two tenants that both fall back to the Default connection string share a DbContext instance. UnitOfWorkDbContextProvider keys cached DbContexts as {DbContextType}_{SHA256(connectionString)}, so identical connection strings collapse to one context — leaving only the EF Core query filter between two offices in a system whose whole isolation story is 'separate databases'.

Background jobs run as HOST unless the args class opts in. BackgroundJobExecuter takes the tenant from job args only if that type implements IMultiTenant, otherwise it inherits the ambient tenant, which in a worker is null. ABP's background-jobs and background-workers documentation pages contain zero occurrences of the word 'tenant', so nothing prompts a developer to get this right. A two-hour reflection test covers every job you will ever add.

Every office's SQL Server connection string — credentials included — is cached in Redis under a global, non-tenant-prefixed key. TenantConfigurationCacheItem is decorated [IgnoreMultiTenancy], so the key normalizer omits the t:{tenantId} prefix, and TenantConfiguration serialises its ConnectionStrings property. The cache name resolves to 'Volo.Abp.MultiTenancy.TenantConfiguration'. Anyone who can read Redis holds the keys to all 11 databases.

Redis tenant scoping only happens through ABP's typed IDistributedCache<T>. Inject Microsoft's raw IDistributedCache and you get unprefixed, cross-tenant keys with no warning from the compiler, the framework or code review. This is an easy and natural thing for an SDE 1 to write, and it is invisible in a diff.

For authenticated requests the Host header is irrelevant — the token wins. CurrentUserTenantResolveContributor is inserted at index 0 and short-circuits the chain, so the tenantid claim overrides the hostname. ABP never verifies that the token's tenant matches the host-resolved tenant. A tenant-A token replayed against tenantB.example.com is served tenant A's data. That is not a data leak, but it means your mental model of the system is wrong, and it means token/claims binding is a separate control from host resolution that needs its own test.

ABP's own documentation is wrong about resolver order. Both the multi-tenancy doc and ABP's first-party AI skill file list the domain resolver LAST (position 6, after the cookie resolver). The source inserts it SECOND, immediately after the current-user resolver. If you reason from the docs about whether __tenant can override the hostname, you will reach the wrong conclusion.

ABP's shipped test harness structurally cannot test your architecture. The startup template runs integration tests against a single in-memory SQLite database with a fresh database per test case, and ABP's three testing documentation pages mention tenants zero times. Every green test in that harness is compatible with completely broken connection-string routing. This is the concrete answer to 'what can unit tests against an ORM not prove'.

Kestrel does not validate the Host header at all — Microsoft states this plainly — and host-filtering middleware stays disabled until you define AllowedHosts. In an application where the Host header IS the authorization boundary between eleven medical offices, that default is the whole ballgame, and it is one configuration key.

A single line shares PHI documents across every office: BlobContainerConfiguration.IsMultiTenant = false. ABP documents it neutrally as a feature for sharing blobs between tenants. For a workers' comp document store on MinIO it is the highest-severity one-liner in the codebase, and it looks like ordinary configuration in a pull request.

One line disables the tenant filter application-wide: AbpDataFilterOptions.DefaultStates[typeof(IMultiTenant)] = new DataFilterState(isEnabled: false). ABP's only comment on this is 'Carefully change defaults for global filters'. There is no framework-level guard, no analyzer warning, and no test in the default template that would fail.
disagreements: ABP contradicts itself on tenant resolver order. The multi-tenancy documentation and ABP's own first-party AI skill file (.claude/skills/abp-multi-tenancy/SKILL.md) both list resolution as: user claims, query string, route, header, cookie, then domain/subdomain LAST. The source disagrees: AddDomainTenantResolver calls TenantResolvers.InsertAfter(r => r is CurrentUserTenantResolveContributor, ...), placing the domain resolver SECOND. This materially changes whether ?__tenant= can override the hostname, so trust the source and pin the behaviour with a test. Docs: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/abpframework/abp/dev/docs/en/framework/architecture/multi-tenancy/index.md vs source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/abpframework/abp/dev/framework/src/Volo.Abp.AspNetCore.MultiTenancy/Volo/Abp/MultiTenancy/AbpMultiTenancyOptionsExtensions.cs

ABP and OWASP disagree on whether disabling the tenant filter is a security matter. ABP's strongest wording anywhere is hygiene — 'Always use the Disable and Enable methods it inside a using block to guarantee that the filter is reset' — and its only note specific to disabling the multi-tenancy filter is a functionality caveat about separate databases, not a leakage warning. OWASP ASVS 8.4.1 and API1:2023 treat any path that removes a cross-tenant control as an authorization defect requiring an explicit test. I did not find an ABP page that warns about DataFilter.Disable<IMultiTenant>() in security terms; if one exists I did not open it. Follow OWASP here: treat every disable site as a reviewed exception with a test.

ABP's multi-tenancy documentation never mentions Host header spoofing at all, despite shipping a resolver that derives tenancy from Request.Host and despite OWASP (WSTG-INPV-17), Microsoft ('Host headers aren't validated') and PortSwigger all treating host-derived trust as a distinct vulnerability class. The absence is not a contradiction so much as a gap, but it means an ABP-only reading of the problem will miss the entire attack surface.

Microsoft's own proxy documentation is internally inconsistent about forwarded-header trust. The options table states that requests must match KnownProxies or KnownNetworks before forwarded headers are processed, and that this 'limits header spoofing by not accepting forwarders from untrusted proxies' — while a code sample on the same page shows options.KnownNetworks.Clear(); options.KnownProxies.Clear();, which removes exactly that protection. The page also notes that setting ASPNETCORE_FORWARDEDHEADERS_ENABLED=true 'doesn't enable features such as the KnownProxies option'. Both snippets are widely copy-pasted. Whichever pattern is in your code, assert the resulting behaviour with a spoofed X-Forwarded-Host test rather than reading the config.

WSTG test-ID numbering differs between the 'latest' and 'stable' trees. I verified Host header injection as WSTG-INPV-17 in the latest tree and the authorization-bypass test as WSTG-ATHZ-02 in the stable tree; I did not cross-check either ID across both trees. Cite the version you actually test against.

Semgrep's language-support page advertises C# at 'Generally available' maturity with 170+ Pro rules, but does not state on that page which capabilities require the commercial product versus the OSS CLI. My recommendation relies only on custom rules in the OSS CLI, which is well established, but I could not verify the OSS/paid boundary from the page I opened — if you plan to lean on Semgrep's bundled C# rulesets rather than your own six rules, confirm licensing first.

material_errors: [2] Citation/threshold overreach: OWASP API1:2023 says "Do not deploy changes that make the tests fail" — 'deploy', not 'block merges'. The page also says nothing about 'not by manual review'. And the API5:2023 half of the claim is NOT on the cited API1 URL; it needs its own citation (https://owasp.org/API-Security/editions/2023/en/0xa5-broken-function-level-authorization/), where the denial-by-default line is in 'How to prevent' but the 'don't assume administrative based on URL path' line is under 'Is the API Vulnerable?', not 'How to prevent'.

[6] The cited Kestrel host-filtering page does NOT mention the project template or a wildcard AllowedHosts value. The page's own statement is the opposite framing: 'Host-filtering middleware is disabled by default. To enable the middleware, define an AllowedHosts key'. The template's "AllowedHosts": "*" is a real but separately-sourced fact (dotnet new appsettings.json) and needs its own citation.

[8] The cited AbpAspNetCoreMultiTenancyModule.cs registers ONLY the four resolvers (QueryString, Route, Header, Cookie). It contains no CurrentUserTenantResolveContributor and no AddDomainTenantResolver. Those live in framework/src/Volo.Abp.MultiTenancy/Volo/Abp/MultiTenancy/AbpMultiTenancyModule.cs (TenantResolvers.Insert(0, new CurrentUserTenantResolveContributor())) and framework/src/Volo.Abp.AspNetCore.MultiTenancy/Volo/Abp/MultiTenancy/AbpMultiTenancyOptionsExtensions.cs (InsertAfter(r => r is CurrentUserTenantResolveContributor, ...)). TenantResolverConsts is in Volo.Abp.MultiTenancy.Abstractions, not the cited assembly path. The substance is correct; the single-URL citation is not.

[10] The cookie write is NOT unconditional on query-string resolution: it sits inside 'if (tenant?.Id != _currentTenant.Id)' and inside 'if (_tenantResolveResultAccessor.Result != null && ...AppliedResolvers.Contains(QueryStringTenantResolveContributor.ContributorName))'. Also, 'persistent' is not shown on the cited file — the 10-year Expires (DateTimeOffset.Now.AddYears(10), Path=/, HttpOnly=false, IsEssential=true) is in AbpMultiTenancyCookieHelper.cs. Cite both files.

[13] The cited DistributedCacheKeyNormalizer.cs supports only the key format and the two omission conditions. The TenantConfigurationCacheItem facts ([IgnoreMultiTenancy], CacheKeyFormat "i:{0},n:{1}") are in Volo.Abp.MultiTenancy.Abstractions/Volo/Abp/MultiTenancy/TenantConfigurationCacheItem.cs, and the FullName-minus-'CacheItem' naming rule is in Volo.Abp.Caching/CacheNameAttribute.cs. All three sub-facts are true but need those citations.

[14] The cited data-filtering.md does not contain two of the four listed constructs: [IgnoreMultiTenancy] on a DbContext and BlobContainerConfiguration.IsMultiTenant = false appear nowhere in that document. Its AbpDataFilterOptions example also uses typeof(ISoftDelete), not typeof(IMultiTenant), and its Disable<T>() example uses ISoftDelete. BlobContainerConfiguration.IsMultiTenant (default true) is in framework/src/Volo.Abp.BlobStoring/Volo/Abp/BlobStoring/BlobContainerConfiguration.cs.

[16] 'the only in-database isolation control' is not supported: the same file also builds a database-side variant via AbpEfCoreDataFilterDbFunctionMethods.MultiTenantFilter when UseDbFunction() is true, and database-per-tenant separation via MultiTenantConnectionStringResolver is a second in-database control. The 'raw SQL is outside the filter' caveat is true of EF Core global filters generally but is not stated on this page.

The string 'IgnoreMultiTenancy' and any mention of BlobContainerConfiguration appear ZERO times in this document.
