research.area: Area 14 — What HIPAA actually requires of code and CI (45 CFR Part 164 Subpart C technical safeguards, 164.308(a)(8) evaluation, the Jan 2025 Security Rule NPRM and its 2026 status, NIST SP 800-66r2)
research.standard_summary: NOT LEGAL ADVICE — this is a technical reading of primary regulatory text for engineering planning; a healthcare attorney should confirm anything you rely on. As of 28 Aug 2026 the operative law is still the 2013-amended Security Rule (45 CFR 164.306, .308, .312, .316). It is deliberately technology-neutral and prescribes almost nothing about code: of the five technical safeguards in 164.312, only two implementation specifications are unconditionally Required (unique user identification and emergency access procedure). Automatic logoff, encryption at rest, integrity-authentication of ePHI, transmission integrity controls and transmission encryption are all "Addressable", meaning 164.306(d)(3) lets you skip them only if you document why and implement an equivalent alternative where reasonable. MFA, SAST, SBOMs, secure coding, penetration testing and vulnerability scanning appear nowhere in the current rule. The January 6, 2025 NPRM (90 FR 898, RIN 0945-AA22) would change that substantially — deleting the addressable/required distinction, mandating encryption of all ePHI at rest and in transit, MFA, automated vulnerability scanning at least every six months, penetration testing at least every 12 months by a qualified person, and an annual compliance audit — but it has NOT been finalised or withdrawn: the current Unified Agenda (Publication ID 2026) places it in "Long-Term Actions" with a projected Final Action of July 2027. The practical consequences for this team are therefore: (a) build the required system properties and, critically, the *documented evidence* of them, because 164.316(b)(2)(i) demands six-year retention and GitHub Actions caps artifacts at 400 days; (b) start the recognized-security-practices clock now, because 42 U.S.C. 17941 gives enforcement mitigation only for "not less than the previous 12 months" of demonstrated practice; and (c) justify SAST/lint/CI gates as risk management under 164.308(a)(1)(ii)(B), not as things HIPAA names, because it does not name them.

standards.claim: 45 CFR 164.312(a)(2) has exactly two Required implementation specifications — Unique user identification ('Assign a unique name and/or number for identifying and tracking user identity') and Emergency access procedure. Automatic logoff (a)(2)(iii) and Encryption and decryption (a)(2)(iv) are both Addressable. FOR CODE: every action against ePHI must be attributable to a distinct identity — no shared service accounts writing on behalf of users, and a break-glass path must exist. FOR CI: an automated test can assert that the audit-trail user id is never null/system for user-initiated ePHI operations, and that a break-glass code path exists and is itself logged.
standards.threshold: 164.312(a)(2)(i) Required; (a)(2)(ii) Required; (a)(2)(iii) Addressable; (a)(2)(iv) Addressable
standards.source_name: GPO govinfo, CFR Title 45 Vol 2 (rev. Oct 1, 2024), § 164.312 — official XML granule
standards.notes: Fetched the raw CFR XML and read the (Required)/(Addressable) tags verbatim; Cornell LII returned identical designations. Section last amended 78 FR 5694 (Jan 25, 2013) per the CITA element — no amendment since, which I separately confirmed by finding no post-2013 final rule under RIN 0945-AA22.

standards.claim: 45 CFR 164.306(d)(3) defines what 'Addressable' actually obliges: the entity must assess whether the specification is reasonable and appropriate, then either implement it, or (i) document why it would not be reasonable and appropriate AND (ii) implement an equivalent alternative measure if reasonable and appropriate. Addressable is not optional. FOR CODE/CI: a decision to skip, say, field-level encryption at rest is a documented artifact you must be able to produce, ideally a versioned ADR in the repo with the risk-analysis reference.
standards.source_name: GPO govinfo, CFR Title 45 Vol 2, § 164.306 Security standards: General rules
standards.notes: Cross-referenced against the NPRM preamble, which states HHS is 'concerned that some regulated entities proceed as if compliance with an addressable implementation specification is optional' and that this is a misreading. 164.306(b)(2) also lets you weigh size, capabilities, technical infrastructure and cost — the explicit statutory basis for a two-person team scaling down.

standards.claim: 45 CFR 164.312(b) Audit controls is a standard with NO implementation specifications: 'Implement hardware, software, and/or procedural mechanisms that record and examine activity in information systems that contain or use electronic protected health information.' OCR/CMS guidance states plainly that 'the Security Rule does not identify data that must be gathered by the audit controls or how often the audit reports should be reviewed.' FOR CODE: you choose the event schema, but it must cover ePHI access, not just writes. FOR CI: assert that read paths to ePHI emit audit records, since ABP/EF Core change-tracking captures mutations by default but reads are the ones that get missed.
standards.threshold: n/a — no prescribed data set, no prescribed review frequency
standards.source_name: HHS/CMS HIPAA Security Series, Vol. 2 Paper 4, 'Security Standards: Technical Safeguards' (5/2005, rev. 3/2007)
standards.notes: Downloaded the PDF and extracted the text directly (17 pages) rather than relying on a summarizer. This paper is still the document NIST SP 800-66r2 cites as 'Security Standards: Technical Safeguards'. It is old (2007) but has not been superseded and is still hosted by HHS.

standards.claim: 45 CFR 164.308(a)(1)(ii)(D) Information system activity review is REQUIRED: 'Implement procedures to regularly review records of information system activity, such as audit logs, access reports, and security incident tracking reports.' Writing audit logs is not sufficient — somebody must regularly review them and that review must be documented. FOR CODE: build a queryable review surface (anomalous cross-tenant access attempts, failed logins, bulk document downloads) rather than raw log dumps. FOR CI: this is the one obligation that CI cannot discharge; it needs a scheduled human ritual with a retained artifact.
standards.threshold: 164.308(a)(1)(ii)(D) — Required; frequency is 'regularly', undefined by the rule
standards.source_name: GPO govinfo, CFR Title 45 Vol 2, § 164.308 Administrative safeguards
standards.notes: Extracted verbatim from the CFR XML. This is the most commonly missed code-adjacent requirement: teams build audit logging to satisfy 164.312(b) and never build the review step that 164.308(a)(1)(ii)(D) separately requires.

standards.claim: 45 CFR 164.312(d) Person or entity authentication is a bare standard with no implementation specifications and names no method. Multi-factor authentication is NOT required by the current Security Rule. OCR's June 2023 cybersecurity newsletter frames it as a recommendation: regulated entities 'should consider implementing multi-factor authentication solutions, including phishing-resistant multi-factor authentication, where appropriate.' FOR CODE: with OpenIddict, MFA is a risk-management choice you document, not a regulatory checkbox — but see the NPRM entry below, which would make it mandatory.
standards.threshold: n/a — no method prescribed; MFA is 'consider', not required
standards.source_name: HHS OCR Cybersecurity Newsletter, June 2023, 'HIPAA and Cybersecurity Authentication'
standards.notes: The newsletter cites NIST SP 800-63, SP 800-63-4 (then draft) and SP 1800-17. OCR's Q1 2022 newsletter separately ties weak authentication to 164.312(d) and 164.312(a)(1), stating 'Weak password rules and single factor authentication are among the practices that can contribute to successful attacks' — so the regulator's practical expectation is stronger than the rule text.

standards.claim: 45 CFR 164.312(e) Transmission security is a Required standard, but BOTH of its implementation specifications — Integrity controls (e)(2)(i) and Encryption (e)(2)(ii) — are Addressable. OCR guidance states 'The Security Rule allows for EPHI to be sent over an electronic open network as long as it is adequately protected' and that where risk analysis shows significant risk of unauthorized access, 'a covered entity must encrypt those transmissions under the addressable implementation specification for encryption.' FOR THIS APP: moving from an office LAN to the public internet is exactly the risk-analysis change that converts 'addressable' into 'you must'. FOR CI: assert HSTS, secure/HttpOnly/SameSite cookie flags, HTTPS redirect, and that no ePHI or tenant identifier appears in query strings or logs.
standards.threshold: 164.312(e)(2)(i) Addressable; 164.312(e)(2)(ii) Addressable; standard (e)(1) itself Required
standards.source_name: HHS/CMS HIPAA Security Series Vol. 2 Paper 4 + GPO CFR 45 § 164.312
standards.notes: Whether your TLS termination uses a FIPS-validated module is a hosting decision and out of scope here; the code-side obligation is to refuse plaintext and to fail CI if the app will serve over HTTP.

standards.claim: Encryption is the breach safe harbor, and it is decided in code and config. 45 CFR 164.402 defines 'unsecured protected health information' as PHI not rendered unusable/unreadable/indecipherable by a technology or methodology the Secretary specifies. HHS's guidance names NIST SP 800-111 for data at rest and NIST SP 800-52, SP 800-77 or SP 800-113 (or others that are FIPS 140-2 validated) for data in motion, and requires decryption keys be stored separately from the encrypted data. FOR CODE: ePHI encrypted to that standard that is compromised is not a reportable breach — the single largest consequence-reducer available to this team, and it lives in the MinIO/SQL Server/TLS configuration, not in a policy document.
standards.threshold: NIST SP 800-111 (at rest); NIST SP 800-52 / 800-77 / 800-113 or FIPS 140-2 validated (in motion); NIST SP 800-88 for media destruction
standards.source_name: HHS, Guidance to Render Unsecured Protected Health Information Unusable, Unreadable, or Indecipherable to Unauthorized Individuals
standards.notes: Note the guidance still says FIPS 140-2, not 140-3 — it dates from 74 FR 42740 (2009) and has not been updated to the current FIPS. The key-separation requirement is the part teams get wrong: encrypting a MinIO bucket with a key stored in the same database defeats the safe harbor.

standards.claim: 45 CFR 164.308(a)(8) Evaluation is a Required standard with no implementation specifications: 'Perform a periodic technical and nontechnical evaluation, based initially upon the standards implemented under this rule and, subsequently, in response to environmental or operational changes affecting the security of electronic protected health information, that establishes the extent to which a covered entity's or business associate's security policies and procedures meet the requirements of this subpart.' Going from office LAN to public internet IS an environmental/operational change that triggers a fresh evaluation. Automated testing is explicitly a valid *input* but cannot satisfy the standard alone: it is silent on the nontechnical half.
standards.threshold: 164.308(a)(8) — Required; frequency is 'periodic' plus event-triggered, undefined
standards.source_name: GPO govinfo, CFR Title 45 Vol 2, § 164.308 Administrative safeguards
standards.notes: Extracted verbatim from the CFR XML. The 'in response to environmental or operational changes' clause is the load-bearing one for this project right now.

standards.claim: NIST SP 800-66r2 §5.1.8 (Evaluation) explicitly contemplates automated tooling as an evaluation collection method: 'Collection methods may include the use of interviews, surveys, and the outputs of automated tools, such as access control auditing tools, system logs, and the results of penetration testing,' and asks 'Has the organization explored the use of automated tools to support the evaluation process?' It also directs entities to 'Implement tools that can provide reports on the level of compliance' and to 'Document Results', and points to NIST SP 800-53A Rev. 5 assessment procedures. So: CI output is admissible evidence for part of 164.308(a)(8); a green pipeline is not the evaluation.
standards.threshold: NIST SP 800-66r2, February 2024, §5.1.8, Table 15
standards.source_name: NIST SP 800-66r2, Implementing the HIPAA Security Rule: A Cybersecurity Resource Guide
standards.notes: Downloaded the 122-page PDF and extracted the full text; quotes are verbatim from the extraction. SP 800-66r2 also says penetration testing should be conducted 'if reasonable and appropriate' and that senior-management written approval should be obtained first — i.e. it is discretionary under the current rule.

standards.claim: NIST SP 800-66r2 contains NO guidance on secure software development. A full-text search of the extracted publication returns zero occurrences of 'SSDF', 'SP 800-218', 'Secure Software Development', 'secure coding', 'SDLC', 'system development life cycle', 'code review' and 'web application'. It is an operations-and-governance guide, not an application-security guide. IMPLICATION: you cannot cite the authoritative NIST HIPAA implementation guide as a reason to run SAST or to gate on code quality; those must be justified as risk-management measures under 164.308(a)(1)(ii)(B).
standards.threshold: 0 occurrences of each of: 800-218, SSDF, secure coding, SDLC, code review, web application
standards.source_name: NIST SP 800-66r2 (Feb 2024) — full-text extraction
standards.notes: Verified by programmatic term counting over a pypdf text extraction of all 122 pages. Caveat: PDF text extraction can miss text rendered in figures; I saw no figures in the relevant sections. 'static' appears twice, both unrelated to static analysis. This is a negative finding, so I flag the method rather than claim certainty about images.

standards.claim: 45 CFR 164.316(b)(2)(i) requires SIX YEARS of documentation retention (Required): 'Retain the documentation required by paragraph (b)(1) of this section for 6 years from the date of its creation or the date when it last was in effect, whichever is later,' where (b)(1)(ii) covers 'a written (which may be electronic) record of the action, activity, or assessment' for anything the subpart requires to be documented. FOR CI: any scan report, test result or evaluation output you intend to cite as compliance evidence must survive six years — 2,190 days.
standards.threshold: 6 years (2,190 days) from creation or last-in-effect, whichever is later
standards.source_name: GPO govinfo, CFR Title 45 Vol 2, § 164.316 Policies and procedures and documentation requirements
standards.notes: Verbatim from CFR XML. 164.316(b)(2)(iii) additionally requires documentation to be reviewed and updated in response to environmental or operational changes — the same trigger as the 164.308(a)(8) evaluation.

standards.claim: GitHub Actions CANNOT hold six years of compliance evidence. GitHub's documentation states 'By default, the artifacts and log files generated by workflows are retained for 90 days before they are automatically deleted,' and the configurable maximum is 90 days for public repositories and 400 days for private repositories. 400 days is roughly 18% of the 2,190 days that 45 CFR 164.316(b)(2)(i) requires. FOR CI: evidence you plan to rely on must be exported out of Actions into durable storage at generation time.
standards.threshold: Default 90 days; maximum 400 days (private/internal), 90 days (public) — vs. 2,190 days required
standards.source_name: GitHub Docs — Configuring the retention period for GitHub Actions artifacts and logs in your organization
standards.notes: Both GitHub pages fetched; the second confirms the 90-day default independently. GitHub also warns custom retention applies only to new artifacts going forward, not retroactively. Where you put the exported evidence is a hosting question and out of scope here.

standards.claim: THE NPRM IS NOT FINAL AND HAS NOT BEEN WITHDRAWN. RIN 0945-AA22 ('HIPAA Security Rule to Strengthen the Cybersecurity of Electronic Protected Health Information') has exactly ONE Federal Register document: the NPRM at 90 FR 898, published January 6, 2025, comments closed March 7, 2025. The most recent Unified Agenda entry (Publication ID 2026, reginfo pubId 202510) lists Agenda Stage of Rulemaking = 'Long-Term Actions', Priority = 'Economically Significant', Major = Yes, and a Timetable of NPRM 01/06/2025 → Final Action 07/00/2027. HHS's own NPRM landing page still says 'While the Department is undertaking this rulemaking, the current Security Rule remains in effect' and is marked 'Content last reviewed December 27, 2024'.
standards.threshold: 90 FR 898 (Jan 6, 2025); comments closed 2025-03-07; Unified Agenda projected Final Action 07/00/2027; stage = Long-Term Actions
standards.source_name: OMB/OIRA Unified Agenda of Regulatory and Deregulatory Actions, RIN 0945-AA22 (Publication ID 2026)
standards.notes: Three independent confirmations: (1) the Federal Register API returns count=1 for RIN 0945-AA22 — no final rule, no withdrawal, no comment-period extension; (2) the Unified Agenda entry above; (3) HHS's own page at hhs.gov/hipaa/for-professionals/security/hipaa-security-rule-nprm/. 'Long-Term Actions' in OIRA parlance means the agency does not expect action within the next 12 months. A projected date in the Unified Agenda is planning data, not a commitment.

standards.claim: IF FINALISED AS PROPOSED, automated vulnerability scanning becomes mandatory at a defined cadence. Proposed 45 CFR 164.312(h)(2)(i)(A): 'Conduct automated vulnerability scans to identify technical vulnerabilities in the covered entity's or business associate's relevant electronic information systems in accordance with the covered entity's or business associate's risk analysis required by § 164.308(a)(2) or at least once every six months, whichever is more frequent.' Proposed (h)(2)(i)(B) additionally requires reviewing and testing the effectiveness of the scanning tooling itself at least once every 12 months. Proposed (h)(2)(ii) requires monitoring authoritative sources (HHS names the NIST National Vulnerability Database and CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities Catalog) for known vulnerabilities on an ongoing basis, with no minimum interval specified.
standards.threshold: Automated vulnerability scans: at least once every 6 months, or more often if risk analysis says so. Scanner effectiveness review: at least every 12 months.
standards.source_name: HIPAA Security Rule To Strengthen the Cybersecurity of ePHI, 90 FR 898 (Jan 6, 2025) — proposed regulatory text
standards.notes: Quoted verbatim from the Federal Register full-text XML (1.46 MB) which I downloaded and searched directly, not from a summary. HHS explicitly requested comment on 'whether once every six months is the appropriate frequency'.

standards.claim: IF FINALISED AS PROPOSED, penetration testing becomes mandatory annually with NO small-entity exemption. Proposed 45 CFR 164.312(h)(2)(iii): 'Perform penetration testing of the covered entity's or business associate's relevant electronic information systems by a qualified person… (B) Penetration testing must be performed at least once every 12 months or in accordance with the covered entity's or business associate's risk analysis required by § 164.308(a)(2), whichever is more frequent.' A 'qualified person' is defined as one 'with appropriate knowledge of and experience with generally accepted cybersecurity principles and methods'. HHS explicitly CONSIDERED and REJECTED exempting small and rural providers, stating that 'setting different requirements for cybersecurity for small and rural health care providers would lead such health care providers to believe that they can limit their investment in cybersecurity.'
standards.threshold: Penetration testing: at least once every 12 months, by a qualified person. No small/rural carve-out.
standards.source_name: 90 FR 898, proposed 45 CFR 164.312(h)(2)(iii) and the Regulatory Impact Analysis
standards.notes: HHS costed this at an average of 3 hours per regulated entity (low 2, high 10) at $119.94/hr for an information security analyst — roughly $360 per entity per year. That figure is not credible for an external test of an internet-facing multi-tenant portal, and HHS itself solicited comment on it ('For regulated entities that have conducted penetration tests, the amount of time and costs of such tests'). See disagreements.

standards.claim: IF FINALISED AS PROPOSED, the addressable/required distinction disappears and encryption + MFA become mandatory. The NPRM proposes to 'remove the distinction between required and addressable implementation specifications and make all implementation specifications required, with specific, limited exceptions.' Proposed 164.312(b)(2): 'Encrypt all electronic protected health information at rest and in transit' except under enumerated exceptions. Proposed 164.312(f)(2)(ii)(A): 'Deploy multi-factor authentication to all technology assets… to verify that a person seeking access to the relevant electronic information system(s) is the user that the person claims to be,' and (B) MFA for any privilege-changing action. Also proposed: 164.308(a)(14) Compliance audit — 'Perform and document an audit at least once every 12 months of… compliance with each standard and implementation specification in this subpart.'
standards.threshold: Encryption of all ePHI at rest and in transit; MFA on all technology assets and all privilege changes; annual compliance audit of every standard and implementation specification
standards.notes: MFA would be defined at proposed 164.304 as verification of at least two of three categories (know / have / are). Note HHS deliberately does NOT name a TLS version or FIPS level — it uses 'prevailing cryptographic standards', explaining that 'a regulated entity using an encryption algorithm that is known to be insecure would not be in compliance', which makes crypto config a recurring review obligation rather than a one-time setting.

standards.claim: IF FINALISED AS PROPOSED, patch timeliness gets hard deadlines that a dependency-scanning SLA can be built against: critical risks within 15 calendar days of identifying the need (or of a patch becoming available, if none exists at identification), and high risks within 30 calendar days on the same terms. Everything else is governed by the entity's own written patch management policy under proposed 164.308(a)(4).
standards.threshold: Critical: 15 calendar days. High: 30 calendar days. Others: per written policy.
standards.source_name: 90 FR 898 preamble discussion of proposed 45 CFR 164.308(a)(5)(ii)(D) / 164.312(h)(2)(iv)
standards.notes: Quoted verbatim from the NPRM full text. These are preamble-stated interpretations of 'reasonable and appropriate period of time' rather than numerals in the proposed regulatory text itself, which matters if the final rule moves them. Even unfinalised, 15/30 days is a defensible, cheap SLA to adopt now for NuGet/Yarn advisories.

standards.claim: NEITHER the current Security Rule NOR the 2025 NPRM regulates how you write code. A full-text search of the 90 FR 898 NPRM (949,067 characters extracted) returns ZERO occurrences of: 'secure coding', 'software development', 'SDLC', 'OWASP', 'application security', 'code review', 'input validation', 'SQL injection', 'static analysis', 'SBOM', 'software bill of materials', 'SSDF' and '800-218'. 'Web application' appears once, and only inside a description of CISA's free Cyber Hygiene Services. HIPAA regulates the properties of the deployed system and the documentation you keep about them — not your development process.
standards.threshold: 0 occurrences of each of 12 application-security terms across the full NPRM text
standards.source_name: Federal Register full-text XML for 90 FR 898 (document 2024-30983) — programmatic term count
standards.notes: Counts run over the stripped-tag text of the official FR XML. Corroborated by the identical negative result in NIST SP 800-66r2. By contrast 'asset inventory' appears 24 times and 'Cybersecurity Framework' 25 times — HHS's attention is on inventory, configuration and operations, not on the build.

standards.claim: 42 U.S.C. 17941 (HITECH § 13412, added by Pub. L. 116-321, Jan. 5, 2021) requires the Secretary to consider whether an entity 'had, for not less than the previous 12 months, recognized security practices in place' when setting fines, deciding whether to terminate an audit early, and agreeing remedies. 'Recognized security practices' means practices developed under 15 U.S.C. 272(c)(15) (the NIST Cybersecurity Framework), the approaches promulgated under section 405(d) of the Cybersecurity Act of 2015 (HHS 405(d) / HICP), and other programs developed under other statutory authorities. Crucially: § 17941(b)(3) says nothing subjects an entity to liability for electing NOT to engage in them, and (b)(4) says they do not substitute for Security Rule compliance.
standards.threshold: 'not less than the previous 12 months' of demonstrated recognized security practices
standards.source_name: 42 U.S.C. § 17941, Recognition of security practices (Office of the Law Revision Counsel, text in effect August 27, 2026)
standards.notes: Fetched the OLRC text directly (it states 'Text contains those laws in effect on August 27, 2026'). Cross-referenced against the NPRM preamble, which cites 'Public Law 116-321, 134 Stat. 5072, adding sec. 13412 (Jan. 5, 2021) (codified at 42 U.S.C. 17941)'. This is the strongest cost/benefit argument available to a two-person team: the 12-month clock is the cheap part, and it only starts when you begin.

standards.claim: IF FINALISED AS PROPOSED, the CI/CD pipeline itself is arguably in regulatory scope. Proposed 45 CFR 164.304 would define 'relevant electronic information system' as one 'that creates, receives, maintains, or transmits electronic protected health information OR THAT OTHERWISE AFFECTS the confidentiality, integrity, or availability of electronic protected health information,' and 'technology asset' as 'the components of an electronic information system, including but not limited to hardware, software, electronic media, information, and data.' A pipeline that can deploy code into the ePHI-handling application plainly affects its integrity and availability. That would pull the CI system into the MFA, audit-logging, vulnerability-scanning and asset-inventory requirements.
standards.threshold: Proposed 164.304 definitions of 'relevant electronic information system' and 'technology asset'
standards.source_name: 90 FR 898, proposed 45 CFR 164.304 definitions
standards.notes: The definitional text is verbatim and verified; the INFERENCE that CI/CD falls inside it is mine, not HHS's — HHS nowhere discusses build systems. I mark this partial because no source states the conclusion. It is a foreseeable-risk flag, not a citable requirement. Even so, applying MFA and least privilege to the GitHub org costs almost nothing and forecloses the question.

recommended_checks.what_it_does: An integration-test suite that boots the API against at least two seeded tenant databases and asserts that a token minted for tenant A can never read, write, list or enumerate any entity, blob or audit row belonging to tenant B — including via ID-guessing, ABP's IRepository/IQueryable surfaces, the Host header, and any endpoint that bypasses the data filter. Should include at least one test that deliberately sets the Host header to another tenant mid-session and asserts rejection.
recommended_checks.tool: xUnit + ABP test host + Testcontainers (or a fixed pair of seeded SQL Server databases); no third-party licence required
recommended_checks.effort_hours: 16-24 to build the harness and 8-12 tests; ~1-2h/month to extend as endpoints are added
recommended_checks.rationale_for_two_person_team: This is the one check that maps to the stated highest-consequence failure mode AND to a Required obligation: 45 CFR 164.312(a)(1) access control plus 164.308(a)(4) information access management. Tenancy resolving from the Host header alone means a single missed data-filter attribute is a multi-tenant PHI breach across 11 offices. It is also the check most likely to catch a real defect per hour spent, and unlike SAST it produces zero false positives, so a two-person team will not learn to bypass it. Note it does not depend on any hosting decision — it runs entirely in CI.
recommended_checks.tool_maintained_evidence: First-party: xUnit and the ABP test host ship with the framework the team already runs (ABP Commercial 10.0.2). No external tool to go stale.

recommended_checks.what_it_does: Tests asserting that every endpoint touching ePHI emits an audit record carrying a non-null, non-system user identity, a tenant identifier, the action, and a timestamp — and specifically that READ paths are covered, not just writes. Plus an architecture test that fails the build if a new controller or application-service method handling a PHI-bearing entity is added without audit coverage.
recommended_checks.tool: xUnit + ABP Audit Logging + NetArchTest or a reflection-based convention test
recommended_checks.effort_hours: 10-16 initial; near-zero ongoing once the convention test exists
recommended_checks.rationale_for_two_person_team: 45 CFR 164.312(b) audit controls is a Required standard with no implementation specifications, and 164.312(a)(2)(i) unique user identification is Required — meaning attributability is not negotiable. ABP/EF Core change tracking gives you writes almost free; reads are the gap and reads are what OCR asks about. The convention test is the part that makes this sustainable: it means the two developers do not have to remember, the build remembers for them.
recommended_checks.tool_maintained_evidence: ABP Audit Logging is a first-party module of ABP Commercial 10.0.2, already a dependency. NetArchTest is optional and replaceable with ~40 lines of reflection if it goes stale.

recommended_checks.what_it_does: Fails the build on high and critical known vulnerabilities in .NET and JS dependencies, including transitive ones, checked against the GitHub Advisory Database at restore time. On .NET 10 this is on by default with NuGetAuditMode defaulting to 'all' (transitive included); set <WarningsAsErrors>$(WarningsAsErrors);NU1903;NU1904</WarningsAsErrors> to gate on high/critical while leaving low/moderate as warnings. Pair with 'yarn npm audit' for the Angular side.
recommended_checks.tool: NuGet Audit (built into .NET 10 SDK / NuGet 7.0) + 'dotnet list package --vulnerable --include-transitive' + Yarn 4 'yarn npm audit'
recommended_checks.effort_hours: 3-5 total, most of it deciding the suppression policy
recommended_checks.rationale_for_two_person_team: Zero new tooling, zero licence, zero maintenance — it is already in the SDK they run. It is the cheapest possible discharge of proposed 164.312(h)(2)(ii) ('monitor authoritative sources for known vulnerabilities on an ongoing basis'), and today it is defensible risk management under Required 164.308(a)(1)(ii)(B). Adopt the NPRM's 15-day-critical / 30-day-high remediation SLA now as written policy; it costs nothing and it is the number HHS has already put in writing. Microsoft documents a pattern for a dedicated audit pipeline so that new advisories do not block unrelated bug fixes — use it, because a two-person team that gets blocked by a 3am advisory will disable the gate.
recommended_checks.tool_maintained_evidence: First-party Microsoft/NuGet feature. The Microsoft Learn doc 'Auditing package dependencies for security vulnerabilities' carries ms.date 2025-10-01 and updated_at 2026-07-07, and documents NuGet 7.0 / .NET 10 SDK behaviour including the new 'dotnet package update --vulnerable' command. https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/nuget/concepts/auditing-packages

recommended_checks.what_it_does: A scheduled (not per-PR) OWASP ZAP baseline scan against a deployed staging instance seeded with synthetic data, covering the newly-anonymous surfaces: registration, login, password reset and document upload. Publishes an HTML/JSON report as a retained artifact. Run it monthly, which beats the proposed six-month floor with margin and gives you twelve dated reports a year.
recommended_checks.tool: OWASP ZAP via the zaproxy/action-baseline GitHub Action
recommended_checks.effort_hours: 8-16 to stand up (most of it getting a seeded staging target and tuning out the initial noise); ~1h/month to triage
recommended_checks.rationale_for_two_person_team: This is the single check that directly produces the artifact proposed 164.312(h)(2)(i)(A) will demand ('automated vulnerability scans… at least once every six months'), and it is admissible today as an input to the Required 164.308(a)(8) evaluation — NIST SP 800-66r2 names 'the outputs of automated tools' as a valid collection method. Deliberately scheduled and NOT a merge gate: a DAST tool wired into every PR is exactly the kind of slow, noisy, occasionally-wrong check that a two-person team learns to bypass. Monthly and advisory keeps it alive. Whether staging is reachable from CI is a hosting question and out of scope here.
recommended_checks.tool_maintained_evidence: ZAP core is very actively maintained: weekly releases, latest w2026-08-26 published 2026-08-26 (https://github.com/zaproxy/zaproxy/releases). The wrapper Action zaproxy/action-baseline last released v0.15.0 on 2025-10-24 — about 10 months old, inside the 12-month window but slowing; if it stalls, the same scan runs from the ZAP Docker image in three lines of YAML.

recommended_checks.what_it_does: Automated assertions against the running app that HTTPS is enforced, HSTS is present, auth cookies carry Secure/HttpOnly/SameSite, session inactivity timeout is enforced server-side, and that no ePHI, tenant identifier or token ever appears in a URL query string or in an application log line. The log-leakage half is a unit/integration test over the logging pipeline; the header half is an assertion in the same job as the DAST scan.
recommended_checks.tool: xUnit integration tests + ZAP baseline rules (both already in the stack above)
recommended_checks.rationale_for_two_person_team: Going from an office LAN to the public internet is precisely the risk-analysis change that converts 164.312(e)(2)(ii) encryption-in-transit from 'addressable' to 'you must, and here is why' — OCR's own guidance says where risk analysis shows significant risk 'a covered entity must encrypt those transmissions'. Automatic logoff (164.312(a)(2)(iii)) is addressable, but an internet-facing PHI portal that never times out is a hard sentence to write in a risk-analysis document. The log-leakage test is disproportionately valuable: ePHI in an application log is a disclosure that no amount of database encryption saves you from, and it is a mistake two developers under feature pressure will make.
recommended_checks.tool_maintained_evidence: No new tooling beyond what checks 1 and 4 already establish.

recommended_checks.what_it_does: A scheduled job that collects the month's compliance-relevant CI output — DAST report, dependency-audit output and resolved SBOM, tenant-isolation and audit-trail test results, the commit SHA and timestamp — into a single dated, hashed bundle and writes it somewhere that survives six years. Also emits a short index file listing what was produced, so the annual evaluation has a table of contents.
recommended_checks.tool: A GitHub Actions workflow + whatever durable store the team already has; SBOM generated by 'dotnet sbom'/CycloneDX or Trivy
recommended_checks.effort_hours: 5-8, plus ~15 min/month to confirm it ran
recommended_checks.rationale_for_two_person_team: 45 CFR 164.316(b)(2)(i) requires six years — 2,190 days — of retention for records of any action, activity or assessment the Security Rule requires to be documented. GitHub Actions caps private-repo artifact retention at 400 days and defaults to 90. Every scan you run and then let expire is money spent producing evidence you will not have when OCR asks. This is the highest evidence-value-per-hour item on the list and the one most likely to be missed, because nothing fails when it is absent — you simply discover in year three that year one is gone. Where the bundle lands is a hosting decision and out of scope; that it leaves Actions is not.
recommended_checks.tool_maintained_evidence: Trivy is very actively maintained: v0.74.0 released 2026-08-14, v0.73.0 on 2026-08-03 (https://github.com/aquasecurity/trivy/releases). OWASP Dependency-Check is also current if preferred — v13.0.0 published 2026-08-03 per its releases Atom feed — though it is redundant with NuGet Audit here and adds NVD API-key friction.

recommended_checks.what_it_does: Not a scanner: a CI check that fails if a listed addressable implementation specification (automatic logoff, encryption at rest, ePHI integrity authentication, transmission integrity controls, transmission encryption) has no corresponding decision record in /docs/security/ carrying a date, the risk-analysis reference, the decision, and — where the answer is 'not implementing' — the equivalent alternative measure. A simple file-presence-and-schema check over Markdown front-matter.
recommended_checks.tool: A ~60-line script in the existing CI (Python or a dotnet tool), plus Markdown ADRs in the repo
recommended_checks.effort_hours: 4-6 to build; 1-3h per decision record to actually write, spread over months
recommended_checks.rationale_for_two_person_team: 45 CFR 164.306(d)(3)(ii)(B) does not let you silently skip an addressable specification — you must document why it is not reasonable and appropriate AND implement an equivalent alternative where that is reasonable. This is the obligation with the highest ratio of legal exposure to engineering effort, and it is invisible to every scanner on the market. Keeping the records in the repo means they are versioned, dated, diffable and survive staff turnover — which is what 164.316(b)(2)(iii)'s 'review and update in response to environmental or operational changes' actually needs. Advisory rather than a gate, because the failure mode is a stale document, not a broken build, and blocking merges on prose is how a two-person team starts bypassing CI.
recommended_checks.tool_maintained_evidence: No third-party dependency; the check is a shell/Python script the team owns. Deliberately chosen over a GRC SaaS product for exactly that reason.

not_worth_it_here: An external third-party penetration test before launch. A larger company books one annually as a matter of course, and the NPRM would require one every 12 months by a 'qualified person'. But the NPRM is in 'Long-Term Actions' with a July 2027 projected final date, and there is no current regulatory requirement — NIST SP 800-66r2 says only to conduct one 'if reasonable and appropriate' and to get written senior-management approval first. HHS costed it at 3 hours; real market cost for an internet-facing multi-tenant portal is one to two orders of magnitude higher. Do the ZAP baseline scan now, budget for one external test in the first year AFTER launch (once there is real PHI and once the NPRM's shape is clearer), and write down that decision as your risk-analysis record.

HITRUST CSF certification, SOC 2 Type II, or any third-party attestation. None of these is required by HIPAA — not by the current rule, not by the NPRM. They are commercial trust signals demanded by enterprise customers. Eleven offices in one workers' comp network are not going to ask, and a two-person team cannot absorb the evidence-collection burden. If a customer does ask later, 42 U.S.C. 17941 recognized security practices (NIST CSF or HHS 405(d) HICP) is the cheaper answer and has actual statutory weight with the regulator that HITRUST does not.

A GRC or continuous-compliance platform (Vanta/Drata class). These automate evidence collection against control frameworks, which sounds exactly like what 164.316 demands. But they charge per-integration and are calibrated for organisations with dozens of systems and a compliance owner. Here the entire evidence set is: a monthly CI bundle, a handful of Markdown decision records, one risk analysis, and one log-review log. That fits in the repository. Buying a platform would add a vendor, a recurring cost, and a second place where the truth lives — and it would still not write the decision records for you.

Real-time security monitoring and alerting on audit logs. Proposed 164.312(d)(2)(i) would require deploying controls that 'monitor in real-time all activity' and alert workforce members. That is not required today, and 164.308(a)(1)(ii)(D) asks only for 'regularly review'. A two-person team with no on-call rotation cannot answer a 3am alert, and an alerting system nobody answers is worse evidence than no alerting system — it documents that you saw the event and did nothing. Do a documented weekly or monthly review with a retained artifact instead, and revisit if the NPRM finalises.

A NIST SP 800-218 SSDF implementation or a CISA secure-software attestation. SSDF is the right framework for a software producer selling to the US federal government; it is not a HIPAA obligation. Neither the current Security Rule nor the NPRM mentions SSDF, secure coding or the SDLC anywhere, and NIST SP 800-66r2 — the authoritative HIPAA implementation guide — does not either. Adopting SSDF's ~40 practices would consume the entire one-developer-week-per-month budget for a year and would not answer a single question OCR asks.

A full authenticated DAST crawl or an IAST agent, as opposed to the unauthenticated baseline scan. Authenticated scanning of an ABP/Angular SPA requires maintaining a session-replay script that breaks every time the login flow changes, and the findings skew heavily toward false positives on framework-generated markup. The anonymous attack surface — registration, login, password reset, document upload — is where the newly-internet-facing risk actually is, and that is exactly what an unauthenticated baseline scan covers. Revisit after the first year.

A formal annual compliance audit of every standard and implementation specification. Proposed 164.308(a)(14) would require exactly this, and a larger company runs it as a project with an external assessor. It is not required today. What IS required today is the 164.308(a)(8) evaluation, which is narrower and which the LAN-to-internet migration triggers regardless. Do that one properly and honestly, once, and let the compliance audit wait for the final rule.
surprises: The controls everyone assumes HIPAA mandates are the ones it does not. Today, encryption at rest, encryption in transit, automatic logoff, integrity-authentication of ePHI and transmission integrity controls are ALL 'Addressable' under 45 CFR 164.312 — and MFA is not in the rule at all. What is unconditionally Required is narrower and less glamorous: unique user identification, an emergency access procedure, audit controls, authentication, the transmission security standard itself, regular review of information system activity, periodic evaluation, and six-year documentation. Teams over-invest in encryption checkboxes and under-invest in the audit-log review obligation, which is the one that is actually Required and has no product feature.

Writing audit logs does not satisfy HIPAA. 164.312(b) requires mechanisms that 'record AND EXAMINE' activity, and 164.308(a)(1)(ii)(D) separately and unconditionally requires procedures to 'regularly review records of information system activity, such as audit logs'. ABP's audit logging module gives you the recording for free and gives you nothing at all for the reviewing. There is no CI check that can discharge this — it needs a recurring calendar event, a query, and a dated artifact saying who looked and what they found. That artifact is what an investigator asks for.

GitHub Actions physically cannot hold your compliance evidence. Artifacts and logs default to 90 days and max out at 400 days for private repositories. 45 CFR 164.316(b)(2)(i) requires six years — 2,190 days. Every DAST report, dependency audit and test result you generate and leave in Actions silently expires at roughly 18% of the required lifetime. Nothing fails when this is wrong; you discover it in year three when the evidence for year one is gone. This is the single most concrete, most checkable, least-anticipated CI consequence of being HIPAA-regulated.

The January 2025 NPRM is neither law nor dead, and the distinction is worth money. Federal Register data shows exactly one document under RIN 0945-AA22 — no final rule, no withdrawal, not even a comment-period extension. The current Unified Agenda places it in 'Long-Term Actions' with a projected Final Action of July 2027, and HHS's own NPRM landing page has not been touched since 27 December 2024. So the six-month scan and annual pen test cadences are planning targets, not present obligations. But adopt the cadence NOW anyway, because 42 U.S.C. 17941 only credits you for 'not less than the previous 12 months' of recognized security practices — the clock is the expensive part and it only starts when you begin.

HIPAA has essentially nothing to say about how you write code. Zero occurrences of 'secure coding', 'SDLC', 'OWASP', 'code review', 'input validation', 'SQL injection', 'static analysis', 'SBOM' or 'SSDF' across the entire 949,000-character NPRM — and zero in NIST SP 800-66r2 as well. It regulates the deployed system's properties and your documentation of them. Practical consequence: you cannot defend a SAST or lint gate to an auditor by saying 'HIPAA requires it', because it does not. Defend it as risk management under Required 164.308(a)(1)(ii)(B), and be honest internally that its justification is engineering quality, not compliance.

'Automated testing satisfies the periodic evaluation' is half true, and the half that is false is the half that gets cited. NIST SP 800-66r2 §5.1.8 explicitly names 'the outputs of automated tools' as a valid collection method and asks whether the organisation has 'explored the use of automated tools to support the evaluation process' — so CI output is admissible evidence. But 164.308(a)(8) requires a TECHNICAL AND NONTECHNICAL evaluation with documented results. A green pipeline is an input to the evaluation, never the evaluation itself, and presenting it as such is how a defensible position becomes an indefensible one.

If the NPRM finalises as written, your CI/CD pipeline is probably in scope. Proposed 164.304 would define a 'relevant electronic information system' as one that 'otherwise affects the confidentiality, integrity, or availability' of ePHI. A pipeline with deploy rights to the PHI-handling application affects all three. HHS never discusses build systems, so this is inference rather than a stated requirement — but MFA and least privilege on the GitHub org cost almost nothing and close the question permanently. Most teams assume CI is categorically outside the regulated boundary.

HHS considered exempting small and rural providers from penetration testing and explicitly refused, on the reasoning that a carve-out 'would lead such health care providers to believe that they can limit their investment in cybersecurity'. There is no small-team relief mechanism in the proposal. The only scaling lever that survives is 164.306(b)(2), which requires HHS to take into account your size, capabilities, technical infrastructure and cost — which is a reason to write those factors explicitly into every decision record you produce, not a reason to skip requirements.

The breach safe harbor is an engineering decision, not a policy one, and it is the largest single consequence-reducer available. Under 164.402, ePHI rendered unusable per HHS's guidance is not 'unsecured PHI', so its compromise is not a reportable breach. The guidance names NIST SP 800-111 for data at rest and SP 800-52 / 800-77 / 800-113 or FIPS 140-2 validated methods in motion, AND requires that decryption keys be stored separately from the encrypted data. That last clause is where implementations fail: encrypting MinIO objects with a key held in the same SQL Server instance forfeits the safe harbor while looking fully compliant on a checklist.

Even the strengthened rule refuses to name a TLS version or cipher suite. The NPRM uses 'prevailing cryptographic standards' deliberately and states that an entity 'using an encryption algorithm that is known to be insecure would not be in compliance'. That converts crypto configuration from a one-time setup task into a standing review obligation tied to your risk analysis. Whatever TLS policy the app ships with needs a calendar reminder attached to it, not just a config file.

The most common OCR finding is not a missing scanner — it is a missing or inadequate risk analysis under Required 164.308(a)(1)(ii)(A). Everything in this document, including every merge gate, is downstream of that one document: proposed 164.312(h)(2)(i)(A) sets scan frequency 'in accordance with the risk analysis… or at least once every six months, whichever is more frequent', so the risk analysis literally sets your CI schedule. A two-person team that builds excellent CI and never writes a risk analysis has optimised the wrong end. HHS's free Security Risk Assessment Tool exists for exactly this size of organisation, though NIST cautions it 'cannot identify technical vulnerabilities' and must be paired with actual scanning.
disagreements: HHS's own cost estimate for penetration testing is contested by HHS. The Regulatory Impact Analysis assumes an average of 3 hours per regulated entity (low 2, high 10) at $119.94/hr for an information security analyst — roughly $360/year. That is far below the market cost of a qualified external test of an internet-facing, multi-tenant, database-per-tenant portal. HHS itself flagged the uncertainty by requesting comment on 'the amount of time and costs of such tests'. Do not plan a budget from the NPRM's figure.

Is MFA required? The letter and the practice diverge. 45 CFR 164.312(d) names no method, and OCR's June 2023 newsletter frames MFA as something entities 'should consider… where appropriate' — a recommendation. But OCR's Q1 2022 newsletter treats 'weak password rules and single factor authentication' as contributing causes of breaches under the same section, and the NPRM would make MFA mandatory on all technology assets. So the rule says optional, the regulator's published expectation says do it, and the proposal says you will have to. For an internet-facing portal with four self-registering external roles, treat MFA as effectively expected and document the decision either way.

'Addressable' means different things to industry and to the regulator. Industry overwhelmingly reads it as optional. HHS states in the NPRM that this is a misreading — that it 'remains concerned that regulated entities believe that flexibility overrides the need for them to protect all ePHI' and that OCR's enforcement experience shows 'addressable' is 'misunderstood to be optional' — and proposes deleting the concept for that reason. The safe reading is HHS's: addressable means implement it or produce a written justification plus an equivalent alternative.

Whether the NPRM will be finalised at all is genuinely open. The Unified Agenda's 'Long-Term Actions' classification and July 2027 projected date are OIRA/HHS planning data, not commitments, and agenda dates slip routinely. Meanwhile HHS's own NPRM page has not been updated since December 2024 and still says only that 'the current Security Rule remains in effect'. Anyone telling this team the six-month scanning requirement is 'coming in 2026' is over-reading the record; anyone calling the NPRM dead is under-reading it. Plan for the cadence, do not budget for the certainty.

NIST SP 800-66r2 (Feb 2024) and the Jan 2025 NPRM point in different directions on testing. SP 800-66r2 treats penetration testing as discretionary — do it 'if reasonable and appropriate', with written senior-management approval — while the NPRM would make it an annual mandate with no small-entity exemption. Both are current documents from the federal government about the same rule. The reconciliation is that SP 800-66r2 describes the rule as it exists and the NPRM describes the rule HHS wants; but a team reading only one of them will reach the wrong conclusion about what is expected.

material_errors: Claim 7 overstates the HHS breach-notification guidance: separate storage of decryption keys is stated as a 'should' (best practice), not a requirement. The safe harbor turns on the encryption meeting the named NIST processes AND the confidential process/key not having been breached — not on where the key is stored. Also note the guidance still names FIPS 140-2, which is stale for a 2026 standard: CMVP stopped accepting FIPS 140-2 submissions in 2021 and 140-2 certificates move to the historical list on 21 September 2026, so a 2026 CI standard should target FIPS 140-3 validation while citing the unrevised HHS text.

Claim 16 states the proposed MFA requirement flatly ('MFA on all technology assets and all privilege changes') while omitting proposed 45 CFR 164.312(f)(2)(iii), which is an explicit 'Exceptions' paragraph — including where 'The technology asset in use does not support multi-factor authentication, and the covered entity or business associate establishes and implements a written plan to migrate electronic protected health information to a technology asset that supports multi-factor authentication.' The claim correctly caveats encryption ('except under enumerated exceptions' at (b)(3)) but not MFA, which materially changes the planning posture for legacy assets.

questions.question: Does ABP Commercial 10.0.2 support Angular 20.3.27, such that the dependabot.yml blocker ("until ABP Commercial supports Angular 20.3+") is stale and the closed Dependabot PRs #415/#416/#417 (20.3.19 -> 20.3.27) can be re-opened and merged?
questions.detail: The blocker is stale and, as written, self-refuting — but not for the reason the comment implies. (a) ABP 10.0.x targets the Angular 20 MAJOR and specifically the 20.0.x line: ABP's own 10.0 quick-start docs state "In this version ABP uses Angular 20.0.x version", ABP's 10.0.2 Angular app template pins every @angular/* package at ~20.0.0, and the published @abp/ng.core 10.0.2 bundle carries Angular partial-compilation markers of version "20.0.7" with linker minVersion 12.0.0/14.0.0/17.0.0. Critically, this holds for ABP COMMERCIAL too, not just open-source: @volo/abp.ng.account 10.0.2 is mirrored on public npm and is likewise compiled at "20.0.7" with no Angular constraint. (c) is the decisive finding: @abp/ng.core 10.0.2 declares NO peerDependencies field at all — verified twice, in the registry manifest and by extracting package/package.json from the published tarball — and the same is true of ng.theme.shared, ng.identity, ng.account, ng.setting-management, ng.permission-management, ng.tenant-management and @volo/abp.ng.account. ABP does express peer ranges when it wants to (@abp/ng.theme.lepton-x 5.0.2 declares peers on @abp/ng.core ~10.0.2), so the absence of an @angular peer is a deliberate convention, not an oversight; consequently no semver peer machinery in Yarn 4 or npm can flag a 20.3.x bump. questions.question: Is SQLite-only backend testing defensible for this app, or must a SQL Server test path exist? (2,261 EF Core tests on Data Source=:memory:, production SQL Server, database-per-tenant, 90 host + 15 tenant migrations, a filtered-unique-index migration now causing a SQLite UNIQUE constraint failure.)
questions.detail: SQLite-only is not defensible here, but the fix is a narrow SQL Server path, not a rewrite of 2,261 tests. Microsoft's own position is explicit and unusually strong: "we recommend either writing your tests against your real database, or if using a test double is an absolute necessity, taking onboard the cost of a repository pattern," and "testing against SQLite does not guarantee the same results as against SQL Server." The decisive finding is not a general principle but a structural one specific to this codebase: ABP's own documentation shows the `*.EntityFrameworkCore.Tests` module builds the SQLite schema with `context.GetService<IRelationalDatabaseCreator>().CreateTables()`, which generates the schema from the EF Core model, not from migrations — so all 105 migrations that actually create your production databases have zero automated coverage, and the schema under test is a SQLite-flavoured artifact that no environment ever runs. That is almost certainly the direct cause of the reported flake: if `Fix_UniqueIndexesExcludeSoftDeleted` wrote the filter into the migration file only and not into `OnModelCreating` via `HasFilter`, `CreateTables()` produces a plain unfiltered unique index and a soft-deleted row keeps blocking reuse of `RequestConfirmationNumber`. I verified that SQLite is not the limiting factor for filtered indexes at all: SQLite has supported UNIQUE partial indexes since 3.8.0 (2013), and EF Core's relational generator appends `" WHERE " + createIndexOperation.Filter` with no override in `EFCore.Sqlite.Core`, so a model-level `HasFilter` would have been honoured — which makes the flake a true-positive signal of model/migration drift, not a SQLite defect to be suppressed. Beyond that one bug, four divergences bite this specific app: uniqueness-with-NULL semantics are opposite (SQL Server "cannot create a unique index on a single column if that column contains NULL in more than one row"; SQLite "NULL values are considered distinct from all other values, including other NULLs"), and EF Core only injects the compensating `IS NOT NULL` filter via the SQL-Server-only `SqlServerIndexConvention`; string comparison defaults are opposite (SQL Server US-English default `SQL_Latin1_General_CP1_CI_AS` is case-insensitive, SQLite defaults to `BINARY` and even `NOCASE` folds "only ASCII characters"); `rowversion`/database-generated concurrency tokens are listed by Microsoft as flatly unsupported on SQLite; and `decimal` and `DateTimeOffset` are types "SQLite doesn't natively support" where "comparison and ordering will require evaluation on the client." For a PHI-handling, host-header-tenanted, database-per-tenant system about to face the public internet, the item I would not ship without is the multi-office tenant-isolation harness: it currently proves isolation against a fake, and cross-tenant leakage is your stated highest-consequence failure. Testcontainers for .NET is alive and well-maintained (Testcontainers.MsSql 4.14.0 published 2026-08-14, 32.4M downloads) and is the right choice over a GitHub Actions `services:` block for a two-person team, because the same tests then run unchanged on both developers' laptops — which is what actually keeps a suite green — whereas `services:` works only inside CI, cannot be used inside composite actions, and needs a hand-written mssql health check against `/opt/mssql-tools18/bin/sqlcmd` with `-No`, a well-known time sink.

evidence.finding: Microsoft's headline recommendation is to test against the real production database system; SQLite as a fake is explicitly discouraged as a general strategy.
evidence.quote: Unfortunately, the above limitations tend to eventually become problematic when testing EF Core applications, even if they don't seem to be at the beginning. As a result, we recommend either writing your tests against your real database, or if using a test double is an absolute necessity, taking onboard the cost of a repository pattern as discussed below. ... We recommend that developers have good test coverage of their application running against their actual production database system.

evidence.finding: Microsoft states directly that SQLite results do not guarantee SQL Server results, and names case-sensitivity as a concrete example of tests passing on SQLite that would fail on SQL Server.
evidence.quote: Fundamentally, this means that testing against SQLite does not guarantee the same results as against SQL Server, or any other database. ... The same LINQ query may return different results on different providers. For example, SQL Server does case-insensitive string comparison by default, whereas SQLite is case-sensitive. This can make your tests pass against SQLite where they would fail against SQL Server (or vice versa).

evidence.finding: The EF Core testing overview page states that at least some tests against the real database are usually necessary, and pushes back on the belief that DB tests are slow.
evidence.quote: Writing at least some tests against your database is usually necessary in any case - to make sure your application actually works against your production database - and tests not involving the database can be limited in what they allow you to test. ... SQLite in-memory mode offers better compatibility with production relational databases, since SQLite is itself a full-fledged relational database. However, there will still be some important discrepancies between SQLite and your production database, and some features cannot be tested at all.

evidence.finding: Microsoft argues DB-backed testing is cheaper than teams assume, citing EF Core's own 30,000+ SQL Server tests running in CI on every commit, and names Testcontainers by name.
evidence.quote: Container-based technologies such as Docker can make this very easy, and libraries like Testcontainers can help automate the lifecycle of containerized databases in your tests. ... EF Core itself contains over 30,000 tests against SQL Server alone; these complete reliably in a few minutes, execute in CI on every single commit, and are very frequently executed by developers locally. Some developers turn to an in-memory database (a "fake") in the belief that this is needed for speed - this is almost never actually the case.

evidence.finding: DECISIVE: ABP's own docs show the startup template's EntityFrameworkCore.Tests module builds the SQLite test schema with IRelationalDatabaseCreator.CreateTables() from the MODEL, bypassing migrations entirely. This means all 90 host + 15 tenant migrations have zero test coverage, and explains the filtered-index flake as model/migration drift.

SQLite DOES support UNIQUE partial (filtered) indexes, since 3.8.0 (2013-08-26). SQLite is therefore not the blocker for the filtered-index migration — this rules out the obvious explanation for the flake.
evidence.quote: A partial index definition may include the UNIQUE keyword. If it does, then SQLite requires every entry in the index to be unique. This provides a mechanism for enforcing uniqueness across some subset of the rows in a table. ... The expression following the WHERE clause may contain operators, literal values, and names of columns in the table being indexed. The WHERE clause may not contain subqueries, references to other tables, non-deterministic functions, or bound parameters.

evidence.finding: EF Core's shared relational migrations generator emits the index filter as a WHERE clause, and EFCore.Sqlite.Core contains no IndexOptions override (search for 'IndexOptions' in src/EFCore.Sqlite.Core returned 0 results). So a model-level HasFilter WOULD be translated on SQLite — confirming the flake points at drift, not a provider gap.
evidence.quote: if (operation is CreateIndexOperation createIndexOperation && !string.IsNullOrEmpty(createIndexOperation.Filter)) { ... .Append(" WHERE ").Append(createIndexOperation.Filter); }

evidence.finding: EF Core auto-generates 'IS NOT NULL' filters for unique indexes over nullable columns ONLY on SQL Server, via SqlServerIndexConvention. This convention never runs in the SQLite test harness, so nullable-column uniqueness is enforced under different rules in test and production.
evidence.quote: if (index.IsUnique && index.IsClustered() != true && GetNullableColumns(index) is { Count: > 0 } nullableColumns) ... .Append(_sqlGenerationHelper.DelimitIdentifier(nullableColumns[i])).Append(" IS NOT NULL");

evidence.finding: SQL Server and SQLite have OPPOSITE NULL semantics in unique indexes. SQL Server treats multiple NULLs as duplicates; SQLite treats every NULL as distinct. Any uniqueness rule over a nullable column is tested under the wrong semantics today.
evidence.quote: You cannot create a unique index on a single column if that column contains NULL in more than one row. Similarly, you cannot create a unique index on multiple columns if the combination of columns contains NULL in more than one row. These are treated as duplicate values for indexing purposes.

evidence.finding: SQLite's counterpart rule, from sqlite.org — the exact opposite of SQL Server's.
evidence.quote: For each UNIQUE constraint on the table, each row must contain a unique combination of values in the columns identified by the UNIQUE constraint. For the purposes of UNIQUE constraints, NULL values are considered distinct from all other values, including other NULLs.

evidence.finding: Collation divergence, both sides confirmed. SQL Server's default for US-English locale is case-insensitive; SQLite defaults to BINARY and its NOCASE only folds ASCII — so non-ASCII patient/provider names behave differently again.
evidence.quote: Every column of every table has an associated collating function. If no collating function is explicitly defined, then the collating function defaults to BINARY. ... NOCASE - ... the 26 upper case characters of ASCII are folded to their lower case equivalents before the comparison is performed. Note that only ASCII characters are case folded. SQLite does not attempt to do full UTF case folding due to the size of the tables required.

evidence.finding: SQL Server side of the collation divergence: the default installation collation for OS locale English (United States) is SQL_Latin1_General_CP1_CI_AS — the _CI suffix meaning case-insensitive.
evidence.quote: For example, for the OS locale "English (United States)" (code page 1252), the default collation during setup is SQL_Latin1_General_CP1_CI_AS ... Case-sensitive (_CS) Distinguishes between uppercase and lowercase letters. ... If this option isn't selected, the collation is case-insensitive.

evidence.finding: EF Core's SQLite limitations page: schemas, sequences and database-generated concurrency tokens (rowversion) are unsupported; decimal, DateTimeOffset, TimeSpan and ulong are not natively supported and fall back to client evaluation for comparison/ordering.
evidence.quote: A couple of these concepts are not supported by the SQLite provider. - Schemas - Sequences - Database-generated concurrency tokens ... SQLite doesn't natively support the following data types. EF Core can read and write values of these types, and querying for equality (where e.Property == value) is also supported. Other operations, however, like comparison and ordering will require evaluation on the client. - DateTimeOffset - decimal - TimeSpan - ulong

evidence.finding: rowversion/[Timestamp] concurrency tokens are a SQL-Server-only feature that some databases, SQLite named explicitly, cannot do at all. Any optimistic-concurrency test on SQLite is testing a different mechanism than production.
evidence.quote: The rowversion type shown above is a SQL Server-specific feature; the details on setting up an automatically-updating concurrency token differ across databases, and some databases don't support these at all (e.g. SQLite).

evidence.finding: SQLite has no date/time storage class at all and DECIMAL gets NUMERIC affinity with silent int coercion — relevant to datetime2 precision assertions and any monetary/decimal fields.
evidence.quote: SQLite does not have a storage class set aside for storing dates and/or times. Instead, the built-in Date And Time Functions of SQLite are capable of storing dates and times as TEXT, REAL, or INTEGER values ... If a floating point value that can be represented exactly as an integer is inserted into a column with NUMERIC affinity, the value is converted into an integer.

evidence.finding: SQL Server datetime2 precision that SQLite cannot model: default 7 fractional digits, 100 ns accuracy.
evidence.quote: Precision, scale | 0 to 7 digits, with an accuracy of 100 nanoseconds (100 ns). The default precision is 7 digits. ... Accuracy | 100 nanoseconds

evidence.finding: Testcontainers for .NET is actively maintained: Testcontainers.MsSql 4.14.0 published 2026-08-14 (two weeks before this research), with a steady monthly-to-six-weekly release cadence and 32.4M total downloads.
The Testcontainers MsSql module's default image, useful for pinning.
evidence.quote: Default Docker image tag: "mcr.microsoft.com/mssql/server:2022-CU14-ubuntu-22.04"

evidence.finding: The GitHub Actions `services:` alternative has two constraints that matter for a small team: it cannot be used inside composite actions, and jobs running directly on the runner must reach it via localhost with explicit port mapping.
evidence.quote: you cannot create and use service containers inside a composite action ... Jobs on runner machines: You must use localhost:<port> or 127.0.0.1:<port> to access services, requiring explicit port mapping.

evidence.finding: Resource headroom check: a private-repo GitHub-hosted Ubuntu runner has 2 CPUs, 8 GB RAM, 14 GB SSD, comfortably above SQL Server's container minimums of 2 GB RAM and 2 GB disk. Developer edition is free and is what the container runs by default.
evidence.quote: At least 2 GB of disk space. At least 2 GB of RAM. ... By default, this quickstart creates a container with the Developer edition of SQL Server.

evidence.finding: GitHub-hosted runner specs (private repos), confirming the SQL Server container fits.
evidence.quote: Private repository runners provide: 2 CPUs, 8 GB RAM, 14 GB SSD storage (x64 architecture).

evidence.finding: A near-free CI gate exists that would have caught the filtered-index drift with no database at all: dotnet ef migrations has-pending-model-changes, added in EF Core 8.0.
evidence.quote: dotnet ef migrations has-pending-model-changes — Note: This command was added in EF Core 8.0. Checks if any changes have been made to the model since the last migration.

evidence.finding: Microsoft's documented isolation techniques for real-DB tests — transaction rollback per test, one DB per test class for parallelism, Respawn for cleanup — i.e. the harness patterns to copy rather than invent.
evidence.quote: One common technique to isolate writing tests is to wrap the test in a transaction, and to have that transaction rolled back at the end of the test. Since nothing is actually committed to the database, other tests don't see any modifications and interference is avoided. ... You may also want to consider using the respawn package, which efficiently clears out a database.

evidence.finding: Respawn is still maintained if cleanup later becomes the bottleneck: 7.0.0 published 2025-11-30, 32.4M total downloads. Secondary caveat: the NuGet page did not itself state SQL Server support in the fetched content, though it is Respawn's primary target.
evidence.quote: The current version is 7.0.0, released on 11/30/2025. ... The package has accumulated 32.4 million total downloads across all versions.

questions.recommended_action:
VERDICT: Keep SQLite as the fast inner loop; add ONE small SQL Server test project. Do NOT port 2,261 tests, and do NOT "fix" the flaky test by relaxing the SQLite assertion — that deletes a true signal.

STEP 0 — free, do it this week (~2 hours, no database)
Add `dotnet ef migrations has-pending-model-changes` as a required CI step for both DbContexts (EF Core 8.0+, verified). This alone catches the class of bug you just hit. Then diagnose the actual flake: check whether `Fix_UniqueIndexesExcludeSoftDeleted` put `HasFilter` in `OnModelCreating` or only in the migration file. SQLite supports UNIQUE partial indexes and EF Core's SQLite provider does emit `WHERE <filter>`, so if the filter is in the model the SQLite schema would have it. It almost certainly is not — because ABP's test module builds the schema with `IRelationalDatabaseCreator.CreateTables()` from the model, never from your 105 migrations. Secondary hypothesis worth 20 minutes: "flakes" rather than "fails" also fits test-order/data accumulation in the single shared `:memory:` database plus a colliding RequestConfirmationNumber generator. Check both.

STEP 1 — the SQL Server path (budget ~3-5 dev-days, fits one month's allocation)
One new xUnit project, Testcontainers.MsSql (4.14.0, published 2026-08-14 — actively maintained), image pinned to the SQL Server version you will actually run in production. Target 30-60 tests, not 2,261. Contents, in priority order:
1. Migration gate: apply all 90 host and all 15 tenant migrations from empty against real SQL Server, assert success. Today nothing tests the artifact that builds production.
2. Tenant isolation harness — MOVE IT, do not copy it. Two real tenant databases, real host-header resolution. Cross-tenant leakage is your highest-consequence failure and it is currently proven only against a fake.
3. Every uniqueness/constraint rule: RequestConfirmationNumber, email/username, and specifically soft-delete + filtered-unique-index interactions. SQL Server and SQLite have opposite NULL-uniqueness semantics and EF Core's `IS NOT NULL` auto-filter is SQL-Server-only.
4. Case-sensitivity-dependent lookups (email, name, confirmation-number search). SQL Server US-English default is CI; SQLite is BINARY.
5. Any `rowversion`/`[Timestamp]` concurrency token (SQLite cannot model these at all) and any `decimal` precision assertion.
Isolation: use Microsoft's documented pattern — transaction-per-test rolled back, one database per test class for the write-heavy classes. Skip Respawn until cleanup is measurably the bottleneck.

TESTCONTAINERS vs GITHUB ACTIONS `services:` — pick Testcontainers.
`services:` is marginally less YAML, but it only works in CI. Testcontainers makes the identical test run on both laptops with zero setup, which is what actually determines whether a two-person team keeps a suite green rather than routing around it. Concretely: `services:` cannot be used inside a composite action, requires explicit port mapping plus a hand-written mssql health check against `/opt/mssql-tools18/bin/sqlcmd` with `-No` (a well-known trap since the tools18 secure-by-default change), and needs a second connection-string code path for local runs. Testcontainers handles readiness, random ports and generated passwords in ~10 lines of C#. Resource fit is fine either way: private-repo Ubuntu runners give 2 CPU / 8 GB / 14 GB SSD against SQL Server's 2 GB RAM / 2 GB disk minimum.

MERGE GATE SHAPE
SQLite suite: every push and every PR. SQL Server suite: required on PRs to main. Given PHI, first public exposure and database-per-tenant, I would not demote it to nightly-only. Cache the image pull. If wall-clock becomes painful, shed test 4-5 to nightly before you shed 1-3.

WHAT A LARGER COMPANY WOULD DO THAT IS NOT WORTH IT HERE
- Running all 2,261 tests against SQL Server. The EF Core team does exactly this with 30,000 tests — they have dozens of engineers. Porting yours is months of work and ~90% of those tests exercise application logic where the provider is irrelevant.
- Adopting the repository pattern, which is Microsoft's own first-choice recommendation for test doubles. It is a rearchitecture of 53k lines and fights ABP's built-in repository/DDD conventions. Explicitly reject this one; the docs even concede it "can incur significant cost to implement and maintain."
- Per-test database provisioning, Respawn-based reset infrastructure, or a version matrix across SQL Server 2019/2022/2025. Pin one version; add the rest only when something forces it.
- Mutation testing and dedicated DB performance benchmarks. Later, if ever.

ONE INFRASTRUCTURE-DEPENDENT LINE (not designed here): confirm the collation your production SQL Server databases are actually created with and pin the same value on the test container via MSSQL_COLLATION — otherwise the new SQL Server tests validate the wrong string semantics.
