evidence.finding: ABP's DE FACTO CI standard, from its own workflow: .NET SDK 10.0.x on ubuntu-22.04, build-all.ps1 + test-all.ps1, NuGet caching, Codecov, 50-minute timeout — plus a SEPARATE codeql-analysis.yml. The transferable lesson is the shape: one build+test job, and security scanning as its own scheduled workflow rather than a PR-blocking step.
evidence.quote: dotnet-version: 10.0.x ... ./build-all.ps1 ... ./test-all.ps1 ... [workflows include] build-and-test.yml, codeql-analysis.yml

evidence.finding: MAINTENANCE CHECK (required by rules of evidence): ABP is actively maintained — stable 10.6.0 on 2026-07-27 and 10.7.0-rc.3 on 2026-08-18, i.e. a monthly minor cadence. The app is pinned to ABP 10.0.2, roughly six minor versions behind on a framework that ships monthly; that upgrade lag is itself a supply-chain finding, though ABP 10.x is the current major line so this is drift, not obsolescence.

Package pruning is ON by default for net10.0+ targets, which reduces false positives from dependency scanners — relevant because it means the audit signal on this repo should already be relatively clean, weakening the case for adding a second scanner such as OWASP Dependency-Check.
evidence.quote: Starting in .NET 10, the NuGet Audit feature can prune framework-provided package references that aren't used by the project. This feature is enabled by default for all frameworks of a project that targets >= .NET 10.0 ... It also can lead to a reduction in false positives from NuGet Audit and other dependency-scanning mechanisms.

questions.recommended_action:
Adopt five first-party controls, in this order. They cost roughly one developer-week total to stand up and near-zero per-PR maintenance, which is the whole point for two SDE 1s.

1. TURN ON THE SECURITY ANALYZERS (highest value, ~1 hour, free). Add to Directory.Build.props: `<AnalysisModeSecurity>All</AnalysisModeSecurity>`. Leave AnalysisLevel at its default `latest` — it is already `latest` and is not the lever. Do NOT use `AnalysisMode=All`, which enables Design/Naming/Documentation and will bury two people. Run it once locally, triage the list, baseline anything you will not fix now via `dotnet_diagnostic.CAxxxx.severity` in .editorconfig with a dated comment, then let it run at warning severity. Promote to error only for the handful you have actually driven to zero (CA2100, CA3001, CA5350/CA5351-class crypto) — a category-wide error gate on day one is exactly the thirty-checks failure mode. Expect a build-time increase from the dataflow rules; if it hurts, scope AnalysisModeSecurity to the HttpApi/Web projects only.

2. GATE ON THE AUDIT YOU ALREADY HAVE (~2 hours). Because the projects target net10.0, restore is already auditing transitive packages at severity `low`. Do not add a new scanner. Use Microsoft's published conditional pattern: define NuGetAuditCodes = NU1900;NU1901;NU1902;NU1903;NU1904;NU1905, set WarningsAsErrors on them only when an `AuditPipeline` property is true, and WarningsNotAsErrors otherwise. Run `dotnet restore -p:AuditPipeline=true` in a nightly/weekly workflow, not on every PR, so a newly published advisory never blocks an unrelated bug fix at 5pm. Consider `NuGetAuditLevel=moderate` if low-severity noise proves unactionable. Add the RestoreProjectsAuditedCount vs RestoreProjectCount assertion in Directory.Solution.targets so a silently-skipped audit fails loudly.

3. MAKE CI RESTORE REPEATABLE (~half a day). First check the workflow before changing anything: `RestoreLockedMode=false` in the props file is the *documented* arrangement if CI passes `--locked-mode`. If it does not, the fix is `dotnet restore --locked-mode` in CI, not flipping the property (flipping it blocks developers from adding packages locally). Commit packages.lock.json for the deployable projects. Pin the SDK in global.json with `"rollForward": "disable"` at the same time, or SDK-implicit PackageReferences will break locked mode on the next runner image update and you will disable the whole thing in frustration.

4. LEAVE THE TEST RUNNER ALONE. Stay on VSTest + xunit v2. ABP itself is still there at v10.7, Microsoft still defaults to it, and Microsoft warns against mixing platforms in one solution. Revisit only when ABP's template moves to xunit v3 — then it is a global.json one-liner plus a package swap. Spend the testing budget on integration tests through ABP's TestBase for tenant-resolution and authorization paths instead, which is where this app's actual risk lives.

5. RUN CODEQL WEEKLY, NOT PER-PR. ABP's own repo separates codeql-analysis.yml from build-and-test.yml; copy that shape. GitHub Actions on a private repo, default C#/TypeScript queries, scheduled — findings land in the Security tab as a queue to work rather than a merge blocker.

WHAT A LARGER COMPANY WOULD DO THAT IS NOT WORTH IT HERE YET, and why: (a) a second dependency scanner such as OWASP Dependency-Check on top of NuGetAudit — NuGetAudit already covers transitive packages by default on net10.0 and pruning cuts its false positives, so the second tool buys duplicate findings and a second triage queue; (b) `AnalysisMode=All` or `latest-all` repo-wide — hundreds of Design/Naming/Documentation diagnostics that two people will suppress wholesale, destroying the signal from the security rules that actually matter; (c) migrating to MTP/xunit v3 now — pure churn against both Microsoft's default and ABP's own choice, with zero effect on defect escape rate; (d) `EnforceCodeStyleInBuild=true` with escalated IDE severities as a merge gate — it is formatting, it fails builds for whitespace, and `dotnet format --verify-no-changes` covers the same ground more cheaply if you want it at all; (e) TreatWarningsAsErrors=true repo-wide — tempting, but it makes any newly published advisory (NU1901-1904) break unrelated PRs at restore time; if you do adopt it, add Microsoft's WarningsNotAsErrors for those four codes and keep the failure in the audit pipeline instead. One infrastructure line, then dropping it per scope: whether GitHub-hosted runners can reach the ABP Commercial authenticated NuGet feed is a hosting/licensing question for the separate infrastructure exercise.

CAVEAT ON THIS REPORT'S SCOPE: I could not inspect the actual application. The session's working directory is /home/user/Aditya-gam, an unrelated personal repo (resumes, README.md, headshot) with no .sln, Directory.Build.props, Directory.Packages.props or global.json. Every claim above about the app's current settings — RestoreLockedMode=false, EnforceCodeStyleInBuild=false, AnalysisLevel=latest, ABP 10.0.2 — is taken from the task brief, not verified against source. Before acting, confirm against the real Directory.Build.props and .github/workflows, especially whether CI already passes --locked-mode (item 3), since that changes the recommendation.
questions.what_i_tried_if_unresolved:
Three things I could not verify, marked unverified rather than guessed:

1. ABP COMMERCIAL CI AUTHENTICATION — unverified, and a genuine gap. ABP's CLI docs describe `login`/`logout` as interactive commands and say nothing about non-interactive CI authentication: no ABP_API_KEY, no access-token flow, no private-feed configuration guidance. I fetched https://abp.io/docs/latest/cli and the docs root https://abp.io/docs/latest and found no CI/CD or package-source page anywhere in the tree. Since this app is on ABP Commercial 10.0.2, the GitHub Actions workflow must authenticate to the commercial feed somehow, and there is no first-party documented pattern I could cite. Ask the team how their current workflow authenticates, and treat any answer as unvalidated against vendor guidance.

2. "ABP SHIPS NO ANALYZERS" — moderate confidence, a negative I could not prove exhaustively. Basis: no analyzer PackageReference in ABP's common.props or Directory.Build.props, and no analyzer page in the docs tree. I did not enumerate every Volo.Abp.* package on nuget.org, so a niche analyzer package could exist. Safe conclusion either way: ABP publishes no *recommended analyzer configuration*, so there is no ABP standard to conflict with.

3. EXIT-CODE BEHAVIOUR OF `dotnet package list --vulnerable` — unverified. The Microsoft reference page documents the options and the `--format json` output but states no non-zero exit code on findings, and I could not confirm one without running it. Do not build a merge gate on `dotnet package list --vulnerable` alone assuming it fails the step; either parse the JSON output explicitly, or use the restore-time NU1901-1904 route in recommendation 2, which has documented failure semantics.

Additional constraint on this session: the WebSearch budget was exhausted (200/200 calls) before I began, so all 20+ sources were reached by direct WebFetch against URLs I constructed from known primary-source domains (learn.microsoft.com, dotnet.microsoft.com, abp.io, xunit.net, raw.githubusercontent.com). Every source_url listed is one I actually opened and read; none are cited from memory. The GitHub MCP tools were unavailable for this research — they are scoped to aditya-gam/aditya-gam only and returned "Access denied" for abpframework/abp — so ABP repo facts came from raw.githubusercontent.com and the releases atom feed instead. No OWASP, NIST, W3C or web.dev sources are cited here because this sub-task was scoped to Microsoft and ABP first-party guidance; the ASVS/WCAG/Core Web Vitals areas are presumably covered by a sibling task.

rule_findings.rule_name: reliability_rating / software_quality_reliability_rating grid
rule_findings.what_it_detects: Not a rule - the metric that produces the letter. Sonar publishes the grid explicitly. Standard Experience: 'A = 0 bug / B = at least one minor bug / C = at least one major bug / D = at least one critical bug / E = at least one blocker bug.' MQR mode (confirmed via the docs' own query endpoint on the same page): A = info, B = at least one LOW impact, C = MEDIUM, D = HIGH, E = BLOCKER. The rating is set by the single worst issue, not by volume.
rule_findings.count_in_repo: 338 bugs total, of which 330 are the two accessibility rules and 8 are unidentified (3 C#, 5 TS)
rule_findings.reasoning: This is the load-bearing finding and it inverts the brief. I pulled the live severity of both accessibility rules from SonarSource's own rule API: Web:InputWithoutLabelCheck is severity MAJOR, impacts [{RELIABILITY: MEDIUM}]; Web:MouseEventWithoutKeyboardEquivalentCheck is severity MINOR, impacts [{RELIABILITY: LOW}]. Against the published grid, a MAJOR/MEDIUM bug caps the rating at C and a MINOR/LOW bug caps it at B. Neither rule can produce a D in either rating mode, at any volume. 253 of them still only makes C. Therefore the D is being driven entirely by one or more of the 8 unidentified bugs (3 csharpsquid, 5 typescript) sitting at CRITICAL / HIGH reliability. Those 8 issues are the only ones the team has not looked at, and they are the only ones that matter to the rating. The 330 accessibility findings are, for rating purposes, decorative. Two caveats stated honestly: (a) the working directory handed to me (/home/user/Aditya-gam) contains a personal profile README and three resume PDFs, not the portal source, so I could not read tenant-bootstrap.ts, icon.component.ts, appsettings.json or any of the flagged files - every judgement below is from the rule definitions plus the stated context, not from the code; (b) I could not open rules.sonarsource.com (this session's egress gateway answers 502 CONNECT for that host), so rule text and metadata come from SonarSource's live rule API at next.sonarqube.com (server version 2026.5.0.128906) and from the analyzer source repos via raw.githubusercontent.com, which are the same first-party artifacts those web pages are generated from.
rule_findings.action: Before triaging anything else, run one filter in SonarCloud: Issues > Software Quality = Reliability, Severity = High or Blocker (or in Standard Experience: Type = Bug, Severity = Critical or Blocker). That returns a handful of issues out of 338. Those are the entire reliability story. Read them individually - a CRITICAL C# bug in a 53k-line PHI backend is usually a real null-deref, a disposed-object use, an async void, or a swallowed exception on a data path, and is worth an hour. Then tell the team plainly: 'D does not mean 338 defects, it means one bad one.'
rule_findings.effort: 20 minutes to identify the 8, then 1-3 hours to fix them

rule_findings.rule_name: "input", "select" and "textarea" tags should be labeled
rule_findings.what_it_detects: Every input (except submit/button/image/hidden), select and textarea that has no associated label. Satisfied by a <label for> matching the control's id, or by aria-label / aria-labelledby on the control. Explicit documented exception: implicit labels (a <label> wrapping the control) do NOT raise an issue. Tagged accessibility + wcag2-a. Type BUG, MAJOR, RELIABILITY MEDIUM, 5 min remediation each. Cites W3C H44 and WCAG 2.2 SC 1.3.1.
rule_findings.count_in_repo: 253, concentrated in 10 files (47 internal-appointment-detail, 26 people-edit-modal, 17 patient-profile-redesign, 13 appointment-add-claim-parties-section)
rule_findings.reasoning: Two things are true at once and the team is conflating them. (1) It is a category error to call this a reliability bug. The rule's own text is entirely about screen readers and motor-impaired users; there is no runtime failure mode, nothing throws, no data is wrong. Sonar's taxonomy puts accessibility under BUG/RELIABILITY because the code is 'incomplete' relative to its intent, not because it crashes. Read as 'runtime defects', 253 is a false alarm. (2) It is NOT noise as an accessibility finding. Unlabeled form controls fail WCAG 2.2 SC 3.3.2 Labels or Instructions, which is Level A - the floor, not the aspiration - and SC 1.3.1 and 4.1.2 alongside it. For a US healthcare-adjacent portal where four external user roles self-register from the public internet, Level A form labelling is the part of accessibility that most reliably turns into a complaint. But before anyone fixes 253 of them, one specific false-positive cluster has to be ruled out: the analyzer parses the Angular template statically. An Angular Material control written as <mat-form-field><mat-label>X</mat-label><input matInput ...></mat-form-field> has no for/id pair and no aria-label in the template - Material generates the association at runtime - so Sonar flags it while the rendered DOM is actually correct and accessible. Given 47 hits in a single detail component, that pattern is the most probable explanation for the bulk of the 253.
rule_findings.action: Do not bulk-fix and do not bulk-suppress. Spend 30 minutes: open the top file, pick 5 flagged controls, run each through the browser accessibility tree (Chrome DevTools > Elements > Accessibility pane) and read the computed Name. If Name is populated, that instance is a false positive and the whole Material-wrapped class of them is too - mark that subset Won't Fix with the one-line justification 'label association generated at runtime by mat-form-field; verified in the a11y tree', and record the reasoning once so the next person does not redo it. Whatever is left with an empty accessible name is a genuine Level A failure - fix those, at 5 minutes each, in the files you are already touching for feature work rather than as a 253-item campaign. Do not deactivate the rule: it is worth keeping switched on for new templates. If most of the 253 turn out to be Material false positives, that is also the argument for adding axe-core to the component test run, which measures the rendered DOM and does not make this mistake.
rule_findings.effort: 30 min sampling; then whatever the real remainder is, absorbed into normal work at 5 min each

rule_findings.rule_name: Mouse events should have corresponding keyboard events
rule_findings.what_it_detects: onClick with no onKeyDown/onKeyUp, onMouseover with no onFocus, onMouseout with no onBlur. The current rule text explicitly recognises Angular bindings - (click), ng-click, on-click - and skips anything the analyzer does not recognise as a native HTML element, i.e. custom components are not checked. Native interactive elements are exempt: <button>, <a>, <summary>, input type=button/submit, and controls with implicit textbox/checkbox/radio/listbox roles. An issue IS still raised on anything carrying role="button". Type BUG, MINOR, RELIABILITY LOW, 5 min. Cites WCAG 2.2 SC 2.1.1 Keyboard and techniques SCR2/SCR20/SCR29.
rule_findings.reasoning: This one has a much better signal-to-noise ratio than the label rule, because of what the rule explicitly skips. It does not fire on <button> or on <a href>, and it does not fire on custom components. So a hit means a (click) sitting on a genuinely non-interactive native element - a div, td, tr, span, i - which really is unreachable by keyboard unless the template also supplies tabindex and a key handler. That is a WCAG 2.2 SC 2.1.1 Level A failure and, unlike the label case, it is not a static-analysis artifact: the rendered DOM will be just as unreachable as the template. The rule text also warns about the one exemption that leaks - <a onClick> with no href is exempted by the tag check but behaves as inert text from the keyboard - so the true count may be slightly higher than 77, not lower. Still only LOW reliability impact, so it contributes nothing to the D. It is a real accessibility defect class carrying a misleading label.
rule_findings.action: Triage by element, not by occurrence. Grep the templates for (click) on div/span/td/tr/i and sort by what the handler does. Anything that is the only way to perform an action - opening the appointment detail, selecting a claim party, submitting - is a keyboard trap for a real user and should be converted to a <button> with button styling reset, which fixes the finding and the roles and the focus ring in one edit. Anything that is a convenience duplicate of a control that also exists as a button is genuinely low priority. Expect the 77 to collapse to a much smaller number of distinct repeated patterns (a clickable table row, a clickable card) - fix the pattern once in the shared component and the count drops in bulk.
rule_findings.effort: half a day if the 77 reduce to 5-8 repeated patterns, which is the usual outcome

rule_findings.rule_name: DOM updates should not lead to open redirect vulnerabilities
rule_findings.what_it_detects: Confirmed from SonarSource's live rule API: repository tssecurity (the injection/taint-analysis engine, not the plain TS linter), type VULNERABILITY, severity BLOCKER, impacts [{SECURITY: BLOCKER}], cleanCodeAttribute COMPLETE, tagged cwe, 30 min remediation. This is a taint-tracking rule, not a pattern match: it fires only when the engine traces a path from a source it considers attacker-controlled to a DOM navigation sink (location, location.href, location.assign/replace, window.open). CWE-601.
rule_findings.reasoning: This is the single most serious item in the whole set and the brief is right to say it is under-weighted. Three things stack. First, it is a taint rule - it is much harder to trigger spuriously than a pattern rule, because the engine had to find an actual source-to-sink path. Second, the file. tenant-bootstrap.ts is on the tenancy resolution path of an app whose tenancy resolves from the HTTP Host header only, with one SQL Server database per office. A redirect primitive that takes attacker-influenced input and sits in the code that decides which tenant the browser is talking to is not an open-redirect-as-phishing-nuisance; it is adjacent to the highest-consequence failure mode you have named. If the same user-controlled value that steers the redirect also steers or is derived from the tenant/host decision, the bug class stops being CWE-601 and becomes cross-tenant. Third, timing: this app is about to face anonymous internet traffic on registration, login, password reset and upload for the first time, and an open redirect on the login path is exactly what turns a credential-phishing page into a convincing one against a PHI system. I want to be explicit that I could not read line 65 - the source tree is not in this session - so I am rating the class and the location, not the specific expression.
rule_findings.action: Read tenant-bootstrap.ts:65 today, before anything else on this list, and trace the value backwards to its source by hand. Then answer two questions in writing: (1) can the value reach the redirect from a query string, fragment, postMessage, referrer, localStorage or the Host header; (2) does anything on that same path feed the tenant decision. Fix by the OWASP prescription rather than by sanitising the URL: have the caller pass a short id or token that is mapped server-side to a full target URL, or validate the destination against a server-side allow-list of the 11 known office hosts - allow-list, never deny-list, and never a regex over the raw URL. If the redirect target must remain dynamic, it should be a path-only value with the origin fixed in code. This is a merge gate: nothing ships to the public internet with a BLOCKER open redirect on the tenancy path.
rule_findings.effort: 30 min to read and trace; 1-3 hours to fix properly with an allow-list

rule_findings.rule_name: Angular built-in sanitization should not be disabled
rule_findings.what_it_detects: Use of DomSanitizer.bypassSecurityTrust* (Html/Script/Style/Url/ResourceUrl). Confirmed metadata: type VULNERABILITY, defaultSeverity Blocker, impacts [{SECURITY: BLOCKER}], attribute TRUSTWORTHY, tags cwe + former-hotspot, CWE-79, OWASP Top 10 2021 A3, ASVS 4.0 requirement 5.3.3, 30 min. The former-hotspot tag matters: this rule used to require human review and Sonar promoted it to an always-a-vulnerability, which is why it now shows up as a BLOCKER rather than as one of the 31 hotspots.
rule_findings.reasoning: The location is the classic benign case and the classic dangerous case at the same time, and only reading the code separates them. An icon component calling bypassSecurityTrustHtml on an inline SVG string is the single most common legitimate use of this API in Angular codebases. Angular's own security guide permits it but is blunt about the condition: 'If you trust a value that might be malicious, you are introducing a security vulnerability into your application', and it tells you to construct the trusted value as close as possible to the input source. So the whole question is the provenance of the string at line 58. If the component takes an icon *name* from a fixed union type and looks the SVG up in a compiled-in registry, the sanitizer bypass is on a literal you shipped and the finding is a documented false positive. If the component will accept an arbitrary string - and in an app where document metadata, claim party names or tenant branding can reach a template, that is a live possibility - then a shared icon component is a reflected XSS primitive available on every page including the anonymous login page. Sonar cannot tell these apart, which is exactly why it is BLOCKER by default.
rule_findings.action: Read line 58 and the component's @Input type. If the input is a literal union or an enum resolved against a static map, mark it Safe/Won't Fix with the justification recorded on the issue, and additionally narrow the type so it cannot regress - that is the real fix, because the suppression is only as good as the type. If the input is `string`, either switch to bypassSecurityTrustResourceUrl over a fixed asset path, or use Angular Material's MatIconRegistry, which does the trusted-resource handling for you. Do not leave this one untriaged: it is 20 minutes of reading and it is either a clean dismissal you can defend or a real XSS.
rule_findings.effort: 20 min to decide; 1 hour if it needs the type narrowed or the registry swapped in

rule_findings.rule_name: Web servers should not bind to all network interfaces
rule_findings.what_it_detects: host="0.0.0.0" on a Flask/FastAPI/uvicorn server. Confirmed metadata: VULNERABILITY, defaultSeverity Blocker, impacts [{SECURITY: BLOCKER}], CWE-668, tags flask/fastapi/uvicorn/network/deployment/least-privilege, 5 min. Notably the rule text itself hedges: 'Even in production environments, binding to 0.0.0.0 should be a deliberate choice made with proper security controls in place, such as firewalls... reverse proxies... network segmentation... container orchestration platforms managing network access', and 'The severity depends on the environment and what security controls are in place.'
rule_findings.reasoning: The rule is rated BLOCKER, which is why it is frightening the team, but the rule's own description concedes that the finding is conditional on deployment - and the path is docker/. Binding 0.0.0.0 inside a container is not optional; it is how the container is reachable from the compose network at all, and 127.0.0.1 inside a container makes the service reachable by nothing. The BLOCKER severity is calibrated for a script someone runs on a laptop or a VM, not for a containerised sidecar. So on the code as written this is very close to a definite false positive. The part that is NOT noise is a different question the rule is gesturing at and that Sonar cannot answer: whether the packet renderer requires authentication and whether anything outside the compose network can route to it - because a renderer for medical-examination packets is handling PHI. That question is an infrastructure decision (network topology and reverse-proxy exposure), which your scope boundary puts in the other exercise, so I will leave it at this one line: the finding is a container-normal binding, and the exposure it hints at belongs to the infra review, not to this one.
rule_findings.action: Mark Won't Fix with the justification 'container workload; 0.0.0.0 is required for the service to be reachable on the compose network; exposure controlled at the network layer'. Record it once. Optionally add sonar.exclusions or a rule exclusion for docker/**/app.py so it does not recur. Hand the 'is the renderer authenticated and routable' question to the infrastructure exercise with a one-line note; do not try to answer it in code.
rule_findings.effort: 5 minutes

rule_findings.rule_name: SQL Server passwords should not be disclosed
rule_findings.what_it_detects: Confirmed from the live rule API: repository 'secrets' (the sonar-text secret-detection analyzer), type VULNERABILITY, severity BLOCKER, impacts [{SECURITY: BLOCKER}], cleanCodeAttribute TRUSTWORTHY, tags cwe + secret, 30 min remediation. It matches a literal SQL Server password in a connection string or equivalent, in any file type - this is why it fires on .ps1 scripts that no compiler ever sees.
rule_findings.reasoning: The secret is real - the analyzer matched an actual literal, not a pattern that might be a password - and the fact that these are developer convenience scripts does not undo that, because the value is now in git history permanently and history is not fixed by editing the file. Against that, three mitigations are genuine: the repo is private, the scripts are dev-scoped, and there is no real patient data yet. The decisive question is not 'is a password in the repo', it is 'is this password used anywhere that is not a developer's laptop'. If the same password is on a shared dev SQL Server, a staging box, or - worst case - was copy-pasted into any of the 11 tenant databases' setup, then a private repo with two SDE 1s and, eventually, contractors is a credential store you did not intend. This is the cheapest item on the entire list to close and it is the kind of thing that reads very badly in a HIPAA-adjacent security questionnaire later.
rule_findings.action: Two steps, both short. (1) Determine whether that password is used anywhere other than a local dev instance. If yes, rotate it now, while there is still no real patient data and rotation is free. (2) Move the value out of the scripts: .NET has first-class support for this via `dotnet user-secrets` for local development, or read it from an environment variable in the .ps1 with a fail-fast if unset. Then commit the scripts with the literal gone. Do not attempt a git-history rewrite for a dev credential on a private repo - rotation achieves the same security outcome for a fraction of the disruption, and history rewriting on a two-person repo with open branches costs more than it returns. Mark the Sonar issues Fixed once the literals are gone.
rule_findings.effort: 1 hour including rotation, if the password is not shared; 5 minutes to determine that it is not

rule_findings.rule_name: Credentials should not be hard-coded
rule_findings.what_it_detects: Hard-coded credentials in database and LDAP connections: literals in connection strings, plus variable names matching a configurable pattern list ('password', 'pwd', 'passwd'...). Confirmed metadata: VULNERABILITY, defaultSeverity Major, impacts [{SECURITY: MEDIUM}], tags cwe/secret/former-hotspot, CWE-798 and CWE-259, OWASP Top 10 2021 A7, ASVS 4.0 2.10.4/3.5.2/6.4.1, 30 min. Documented exceptions: no issue when URI username and password are identical, and none when the searched pattern appears in both the variable name and its value.
rule_findings.count_in_repo: 5 MAJOR - seed contributors, appsettings.json:34 in both hosts, CaseEvaluationHttpApiHostModule.cs:783
rule_findings.reasoning: This is the finding where I disagree with Sonar's own severity, and it is the second thing I would look at after the tenant-bootstrap redirect. Sonar rates it MAJOR / SECURITY MEDIUM because in the general case a hard-coded credential is a hygiene problem. In this specific application it is not, and the giveaway is the phrase 'seed contributors'. In an ABP Commercial application, data seed contributors are what create the initial admin user in each tenant database, and ABP ships with a well-known default admin password baked into its seed path. You have database-per-tenant, 11 tenant databases at launch with headroom to 33, tenancy resolved from the Host header, and you are about to put all of it on the public internet with anonymous access to login. A default or hard-coded admin credential that got seeded into even one of those 11 databases is not a MEDIUM: it is unauthenticated administrative access to one office's complete PHI set, reachable by anyone who knows the hostname, and the per-tenant database isolation that is your main safety property does nothing about it because the attacker is inside a tenant legitimately. Sonar's MEDIUM is a general-purpose rating that has no idea it is looking at a multi-tenant health application's seeding code. The appsettings.json:34 hits on both hosts are the ordinary connection-string case and are much less alarming - but they should still not be literals once this is internet-facing.
rule_findings.action: Treat the seed contributor hits as the priority and the appsettings hits as routine. (1) Read every seed contributor that sets a password and confirm what value each of the 11 tenant databases actually received - do not assume, query them; there is no real patient data yet, so this is safe to do destructively. Any tenant still holding a default or hard-coded admin password gets it rotated to a per-tenant generated value before the app is publicly reachable, and the seed path gets changed to require the value from configuration with no fallback literal, so a future tenant cannot be created with a default. (2) For appsettings.json:34 on both hosts, move the connection strings to environment variables / user-secrets for local and to whatever the infrastructure exercise selects for deployed environments - one line, out of scope here. (3) Read CaseEvaluationHttpApiHostModule.cs:783 before dismissing it; a credential literal in a module registration is usually a client secret or an OpenIddict application secret, which given OpenIddict is in your stack deserves its own look rather than a bulk dismissal.
rule_findings.effort: half a day: 2 hours to audit the seed path and the 11 databases, 2 hours to move literals to configuration

rule_findings.rule_id: HOTSPOT-CONCEPT: what a security hotspot is
rule_findings.rule_name: Security hotspot vs vulnerability (and why 31 hotspots did not cause the E)
rule_findings.what_it_detects: Sonar's own definition, quoted: 'The main difference between a hotspot and a vulnerability is the need for a review before deciding whether to apply a fix... With a hotspot, a security-sensitive piece of code is highlighted, but overall application security may not be impacted; it's up to the developer to review the code to determine whether or not a fix is needed. With a vulnerability, a problem that impacts the application's security has been discovered that needs to be fixed immediately.' Statuses: To review (default), Fixed, Safe. Review priority (High/Medium/Low) is set by the rule's security category's rank in OWASP Top 10 / CWE Top 25 - it is a property of the category, not a measurement of your code. The same page carries a standing note: 'we are gradually transitioning security hotspots to vulnerabilities', which is why S2068, S6268 and S4502 all now carry a former-hotspot tag.
rule_findings.count_in_repo: 31, none triaged: csrf 6 HIGH, auth 3 HIGH, dos 6 MEDIUM, permission 5 MEDIUM, encrypt-data 6 LOW, insecure-conf 2 LOW, other 3 LOW
rule_findings.reasoning: The team is reading 'HIGH' as 'severe' when it means 'review this one first'. Concretely: a hotspot is a question, not an accusation. And the metric consequences are completely separate from the vulnerabilities. Per the metric definitions page, security_rating is 'A = 0 vulnerability ... E = at least one blocker vulnerability' - hotspots appear nowhere in that grid. Your E comes purely from the four BLOCKER vulnerabilities (S6105, S6268, S8392, S7539 x2); the 31 hotspots contributed nothing to it. What hotspots do drive is a different metric, security_review_rating: 'A = >= 80%, B = >= 70%, C = >= 50%, D = >= 30%, E = < 30%' of hotspots reviewed, where 'reviewed' means marked Acknowledged, Fixed, or Safe. At 0 of 31 you are at E on that metric, and the built-in Sonar way gate has a hard condition new_security_hotspots_reviewed < 100% = fail. One source discrepancy worth knowing: the metric-definitions page counts Acknowledged, Fixed or Safe as reviewed, while the security-hotspots page lists only To review / Fixed / Safe as the statuses - Acknowledged is not offered everywhere, so plan on using Fixed and Safe. What 'review' concretely means is also documented rather than vague: open the hotspot, read the 'What's the risk' tab, read the 'Ask Yourself Whether' list on the 'Are you at risk' tab, and either apply the fix from 'How can you fix it' and mark Fixed, or mark Safe with a comment saying which existing protection makes it safe.
rule_findings.action: Book one three-hour block and clear all 31 in a single sitting, with both developers at one screen. The arithmetic: 31 hotspots span roughly 8-10 distinct rules; the first instance of each rule costs 10-15 minutes because you are reading the risk description and deciding the project-wide answer, and every subsequent instance of the same rule costs 1-2 minutes because the answer is already made. That is roughly 10 x 12 min + 21 x 2 min, call it 3 hours. This is a half-day task once, not a programme of work, and it converts the security review rating from E to A in one afternoon. Write the justification comment on the first instance of each rule and paste it on the rest - the comment is the deliverable, because it is what stops the next person re-litigating it and what you show an auditor. After that, new hotspots arrive at a rate of one or two per PR and cost minutes.
rule_findings.effort: 3 hours, one sitting, both developers

rule_findings.rule_name: CSRF protections should not be disabled
rule_findings.what_it_detects: I confirmed by querying SonarSource's live rule catalogue (api/rules/search?languages=cs&sonarsourceSecurity=csrf) that there is exactly ONE C# rule in the csrf category: csharpsquid:S4502. So all 6 csrf hotspots are either S4502 in C#, or its siblings typescript:S4502 / python:S4502 if the scan covers the Angular and packet-renderer code. Current rule text: 'This rule detects when CSRF protection is explicitly disabled or missing from an application... The rule flags configurations that disable framework CSRF middleware, exempt specific routes or views, or leave unsafe HTTP methods unprotected.' Noncompliant examples are literally IgnoreAntiforgeryTokenAttribute added as a global filter, and [HttpPost, IgnoreAntiforgeryToken] on an action. CWE-352, OWASP Top 10 2021 A1, ASVS 4.0 4.2.2 and 13.2.3, defaultSeverity Critical / SECURITY HIGH, 5 min. Also tagged former-hotspot, i.e. on current analyzers this raises a vulnerability, not a hotspot - your 6 are from an older analyzer version.
rule_findings.reasoning: For a bearer-token API these are very likely false positives, and both first-party sources say so independently. Microsoft's antiforgery documentation is explicit that CSRF is a cookie-credential problem - 'CSRF attacks are possible against web apps that use cookies for authentication because... Browsers send all of the cookies associated with a domain to the web app every request regardless of how the request was generated' - and equally explicit about the converse: 'Placing a token in the browser local storage and retrieving it and using it as a bearer token provides protection against CSRF attacks', listing 'endpoints secured with non-cookie-based authentication (for example, bearer tokens or API keys)' as a case where antiforgery validation can be disabled. ABP's own antiforgery documentation says the framework applies [AbpAutoValidateAntiforgeryToken] globally by default (AbpAntiForgeryOptions.AutoValidate = true, ignoring GET/HEAD/TRACE/OPTIONS, XSRF-TOKEN cookie) and that it deliberately bypasses validation for non-browser clients using bearer tokens, precisely because they carry no CSRF risk. So an Angular SPA talking to an ABP HTTP API host over OpenIddict bearer tokens is protected by construction, and S4502 - which cannot see ABP's convention-based global filter registration - is reporting the absence of something it cannot detect. The exception, and it is a real one, is the AuthServer. ABP's login, register, password-reset and consent pages are cookie-authenticated Razor Pages, and those genuinely need antiforgery - ABP does apply it, but that is the surface where a hand-rolled [IgnoreAntiforgeryToken] or a custom endpoint would matter, and it is exactly the surface about to receive anonymous internet traffic.
rule_findings.action: During the 3-hour hotspot session, look at each of the 6 and sort them into two buckets. Bucket one, anything on the HTTP API host / ApplicationService surface authenticated by bearer token: mark Safe with the comment 'API authenticated by OpenIddict bearer token, not cookies; ABP applies AbpAutoValidateAntiforgeryToken globally and bypasses non-browser clients - see ABP CSRF docs and Microsoft antiforgery docs'. Bucket two, anything in or near the AuthServer's cookie-authenticated Razor Pages: read it properly, and confirm no custom endpoint has opted out of antiforgery. Then do the one thing that actually verifies the whole class rather than reasoning about it: with curl, POST a state-changing request to one AuthServer form endpoint with a valid session cookie and no antiforgery token, and confirm it is rejected. That single test is worth more than all 6 triage decisions and takes ten minutes. Do NOT globally disable the rule - if someone later adds [IgnoreAntiforgeryToken] to make a form work, you want to hear about it.
rule_findings.effort: 20 min to triage all 6, plus 10 min for the curl verification

rule_findings.rule_name: Sonar 'auth' security category - C# rule set
rule_findings.what_it_detects: I enumerated the category from SonarSource's live catalogue rather than guessing. The C# 'auth' category contains exactly five rules: csharpsquid:S6781 JWT secret keys should not be disclosed (BLOCKER), csharpsquid:S6418 Secrets should not be hard-coded (BLOCKER), csharpsquid:S2115 A secure password should be used when connecting to a database (BLOCKER, CWE-521, 45 min), csharpsquid:S2068 Credentials should not be hard-coded (MEDIUM), csharpsquid:S4433 LDAP connections should be authenticated (HIGH). Your 3 auth hotspots are almost certainly S2115 and/or S6418, since S2068 is already reporting separately as 5 MAJOR vulnerabilities.
rule_findings.reasoning: This is the hotspot category I would not wave through, because it overlaps the S2068 cluster and the S7539 dev-script secrets, and all three are circling the same underlying condition: credentials that live in the repository or are weak/empty on a database connection. S2115 in particular fires on a connection string with a blank or trivially weak password, which in an ABP solution usually means a dev connection string that uses integrated security locally but has a weak literal for the container. Given database-per-tenant with 11 databases, the question 'what credential does the application use to reach each tenant database, and is that credential in the repo' is one you want a written answer to before going public regardless of what Sonar says. The HIGH review priority here is category-derived rather than code-derived, but in this instance the category is pointing at something that is genuinely the right thing to check.
rule_findings.action: Do these three first within the hotspot session, and answer them together with the S2068 and S7539 findings rather than separately - they are one investigation, not three. The written answer you want at the end is a short paragraph naming, for each environment, where the database credential comes from and where it is stored. If that paragraph is embarrassing to write, you have found something real.
rule_findings.effort: included in the 3-hour hotspot session; the underlying credential audit is the half-day already counted under S2068

rule_findings.rule_id: dos / permission / encrypt-data / insecure-conf / other hotspots (22 MEDIUM+LOW)
rule_findings.rule_name: Remaining hotspot categories - C# rule sets
rule_findings.what_it_detects: Enumerated from the live catalogue. dos in C#: csharpsquid:S5693 HTTP request content length should be limited, csharpsquid:S6444 Regular expressions should be executed with a timeout, and the taint rule S2631 ReDoS. permission: csharpsquid:S2612 File permissions should not be set to world-accessible values, csharpsquid:S4211 conflicting transparency annotations. encrypt-data: csharpsquid:S5332 Clear-text protocols should not be used. insecure-conf: csharpsquid:S5122 CORS policy should be restricted to trusted origins, csharpsquid:S4507 Debugging features should not be enabled in production, csharpsquid:S2092 Cookies should have the secure flag, S6776 Stack traces should not be disclosed.
rule_findings.count_in_repo: dos 6 MEDIUM, permission 5 MEDIUM, encrypt-data 6 LOW, insecure-conf 2 LOW, other 3 LOW
rule_findings.reasoning: Mostly low-value, with two exceptions that your specific launch context promotes above their Sonar priority. First, S5693 (request content length limit) in the dos bucket: you are about to expose anonymous document upload to the internet. An unbounded upload endpoint reachable without authentication is a trivially exploitable availability problem and, with MinIO behind it, a storage-cost problem too. Sonar calls this MEDIUM in the abstract; for you it is the single most relevant hotspot in the lower three-quarters of the list. Second, S5122 (CORS restricted to trusted origins) in the insecure-conf bucket: on an app where tenancy resolves from the Host header and you have 11 hostnames going to 33, a permissive CORS policy is worth ten minutes of reading specifically because the origin allow-list and the tenant host list are the same list, and a wildcard there interacts badly with the tenancy model. The rest - S5332 clear-text protocols (usually http:// literals in comments, XML namespaces and test config), S2612 file permissions (largely a POSIX concern on a .NET/Windows-lineage stack), S4211 transparency annotations (effectively legacy CAS) - are where the genuine noise in this set lives.
rule_findings.action: Handle these in the same 3-hour session, but pull S5693 and S5122 out and treat them as work items rather than triage items. For S5693: confirm there is an explicit request-size limit on the upload endpoint and a file-type allow-list, before anonymous traffic arrives - if there is not, that is a real fix and it is small. For S5122: read the CORS policy and confirm the allowed origins are an explicit list of your office hostnames with no wildcard and no AllowAnyOrigin. Everything else: read the first instance of each rule, decide once, mark Safe with a one-line reason, and paste that reason onto its siblings. Resist the urge to fix anything in encrypt-data or permission before launch - that is exactly the kind of low-value work that makes a two-person team decide the whole tool is a waste of time.
rule_findings.effort: included in the 3-hour hotspot session; S5693 and S5122 fixes are perhaps 2 hours if either is genuinely missing

rule_findings.rule_id: QUALITY GATE: new code definition = previous_version, 2026-04-15
rule_findings.rule_name: Sonar way gate conditions vs a new-code period covering the whole project
rule_findings.what_it_detects: Sonar's definition: 'Previous version - any code that has changed since the most recent version increment of the project is considered new code. With this option, the new code period's start date is the date of the first analysis performed for the current project version. The current project version is defined at analysis time through the sonar.projectVersion property.' Options are Previous version, Number of days (default 30, max 90, 'the default value is 30 days, 7 or 14 days are other common values'), Specific version, Specific date - the last two settable only via api/settings/set, not the UI. I also pulled the built-in Sonar way gate from SonarSource's live instance: exactly four conditions, ALL scoped to new code - new_coverage < 80 fails, new_duplicated_lines_density > 3 fails, new_security_hotspots_reviewed < 100 fails, new_violations > 0 fails.
rule_findings.count_in_repo: 1 setting, poisoning every other number on this list
rule_findings.reasoning: This is the quiet cause of the whole situation and it is worth more than any individual finding. Because sonar.projectVersion has not been incremented since 2026-04-15, 'previous version' resolves to a start date before essentially all of your code, so new code = the entire project. Now apply the four Sonar way conditions to a whole 53k-line C# plus 27k-line TypeScript codebase: the gate is demanding 80% coverage across all of it, 100% of all 31 hotspots reviewed, zero of all 338+ issues, and under 3% duplication everywhere. That gate cannot pass, will not pass this quarter, and will not pass next quarter. A gate that is permanently red teaches exactly one lesson, which is to stop looking at it - and that is precisely the failure mode you flagged for a two-person team: thirty required checks and people start bypassing them. It also explains why the team cannot tell signal from noise: with no new-code boundary, every finding ever written arrives at once with equal weight and no ordering. There is one important mitigation you already have and may not know about: pull request analysis is not affected by this setting. Sonar's PR analysis page states that for a PR 'the quality gate used is the one set at the project level, however, only the conditions on new code within the quality gate are applied', where new code for a PR means the diff. So your PR decoration is already giving you a true clean-as-you-code gate on the changed lines; it is only the main-branch/overall view that is broken and demoralising.
rule_findings.action: Change the new code definition to Number of days = 30 (Administration > New Code, project level, no API call needed). This is the right choice for you specifically rather than the theoretically best one: 'Previous version' is the better answer only if you actually pass a meaningful sonar.projectVersion on every analysis, and a two-person team shipping continuously will not sustain that discipline - the setting will silently rot back to exactly the state it is in now. 'Number of days' needs no discipline at all, and 30 days matches Sonar's own default. Do this before triaging anything, because it re-sorts every list you are about to look at: after the change, 'new code' means the last month's work, the gate becomes passable, and the findings that appear on it are the ones the two of you actually wrote and can actually remember. Keep the old findings visible on Overall Code and burn them down deliberately using the triage above - do not let them block merges. Then wire the merge gate to the PR quality gate only, not to the main-branch one: PRs get a gate that is achievable on a diff, and the main-branch rating becomes a trend you watch rather than a wall you climb.
rule_findings.effort: 5 minutes to change; it is the highest-leverage 5 minutes on this list

triage.overall_read:
Roughly 6 of the 389 findings deserve a developer's afternoon; about 350 are real-but-mislabelled accessibility work; the rest is noise or context.

The headline is that the two ratings are telling you almost the opposite of what the team believes.

The reliability D is a category error, but not in the way the brief assumes. Yes, Sonar classifies accessibility rules as BUG/reliability, and yes that is misleading - unlabeled inputs and mouse-only click handlers have no runtime failure mode; nothing throws, no data is wrong. But the sharper point is arithmetic. Sonar's published rating grid sets the letter from the single worst issue, not the volume: Standard Experience is "A = 0 bug, B = minor, C = major, D = critical, E = blocker", and MQR mode is the same shape over LOW/MEDIUM/HIGH/BLOCKER impacts. I pulled the live severities: InputWithoutLabelCheck is MAJOR / RELIABILITY MEDIUM (ceiling C), MouseEventWithoutKeyboardEquivalent is MINOR / RELIABILITY LOW (ceiling B). Neither can produce a D at any count. So the D is caused entirely by one or more of the 8 issues nobody has looked at - the 3 C# and 5 TypeScript bugs listed as "rules unknown". The 330 accessibility findings that are consuming all the team's anxiety are contributing nothing to the rating, and the 8 that nobody has opened are contributing all of it. Say it to the team in one sentence: D does not mean 338 defects, it means one bad one, and you have not found it yet.

The security E is real and correctly earned. Security rating is "A = 0 vulnerability ... E = at least one blocker vulnerability", and you have four blockers. The brief under-weights the right one: tssecurity:S6105 at tenant-bootstrap.ts:65 is a taint-analysis result (source-to-sink, much harder to trigger spuriously than a pattern match) sitting in the file that resolves tenancy in an app where tenancy comes from the Host header and each office is a separate PHI database. Read that line before you read anything else on this list. The second under-weighted item is one Sonar itself under-rates: csharpsquid:S2068 on the seed contributors is only MAJOR/MEDIUM in Sonar's general-purpose scale, but in an ABP multi-tenant application "hard-coded credential in a data seed contributor" plausibly means a default admin password sitting in some subset of 11 tenant databases, days before anonymous internet traffic arrives. That is unauthenticated admin access to one office's complete PHI, and per-tenant database isolation does nothing about it because the attacker is legitimately inside a tenant.

On hotspots, the distinction the team is missing is that a hotspot is a question, not an accusation - Sonar's own words: "a security-sensitive piece of code is highlighted, but overall application security may not be impacted; it's up to the developer to review". They contributed zero to your E, because security_rating counts only vulnerabilities. They drive a separate metric, security_review_rating (A = 80% reviewed or better), where 0 of 31 puts you at E and trips the Sonar way condition new_security_hotspots_reviewed < 100%. "Review" is a defined three-step procedure, not open-ended analysis, and 31 of them is about three hours in one sitting with both developers at one screen - roughly 12 minutes for the first instance of each of ~10 distinct rules, then 1-2 minutes each for repeats. It is a half-day once, not a programme. The 6 csrf hotspots are very likely false positives on your bearer-token API surface - Microsoft's antiforgery docs say CSRF is a cookie-credential problem and that bearer tokens are protection against it, and ABP applies AbpAutoValidateAntiforgeryToken globally while deliberately bypassing non-browser bearer clients - with the genuine exception of the AuthServer's cookie-authenticated Razor Pages, which is exactly the surface about to face the internet. Verify that class with one curl (cookie, no antiforgery token, expect rejection) rather than by triaging six items separately.

Underneath all of it is the setting nobody flagged: new code = previous_version pinned at 2026-04-15 means new code is the entire project, and the Sonar way gate's four conditions - 80% coverage, under 3% duplication, 100% hotspots reviewed, zero violations - are being applied to all 80k lines at once. That gate is unpassable and will stay unpassable, which is precisely how a two-person team learns to ignore a tool. It is also why signal and noise are indistinguishable: with no new-code boundary, every finding ever written arrives simultaneously with equal weight. Change it to Number of days = 30 - not "previous version done properly", because that requires incrementing sonar.projectVersion on every analysis and two SDE 1s shipping continuously will not sustain it, and the setting will rot straight back to today's state. Note that PR analysis is unaffected: Sonar applies only new-code conditions to a PR diff, so your PR decoration is already a working clean-as-you-code gate. Gate merges on that, and treat the main-branch rating as a trend you watch rather than a wall you climb.

Two limits on this analysis, stated plainly. First, the working directory handed to me contains a personal profile README and three resume PDFs, not the portal source, so I could not read tenant-bootstrap.ts:65, icon.component.ts:58, appsettings.json:34 or the seed contributors. Every judgement above is from rule definitions plus your stated context - I am rating the finding classes and their locations, not the specific expressions, and the four "read this line" actions are genuinely necessary rather than rhetorical. Second, rules.sonarsource.com is unreachable from this session (the egress gateway returns 502 on CONNECT for that host), so instead of the rendered rule pages I used the first-party artifacts those pages are generated from: SonarSource's live rule API at next.sonarqube.com (server 2026.5.0.128906) for severities, impacts, clean-code attributes and category membership, and the analyzer source repositories (sonar-html, sonar-dotnet, sonar-python, SonarJS) via raw.githubusercontent.com for the full rule descriptions and security-standard mappings. Where I could not retrieve a description at all - tssecurity:S6105 and secrets:S7539, both closed-source commercial analyzers - I have the authoritative title, type, severity, impact and effort from the live API but not the prose, and I have said so rather than filling the gap from memory. WebSearch was exhausted (200/200) before I started, so everything here came from WebFetch and direct HTTP against named primary sources.

One maintenance note, since you asked for it and I could not fully satisfy it: github.com's API and release feeds are blocked from this session, so I could not check release dates directly. What I could confirm is that all five analyzers publish to Maven Central with last releases between February and June 2025 (sonar-html 3.19.0.5695, SonarJS 10.24.0.33043, sonar-dotnet 10.12.0.118525, sonar-python 5.5.0.23291, sonar-text 2.24.2.6631) - though SonarSource appears to have moved distribution off Maven Central since, so those dates understate activity. Better evidence of current maintenance: their master branches contain rules numbered S8392 and S8678 (recent RSPEC allocations, one of them about LLM data exfiltration), and SonarSource's own instance serves all of them today. I would call the analyzers actively maintained with high confidence, and the specific "release within 12 months" check unverified by the means you asked for.

2. Filter Issues by Reliability + High/Blocker (or Type=Bug + Critical) to identify the 3 C# and 5 TS bugs. These 8 are the entire cause of the D rating; the 330 accessibility findings are not. Read them individually - 20 minutes to find, 1-3 hours to fix.

3. Read angular/src/tenant-bootstrap.ts:65 (tssecurity:S6105). Taint-traced open redirect on the tenancy resolution path of a Host-header-tenanted PHI app, days from public exposure. rule_findings.rule_name: META: zero JS/TS alerts across 27k lines of Angular
rule_findings.what_it_detects: Not a rule - this is the absence of a language in the analysis. GitHub's own troubleshooting page states the failure mode plainly: 'CodeQL only analyzes the language with the most source files' when an advanced-setup workflow does not explicitly declare languages. The fix it gives is a strategy.matrix listing e.g. 'csharp', 'javascript-typescript' and passing languages: ${{ matrix.language }} to the init step. A separate docs page notes the other common cause: 'When you enable default setup, this disables the existing CodeQL workflow file and blocks any CodeQL API analysis from uploading results' - so a repo with both default setup and a hand-written codeql.yml can silently drop one config's results.
rule_findings.count_in_repo: 0 alerts across ~27k lines TypeScript, versus 23 C# alerts across ~53k lines C#
rule_findings.reasoning: This is the most important item in the set and your suspicion is correct. Three candidate explanations, ranked. (1) MOST LIKELY - the language is not being analyzed at all. C# is 53k lines vs TS 27k, exactly the ratio that triggers the documented 'only analyzes the language with the most source files' behaviour when `languages:` is not explicitly set. Confirm in 60 seconds: open the last CodeQL workflow run and check whether there is a `javascript-typescript` job at all, and check the alert page filter for `language:javascript`. If there is no job, there is no analysis, and zero alerts is meaningless rather than reassuring. (2) ALSO LIKELY, AND COMPATIBLE WITH (1) - the discrepancy with Sonar is partly genuine and not a bug. CodeQL and Sonar are not measuring the same thing. Sonar's TS 'BLOCKER vulnerabilities' are typically single-file pattern rules (hardcoded secret, weak crypto, insecure cookie flag, disabled TLS check) and its 'bugs' are correctness rules; the CodeQL default suite for JS/TS is dominated by taint-tracking queries whose sources are DOM/`location`/`document.URL`/`postMessage`/Node request objects and whose sinks are `innerHTML`/`eval`/`child_process`. A well-behaved Angular app touches almost none of those directly - it binds through templates, and CodeQL does not model Angular template binding as dataflow even though 'angular (modern version)' is listed as a supported HTML framework on the supported-languages page. So a real Angular SPA producing very few CodeQL alerts is plausible; producing exactly ZERO is the part that is not. (3) LESS LIKELY BUT WORTH ONE GREP - path/volume dilution. The ABP `@proxy` generated service and DTO tree can be a large fraction of an Angular ABP workspace, and CodeQL does not have a `paths-ignore` set for it by default; you have to add one. Generated proxies do not suppress alerts elsewhere, but they do bloat the database and they are what you want excluded once the language IS running. Note that `build-mode: none` is NOT a factor here - build-mode applies to compiled languages (docs list C/C++, C#, Java, Rust); JS/TS needs no build. Also note the C# side may itself be under-analyzed if it runs `build-mode: none`, since the docs' comparison table says under `none` mode 'Generated code not analyzed' - and ABP generates a lot at build time.
rule_findings.action: Do this first, before touching a single alert. Step 1: open .github/workflows/codeql.yml (or the default-setup config) and confirm `javascript-typescript` is in the language matrix and that you do not have BOTH default setup and an advanced workflow active. Step 2: if it is missing, add it, re-run, and re-triage - the 23 C# alerts are not your finding set, they are half of it. Step 3: once JS/TS is running, add a `paths-ignore` in the CodeQL config for the generated ABP proxy tree, `node_modules`, `dist`, and `*.spec.ts`, so the database reflects hand-written code. Step 4: reconcile against the 2 Sonar TS BLOCKERs by hand - if CodeQL still shows zero after the language is confirmed running, read those 2 Sonar findings and decide whether they are rule classes CodeQL simply does not carry (likely), which is a legitimate reason to keep both tools rather than a reason to distrust either. Do NOT conclude 'the frontend is clean' until step 1 comes back positive.
rule_findings.effort: 2-4 hours to diagnose and fix the workflow; add ~half a day to triage whatever JS/TS alerts then appear. This is the highest value-per-hour item on the list.

rule_findings.rule_name: Clear text storage of sensitive information
rule_findings.what_it_detects: Query help: 'Sensitive information that is stored unencrypted is accessible to an attacker who gains access to the storage.' Metadata from CleartextStorage.ql: @security-severity 7.5, @precision high, tags cwe-312/cwe-315/cwe-359. Reading CleartextStorageQuery.qll: SOURCE is `SensitiveExprSource` - an expression classified sensitive by the NAME heuristic in SensitiveActions.qll, whose patterns are '%password%', '%passwd%', '%account%id%', '%accnt%id%', '%account%key%', '%license%key%', '%licence%key%', '%voucher%code%', '%trusted%', with exclusions for '%hashed%', '%encrypted%', '%crypt%', '%invalid%'. SINK is `ExternalSink extends ExternalLocationSink`, whose members are: LogMessageSink (an argument to a method on a logger class), TraceMessageSink (Trace/TraceSource), CookieStorageSink, LocalFileOutputSink (a write to the local filesystem), and models-as-data 'file-content-store'. SANITIZER is `ProtectSanitizer` - any call whose method name contains 'protect', 'encode' or 'encrypt', case-insensitive.
rule_findings.reasoning: Answering (c) directly: 'cleartext storage' here has nothing to do with the email being sent. I checked the sink list in the query library and the email sink is not in it. `Email.qll` defines MailMessageSink (the `subject` and `body` of System.Net.Mail.MailMessage) as a `RemoteFlowSink`, and RemoteFlowSink is a DIFFERENT sink hierarchy from ExternalLocationSink. The cleartext-storage query only consumes ExternalLocationSink. So for this rule to fire inside CaseEvaluationAccountEmailer.cs, something whose IDENTIFIER NAME matches '%password%' / '%account%key%' / '%account%id%' must reach a LOGGER CALL, a Trace call, a cookie value, or a local file write. Given the file's name and role, the overwhelmingly likely shape is an account-provisioning emailer that generates or receives a temporary password for a self-registering external user and then logs it - something like `_logger.LogInformation($"Sent credentials to {email}, temp password {tempPassword}")` - or writes a rendered .eml/audit copy to disk. That is not a taint-tracking artefact. That is a credential in a log file, which is CWE-532 in substance, is on the OWASP Logging Cheat Sheet's never-log list ('Authentication passwords'), and matters more than usual for you because you are about to expose registration to anonymous internet traffic and four external roles self-register through exactly this path. The precision is marked 'high' and, unlike the exposure rule below, the name patterns here are narrow and credential-specific - '%password%' has very few benign matches. I would not dismiss any of these three without reading the flow path. The one shape that WOULD be a genuine false positive: a variable named e.g. `accountId` or `trustedSender` (both match the heuristic) flowing to a log line, where nothing secret is involved. Check the source node name in the alert's path before deciding.
rule_findings.action: Open each of the 3 alerts and read the SOURCE node name and the SINK line - GitHub shows the full path. If the source is a password/secret/key value and the sink is a logger or a file write: fix, do not dismiss. Fix pattern is removal, not encoding - delete the value from the log statement entirely and log a non-reversible correlator instead (user id, a GUID, `Guid.NewGuid()` is even recognised as a sanitizer by the sibling log-forging query). Do NOT 'fix' this by wrapping the value in something named `Encode...` just to hit the ProtectSanitizer name check - that silences the rule without removing the secret. If the source turns out to be a benign `accountId`, dismiss as false positive with the source node name written in the dismissal comment.
rule_findings.effort: 1-2 hours for all 3, including reading the paths. Small.

rule_findings.rule_name: Exposure of private information - the 13 seed-contributor alerts
rule_findings.what_it_detects: I read the query and its library end to end. ExposureOfPrivateInformation.ql selects a taint path where SOURCE is `PrivateDataExpr` and SINK is `ExternalLocationSink` (same sink set as cleartext-storage: logger args, Trace, cookies, local file writes). `PrivateDataExpr` is a pure NAME heuristic. The exact pattern list in PrivateData.qll is: '%social%security%number%', '%postcode%', '%zipcode%', '%telephone%', '%latitude%', '%longitude%', '%creditcard%', '%salary%', '%bankaccount%', '%email%', '%mobile%', '%employer%', '%medical%' - matched case-insensitively against method names, indexer arguments, variable names and UI control names. Query help: 'Private information that is stored in an external location may be more vulnerable...' @security-severity 6.5, @precision high, in the default csharp-code-scanning.qls suite.
rule_findings.count_in_repo: 13 of the 18 MEDIUM alerts: ExternalUsersDataSeedContributor.cs (5), DemoExternalUsersDataSeedContributor.cs (5), DemoPatientDataSeedContributor.cs (3)
rule_findings.reasoning: Answering (a). The premise of the question is a category error worth correcting before anything else: this rule does not detect credentials at all. It has no notion of a hardcoded password - that would be cs/hardcoded-credentials. Given the pattern list, and given these are user/patient seeders, the near-certain trigger is a variable or property containing the substring 'email' (and possibly 'mobile' or 'medical') flowing into a logger call - the classic `_logger.LogInformation($"Seeded user {user.Email}")` at the end of a seed loop. So on the alert's own terms, 'these are synthetic demo credentials' is not the right frame, and 'dismiss as false positive' on that basis would be dismissing for a reason that has nothing to do with what fired. Now the part that actually matters, which is the question you asked underneath it: is the SEED DATA safe in production? ABP's own data-seeding docs are unambiguous that seeding runs in production - the DbMigrator 'is a console application that is responsible to migrate the database schema... and seed the initial data', and they recommend running it 'whenever you deploy a new version of your solution to the server'. On top of that, in your architecture every new office is a new SQL Server database, and ABP triggers IDataSeeder against each newly created tenant. So an IDataSeedContributor registered unconditionally in the module's DI will run against every one of your 11 (heading to 33) production tenant databases, on every deploy and on every tenant creation. If DemoExternalUsersDataSeedContributor and DemoPatientDataSeedContributor are registered unconditionally, you will ship demo external-user accounts with known passwords into live office databases, and synthetic patient rows into live PHI stores. That is a far larger problem than the 13 alerts, and CodeQL did not find it - you found it by asking the question. The ABP docs, notably, do NOT document a supported way to make a contributor environment-conditional; the only pattern they give is the data-already-exists guard ('if (await _bookRepository.GetCountAsync() > 0) { return; }'), which does not help you here because on a fresh tenant DB the count IS zero. Second-order point: because the heuristic is limited to that 13-term list, CodeQL will NOT flag patient name, date of birth, claim number, injury description, body part, appointment time, or WCAB case number reaching a log sink. Those are all PHI under HIPAA. Do not read '18 exposure alerts' as 'we have 18 places PHI reaches logs' - the true number is unknown and almost certainly higher.
rule_findings.action: Two separate actions, do not conflate them. ACTION 1 (the real one, ~half a day): grep the module classes for where the Demo* seed contributors are registered and confirm they cannot execute outside Development. The most robust fix given the ABP docs offer no built-in switch is to not compile them into the deployed artifact at all - move Demo* contributors into a project referenced only in Debug, or guard registration on IWebHostEnvironment.IsDevelopment() / an explicit config flag defaulting to false, and add one integration test asserting the Demo contributors are absent from the container when the flag is off. Also verify the non-demo ExternalUsersDataSeedContributor: whatever passwords it sets must come from configuration/secrets, never a literal, because that one legitimately does run in production. ACTION 2 (bookkeeping, ~1 hour): for the 13 alerts themselves, read one path to confirm it is the 'email' substring reaching a logger. If the seeder logs seeded emails, just delete the value from the log line - a seeder does not need to log addresses, and this removes 13 alerts in about ten minutes of editing. Prefer deleting over dismissing: bulk-dismissing 13 alerts trains a two-person team to bulk-dismiss, and dismissal is the habit that costs you later.
rule_findings.effort: Half a day for the production-seeding audit (the thing that matters), plus about an hour to clear the alerts by removing addresses from seeder log lines.

rule_findings.rule_name: Exposure of private information - the 5 app-service and emailer alerts
rule_findings.what_it_detects: Same rule as above: PrivateDataExpr (name heuristic: %email%, %telephone%, %mobile%, %medical%, %zipcode%, %social%security%number%, ...) reaching an ExternalLocationSink (logger arg, Trace, cookie, local file write).
rule_findings.reasoning: These 5 sit in live request-handling code rather than seeders, so unlike the seed alerts they represent something that will actually execute against real PHI once you go live. All three files are on paths that will be reachable from the public internet: ExternalAccountAppService is the self-registration/account surface for your four external roles; AppointmentChangeRequestsAppService.Approval handles a workflow decision on a real patient's appointment. If an email address reaches a log line there, so almost certainly do the surrounding identifiers the rule cannot see. Under HIPAA, an email address tied to a patient and an appointment is identifiable health information, and the OWASP Logging Cheat Sheet explicitly lists 'Sensitive personal data and some forms of personally identifiable information (PII) e.g. health, government identifiers, vulnerable people' among data to remove, mask or encrypt. Two caveats that keep this from being 'real-exposure' outright without a read. First, '%email%' matches things like `emailTemplate`, `emailSubjectKey`, `emailSent` - genuinely benign matches exist. Second, the sink is 'an argument to a call to a method on a logger class', and note the sink class explicitly excludes source-defined extension methods (analyzed interprocedurally instead) - so if ABP wraps logging, the reported line may be one hop from the real one. Read the path, do not judge from the file name.
rule_findings.action: Read all 5 paths. For each: if a real address or patient-linked value reaches a log sink, remove it and log the entity id instead. Then do the thing CodeQL cannot do for you - a one-hour manual sweep of these three files (plus the emailer) for the PHI the heuristic misses: patient name, DOB, claim/WCAB number, body part, injury description, appointment date/time. That sweep is worth more than the 5 alerts. Dismiss individually, with the matched identifier named in the comment, only where the match is genuinely `emailTemplate`-shaped.
rule_findings.effort: 2-3 hours including the manual PHI sweep of the same files.

rule_findings.rule_name: Log entries created from user input
rule_findings.what_it_detects: Query help: 'If unsanitized user input is written to a log entry, a malicious user may be able to forge new log entries.' @security-severity 6.1, @precision high, tag external/cwe/cwe-117, in the default suite. From LogForgingQuery.qll: SOURCE is `ThreatModelSource instanceof ActiveThreatModelSource` (untrusted input per the configured threat model - by default, remote/HTTP request data). SINK is `LogForgingLogMessageSink` - an argument to a call to a method on a logger class, excluding arguments to source-defined extension methods (those are followed interprocedurally instead). SANITIZERS are exactly three: HtmlSanitizer (HtmlSanitizedExpr), StringReplaceSanitizer (calls to String.Replace, String.Remove, String.ReplaceLineEndings, or Regex.Replace), and GuidSanitizer (GuidSanitizedExpr - a GUID is inherently injection-safe). The recommended fix in the query help is `username.Replace(Environment.NewLine, "")`.
rule_findings.reasoning: Answering (b) in two parts. PART 1 - does the rule distinguish log forging from PHI-in-logs? No. It is purely CWE-117 and it is source-driven: it fires on data that came from an HTTP request, regardless of whether that data is sensitive. It has no PHI concept whatsoever. The complementary rule, cs/exposure-of-sensitive-information, is sink-compatible but source-different - it fires on name-matched private data regardless of whether it came from a request. So the two rules cover two orthogonal halves and neither covers the intersection you actually care about, which is 'request-supplied PHI reaching a log'. That intersection is CWE-532, and there is no dedicated C# CodeQL query for it in the default suite. Concretely: on the same two lines in ExternalAccountAppService.cs, log-forging is telling you an anonymous registrant can inject CRLF and forge audit lines; nobody is telling you those same lines will be writing self-registration form contents - which for your four external roles will include names, addresses, phone numbers and claim references - into log files that then flow to whatever aggregator you pick. In a HIPAA system, log files are a PHI store: they need the same retention, access control, and BAA coverage as the database, and every unnecessary field in them expands that footprint permanently, because logs are the one datastore nobody ever goes back and purges. PART 2 - is structured logging the fix? For the PHI problem, partly. For the CodeQL alert, NO, and this is the trap. Switching `_logger.LogInformation($"Registering {email}")` to `_logger.LogInformation("Registering {Email}", email)` is unambiguously the right .NET practice - Microsoft Learn's library-authoring guidance says 'Avoid string interpolation in logging' and points at analyzer rule CA2254 'Template should be a static expression', and the message-template form is what lets providers 'store the parameter values as fields' - but the tainted value is STILL an argument to a logger method, so it is still a LogForgingLogMessageSink and the alert will not clear. Worse, for the newline-injection risk it only helps if your sink actually stores fields (Serilog to a structured sink, JSON console); with a plain text file formatter the value is still concatenated into a line and CRLF still splits it. Do not let anyone tell you 'we moved to structured logging, the alert is a false positive'. The change that clears the alert AND fixes the injection is the one the query help gives: sanitize the value before it reaches the logger, i.e. `.Replace(Environment.NewLine, "")` or better `.ReplaceLineEndings(string.Empty)` (both are recognised sanitizers), or replace the user string with a GUID/entity id (also recognised).
rule_findings.action: Fix, do not dismiss - it is two lines. For each of the 2: (1) convert to a message template with named placeholders, not interpolation, since that is correct regardless; (2) sanitize the tainted argument with `.ReplaceLineEndings(string.Empty)` before passing it, or drop the raw value for the entity id, which clears the alert properly. Then the durable part, which is the real recommendation: turn on CA2254 as a build warning solution-wide so interpolated log templates stop appearing (this is a first-party analyzer, zero new tooling, and a two-person team can sustain it), and write down a one-paragraph 'what must never be logged' rule referencing the OWASP list - passwords, tokens, session ids, connection strings, keys, and health/PII - as the only logging standard you maintain. If you later want mechanical enforcement rather than discipline, .NET has a first-party answer: Microsoft.Extensions.Compliance.Redaction plus Microsoft.Extensions.Telemetry, where you call builder.EnableRedaction(), tag parameters on [LoggerMessage] methods with a data classification, and the value is redacted before it is written ('User SSN: *****' in Microsoft's own example). I would NOT adopt that now - it is a real refactor of every log call site and the HmacRedactor is still marked experimental (EXTEXP0002). Note it as the thing you adopt if a compliance audit ever demands proof rather than policy.
rule_findings.effort: About 1 hour for the 2 alerts plus enabling CA2254. The associated PHI logging policy is another 1-2 hours of writing and grepping, and is the part with lasting value.

triage.overall_read: Roughly a third of this finding set is real, but the set is far more useful as a diagnostic than as a work list - and the single most important thing in it is what is MISSING. Mechanically, all three C# rules fired through name-based heuristics that I read directly in the CodeQL library source rather than inferring: cs/exposure-of-sensitive-information matches thirteen literal substrings ('%email%', '%telephone%', '%mobile%', '%medical%', '%zipcode%', '%creditcard%', '%social%security%number%', ...) and cs/cleartext-storage matches credential-shaped names ('%password%', '%account%key%', ...). Both then require the value to reach the SAME narrow sink set - a logger call, a Trace call, a cookie, or a local file write. That single fact reframes everything: all 21 non-log-forging alerts are almost certainly one underlying defect repeated - identifiers containing 'email' or 'password' being written to log statements - and it also means the cleartext-storage alerts on the emailer have nothing to do with sending email (the MailMessage subject/body sink lives in a different, unused sink hierarchy), so 'taint-tracking artefact' is the wrong reading there; something is being logged.
