Consequences for triage: (1) the 13 seed-contributor alerts are mostly cosmetic AS ALERTS, but the question behind them exposes a genuine and much larger risk - ABP's own docs confirm data seeding runs in production via DbMigrator on every deploy, and with database-per-tenant it also runs on every new office, so unconditionally-registered Demo* contributors will seed demo accounts and synthetic patients into live tenant databases; (2) the cleartext-storage findings are the likeliest true positives and sit on the anonymous self-registration path you are about to expose; (3) log-forging is real but small, and the important insight is that CodeQL has no rule for the thing that actually matters to you - request-supplied PHI landing in logs (CWE-532) - because log-forging is source-driven with no PHI concept and the exposure rule's 13-term list cannot see patient name, DOB, claim number, injury description or appointment time. Treat '18 exposure alerts' as a floor, not a count. And (4), the finding that should change your plan: zero JS/TS alerts across 27k lines is not credible as a clean bill of health. GitHub's own troubleshooting docs describe exactly your symptom - without an explicit language matrix, 'CodeQL only analyzes the language with the most source files', and your C# is roughly twice your TypeScript. Some genuine gap between CodeQL and Sonar on TypeScript is expected (different rule classes; CodeQL's JS taint queries need DOM/Node sources that a template-bound Angular app rarely touches), but exactly zero points at configuration, not cleanliness. Tooling maintenance check as requested: github/codeql-action is very actively maintained - v4.37.9 and v3.37.9 both published 26 Aug 2026, CodeQL Bundle v2.26.4 the same day, two days before today's date. Sustainability note for two SDE 1s at one dev-week per month: the entire C# list is roughly one day of work if you fix rather than argue, because it is one defect class. Spend the rest of the week on the workflow fix and the seeder audit. What a larger company would do here that is NOT worth it yet: adopting Microsoft.Extensions.Compliance.Redaction with a formal data-classification taxonomy across every log call site (real refactor, HmacRedactor still experimental under EXTEXP0002), writing custom CodeQL query packs to model your own PHI types as PrivateDataExpr, and running security-extended instead of the default suite - the docs are explicit that security-extended 'may return a greater number of false positive code scanning results', and a team of two drowning in low-precision alerts stops reading all of them, including the true ones. Stay on the default suite, fix what it finds, and buy your PHI-in-logs assurance with a one-page written rule plus CA2254 as a build warning rather than with tooling.
triage_order: 1. Check .github/workflows/codeql.yml for an explicit `javascript-typescript` entry in the language matrix, and check that you do not have both default setup and an advanced workflow enabled. If JS/TS is absent, fix it and re-run BEFORE triaging anything else - the 23 C# alerts are half a picture. (2-4 hours)

2. Audit where DemoExternalUsersDataSeedContributor and DemoPatientDataSeedContributor are registered. ABP seeding runs in production and per-tenant; confirm these cannot execute outside Development, ideally by not compiling them into the deployed artifact. Verify the non-demo ExternalUsersDataSeedContributor takes its passwords from configuration, not literals. (half a day)

3. Read the 3 cs/cleartext-storage paths on CaseEvaluationAccountEmailer.cs and NotificationDispatcher.cs. Check the SOURCE node name: if it is a password or key reaching a logger or file write, delete the value from the statement. Do not silence it by renaming through an 'Encode' method. (1-2 hours)

4. Read the 5 cs/exposure paths in ExternalAccountAppService.cs, CaseEvaluationAccountEmailer.cs and AppointmentChangeRequestsAppService.Approval.cs - live request paths reachable from the public internet - and while in those files do a manual sweep for the PHI the heuristic cannot see: patient name, DOB, claim/WCAB number, body part, injury description, appointment time. (2-3 hours)

5. Fix the 2 cs/log-forging alerts in ExternalAccountAppService.cs: named message-template placeholders instead of interpolation, plus .ReplaceLineEndings(string.Empty) on the tainted argument (or substitute the entity id). Structured logging alone will not clear these. (30 minutes)
6. Clear the 13 seed-contributor alerts by removing addresses from seeder log lines rather than bulk-dismissing them. (1 hour)

7. Enable CA2254 as a build warning solution-wide and write the one-paragraph 'never log' rule (passwords, tokens, session ids, connection strings, keys, health/PII) citing the OWASP Logging Cheat Sheet. This is the durable control; skip the redaction-library refactor. (1-2 hours)

rule_findings.rule_name: Secret scanner that passes when it is not installed
rule_findings.what_it_detects: Claims to block commits/pushes containing secrets: `gitleaks protect --staged` on commit and `gitleaks detect` full-tree on push.
rule_findings.reasoning: This is the purest instance of the pattern the requester described, and it is the one I would fix first. The hook prints a warning and exits 0 when gitleaks is not on PATH. A developer who has never installed gitleaks gets an unbroken run of green commits and concludes local secret scanning is working. The failure mode is perfectly inverted: the machine MOST likely to lack the binary (new laptop, fresh onboard, CI container, a dev who cloned and started working) is the machine whose commits are unscanned, and nothing in the output distinguishes 'scanned, clean' from 'not scanned at all'. Every downstream layer then compounds it, because trufflehog-pr.yml is continue-on-error too, so nothing catches the miss. NIST SP 800-218 PO.3.3 requires tools be configured to 'generate artifacts of their support of secure software development practices', with the document's own footnote defining an artifact as 'a piece of evidence' and evidence as 'grounds for belief or disbelief'. A hook that emits a pass when it did not run generates counter-evidence. This matters more than usual here: OpenIddict signing keys, per-tenant SQL Server connection strings (one per office, 11 at launch) and MinIO credentials are exactly what a workers'-comp PHI repo has lying around, and the repo is about to face the public internet.
rule_findings.action: Two-line fix, do it this week: replace the soft check with a hard one — `command -v gitleaks >/dev/null || { echo 'gitleaks not installed — see CONTRIBUTING'; exit 1; }` — in both hooks. Apply the same treatment to the `lint-staged only if angular/node_modules exists` conditional, which fails open identically. Then DELETE the pre-push full-tree `gitleaks detect`: it rescans unchanged history on every push, it is the slowest hook, and it is what pushes developers to `--no-verify`. Keep one staged-diff scan at commit. Do not add a third scanner; see the trufflehog entry.
rule_findings.effort: 1-2 hours

rule_findings.rule_id: sonarcloud.yml — continue-on-error: true AND sonar.qualitygate.wait=false, plus the README claim
rule_findings.rule_name: A quality gate that cannot fail, documented as a gate that does
rule_findings.what_it_detects: Claims to run SonarCloud static analysis and gate new-code coverage on pull requests.
rule_findings.reasoning: This one is disabled twice over, which is the tell that nobody understood which switch was doing the work. `sonar.qualitygate.wait=false` means the scanner step returns as soon as it has uploaded, without waiting for the gate verdict; `continue-on-error` then guarantees the step's outcome is discarded anyway. Per the GitHub Actions workflow syntax reference, step-level continue-on-error 'Prevents a job from failing when a step fails', and job-level 'Prevents a workflow run from failing when a job fails'. Combined with branch protection, which per GitHub's protected-branches doc requires checks to 'have a successful, skipped, or neutral status before collaborators can make changes to a protected branch', the check is structurally incapable of blocking anything. What makes it worse than nothing rather than merely useless is the README sentence asserting 'SonarCloud is live and gates new-code coverage on PRs'. That is a written attestation to a control that does not exist, in a HIPAA-regulated system — the exact document a customer, auditor or acquirer reads instead of the YAML. Compounding it: the check has been RED on main since 2026-07-08, so every cascade merge is a named bypass, which has trained both developers that a red Sonar tick is normal and ignorable. That habit is the real damage, and it will carry over to the checks you eventually make real. NIST SSDF PO.4.1 asks you to 'Define criteria for software security checks and track throughout the SDLC' and to 'Ensure that the criteria adequately indicate how effectively security risk is being managed'; a permanently-red non-blocking gate inverts this.
rule_findings.action: Pick one and do it this month, do not leave the third state. EITHER (a) delete sonarcloud.yml and the README sentence outright — defensible for two SDE 1s, since you keep CodeQL for security and Roslyn analyzers for quality; OR (b) make it real: drop `continue-on-error`, set `sonar.qualitygate.wait=true`, fix the red on main FIRST, then add it to required checks. Do not do (b) before the main branch is green, or you block yourselves on day one and reach for admin bypass. Delete the README sentence today regardless of which path you choose — that is a five-minute change and it is the part with legal weight.
rule_findings.effort: Option (a) 1 hour; option (b) 1-2 days including clearing the existing red

rule_findings.rule_id: dependabot.yml — target-branch: chore/dependency-updates combined with open-pull-requests-limit: 0
rule_findings.rule_name: Dependency updates routed to a dead branch and throttled to zero
rule_findings.what_it_detects: Claims to keep NuGet, npm/Yarn and GitHub Actions dependencies patched across all ecosystems.
rule_findings.count_in_repo: 1 config file, all ecosystems; 88 open alerts accumulated
rule_findings.reasoning: This is the load-bearing misunderstanding, and the mechanism is the opposite of what most people assume in BOTH directions, so it is worth being precise. GitHub's Dependabot options reference states that with open-pull-requests-limit, 'Security update pull requests are not subject to this limit and do not count toward it', and that setting it to zero 'temporarily disable[s] version updates for a package manager'. So limit: 0 alone would have been the CORRECT way to get security-only updates — that half is fine. The kill switch is target-branch. GitHub's own guidance on configuring Dependabot security updates says explicitly that 'you should not specify a target-branch' when configuring Dependabot for security updates. The two options together produce the worst available outcome: version updates off by the limit, and security updates either suppressed or aimed at chore/dependency-updates — a branch last touched 2026-05-22, 465 commits behind main, never merged once. Every Dependabot PR closed. Why worse than nothing: a dependabot.yml in the repo root is universally read as 'dependency management is handled', by the two developers, by any future reviewer, and by anyone assessing the vendor. Meanwhile 88 alerts sit unrouted against a .NET 10 / Angular 20 / ABP 10 stack that is about to accept anonymous registration, login, password reset and document upload from the public internet. A repo with NO dependabot.yml would at least prompt someone to ask the question.
rule_findings.action: Highest value-per-minute change on the list. Delete the `target-branch` key entirely and delete `open-pull-requests-limit: 0` (or set it to 5 for npm and 5 for nuget) so PRs land on main. Confirm Dependabot security updates are enabled in repo Settings — that is a repo-level toggle, not a dependabot.yml setting. Then triage the 88 alerts ONCE by severity, not by count: with database-per-tenant and host-header tenancy, prioritise anything in the auth, HTTP-pipeline, serialization or file-upload path. Group updates by ecosystem so two devs see ~2 PRs a week rather than 20. A larger company would run a full SCA platform with license policy and SBOM attestation on top; skip that here — Dependabot alerts plus dependency-review is the right depth for 53k lines of C# and 27k of TS with one dev-week a month.
rule_findings.effort: 30 minutes to fix routing; 1-2 days spread over a month to drain the 88-alert backlog

rule_findings.rule_id: ci.yml:248 — frontend test step skipped when no *.spec.ts is found
rule_findings.rule_name: Test guard that greens the build when the tests disappear
rule_findings.what_it_detects: Claims to run the Angular/Karma unit test suite on every PR.
rule_findings.reasoning: Dead today and dangerous precisely because it is dead — nobody will notice it until it fires, and when it fires it fires silently in the wrong direction. The guard emits a warning and skips instead of failing, so the conditions that trigger it are all indistinguishable from success: a PR that deletes the last spec, a glob or path change during a folder reorg, a Yarn 4 Berry PnP resolution problem, a partial checkout, or a rename of the angular/ directory. Each of those is a plausible Tuesday for a two-person team mid-refactor, and each produces a green 'Frontend: Build' — one of only two required checks on this repo. Per GitHub's protected-branches documentation a required check passes on 'successful, skipped, or neutral' status, so a skip is indistinguishable from a pass at the merge gate: the branch protection UI cannot tell you the difference. The general principle is that a guard which converts 'I could not find the thing I am supposed to check' into a pass has exactly inverted the meaning of its own output. Absence of tests is the single strongest signal a test step can produce, and this code discards it.
rule_findings.action: Delete the guard block. Let the runner's own behaviour surface it, and additionally assert a floor: `test $(find angular/src -name '*.spec.ts' | wc -l) -ge 60 || exit 1`. That is three lines, needs no maintenance, and turns the silent case into a loud one. Same review pass should confirm no other step in ci.yml uses find-then-skip.
rule_findings.effort: 30 minutes

rule_findings.rule_name: Workflow whose entire body is commented out
rule_findings.what_it_detects: Nominally claims to validate documentation structure. Its only live step is an echo.
rule_findings.reasoning: Confirmed as given, and I would rank it slightly less urgent than the four above only because docs structure is not a PHI control — but the mechanism is the canonical one and it should go in the same PR. It consumes a runner, posts a green check named as though it validates documentation, and occupies a line in the PR checks list. Its cost is not the compute; it is that it inflates the apparent check count. A team of two looking at a wall of ~17 workflows and a dozen green ticks reasonably concludes the pipeline is thorough, and that impression is doing active harm because it suppresses the question 'what is actually gating this merge?' — to which the real answer is: two build jobs that do not run tests. It is also strong evidence for how the rest of the pipeline got this way: someone disabled a check by commenting it out rather than deleting it, and the green tick meant nobody ever revisited it. Every continue-on-error in this repo is the same decision made a different way.
rule_findings.action: Delete the file. Do not 'fix' it — the Docs Structure job already in ci.yml covers the same ground, and documentation-structure linting is not worth a dedicated workflow for two developers. If the commented-out body contains logic worth keeping, it is in git history.
rule_findings.effort: 10 minutes

rule_findings.rule_name: Redundant warnings-as-errors step (with a correction to the stated premise)
rule_findings.what_it_detects: Claims to surface compiler warnings as errors, separately from the main build.
rule_findings.reasoning: Remove it — but the stated justification is not quite right, and the difference changes what you should do next, so I am flagging it rather than silently agreeing. Microsoft Learn's C# compiler-options reference documents `TreatWarningsAsErrors` and `-warnaserror` as MSBuild-property and csc-switch forms of the same option, but then states explicitly: 'There are two subtle differences between using the <TreatWarningsAsErrors> element in your csproj file, and using the warnaserror MSBuild command line switch. TreatWarningsAsErrors only impacts the C# compiler, not any other MSBuild tasks in your csproj file. The warnaserror command line switch impacts all tasks.' So the extra step is NOT strictly redundant in coverage — the command-line switch is broader, catching warnings from non-csc MSBuild tasks, which in an ABP Commercial 10 solution means code generation, resource and packaging targets. What makes the step worthless is different and simpler: it is continue-on-error, so it cannot fail, and it is 'informational', so its output scrolls past in a log nobody opens. It is a second full build of a 53k-line solution — real minutes of CI on every PR — producing a signal that is structurally discarded. That is worse than nothing because the step's existence is the reason nobody has asked whether warnings are enforced at all.
rule_findings.action: Delete the step. Then, to keep the coverage you would otherwise lose, add `-warnaserror` to the ONE real `dotnet build` invocation in the Backend: Build job. Net effect: one build instead of two, strictly broader enforcement than today, and a failure that actually blocks because Backend: Build is a required check. Verify the main build stays green with the switch on before merging — ABP's generated code is the likely source of surprises.
rule_findings.effort: 2-4 hours including fixing whatever the broader switch surfaces

rule_findings.rule_id: continue-on-error on ci.yml Backend Format and Frontend Format steps
rule_findings.rule_name: Format checks inside a required job that cannot fail it
rule_findings.what_it_detects: Claims to enforce dotnet format and Prettier/ESLint formatting on every PR.
rule_findings.count_in_repo: 2 steps, inside the two required check jobs
rule_findings.reasoning: Worse than the standalone masked workflows, because these live INSIDE the only two required checks. Per the workflow syntax reference, step-level continue-on-error 'Prevents a job from failing when a step fails' — so a formatting failure is absorbed into a green 'Backend: Build' or 'Frontend: Build', which branch protection then accepts. The merge gate reports success while a step inside it failed, and the PR checks list gives no indication. This is the most literally misleading tick in the inventory: it is not a check that does nothing, it is a check that ran, failed, and reported pass. The practical harm is diff noise. Two developers with no reviewer bandwidth cannot afford PRs where formatting churn hides logic changes, and in a codebase where the highest-consequence bug class is a missing tenant filter on an EF Core query, review signal-to-noise is a security control, not a style preference.
rule_findings.action: Remove `continue-on-error` from both format steps and let them block — formatting failures are auto-fixable in seconds, so this is the rare gate that costs nothing to satisfy. Alternatively, and better for a two-person team: delete the CI format steps entirely and rely on the pre-commit `dotnet format` and lint-staged hooks, which fix rather than complain — but only after the hook silent-degradation fix above lands, because right now lint-staged skips itself when node_modules is missing. Do not keep both a non-blocking CI check and a hook.
rule_findings.effort: 1-2 hours

rule_findings.rule_name: The only SAST tool, configured so its own failure is invisible
rule_findings.what_it_detects: Claims to run CodeQL static analysis for C# and TypeScript on pull requests.
rule_findings.reasoning: CodeQL is the only real SAST in this pipeline and the one control most likely to catch the failure mode that matters here — a query path missing a tenant filter, an unvalidated redirect on the new anonymous password-reset flow, an unsafe deserialization on document upload. continue-on-error does something specific and nastier than 'ignores findings': it hides RUN failures. If the CodeQL autobuild fails against a .NET 10 / ABP Commercial solution, or extraction OOMs on 53k lines of C# plus 27k of TS, the analyze step fails, NO SARIF is uploaded, and the Security tab keeps showing the previous alert count — or zero. Zero alerts then reads as 'clean' rather than 'never analysed', and there is no green/red difference to prompt a second look. That is the definitional case of a check counted as protection while providing none. The action itself is healthy and actively maintained: latest release v4.37.9 on 26 August 2026, with the v3 line still receiving parallel updates the same day, so there is no tooling reason for the masking.
rule_findings.action: Remove `continue-on-error`. Keep CodeQL non-required at the merge gate for now — findings triage is real work and two SDE 1s will drown if every CodeQL alert blocks — but a workflow FAILURE must be red so you know analysis stopped happening. Pin to v4. Set the PR alert threshold to error-severity only for the first quarter so the signal stays triageable. A larger company would add a second commercial SAST and a mandated triage SLA; not worth it here — one well-maintained analyser you actually read beats two you ignore.
rule_findings.effort: 2-3 hours

rule_findings.rule_id: dependency-review.yml — continue-on-error: true AND fail-on-severity: critical
rule_findings.rule_name: Supply-chain gate disabled by two independent mechanisms
rule_findings.what_it_detects: Claims to block PRs that introduce vulnerable dependencies.
rule_findings.reasoning: Disabled twice, like sonarcloud.yml, which again suggests nobody was sure which knob mattered. The action's own README documents fail-on-severity as 'Defines the threshold for the level of severity. The action will fail on any pull requests that introduce vulnerabilities of the specified severity level or higher' with a DEFAULT of `low`. Someone deliberately moved it to `critical`, discarding low, moderate and high — and in practice the overwhelming majority of npm and NuGet advisories land in moderate/high, so `critical` alone filters out nearly everything real. Then continue-on-error makes even a critical finding non-blocking. Two safety catches were engaged on a gate that was already the cheapest one available. Worse than nothing because it produces a green 'dependency-review' tick on every PR, which is a direct visual affirmation that new dependencies were vetted. Note the scope limit that makes the current state indefensible: dependency-review only inspects manifest changes in the PR, so it was never going to touch the 88 existing alerts — it is purely a don't-make-it-worse ratchet, and a ratchet set to `critical` and non-blocking does not ratchet. The action is maintained: v5.0.0 released 8 May 2026.
rule_findings.action: Remove `continue-on-error` and set `fail-on-severity: high`. High rather than the default `low` is the deliberate sustainability call for two developers — low/moderate advisories on transitive dev dependencies would generate weekly friction with little real risk, whereas high-and-above on a public-facing PHI app is worth stopping for. Pin to v5. This becomes your don't-regress ratchet while you drain the Dependabot backlog separately.
rule_findings.effort: 1 hour

rule_findings.rule_id: trufflehog-pr.yml — continue-on-error, third redundant secret scanner
rule_findings.rule_name: Redundant non-blocking secret scanner
rule_findings.what_it_detects: Claims to scan PRs for committed secrets.
rule_findings.count_in_repo: 1 workflow — the third secret scanner alongside pre-commit and pre-push gitleaks
rule_findings.reasoning: Three secret scanners, zero of which can fail a merge. The harm is not the tool — TruffleHog is actively maintained, v3.97.1 tagged 24 August 2026 — it is that three overlapping non-blocking scanners create a diffusion of responsibility that is measurably worse than one blocking scanner. Each layer looks like backup for the others, so nobody checks whether any of them is load-bearing, and in fact none is: the hooks fail open when gitleaks is absent, and this workflow is continue-on-error. The visible redundancy is the thing that makes the gap invisible. This is also the clearest illustration of the team-size point in the brief: seventeen workflows and three secret scanners on a two-person team is precisely the surface area that produces bypass habits, and the bypass habit is already documented here in the form of routine merges past a red Sonar check.
rule_findings.action: Delete trufflehog-pr.yml. Keep exactly ONE secret scanner and make it blocking: gitleaks at pre-commit with the hard PATH check from the first finding. Separately, check whether GitHub secret scanning with push protection is available on this private repo under your plan and enable it if so — a server-side control cannot be bypassed with `--no-verify`, which is the failure mode local hooks structurally cannot cover. I could not verify the current private-repo entitlement for push protection from primary docs in this session (confidence: unverified for that sub-point); check Settings > Code security directly, it takes a minute.
rule_findings.effort: 1 hour

rule_findings.rule_id: commitlint.yml — continue-on-error, duplicating the commit-msg hook
rule_findings.rule_name: Non-blocking CI duplicate of a local hook
rule_findings.what_it_detects: Claims to enforce Conventional Commits format on PR commits.
rule_findings.reasoning: Merely useless rather than dangerous — nobody is harmed by an unenforced commit message convention — but it earns removal on the sustainability argument, which for this team is the whole point. The commit-msg hook already enforces commitlint at the only moment it can be fixed cheaply. The CI job re-checks it after the fact, cannot fail, and adds a runner, a queue slot and a row in the PR checks list. Its real cost is attention: it is one of roughly a dozen ticks a developer scans past, and every meaningless tick raises the price of noticing a meaningful one. The requester's framing is right — a team of two facing thirty checks starts bypassing them — and the way you avoid that is by deleting the ones that carry no information, not by hoping people read carefully.
rule_findings.action: Delete the workflow. Keep the commit-msg hook. If you later want server-side enforcement that a hook cannot bypass, fold it into pr-title.yml rather than running both.
rule_findings.effort: 15 minutes

rule_findings.rule_id: lint-meta.yml — yamllint and markdownlint, both continue-on-error, with 'Phase C flips them to blocking'
rule_findings.rule_name: Promissory TODO comment standing in for a control
rule_findings.what_it_detects: Claims to lint YAML and Markdown across the repo.
rule_findings.reasoning: The comment is the harmful part. 'Phase C flips them to blocking' converts an indefinitely-deferred intention into something a reader parses as a scheduled control, and there is no Phase C on a two-person team with one dev-week a month — the comment has already outlived the plan. It also sets the precedent visible throughout this repo: disable now, promise later, never revisit, with a green tick suppressing the reminder in the meantime. That said, the two linters are not equal and I would not remove both. yamllint over .github/workflows specifically has real value here that is easy to miss: a syntactically malformed workflow file does not fail loudly, it simply does not run — which would silently remove a check from the PR gate, the exact failure class this whole review is about. markdownlint over docs has no such property.
rule_findings.action: Split them. Keep yamllint, scoped to `.github/**` only, and make it blocking — it is fast, near-zero false positives on workflow files, and it protects the pipeline's own integrity. Delete markdownlint and delete the workflow-wide Markdown scope. Delete the 'Phase C' comment either way: if a check is not blocking today, the file should say why in the present tense or not mention it.
rule_findings.effort: 2 hours

rule_findings.rule_name: Workflow named 'deploy' that does not deploy, holding one of only two post-merge test runs
rule_findings.what_it_detects: The name claims deployment to the dev environment. It actually runs build plus test and opens a PR.
rule_findings.reasoning: Two separate lies stacked. First the name: 'deploy-dev' in the workflow list tells both developers and any future reader that deployment is automated and gated, which is false, and that misreading is dangerous at exactly the moment this system moves to the public internet, because it implies a promotion path with checkpoints that does not exist. Second and more serious, this workflow and promote-staging.yml are the ONLY places `dotnet test` runs as a post-merge gate, and neither has run meaningfully since 2026-05-01. So the backend test suite for a HIPAA-regulated, database-per-tenant application has not gated anything for nearly four months, while the workflow list continues to imply a build-test-deploy pipeline. The green history of past runs makes this worse: the evidence trail suggests tests are running. Placing your only test execution in post-merge automation that stopped moving is a structural error independent of the naming — post-merge gates on a two-person repo with no on-call are gates nobody reads.
rule_findings.action: Rename or delete the workflow, but the load-bearing change is to MOVE `dotnet test` into ci.yml as a PR-blocking job and add 'Backend: Test' and 'Frontend: Test' to required checks. Right now only Backend: Build and Frontend: Build are required, meaning nothing in the merge gate executes a single test. That is the largest single gap this inventory reveals, and it is created by removal work rather than addition: once the fake gates are gone, the missing real one is obvious.
rule_findings.effort: 1-2 days including making the suite reliably green in CI

rule_findings.rule_name: Dormant promotion machinery for a pipeline that stopped moving
rule_findings.what_it_detects: Claims an automated dev to staging to production promotion and release flow.
rule_findings.reasoning: Collectively these describe a four-stage promotion pipeline that has not executed in four months. Dormant workflows are worse than absent ones for three reasons here. They carry credentials and permissions that remain granted while nobody watches the runs. They will fail confusingly if anyone triggers them, because they encode assumptions about branches and environments that have drifted 465 commits. And most importantly they make the repo LOOK like it has release discipline, which is precisely the impression you do not want going into a first public launch with no DevOps and no QA — the gap between the apparent pipeline and the real one is where a launch goes wrong. Whether staging and production restart is an infrastructure question and out of scope; the point that stands regardless is that these files should not sit dormant advertising a flow nobody exercises.
rule_findings.action: Delete promote-staging.yml and auto-pr-dev.yml now, after first extracting the `dotnet test` invocation into ci.yml per the previous finding. Keep release.yml only if you actually cut tagged releases; if the last tag predates 2026-05-01, delete it too. Recreate from git history when the promotion path genuinely restarts — recreating a workflow is an afternoon, and debugging four months of silent drift is not.
rule_findings.effort: 2-4 hours

rule_findings.rule_name: Privileged trigger on a near-valueless workflow
rule_findings.what_it_detects: Claims to auto-apply labels to pull requests based on changed paths.
rule_findings.reasoning: This is a risk/value ratio problem rather than a false-green problem, and it belongs on the remove list because the value side is close to zero. GitHub Security Lab documents that 'Workflows triggered via pull_request_target have write permission to the target repository. They also have access to target repository secrets', and that it 'runs in the context of the target repository of the PR, rather than in the merge commit' — the mechanism behind the pwn-request class, where untrusted PR content executes with write access and secret availability. Mitigating factors here are genuine: the repo is private, there are two developers and no forks, so the realistic attack path is narrow today. But the counterweight is that automatic labels on a two-author repo where both people see every PR provide essentially no information, so you are holding a privileged trigger for no return. The residual concern is precedent — pull_request_target in the repo is a pattern that gets copied into the next workflow, one that does check out PR head and run `yarn install`.
rule_findings.action: Delete labeler.yml. If you decide labels are worth keeping, switch the trigger to `pull_request` and add explicit least-privilege `permissions: pull-requests: write`, and never check out PR head under pull_request_target. Recommendation for this team is deletion — it is one less workflow in a list that is already too long to read.
rule_findings.effort: 30 minutes

rule_findings.rule_name: Three enforcement points for commit and PR text conventions
rule_findings.what_it_detects: pr-title claims Conventional-Commits-style PR titles; pr-size claims to flag oversized PRs.
rule_findings.count_in_repo: 2 workflows, overlapping with commit-msg hook and commitlint.yml
rule_findings.reasoning: Not harmful individually; harmful in aggregate, and aggregate is what determines whether a two-person team follows the process. Between the commit-msg hook, commitlint.yml and pr-title.yml there are three enforcement points for message formatting on a repo with two authors and effectively single-author PRs. Every one of them occupies a slot in the checks list with the same visual weight as CodeQL. The requester's premise is the governing consideration: thirty required checks produces bypass behaviour, and bypass behaviour is already established here through routine merges past a red Sonar check. Removing low-information checks is how you buy back the attention needed for the high-information ones. pr-size is the more defensible of the two — PR size genuinely correlates with review quality, and review quality is your main defence against a missing tenant filter — but as an advisory label on a repo where PRs are self-reviewed it changes no behaviour.
rule_findings.action: Keep pr-title.yml as the single server-side convention check (it survives `--no-verify`, which the hook does not) and delete commitlint.yml per the earlier finding. Delete pr-size.yml. Target roughly six to eight total checks on a PR, of which four are required — that is a list two people will actually read.
rule_findings.effort: 30 minutes

rule_findings.rule_id: sonar coverage exclusions: angular/src/**/*.ts and angular/src/**/*.html
rule_findings.rule_name: Frontend coverage generated in CI, then discarded by configuration
rule_findings.what_it_detects: Claims project coverage measurement; the reported number describes backend only.
rule_findings.count_in_repo: 2 exclusion patterns covering all 27k lines of TypeScript
rule_findings.reasoning: Sonar's analysis-scope documentation describes sonar.coverage.exclusions as excluding 'source files from code coverage analysis' — the files are still analysed for issues, they simply contribute no coverage measurement. The result is that CI spends minutes on every PR generating a frontend LCOV report that the scanner is configured to throw away. Two distinct harms. The wasted compute is trivial; the misattribution is not. A single coverage percentage is displayed on the project and read as the coverage of the project, when it in fact describes only the ~53k lines of C# and silently omits all 27k lines of TypeScript. Anyone reasoning about test adequacy — a developer deciding whether a refactor is safe, or an auditor asking about testing rigour for a PHI-handling system — gets a number that is confidently wrong about half the codebase. That is worse than reporting no frontend coverage at all, which would at least prompt the question. It also interacts with the ci.yml:248 spec-file guard: if every spec vanished, neither the CI step nor the coverage metric would register the loss.
rule_findings.action: Delete both coverage exclusion patterns and let the frontend LCOV you are already generating actually land. If the resulting number is embarrassing, that is the finding — record the real baseline rather than hiding it. If you instead decide frontend coverage is not worth tracking yet, then delete the LCOV generation step from ci.yml too; do not keep paying to produce a report you configured away. Either resolution is fine, the current halfway state is not.
rule_findings.effort: 2-3 hours

rule_findings.rule_id: sonar new-code period: previous_version, frozen at 2026-04-15
rule_findings.rule_name: New-code window that has been growing for four and a half months
rule_findings.what_it_detects: Claims to measure quality and coverage on new code only.
rule_findings.reasoning: Sonar's new-code documentation defines the Previous version option as 'Any code that has changed since the most recent version increment of the project is considered new code', with the period's start date being the date of the first analysis of the current project version, set via sonar.projectVersion. Because projectVersion has not been incremented since 2026-04-15, the 'new code' window has been widening for over four months and now spans a large fraction of active development. That defeats the entire purpose of the clean-as-you-code model: new-code thresholds are achievable precisely because the window is small, and a four-month window makes them neither achievable nor informative. This is very likely a direct contributor to the check being RED on main since 2026-07-08 and therefore to the established bypass habit — the gate became unsatisfiable, so the team learned to merge past it. A metric labelled 'new code' that actually measures a third of the project's history is a mislabelled number, which is the same defect class as the coverage exclusions above.
rule_findings.action: Remove the previous_version setting and switch the new code definition to reference branch = main, which needs no version bumping discipline and therefore cannot silently rot the way this did. Do this BEFORE re-enabling any Sonar blocking, in the same piece of work as clearing the red on main — reversing that order guarantees you block yourselves.
rule_findings.effort: 1 hour for the setting; folds into the Sonar remediation above

rule_findings.rule_name: Suppression list against a gate that does not gate
rule_findings.what_it_detects: Claims to suppress framework-shaped false positives.
rule_findings.reasoning: Do NOT mass-delete these, and I want to separate them because the categories differ sharply in defensibility. The ABP dependency-injection constructor-parameter-count suppressions and the permission-string duplication suppressions are legitimate: ABP Commercial's conventions genuinely produce wide constructors and repeated permission constants, and those rules fire on framework shape rather than on defects. The email-template HTML suppressions are the ones I would look at hard, because HTML rules suppressed on email templates can mask injection and escaping problems, and this application emails content around workers'-comp medical examinations — content adjacent to PHI, rendered by mail clients you do not control. The category-level point that applies to all 19: a suppression is a claim that a finding is not worth acting on, and that claim can only be evaluated against a gate that is enforced. Since the Sonar gate cannot fail and has been red for weeks, none of these suppressions has been meaningfully justified for months — they are unreviewed assertions attached to an unenforced control, which is why they belong in a removal review even though some should survive it.
rule_findings.action: Do not touch them until Sonar is either deleted or made blocking — that decision comes first, since deleting Sonar deletes this question. If you keep Sonar: re-run analysis with all 19 disabled, delete every suppression whose rule no longer fires (dead suppressions cost nothing to remove and there will be several after 465 commits), then hand-review the email-template HTML entries specifically and require a one-line justification comment on each survivor. Budget one afternoon, not a project. A larger company would demand a documented justification and expiry date per suppression; skip the expiry ceremony here, but the email-template review is worth the hour.
rule_findings.effort: Half a day, only after the Sonar keep/delete decision

rule_findings.rule_id: wildcard CORS header on a dead endpoint
rule_findings.rule_name: Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * on an unused route
rule_findings.what_it_detects: Nothing. It is a permissive header left on an endpoint no longer in use.
rule_findings.reasoning: Worth being precise about the actual exposure rather than overstating it. Per MDN's CORS documentation, the wildcard works only for requests without credentials: 'When responding to a credentialed request, the server must specify an origin in the value of the Access-Control-Allow-Origin header, instead of specifying the * wildcard', and if a request carries a Cookie header while the response has the wildcard, 'the browser will block access to the response, and report a CORS error in the devtools console'. So this is not a direct credentialed-read vulnerability — the browser refuses the combination. The reasons it still must go are three. It exposes whatever the dead endpoint returns to any origin for unauthenticated reads, and 'dead' endpoints are frequently still routed. It is a template: the next developer adding a CORS policy copies the existing one, and this codebase resolves tenancy from the HTTP Host header alone, making origin handling security-relevant in a way it is not in a single-tenant app. And it produces a false negative in review — a reader sees CORS configured and moves on. Dead code carrying a permissive security header is the specific combination that survives audits, because nobody tests what nobody calls.
rule_findings.action: Delete the endpoint, not just the header — an unused route on a service about to face the public internet is attack surface regardless of its CORS policy. Then grep the solution for other `*` CORS values and for the ABP CORS origins configuration, and confirm the real API uses an explicit per-tenant origin allowlist. Given host-header tenancy, that allowlist is genuinely load-bearing and deserves a test.
rule_findings.effort: 2-4 hours including the grep and the allowlist check

rule_findings.rule_name: Self-certifying freshness stamp on stale content
rule_findings.what_it_detects: Claims to document the current test layout and strategy. Describes a layout that no longer exists and still references the ABP 'Books' sample.
rule_findings.reasoning: The 'last verified' line is the harmful element, more than the stale body. Stale documentation is ordinary and readers discount it automatically; a document asserting it was verified on a specific recent date defeats that discount and converts staleness into positive false assurance. It is the documentation-layer equivalent of continue-on-error — a green tick applied by hand. That it still references the ABP 'Books' sample means it has probably never described this application's real test layout, so the verification date is not merely stale, it attests to something that was never checked. In a HIPAA context this is the artefact an auditor or an acquirer's technical reviewer reads to assess testing rigour, and it will be read as current because it says it is. NIST SSDF PO.4.1 Example 4 asks you to 'Review the artifacts generated as part of the software development workflow system to determine if they meet the criteria' — an unreviewed artefact carrying a review stamp inverts that.
rule_findings.action: Delete the file. Do not rewrite it now — with one dev-week a month you will not maintain a strategy document, and an unmaintained one returns to this state within a quarter. Replace it with a ten-line README section stating what actually runs and where, which is cheap enough to keep true. Remove every 'last verified' stamp in docs/ unless something automatically enforces the date; a stamp no process updates is a stamp that will eventually lie.
rule_findings.effort: 1 hour

rule_findings.rule_id: README badges: Node 20 vs ci.yml Node 22 vs security.yml Node 20
rule_findings.rule_name: Status badge asserting the wrong runtime, and a scanner on a different Node than the build
rule_findings.what_it_detects: The badge claims the project's Node version. CI actually uses Node 22; security.yml uses Node 20.
rule_findings.reasoning: Two problems of different weight. The badge is minor — a wrong badge on a private repo misleads only the two people who wrote it, though a badge is by construction a status assertion, so a wrong one is a small instance of the same defect as the false SonarCloud README claim. The version divergence underneath it is the real finding: security.yml scans on Node 20 while the application builds and ships on Node 22. That means the dependency tree, the resolved lockfile graph under Yarn 4 Berry, and any engine-gated packages that the security scan examines are not necessarily the ones that get built. Findings therefore describe a configuration that does not ship, in either direction — missed vulnerabilities or phantom ones. A security scan running against a different runtime than the artefact is a check whose output does not describe the thing it appears to describe.
rule_findings.action: Delete the Node badge (private repo, no audience). Then pin one Node version in one place — a root .nvmrc or the engines field — and have every workflow read from it rather than hardcoding, so ci.yml and security.yml cannot diverge again. Same pass should confirm the Yarn 4 Berry version is pinned identically across workflows.
rule_findings.effort: 2 hours

rule_findings.rule_id: .husky/pre-push — dotnet build -c Debug with no tests
rule_findings.rule_name: Pre-push build that duplicates CI and gates nothing
rule_findings.what_it_detects: Implies push is gated on the solution compiling.
rule_findings.reasoning: Mostly waste, with a secondary false-assurance component that keeps it on the list. A Debug build of a 53k-line ABP solution on every push costs each developer real time repeatedly per day, and produces a signal CI reproduces minutes later at no human cost. Its notable property is what it omits: it builds but runs no tests, so the one thing a local pre-push gate could offer that CI does not — fast feedback before the PR — is exactly what it declines to provide. Meanwhile 'pre-push runs a build' reads to the team as push being gated on something meaningful. The practical danger is behavioural: slow hooks are the single most reliable cause of habitual `--no-verify`, and `--no-verify` also skips the gitleaks and commitlint hooks that you do want. So this step actively undermines the controls beside it.
rule_findings.action: Delete the pre-push build. Keep pre-push cheap or delete the hook entirely. If you want a local test gate, run only the affected test project rather than a full build, and only if it finishes in under about twenty seconds — otherwise it will be bypassed and take the secret scanner with it.
rule_findings.effort: 30 minutes

rule_findings.rule_id: branch protection: enforce_admins: false with 1 required review on a single-author repo
rule_findings.rule_name: Merge gate that is advisory by configuration
rule_findings.what_it_detects: Claims code review and protected-branch enforcement on main.
rule_findings.reasoning: The setting that makes everything else on this list moot. GitHub's protected-branches documentation describes the enforcement option as overriding the default in which 'the restrictions of a branch protection rule do not apply to people with admin permissions'. With enforce_admins false on a repo where both developers are almost certainly admins, every protection is advisory — which is consistent with the observed reality that Sonar has been red on main since 2026-07-08 and cascade merges proceed as named bypasses. A review requirement that the reviewer can dismiss for themselves is not a control; it is a record of intent. required_conversation_resolution: false additionally means review comments can be left unresolved at merge, so even completed reviews do not have to be acted on. Worse than nothing because branch protection being 'on' is the fact anyone would cite when asked whether main is protected. The subtlety worth stating: the review requirement itself is NOT the thing to remove — with exactly two developers, one review each way is genuinely achievable, and peer review is your strongest available defence against the tenant-filter bug class given there is no QA and no architect. What must be removed is the configuration that makes it optional.
rule_findings.action: Set enforce_admins: true and required_conversation_resolution: true. Both are one-click and cost nothing until the day they matter. Leave required_linear_history alone — it is a merge-hygiene preference, not a control, and adding rebase friction to a two-person team buys nothing. Then expand required checks beyond the two build jobs to include the test jobs, once the tests actually run per the deploy-dev finding. Getting to four real required checks that always mean something is the goal; that is a list two people can sustain, and it is roughly a quarter of what a larger company would impose.
rule_findings.effort: 1 hour for the settings; gated on the test-job work above

triage.overall_read:
Substantially all of it is real, and the inventory is more uniform than it first appears: of ~23 removal candidates, roughly 15 are genuinely harmful false assurance rather than mere clutter, and they nearly all reduce to one mechanism applied through four different surfaces. The mechanism is verified. GitHub's workflow syntax reference states that step-level continue-on-error "Prevents a job from failing when a step fails" and job-level "Prevents a workflow run from failing when a job fails"; GitHub's protected-branches documentation states that required checks need only "a successful, skipped, or neutral status before collaborators can make changes to a protected branch". Those two facts together mean every continue-on-error check in this repo emits a status indistinguishable from a genuine pass, and the merge gate is structurally unable to tell the difference. The same inversion then reappears without continue-on-error in the ci.yml:248 spec-file guard (missing tests become a pass), in the hooks (missing gitleaks binary becomes a pass), and in prose (a README asserting a SonarCloud gate that does not gate, a TESTING-STRATEGY.md stamped "last verified"). Four surfaces, one defect: absence of checking reported as successful checking. NIST SP 800-218 PO.3.3 requires tools be configured to generate artifacts of their support of secure development practices, with the document's own footnote defining an artifact as "a piece of evidence" and evidence as "grounds for belief or disbelief" — this pipeline generates grounds for belief where none exists, which is why it is worse than an empty .github directory.

Two items materially change the picture beyond confirming the brief. First, the Dependabot mechanism is the opposite of the common assumption in both directions and the given diagnosis is half wrong: GitHub's options reference states "Security update pull requests are not subject to this limit and do not count toward it", so open-pull-requests-limit: 0 was actually the correct way to get security-only updates and is not the fault. The kill switch is target-branch — GitHub's security-updates guidance says explicitly "you should not specify a target-branch" — which is what routes everything at a branch 465 commits behind that has never merged. That makes the fix a one-line deletion rather than a config rewrite, and it is the best value-per-minute item on the list. Second, the -warnaserror premise is not quite right: Microsoft Learn states that TreatWarningsAsErrors "only impacts the C# compiler, not any other MSBuild tasks in your csproj file. The warnaserror command line switch impacts all tasks." So the step is broader than the props file, not redundant to it — it should still be deleted, but the switch should move onto the one real build rather than being dropped, or you lose coverage you currently have.

The largest finding is what the removals reveal rather than any single removal: strip out everything that cannot fail, and the merge gate is two build jobs that execute no tests at all. dotnet test runs only in deploy-dev.yml and promote-staging.yml, neither of which has run meaningfully since 2026-05-01 — so a HIPAA-regulated, database-per-tenant application has had no test gate for nearly four months while the workflow list implied a build-test-deploy pipeline. With enforce_admins: false, even the two required build checks are advisory, which is corroborated by the observed behaviour: Sonar red on main since 2026-07-08 with every cascade merge a named bypass. The bypass habit is already established, and that is the thing to fix, because it will carry over to whatever real checks you add next.

On sustainability, the honest read is that removal IS the sustainable path here — this list is roughly 60% deletion, and executing all of it plus the four real fixes is well inside one dev-week a month over about two months. Target six to eight PR checks with four required, down from seventeen workflows. Explicitly NOT worth it for two SDE 1s: a second commercial SAST alongside CodeQL; a full SCA platform with license policy and SBOM attestation (Dependabot plus dependency-review is right at this size); per-suppression justification-with-expiry ceremony; DAST/ZAP in CI; performance budgets and Lighthouse CI gating; automated WCAG 2.2 gating (do a manual keyboard-and-contrast pass on the four anonymous flows instead); and required linear history. Each is defensible at fifty engineers and each would be bypassed within a month at two.

Confidence notes. Fully verified against primary sources: the continue-on-error semantics, required-check status semantics, Dependabot limit-and-target-branch behaviour, dependency-review fail-on-severity default of low, TreatWarningsAsErrors versus -warnaserror, Sonar's Previous-version new-code definition, sonar.coverage.exclusions scope, pull_request_target privileges, and CORS wildcard-with-credentials behaviour. Tool liveness confirmed, all active within the last twelve months: gitleaks v8.30.1 (2026-03-21), TruffleHog v3.97.1 (2026-08-24), CodeQL Action v4.37.9 (2026-08-26), dependency-review-action v5.0.0 (2026-05-08). Unverified, and I say what I tried: I could not retrieve a primary Sonar page documenting sonar.qualitygate.wait's default — docs.sonarsource.com returned 404s on five URL patterns and its ?ask= endpoint timed out — so that parameter's semantics are stated from the surrounding configuration rather than quoted, though the conclusion does not depend on it since continue-on-error alone neutralises the step. I also could not confirm whether GitHub secret-scanning push protection is available for private repos on your current plan; check Settings > Code security directly. My WebSearch budget was exhausted early in this session, so all evidence above comes from direct WebFetch of specific primary URLs, each of which I opened.
triage_order: WEEK 1, roughly one day total, all four are small and all four are currently lying to you: (1) gitleaks hard PATH check in both husky hooks, replacing silent degradation with exit 1 — two lines, highest value on the list; (2) delete target-branch and open-pull-requests-limit: 0 from dependabot.yml so security PRs reach main, and confirm security updates are enabled in repo Settings; (3) delete the false 'SonarCloud gates new-code coverage' sentence from README and delete the 'last verified 2026-06-01' stamp from docs/devops/TESTING-STRATEGY.md — these are the written attestations with the most weight in a HIPAA context; (4) delete the ci.yml:248 spec-file guard and replace it with a minimum-spec-count assertion.

WEEK 2, the structural gap the removals exposed: move dotnet test out of the dormant deploy-dev.yml and promote-staging.yml into ci.yml as PR-blocking jobs, then set enforce_admins: true and required_conversation_resolution: true, and add Backend: Test and Frontend: Test to required checks. Until this lands the repo has no test gate at all and the two existing required checks are advisory. Everything else on the list is cosmetic next to this.

WEEK 3, un-mask the security checks that already exist and are already paid for: remove continue-on-error from codeql-pr.yml (a masked run failure means no SARIF uploads and zero alerts reads as clean) and from dependency-review.yml, and change fail-on-severity from critical to high. Delete trufflehog-pr.yml so exactly one secret scanner remains and it is the blocking one.

WEEK 4, delete the clutter in a single PR to buy back attention for the checks that now mean something: doc-check.yml, commitlint.yml, pr-size.yml, labeler.yml (privileged pull_request_target for near-zero value), auto-pr-dev.yml, promote-staging.yml, the ci.yml:100-106 -warnaserror step (moving -warnaserror onto the real build so you keep the broader MSBuild-task coverage), the pre-push dotnet build, the markdownlint half of lint-meta.yml plus its 'Phase C' comment, and the Node badge. Target six to eight checks with four required.

MONTH 2, the Sonar keep-or-kill decision, which must be one or the other and not the current third state: if killing, delete sonarcloud.yml and stop there — CodeQL plus Roslyn analyzers is defensible coverage at this size. If keeping, do it in this order or you will block yourselves on day one: switch new-code definition from previous_version to reference branch = main, remove the angular/src coverage exclusions so the frontend LCOV you already generate is no longer discarded, clear the red that has stood on main since 2026-07-08, THEN set sonar.qualitygate.wait=true and remove continue-on-error, and only then make it required.

MONTH 2, security review of the two code-level items, which need a developer reading code rather than editing YAML: delete the dead endpoint carrying the wildcard CORS header (not just the header), grep for other '*' CORS values, and verify the real API uses an explicit per-tenant origin allowlist with a test — load-bearing because tenancy resolves from the Host header alone. Then, only after the Sonar decision is made, review the 19 multicriteria suppressions: keep the ABP DI and permission-string entries, delete any whose rule no longer fires, and hand-review the email-template HTML suppressions specifically, since that application emails PHI-adjacent content.
